title: German A2
description: The second step in German, from A1 to CEFR level A2, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat A2. Lessons cover talking about the past, reasons and opinions with weil and dass, reflexive verbs, verbs with prepositions, adjective endings, comparisons, two-way prepositions, polite requests with würde and könnte, and writing short messages and e-mails. About 670 new words build on the 717 from German A1 for about 1,380 in all, and a reading list suggests graded readers for this level. Unlocks when German A1 is complete.
author: Erudior
changelog: Honors lessons with longer texts and culture, pictures and diagrams in every lesson, new question types and vocabulary; corrections from a second full review.

lessons.title: Your life so far: the perfect, extended
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At the end of A1 you learned to talk about last weekend: *Ich habe eingekauft*, *Wir sind ans Meer gefahren*. That was the **[[perfect tense]]**, the past tense Germans use most when they speak. At A2 you use the same tense for something bigger: your whole life. Where were you born, where did you grow up, what did you study, when did you move, what have you experienced?

To tell that story you need more verbs, and many of the verbs that describe a life are a little special: *aufwachsen* (to grow up) uses *sein*, *verlassen* (to leave) has no *ge-*, *studieren* has no *ge-* either, and *nennen* (to name) changes its vowel but ends in *-t*. This lesson reviews the rules from A1 quickly, then fills in the patterns you only met briefly: verbs with inseparable prefixes, verbs in *-ieren* and mixed verbs. It finishes with years and ages, so you can put dates into your story.

## The perfect in one minute

The perfect has two parts. An **[[auxiliary verb]]**, *haben* or *sein*, takes the person ending and stands in position 2. The **[[past participle]]** goes to the very end. Everything else sits between them, inside the **[[sentence bracket]]**.

| position 1 | auxiliary (position 2) | middle | participle (end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | habe | in Köln Medizin | studiert. |
| Meine Eltern | sind | 1995 nach Deutschland | gekommen. |
| Nach dem Abitur | hat | sie eine Ausbildung | gemacht. |
| Wo | bist | du | aufgewachsen? |

*Das Abitur* is the school-leaving exam you need for university in Germany (in Austria and Switzerland it's *die Matura*). *Die Ausbildung* is vocational training, usually two or three years of work in a company plus classes at a vocational school.

### haben or sein?

The rule hasn't changed since A1. Most verbs use *haben*, and every verb with an accusative object does. *sein* is used for:

- movement from one place to another: *gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, rennen, umziehen*;
- a change of state: *aufwachsen* (to grow up), *sterben* (to die), *werden* (to become), *aufstehen*, *einschlafen*;
- three verbs you just learn: *sein, bleiben, passieren*.

Life stories are full of the second group:

- *Ich bin in einem kleinen Dorf aufgewachsen.* — I grew up in a small village.
- *Mein Großvater ist 2019 gestorben.* — My grandfather died in 2019.
- *Mit 25 ist sie Mutter geworden.* — At 25 she became a mother.
- *Wir sind dreimal umgezogen.* — We moved house three times.

The same questions as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: haben or sein in the perfect?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the auxiliary. If the verb has an accusative object, use haben. Otherwise, if it describes movement from one place to another, such as fahren or umziehen, use sein. If it describes a change of state, such as aufwachsen, sterben or werden, use sein. The three verbs sein, bleiben and passieren also take sein. Everything else takes haben.
  A["Does the verb have an accusative object?"] -- yes --> H["haben"]
  A -- no --> B["Movement from A to B? fahren, umziehen"]
  B -- yes --> S["sein"]
  B -- no --> C["Change of state? aufwachsen, sterben, werden"]
  C -- yes --> S
  C -- no --> D["sein, bleiben or passieren?"]
  D -- yes --> S
  D -- no --> H
```

## Participles: the patterns you know

A quick review of the main types from A1:

| type | how it's built | examples |
|---|---|---|
| **[[weak verb]]** (regular) | ge- + stem + -t | *heiraten → geheiratet*, *wohnen → gewohnt*, *gründen → gegründet* |
| **[[strong verb]]** | ge- + stem + -en, often a new vowel | *schreiben → geschrieben*, *finden → gefunden*, *sterben → gestorben* |
| **[[separable verb]]** | prefix + ge + participle | *aufwachsen → aufgewachsen*, *umziehen → umgezogen*, *anfangen → angefangen* |

Stems ending in *-t* or *-d* add an *e* so you can pronounce them: *heiraten → geheiratet*, *gründen → gegründet* (to found, to start a company or a family), *arbeiten → gearbeitet*.

*wechseln* (to change, to switch) is a weak verb: *Ich habe die Stelle gewechselt.* — I changed jobs. In the present tense, *ich wechsle* drops the second *e*.

## Inseparable prefixes: no ge-

Some prefixes are glued to their verb for good. They are never stressed, they never split off, and the participle gets no *ge-*. There are only a few, and these seven are the ones you need:

| **[[inseparable prefix]]** | infinitive | participle | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| be- | bekommen, beginnen, besuchen | bekommen, begonnen, besucht | to get, to begin, to visit |
| emp- | empfehlen | empfohlen | to recommend |
| ent- | entscheiden | entschieden | to decide |
| er- | erleben, erzählen, erreichen | erlebt, erzählt, erreicht | to experience, to tell, to reach |
| ge- | gehören, gefallen | gehört, gefallen | to belong, to please |
| ver- | verlassen, verstehen, vergessen | verlassen, verstanden, vergessen | to leave, to understand, to forget |
| zer- | zerstören | zerstört | to destroy |

Notice what happens: you build the participle exactly as for the verb without the prefix, then you simply don't add *ge-*. *Stehen* has the participle *gestanden*, so *verstehen* has *verstanden*. *Lassen* has *gelassen*, so *verlassen* has *verlassen*. For some verbs the participle looks just like the infinitive: *bekommen → bekommen*, *vergessen → vergessen*, *verlassen → verlassen*. Only the auxiliary tells you it's the past.

- *Mit 19 habe ich mein Elternhaus verlassen.* — At 19 I left my parents' house.
- *In Spanien habe ich viel erlebt.* — I experienced a lot in Spain.
- *Wann hat der Kurs begonnen?* — When did the course begin?
- *Sie hat sich für ein Studium entschieden.* — She decided to go to university. (*sich entscheiden für* = to decide on; take it as a chunk for now.)

### Separable or inseparable?

Listen for the stress. Separable prefixes are stressed: AUF-wachsen, UM-ziehen. Inseparable ones never are: be-KOM-men, ver-LAS-sen. A few verbs only look as if they have a prefix: *heiraten* is not *he-* + *raten*; it's one simple weak verb, so it takes ge-: *geheiratet*.

Be careful with *gefallen* and *gehören*: the *ge-* at the start is part of the verb, and you don't add another one. *Das Buch hat mir gefallen* (I liked the book), never *gegefallen*.

## Verbs in -ieren: no ge- either

Verbs ending in *-ieren* come from French or Latin. They are always weak and they take no *ge-*: the participle just replaces *-en* with *-t*. The stress is always on the *-ie-*.

- *studieren → studiert*: *Er hat in Wien Informatik studiert.* — He studied computer science in Vienna.
- *fotografieren → fotografiert*, *telefonieren → telefoniert*, *reparieren → repariert*, *organisieren → organisiert*
- *passieren → ist passiert* (with *sein*, as you know)

So two groups have no *ge-*: verbs with an inseparable prefix and verbs in *-ieren*. Everything else has one somewhere.

This chart puts all the participle rules of this lesson in the order to check them:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to build a past participle
  accDescr: A decision chart. First ask whether the verb ends in -ieren; if so, there is no ge- and the ending is -t, as in studiert. If not, ask whether it has an inseparable prefix such as be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver- or zer-; if so, there is no ge-, as in verstanden. If not, ask whether it has a separable prefix; if so, -ge- goes between the prefix and the verb, as in aufgewachsen. Otherwise the participle starts with ge-: weak verbs end in -t (geheiratet), strong verbs in -en (geschrieben), and mixed verbs change the vowel and end in -t (genannt).
  A["Verb ends in -ieren?"] -- yes --> A1["no ge-, ending -t: studiert"]
  A -- no --> B["Inseparable prefix? be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer-"]
  B -- yes --> B1["no ge-: verstanden, erlebt"]
  B -- no --> C["Separable prefix? auf-, um-, an- …"]
  C -- yes --> C1["prefix + ge + participle: aufgewachsen"]
  C -- no --> D["ge- at the front"]
  D --> D1["weak: ge…t (geheiratet)"]
  D --> D2["strong: ge…en (geschrieben)"]
  D --> D3["mixed: new vowel + t (genannt)"]
```

## Mixed verbs

A small group of verbs behaves partly like weak verbs and partly like strong ones: they change their vowel, but the participle ends in *-t*. These are the **[[mixed verbs]]**. You met four at A1. Two more are useful at A2:

| infinitive | participle | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| bringen | hat gebracht | to bring |
| denken | hat gedacht | to think |
| kennen | hat gekannt | to know (a person) |
| wissen | hat gewusst | to know (a fact) |
| nennen | hat genannt | to name, to call |
| rennen | ist gerannt | to run (fast) |

- *Meine Eltern haben mich nach meiner Oma genannt.* — My parents named me after my grandma.
- *Ich bin zum Bahnhof gerannt, aber der Zug war weg.* — I ran to the station, but the train was gone.
- *Das habe ich nicht gewusst!* — I didn't know that!

*rennen* is faster than *laufen*: you *laufen* in the park, you *rennen* to catch the bus.

## Years, ages and dates in a life story

German reads years before 2000 in hundreds: *1998* is *neunzehnhundertachtundneunzig* (nineteen hundred ninety-eight). From 2000 on, you read them as thousands: *2010* is *zweitausendzehn*, *2024* is *zweitausendvierundzwanzig*.

The biggest difference from English: German says a year on its own, with no preposition. Never say *in 2010*.

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *2010 bin ich umgezogen.* | In 2010 I moved. |
| *Im Jahr 2010 bin ich umgezogen.* | In (the year) 2010 I moved. (a bit more formal) |
| *mit 18* | at 18, at the age of 18 |
| *von 2012 bis 2015* | from 2012 to 2015 |
| *seit 2020* | since 2020 |
| *in den Neunzigerjahren* | in the nineties |

For your birth, use *geboren* (born) with *sein*: *Ich bin 1993 in Linz geboren.* — I was born in Linz in 1993. *Wo bist du geboren?* — Where were you born? (In a formal CV or for someone who has died you'll also see *wurde … geboren*; that's lesson 2.)

*erst* means "only" or "not until", when something happened later than you'd expect:

- *Ich habe erst mit 30 Auto fahren gelernt.* — I didn't learn to drive until I was 30.
- *Er ist erst seit zwei Wochen hier.* — He's only been here for two weeks.

## Words for a life

Most of the new words in this lesson name stages and events of *das Leben* (life): *die Geburt* (birth), *die Kindheit* (childhood), *die Jugend* (youth, the teenage years), *der Abschluss* (a qualification), *das Studium* (a degree course), *die Hochzeit* (wedding), *der Umzug* (a move to a new home) and *die Heimat* (the place where you feel you belong).

*die Erfahrung* is experience you gain over time (*Ich habe viel Erfahrung mit Kindern*); *das Erlebnis* is one memorable thing that happened to you (*Die Reise war ein tolles Erlebnis*). To retire is *in Rente gehen*: *Mein Vater ist letztes Jahr in Rente gegangen.* A retired person is *ein Rentner* or *eine Rentnerin*. A CV is *der Lebenslauf*, literally "the run of a life". *Die Vergangenheit* is the past, and it's also the grammar word for past tenses.

![Five pictures on a timeline labeled das Leben: a pram for die Geburt (birth), a graduation cap for der Abschluss (a qualification), two wedding rings for die Hochzeit (wedding), a moving van with boxes for der Umzug (a move) and a rocking chair for die Rente (retirement, pension).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: An interview for the club newsletter

Tomasz Nowak has joined a choir in Leipzig, and the club newsletter interviews every new member.

> Interviewerin: Herr Nowak, erzählen Sie doch ein bisschen von sich. Wo sind Sie geboren?
>
> Tomasz: Ich bin 1987 in Breslau geboren, auf Polnisch heißt die Stadt Wrocław. Dort bin ich auch aufgewachsen. Meine Kindheit war sehr schön, wir haben direkt an der Oder gewohnt.
>
> Interviewerin: Und wie sind Sie nach Leipzig gekommen?
>
> Tomasz: Nach dem Abitur habe ich zuerst in Krakau Chemie studiert. Das Studium hat mir gefallen, aber nach dem Abschluss habe ich keine Stelle gefunden. 2013 habe ich dann ein Angebot aus Leipzig bekommen, und ich habe meine Heimat verlassen. Das war keine leichte Entscheidung.
>
> Interviewerin: Haben Sie damals schon Deutsch gesprochen?
>
> Tomasz: Ein bisschen. Ich habe es in der Schule gelernt, aber ich habe fast alles vergessen. Die ersten Monate waren schwer. Erst nach einem Jahr habe ich die Kollegen wirklich verstanden.
>
> Interviewerin: Und privat?
>
> Tomasz: 2016 habe ich meine Frau kennengelernt, im Chor übrigens! Wir haben 2018 geheiratet. Die Hochzeit haben wir in Polen gefeiert, mit über hundert Gästen. Meine Mutter hat drei Tage lang gekocht.
>
> Interviewerin: Was war Ihr schönstes Erlebnis in Deutschland?
>
> Tomasz: Die Geburt von unserer Tochter. Wir haben sie Hanna genannt, so heißt auch meine Oma. Und letztes Jahr haben wir eine kleine Firma gegründet, wir reparieren alte Klaviere.
>
> Interviewerin: Haben Sie den Umzug nach Deutschland nie bereut?
>
> Tomasz: Nein, nie. Ich habe hier so viele Erfahrungen gemacht. Aber ich habe zwei Heimaten, das sage ich immer.

In English:

> Interviewer: Mr Nowak, tell us a little about yourself. Where were you born?
>
> Tomasz: I was born in 1987 in Breslau; in Polish the city is called Wrocław. I grew up there too. My childhood was very happy; we lived right on the Oder.
>
> Interviewer: And how did you come to Leipzig?
>
> Tomasz: After my Abitur I first studied chemistry in Kraków. I liked the course, but after graduating I didn't find a job. Then in 2013 I got an offer from Leipzig, and I left my home country. That wasn't an easy decision.
>
> Interviewer: Did you already speak German back then?
>
> Tomasz: A little. I learned it at school, but I'd forgotten almost everything. The first months were hard. It was only after a year that I really understood my colleagues.
>
> Interviewer: And in your private life?
>
> Tomasz: In 2016 I met my wife, in the choir, by the way! We got married in 2018. We celebrated the wedding in Poland, with over a hundred guests. My mother cooked for three days.
>
> Interviewer: What was your best experience in Germany?
>
> Tomasz: The birth of our daughter. We named her Hanna; that's my grandma's name too. And last year we started a small company; we repair old pianos.
>
> Interviewer: Have you never regretted the move to Germany?
>
> Tomasz: No, never. I've had so many experiences here. But I have two homelands, I always say that.

Look at the participles: *aufgewachsen* and *gekommen* take *sein*; *bekommen, verlassen, vergessen, verstanden* have inseparable prefixes and no *ge-*; *studiert* and *repariert* end in *-ieren*; *genannt* is mixed; *geheiratet* and *gegründet* are weak with the extra *e*. *Gefallen* has no extra *ge-*. Also see how the years stand alone: *2013 habe ich …*, *Wir haben 2018 geheiratet*. (*übrigens* = by the way; *bereuen* = to regret; *der Gast, die Gäste* = guest.)

## Pronunciation

- Inseparable prefixes are unstressed and short: be-KOM-men, ver-LAS-sen, er-LE-ben, ent-SCHEI-den.
- Separable prefixes carry the stress: AUF-ge-wach-sen, UM-ge-zo-gen.
- *-ieren* verbs stress the *ie*: stu-DIERT, re-pa-RIERT.
- *das Studium*: stu-DI-um, three clear vowels, *St-* said "sht".
- *die Heimat*: HEI-mat; *der Abschluss*: AB-schluss, with a short *u*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich habe in 2015 geheiratet.* — No *in* before a bare year: *2015 habe ich geheiratet* or *Im Jahr 2015 …*.
- *Ich habe aufgewachsen.* — *aufwachsen* is a change of state: *Ich bin aufgewachsen.* The same goes for *sterben*: *Er ist gestorben*.
- *Ich habe das vergessen.* is right; *Ich habe das gevergessen* is not. No *ge-* after an inseparable prefix: *bekommen, verstanden, erlebt*.
- *Ich habe Biologie gestudiert.* — *-ieren* verbs take no *ge-*: *studiert*.
- *Er hat seinen Sohn Max genennt.* — *nennen* is mixed: *genannt*.
- *Ich bin in 1990 geboren.* / *Ich habe geboren.* — Say *Ich bin 1990 geboren.*
- Mixing up *bekommen* and English "become": *bekommen* means to get. "To become" is *werden*: *Sie ist Ärztin geworden.*

## Key points

- Perfect = *haben* or *sein* in position 2 + participle at the end. Change-of-state verbs like *aufwachsen*, *sterben* and *werden* take *sein*.
- The main inseparable prefixes are be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer-. They are unstressed and the participle has no *ge-*: *bekommen, entschieden, erlebt, verlassen*.
- Verbs in *-ieren* take no *ge-*: *studiert, passiert*.
- Mixed verbs change their vowel and end in *-t*: *gebracht, gedacht, gekannt, gewusst, genannt, gerannt*.
- A year stands alone or with *im Jahr*: *2010* / *im Jahr 2010*, never *in 2010*. *mit 18* = at 18. *Ich bin 1990 geboren.*
- *erst* = only, not until: *erst mit 30*.

lessons.title: When I was a child: the simple past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 1 you told your life story in the perfect. But some verbs sound clumsy in the perfect, and Germans avoid it with them. You already know two: Germans rarely say *Ich bin müde gewesen*; they say *Ich war müde*. At A1 you learned *war* and *hatte*, the **[[simple past]]** of *sein* and *haben*.

This lesson adds the rest of the simple past you need at A2. You'll learn to *use* it for the modal verbs, because *konnte, musste, durfte* are what Germans actually say when they talk about what they could, had to or were allowed to do as children. You'll learn to *recognise* the simple past of other common verbs, because you'll meet them in every story, article and fairy tale you read. And you'll find out when Germans choose which past tense.

The theme is childhood and school days: what was allowed, what was forbidden, who was strict and what you remember.

## Two past tenses, one meaning

German has two everyday past tenses, the perfect (*ich habe gespielt*) and the simple past, also called the **[[Präteritum]]** (*ich spielte*). The important thing for an English speaker: they mean the same. *Ich habe gespielt* and *ich spielte* both translate as "I played", "I have played" or "I was playing". The difference is style, not time.

| | perfect | simple past |
|---|---|---|
| where | conversation, messages, e-mails to friends | books, newspapers, stories, reports, fairy tales |
| which verbs | almost all verbs | *sein, haben, werden* and the modals, in speech too |
| example | *Gestern habe ich Oma besucht.* | *Der König hatte drei Töchter.* |

So in speech you mix the two: the perfect for most verbs, the simple past for *sein, haben* and the modals. *Gestern war ich bei Oma. Wir haben Kuchen gegessen, und ich musste ihr den Computer erklären.* That one sentence uses both, and it's completely normal.

When you're not sure which tense to choose, ask these questions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which past tense should I use?
  accDescr: A decision chart. If you are writing a story, report, biography or fairy tale, use the simple past for all verbs. If you are speaking or writing a message to a friend, check the verb: for sein, haben, werden and the modal verbs, use the simple past, such as war, hatte, konnte; for all other verbs, use the perfect, such as habe gespielt.
  A["Speaking or writing?"] -- "a story, report or fairy tale" --> P["simple past for all verbs: ging, sagte"]
  A -- "speaking, chatting, messages" --> B["Is the verb sein, haben, werden or a modal?"]
  B -- yes --> P2["simple past: war, hatte, wurde, konnte"]
  B -- no --> Q["perfect: habe gespielt, bin gegangen"]
```

In northern Germany people use the simple past a little more in speech than in the south, Austria and Switzerland, where the perfect is almost everything. You won't go wrong with the rule in the table.

## sein, haben and werden

You know *war* and *hatte*. *werden* (to become) has the simple past *wurde*. All three use the same endings, which are also the endings of every simple past form: nothing for *ich* and *er/sie/es*, *-st* for *du*, *-t* for *ihr* and the plural ending *-en* (or *-n*).

| | sein | haben | werden |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte | wurde |
| du | warst | hattest | wurdest |
| er / sie / es | war | hatte | wurde |
| wir | waren | hatten | wurden |
| ihr | wart | hattet | wurdet |
| sie / Sie | waren | hatten | wurden |

- *Mit zwölf wurde ich sehr frech.* — At twelve I became very cheeky.
- *Meine Lehrerin war streng, aber fair.* — My teacher was strict but fair.
- *Wir hatten keinen Fernseher.* — We didn't have a TV.

In lesson 1 you said *Ich bin 1990 geboren.* With *wurde* you can say *Ich wurde 1990 geboren*, which sounds more formal, like a CV. For people who have died, Germans normally use *wurde*: *Mozart wurde 1756 in Salzburg geboren.*

## The modal verbs in the simple past

Modal verbs are rarely used in the perfect. To say what you could, wanted, had to or were allowed to do, use their simple past. The rule is easy: take the infinitive, drop the umlaut if there is one, and add *-te*.

| infinitive | drop umlaut, add -te | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| können | konnte | could, was able to |
| müssen | musste | had to |
| dürfen | durfte | was allowed to |
| wollen | wollte | wanted (to) |
| sollen | sollte | was supposed to |
| mögen | mochte | liked |

*mögen* is the only odd one: the *g* becomes *ch*, *mochte*. And *möchten* has no past of its own: for "wanted to" use *wollte*. *Ich möchte ein Eis* becomes *Ich wollte ein Eis*.

The endings are the same as for *war* and *wurde*:

| | können | müssen | dürfen | wollen | sollen | mögen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | konnte | musste | durfte | wollte | sollte | mochte |
| du | konntest | musstest | durftest | wolltest | solltest | mochtest |
| er / sie / es | konnte | musste | durfte | wollte | sollte | mochte |
| wir | konnten | mussten | durften | wollten | sollten | mochten |
| ihr | konntet | musstet | durftet | wolltet | solltet | mochtet |
| sie / Sie | konnten | mussten | durften | wollten | sollten | mochten |

The word order is the same as in the present: the modal in position 2, the infinitive at the end.

- *Mit sechs konnte ich schon lesen.* — At six I could already read.
- *Wir mussten jeden Tag um sieben aufstehen.* — We had to get up at seven every day.
- *Ich durfte abends nicht fernsehen.* — I wasn't allowed to watch TV in the evenings.
- *Meine Schwester wollte immer Ärztin werden.* — My sister always wanted to become a doctor.
- *Du solltest doch um sechs zu Hause sein!* — You were supposed to be home at six!
- *Als Kind mochte ich keinen Spinat.* — As a child I didn't like spinach.

*Als Kind* means "as a child", a useful chunk; the word *als* gets its own section in lesson 4.

Watch *sollte*: it can also mean "should" in the present (*Du solltest mehr schlafen* — You should sleep more). The context tells you which; lesson 15 covers the "should" meaning properly.

## Recognising the simple past of other verbs

In speech you'll use the perfect for most verbs. But you'll *read* the simple past all the time, so you need to recognise it. There are three patterns, and they match the three participle types from lesson 1.

### Weak verbs: -te

Weak verbs add *-te* to the stem, just like the modals: *sagen → sagte*, *machen → machte*, *spielen → spielte*, *wohnen → wohnte*. Stems ending in *-t* or *-d* add *-ete*: *arbeiten → arbeitete*, *warten → wartete*. If you see *-te* in the middle of a verb, think "past".

### Strong verbs: a new vowel, no ending

Strong verbs change their vowel, and the *ich* and *er/sie/es* forms have no ending at all: *er ging* (he went), *sie kam* (she came). Here are the most common ones in stories:

| simple past | infinitive | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ging | gehen | went |
| kam | kommen | came |
| sah | sehen | saw |
| gab | geben | gave; (es gab) there was, there were |
| fand | finden | found |
| stand | stehen | stood |
| saß | sitzen | sat |
| lag | liegen | lay, was lying |
| las | lesen | read |
| schrieb | schreiben | wrote |
| fuhr | fahren | drove, went |
| lief | laufen | ran |
| blieb | bleiben | stayed |
| nahm | nehmen | took |
| sprach | sprechen | spoke |
| aß | essen | ate |

*es gab* is especially common: *Damals gab es kein Internet.* — Back then there was no internet.

### Mixed verbs: new vowel and -te

The mixed verbs from lesson 1 combine both: a new vowel and *-te*. *denken → dachte*, *bringen → brachte*, *kennen → kannte*, *wissen → wusste*, *nennen → nannte*, *rennen → rannte*.

- *Ich dachte, du kommst heute.* — I thought you were coming today.
- *Das wusste ich nicht.* — I didn't know that.

A dictionary lists the simple past next to the participle: *finden, fand, gefunden*.

## Fairy tales

German fairy tales, *die Märchen*, are told in the simple past and almost always start with *Es war einmal …* (Once upon a time there was …). They're a good way to practise recognising the forms:

*Es war einmal ein Mädchen, das wohnte mit seiner Mutter am Rand von einem großen Wald. Eines Tages sagte die Mutter: „Bring der Großmutter diesen Kuchen. Aber du darfst nicht vom Weg gehen!“ Das Mädchen nahm den Korb und ging los.* — Once upon a time there was a girl who lived with her mother at the edge of a big forest. One day the mother said: "Take this cake to Grandmother. But you mustn't leave the path!" The girl took the basket and set off.

You don't need to produce this style yet; you only need to understand it.

## Remembering

To say you remember something, use *sich erinnern an* + accusative. It's a reflexive verb, which you'll learn properly in lesson 5. For now, use these chunks:

- *Ich erinnere mich an meine erste Lehrerin.* — I remember my first teacher.
- *Erinnerst du dich an unseren Spielplatz?* — Do you remember our playground?
- *Ich kann mich nicht erinnern.* — I can't remember.

The noun is *die Erinnerung* (memory): *Ich habe schöne Erinnerungen an meine Kindheit.*

## School in Germany

Children usually go to *der Kindergarten* from age three, and to *die Grundschule* (primary school) at six. School years are counted in *Klassen*: *Ich war in der dritten Klasse* (I was in third grade, in year 3). *Die Klasse* also means the group of children. A school subject is *das Fach*, and at the end of each half-year children get a report, *das Zeugnis*, with *Noten* (grades) from 1 (sehr gut) to 6 (ungenügend). In Germany a 1 is the best grade, not the worst! Between lessons there's *die Pause*, and children play outside on *der Schulhof* (the schoolyard).

Here is what Opa's report from the text below might have looked like:

![A school report (Zeugnis) from Grundschule Lindenweg for Peter Wolf, Klasse 3b, school year 1961/62, second half-year. Subjects and grades: Deutsch 2, Mathematik 4, Sport 1, Musik 3. The teacher's comment reads: Peter ist fleißig, aber oft frech (Peter works hard but is often cheeky). A signature line is at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Allowed and forbidden

Childhood is full of rules. *erlauben* (to allow) is the verb behind *erlaubt*, which you know from A1, and *das Verbot* (ban, rule against something) is the noun behind *verboten*. Parents want their children to be *brav* (good, well-behaved), but children are often *frech* (cheeky).

- *Meine Eltern haben mir fast alles erlaubt.* — My parents allowed me almost everything.
- *Bei uns gab es ein Verbot: kein Fernsehen vor den Hausaufgaben.* — We had one rule: no TV before homework.
- *Unser Nachbar hat oft geschimpft, denn unser Ball lag immer in seinem Garten.* — Our neighbour often told us off, because our ball was always lying in his garden.
- *Pass auf deinen Bruder auf!* — Keep an eye on your brother! (*aufpassen auf* + accusative = to look after, to watch out for)

## Text: Opa erzählt

Lena's grandfather, born in 1952, tells her about his school days.

> Lena: Opa, wie war die Schule früher?
>
> Opa: Oh, ganz anders als heute. Wir waren fünfunddreißig Kinder in einer Klasse. Unser Lehrer, Herr Krämer, war sehr streng. Wir durften im Unterricht kein Wort sagen.
>
> Lena: Und wenn doch?
>
> Opa: Dann schimpfte er laut, und man musste in der Pause in der Klasse bleiben. Einmal war ich frech und habe eine Maus mitgebracht. Die hat sich unter seinem Tisch versteckt. Er hat sie nie gefunden!
>
> Lena: Was war dein Lieblingsfach?
>
> Opa: Sport. In Mathe hatte ich immer schlechte Noten. Mein Zeugnis wollte ich meinem Vater nie zeigen.
>
> Lena: Und nach der Schule?
>
> Opa: Wir hatten kein Spielzeug wie ihr heute, nur einen alten Ball und eine Puppe für meine Schwester. Wir konnten den ganzen Nachmittag draußen spielen und auf Bäume klettern. Unsere Nachbarin, Frau Lutz, passte auf uns auf. Wir sollten um sechs zu Hause sein, aber das hat selten geklappt.
>
> Lena: Hast du schöne Erinnerungen an diese Zeit?
>
> Opa: Ja, sehr schöne. Wir hatten nicht viel, aber wir waren frei.

In English:

> Lena: Grandpa, what was school like in the old days?
>
> Grandpa: Oh, very different from today. We were thirty-five children in one class. Our teacher, Mr Krämer, was very strict. We weren't allowed to say a word in lessons.
>
> Lena: And if you did?
>
> Grandpa: Then he scolded loudly, and you had to stay in the classroom during break. Once I was cheeky and brought a mouse along. It hid under his desk. He never found it!
>
> Lena: What was your favourite subject?
>
> Grandpa: PE. In maths I always had bad grades. I never wanted to show my report to my father.
>
> Lena: And after school?
>
> Grandpa: We didn't have toys like you do today, just an old ball and a doll for my sister. We could play outside all afternoon and climb trees. Our neighbour, Mrs Lutz, kept an eye on us. We were supposed to be home at six, but that rarely worked out.
>
> Lena: Do you have happy memories of that time?
>
> Grandpa: Yes, very happy ones. We didn't have much, but we were free.

Grandpa speaks naturally: *war, hatte, durften, musste, konnte, wollte, sollten* in the simple past, and *habe mitgebracht, hat gefunden, hat geklappt* in the perfect. *schimpfte* and *passte auf* are simple past too; he's telling an old story, so they slip in. (*Und wenn doch?* = And if you did?; *der Unterricht* = lessons, teaching; *der Lieblings-* = favourite; *der Baum, die Bäume* = tree; *selten* = rarely; *klappen* = to work out.)

## Pronunciation

- *durfte, musste, konnte*: short vowels, no umlaut. Don't say *dürfte* or *müsste*; those are different forms with a different meaning (lesson 15).
- *wurde*: a short *u*, like English "put". Don't confuse it with *würde* (would).
- *das Zeugnis*: ZEUG-nis, *eu* as in "boy", the *g* sounds like *k*.
- *das Märchen*: long *ä*, MÄR-chen.
- *die Grundschule*: GRUND-schu-le, the *d* sounds like *t*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich habe nicht gekonnt schwimmen.* — Use the simple past of the modal: *Ich konnte nicht schwimmen.*
- *Ich möchtete …* — *möchten* has no simple past; use *wollte*: *Ich wollte ein Fahrrad.*
- *Er konntet …* / *Ich musstet …* — The ich and er forms have no ending after *-te*: *ich konnte, er musste*.
- *Ich durfe nicht …* — Don't forget the *t*: *durfte*.
- *Ich mögte …* — The past of *mögen* is *mochte*.
- *Ich bin müde gewesen.* isn't wrong, but it sounds stiff. With *sein* and *haben*, people say *Ich war müde*, *Ich hatte Zeit*.
- Reading *sie ging* as present: a strong verb with a new vowel and no ending is past. *Sie geht* is present, *sie ging* is past.

## Key points

- Perfect and simple past mean the same; the perfect is for speaking, the simple past for writing and stories.
- In speech too, use the simple past for *sein* (*war*), *haben* (*hatte*), *werden* (*wurde*) and the modals.
- Modal past: no umlaut + *-te*: *konnte, musste, durfte, wollte, sollte, mochte*. *möchten* → *wollte*.
- Endings: ich –, du -st, er –, wir -en, ihr -t, sie -en. The ich and er forms are the same.
- Recognise strong pasts by the new vowel (*ging, kam, sah, gab, fand*) and weak pasts by *-te* (*sagte, machte*).
- *Es war einmal …* starts a fairy tale; *es gab* = there was / there were.

lessons.title: Reasons and opinions: weil and dass
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A1 you gave reasons with *denn*: *Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.* That works, but in conversation Germans much more often say *weil*: *Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.* Look at the end of that sentence: the verb *bin* has moved to the last place.

That small move is one of the most important patterns in German. It happens after *weil* (because), after *dass* (that) and after the words in lesson 4 (*wenn, als, ob*). Once you have it, you can give reasons, say what you think, hope and know, and talk about your feelings in longer, more natural sentences. That's exactly what A2 asks of you: not just "I like it", but "I like it because …" and "I think that …".

## Two kinds of clause

A clause is a group of words with its own verb. A **[[main clause]]** can stand alone as a sentence, and its verb is in position 2: *Ich bin krank.* A **[[subordinate clause]]** can't stand alone; it hangs on a main clause and adds information, such as a reason. In a German subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the very end.

| main clause | , | subordinate clause (verb at the end) |
|---|---|---|
| Ich bleibe zu Hause | , | weil ich krank bin. |
| Ich glaube | , | dass sie heute kommt. |

Words like *weil* and *dass*, which start a subordinate clause and push the verb to the end, are called **[[subordinating conjunctions]]**. Words like *und, aber, oder, denn* and *sondern*, which just join two main clauses and change nothing, are **[[coordinating conjunctions]]**.

German always puts a comma between a main clause and a subordinate clause. In English you often don't, so this is a rule to watch when you write.

## weil: giving a reason

*weil* means "because". The subject usually comes right after *weil*, and the verb goes to the end.

- *Ich lerne Deutsch, weil meine Frau aus Österreich kommt.* — I'm learning German because my wife is from Austria.
- *Sie ist froh, weil sie die Prüfung bestanden hat.* — She's glad because she passed the exam.
- *Wir fahren nicht weg, weil wir kein Geld haben.* — We're not going away because we have no money.

### weil or denn?

Both mean "because", and you can usually use either. The difference is only word order:

| | word order | example |
|---|---|---|
| *denn* | main clause: verb in position 2 | *Ich gehe früh ins Bett, denn ich bin müde.* |
| *weil* | subordinate clause: verb at the end | *Ich gehe früh ins Bett, weil ich müde bin.* |

*weil* is more common in speech, and it's the only one you can use to answer a *warum* question on its own:

- *Warum lernst du so viel? – Weil ich nächste Woche eine Prüfung habe.* — Why are you studying so much? – Because I have an exam next week.

A *denn* sentence can't answer alone; it always follows a main clause.

## Two verbs at the end

If the subordinate clause has two verb parts, the conjugated one goes last of all. Everything else from A1 still applies; just pull the conjugated verb to the end.

### Separable verbs join up again

In a main clause a separable verb splits: *Ich stehe früh auf.* In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb moves to the end, right next to its prefix, and they're written as one word again:

- *Ich bin müde, weil ich jeden Tag um fünf aufstehe.* — I'm tired because I get up at five every day.
- *Er ist traurig, weil seine Freundin nicht anruft.* — He's sad because his girlfriend doesn't call.

### Modal verbs: the modal comes last

- *Ich kann nicht kommen, weil ich arbeiten muss.* — I can't come because I have to work.
- *Sie ist stolz, weil sie schon gut Deutsch sprechen kann.* — She's proud because she can already speak German well.

### The perfect: the auxiliary comes last

- *Ich bin enttäuscht, weil du nicht angerufen hast.* — I'm disappointed because you didn't call.
- *Er ist glücklich, weil er eine neue Stelle bekommen hat.* — He's happy because he's got a new job.
- *Wir sind spät gekommen, weil wir den Bus verpasst haben.* — We came late because we missed the bus.

So the order at the end is: participle or infinitive first, conjugated verb last: *angerufen hast, arbeiten muss, aufstehe*.

## dass: what you think, know and hope

*dass* means "that" and introduces what someone thinks, says, knows, hopes or feels. Like *weil*, it sends the verb to the end.

- *Ich glaube, dass er recht hat.* — I think (that) he's right.
- *Ich hoffe, dass das Wetter morgen schön ist.* — I hope (that) the weather is nice tomorrow.
- *Weißt du, dass Paula schwanger ist?* — Do you know that Paula is pregnant?
- *Ich finde, dass das Hotel zu teuer ist.* — I think (that) the hotel is too expensive.

Note *finden* here: besides "to find", it means "to think" when you give your opinion about something. *Wie findest du das Buch?* — What do you think of the book?

The most common verbs before *dass* are *denken, glauben, finden, meinen, hoffen, wissen, sagen*. Also common are adjectives with *sein*:

- *Es ist wichtig, dass du pünktlich bist.* — It's important that you're on time.
- *Ich bin froh, dass du da bist.* — I'm glad you're here.
- *Es ist schade, dass ihr schon fahrt.* — It's a pity that you're leaving already.

### Without dass

In English you can leave out "that", and in German, after verbs of thinking and saying, you can leave out *dass* too. But then the second part is a main clause again, with the verb in position 2:

| with dass | without dass |
|---|---|
| *Ich glaube, dass er krank ist.* | *Ich glaube, er ist krank.* |
| *Sie sagt, dass sie keine Zeit hat.* | *Sie sagt, sie hat keine Zeit.* |

Both are correct, and the version without *dass* is very common in speech. What you can't do is mix the two: *Ich glaube, dass er ist krank* is wrong.

So the word at the start of the second clause decides where its verb goes:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where does the verb go?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the position of the conjugated verb in the second part of a sentence. After und, aber, oder, denn or sondern, the second part is a main clause, and the verb stays in position 2. After weil, dass or another subordinating conjunction, the verb goes to the end of the clause. After verbs like glauben or finden with dass left out, the verb is in position 2 again.
  A["What starts the second clause?"] --> B["und, aber, oder, denn, sondern"]
  A --> C["weil, dass"]
  A --> D["nothing: dass left out after glauben, finden"]
  B --> B1["verb in position 2: denn ich bin müde"]
  C --> C1["verb at the end: weil ich müde bin"]
  D --> D1["verb in position 2: Ich glaube, er ist müde"]
```

Don't confuse *dass* with *das*. *das* (one *s*) is the article or "that" as a pronoun: *Das stimmt.* *dass* (double *s*) is the conjunction. A quick test: if you can replace it with *dies* or *welches*, it's *das*.

## Starting with the subordinate clause

You can put the subordinate clause first, for emphasis. Then the whole subordinate clause counts as position 1, so the verb of the main clause comes straight after the comma, and the subject follows it:

- *Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause.* — Because I'm ill, I'm staying at home.
- *Dass du gekommen bist, finde ich toll.* — I think it's great that you came.

The pattern is easy to remember as "verb, comma, verb": *… bin, bleibe …*. Saying *Weil ich krank bin, ich bleibe zu Hause* is a typical English-speaker mistake.

![Two versions of the same sentence in word boxes. Top: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin. bleibe is in position 2, weil is the conjunction and bin is at the end; a bracket joins weil and bin. Bottom: Weil ich krank bin, bleibe ich zu Hause. The whole weil clause is position 1, so bleibe comes straight after the comma in position 2: verb, comma, verb.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Talking about opinions

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *Meiner Meinung nach ist das falsch.* | In my opinion that's wrong. |
| *Ich bin der Meinung, dass …* | I'm of the opinion that … |
| *Was meinst du?* | What do you think? |
| *Da hast du recht.* | You're right there. |
| *Das stimmt. / Das stimmt nicht.* | That's true. / That's not true. |
| *Ich stimme dir zu.* | I agree with you. |
| *Das ist mir egal.* | I don't mind. / I don't care. |
| *Das ist wahr.* | That's true. |
| *Sag mir bitte die Wahrheit.* | Please tell me the truth. |

*Meiner Meinung nach* counts as position 1, so the verb follows straight away: *Meiner Meinung nach ist …*. *zustimmen* (to agree) is separable and takes the dative: *Ich stimme dir zu. Stimmst du mir zu?* *recht haben* (to be right) uses *haben*, never *sein*: *Du hast recht.*

*unbedingt* means "absolutely" or "definitely", for something you really want or need: *Das musst du unbedingt sehen!* — You absolutely have to see that!

## Talking about feelings

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *froh, glücklich* | glad, happy |
| *zufrieden* | satisfied, content |
| *stolz (auf)* | proud (of) |
| *überrascht* | surprised |
| *traurig* | sad |
| *enttäuscht* | disappointed |
| *wütend* | furious, very angry |
| *nervös* | nervous |

![Five faces with their feelings: glücklich (a big smile), traurig (a frown and a tear), wütend (angry eyebrows and clenched teeth), überrascht (wide eyes and an open mouth) and nervös (a wavy mouth and a drop of sweat).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*froh* is "glad about a situation"; *glücklich* is a deeper "happy" (*ein glückliches Leben*). The nouns *die Angst* (fear), *die Sorge* (worry), *die Hoffnung* (hope), *die Freude* (joy) and *das Gefühl* (feeling) all combine with *dass*:

- *Ich habe Angst, dass ich die Prüfung nicht schaffe.* — I'm afraid I won't pass the exam.
- *Ich habe das Gefühl, dass sie mich nicht mag.* — I have the feeling she doesn't like me.
- *Ich mache mir Sorgen, weil er nicht anruft.* — I'm worried because he isn't calling. (*sich Sorgen machen* = to worry; take it as a chunk.)

## Dialogue: Ab wann ein Handy?

Jana and Murat's son Emil is nine. Over dinner they discuss whether he should get a smartphone.

> Jana: Emil hat heute wieder gefragt, ob er ein Handy bekommt. Was meinst du?
>
> Murat: Ehrlich gesagt finde ich, dass neun zu jung ist. Ich habe Angst, dass er den ganzen Tag nur noch spielt.
>
> Jana: Da hast du schon recht. Aber in seiner Klasse haben fast alle Kinder eins. Er ist traurig, weil er in der Pause nicht mitreden kann.
>
> Murat: Das ist doch kein Grund! Nur weil die anderen eins haben, muss er nicht auch eins haben.
>
> Jana: Ein Handy hat aber auch Vorteile. Für mich ist es wichtig, dass er mich nach dem Training anrufen kann.
>
> Murat: Dafür braucht er kein Smartphone. Ein einfaches Handy ohne Internet reicht doch.
>
> Jana: Gute Idee. Ich glaube, damit ist er nicht ganz zufrieden, aber es ist ein Anfang.
>
> Murat: Und wenn er elf ist, sprechen wir noch einmal darüber. Einverstanden?
>
> Jana: Einverstanden. Ich bin sicher, dass er sich trotzdem freut.

In English:

> Jana: Emil asked again today whether he's getting a phone. What do you think?
>
> Murat: To be honest, I think nine is too young. I'm afraid he'll do nothing but play games all day.
>
> Jana: You're right about that. But almost all the children in his class have one. He's sad because he can't join in the conversation at break.
>
> Murat: That's no reason! Just because the others have one, he doesn't have to have one too.
>
> Jana: But a phone has advantages too. For me it's important that he can call me after training.
>
> Murat: He doesn't need a smartphone for that. A simple phone without internet is enough.
>
> Jana: Good idea. I don't think he'll be completely satisfied with that, but it's a start.
>
> Murat: And when he's eleven, we'll talk about it again. Agreed?
>
> Jana: Agreed. I'm sure he'll be pleased anyway.

Find the verbs at the end: *dass neun zu jung ist*, *dass er … spielt*, *weil er … nicht mitreden kann*, *dass er sich trotzdem freut*. *Ich glaube, damit ist er …* leaves out *dass*, so the verb stays in position 2. *ob* (whether) and *wenn* (when) come in lesson 4, and *sich freuen* (to be pleased) in lesson 5. (*ehrlich gesagt* = to be honest; *mitreden* = to join in a conversation; *reichen* = to be enough; *einverstanden* = agreed; *trotzdem* = anyway; *der Vorteil* = advantage, *der Nachteil* = disadvantage.)

## Pronunciation

- *weil* rhymes with English "mile"; *dass* has a short *a*, like *das*.
- *enttäuscht*: ent-TÄUSCHT; the two *t*s merge, and *äu* sounds like "oy".
- *wütend*: long *ü*, WÜ-tend. *überrascht*: ü-ber-RASCHT.
- *zufrieden*: zu-FRIE-den, long *ie*. *unbedingt*: UN-be-dingt.
- In speech, there's a tiny pause at the comma before *weil* and *dass*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich will in Wien wohnen.* — Verb to the end: *weil ich in Wien wohnen will.*
- *…, weil ich stehe früh auf.* — The separable verb joins up at the end: *weil ich früh aufstehe.*
- *…, weil ich habe den Bus verpasst.* — The auxiliary goes last: *weil ich den Bus verpasst habe.*
- *Ich glaube, dass er ist nett.* — Either *dass er nett ist* or *Ich glaube, er ist nett.*
- *Weil es regnet, ich nehme den Bus.* — Verb, comma, verb: *Weil es regnet, nehme ich den Bus.*
- *Ich bin recht.* — Use *haben*: *Ich habe recht.*
- *Ich denke, das …* written with *das* when you mean the conjunction: the conjunction is *dass*.
- Forgetting the comma: *Ich hoffe dass …* needs a comma: *Ich hoffe, dass …*

## Key points

- *weil* and *dass* start subordinate clauses: the conjugated verb goes to the end, and a comma separates the clauses.
- *weil* and *denn* both mean "because"; *denn* keeps main-clause order, *weil* sends the verb to the end.
- Separable verbs join up at the end (*aufstehe*); modals and auxiliaries come last (*arbeiten muss, verpasst habe*).
- After *glauben, denken, finden, sagen* you can leave out *dass*, but then use main-clause order.
- A subordinate clause in position 1 is followed directly by the main verb: verb, comma, verb.
- Opinions: *Meiner Meinung nach …, Ich finde, dass …, Da hast du recht, Ich stimme dir zu.*
