lessons.title: Verbs with the dative and two objects
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you used the dative after prepositions (*mit dem Bus*, *bei meiner Mutter*) and in chunks like *Kannst du mir helfen?* and *Gib mir das Buch*. This lesson makes the dative a full part of your German. You will learn the verbs that take a dative object instead of an accusative one, the verbs that take both (you give *someone something*), and the rules for putting two objects in the right order: *dem Kind das Buch*, *es dem Kind*, *es ihm*.

The theme fits the grammar: presents, birthdays, lending and borrowing, and saying that something fits, suits or belongs to someone. And because many of these verbs are the ones Germans use to say what they like (*Das gefällt mir*), they will make you sound much more natural.

## The dative forms: a quick review

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| definite | *dem* | *der* | *dem* | *den* (+ *-n* on the noun) |
| indefinite / *kein* / *mein* | *einem, keinem, meinem* | *einer, keiner, meiner* | *einem, keinem, meinem* | *keinen, meinen* (+ *-n*) |

| nominative | *ich* | *du* | *er* | *sie* | *es* | *wir* | *ihr* | *sie* | *Sie* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dative | *mir* | *dir* | *ihm* | *ihr* | *ihm* | *uns* | *euch* | *ihnen* | *Ihnen* |

Two things to notice: the plural noun takes an extra *-n* (*den Kindern*, *meinen Freunden*), unless it already ends in *-n* or *-s* (*den Frauen*, *den Autos*). And *ihr* means both "to her" (dative of *sie*) and "you all" (nominative); context always makes it clear.

## Verbs with only a dative object

A handful of very common verbs take their object in the dative, not the accusative. These are **[[dative verbs]]**, and their object is a **[[dative object]]**. You know *helfen* already. Here are the others to learn at A2:

| verb | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *helfen* | to help | *Ich helfe dir.* |
| *danken* | to thank | *Ich danke Ihnen für die Einladung.* |
| *antworten* | to answer (someone) | *Sie hat mir nicht geantwortet.* |
| *gratulieren* | to congratulate | *Wir gratulieren dir zum Geburtstag!* |
| *vertrauen* | to trust | *Ich vertraue meiner Schwester.* |
| *verzeihen* | to forgive | *Verzeih mir!* |
| *glauben* | to believe (someone) | *Ich glaube dir.* |

There is no logic you can see from English: "I help *you*" looks like a direct object. Think of it as "I give help *to* you", "I give thanks *to* you", "I give my congratulations *to* you": the dative is the "to" person. *gratulieren* adds *zu* + dative for the occasion: *zum Geburtstag, zur Hochzeit*. *danken* adds *für* + accusative for the reason: *Danke für die Blumen.* (*sich bedanken* means the same as *danken* but is reflexive and uses *bei*: *Ich bedanke mich bei dir für die Hilfe.*)

## The "upside-down" verbs: gefallen, gehören, passen …

Some dative verbs work the other way round from English. The thing is the subject, and the person who likes it, owns it or misses it is in the dative:

| verb | literally | English | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *gefallen* | to be pleasing to | to like (how it looks or seems) | *Die Kette gefällt mir.* — I like the necklace. |
| *schmecken* | to taste good to | to like (food) | *Schmeckt dir die Suppe?* — Do you like the soup? |
| *gehören* | to belong to | to belong to | *Der Regenschirm gehört mir.* — The umbrella is mine. |
| *passen* | to fit / suit | to fit, suit, be convenient | *Der Ring passt mir nicht.* — The ring doesn't fit me. |
| *stehen* | to stand (to) | to suit (clothes) | *Die Sonnenbrille steht dir gut.* — The sunglasses suit you. |
| *fehlen* | to be missing to | to miss (someone) | *Du fehlst mir.* — I miss you. |
| *wehtun* | to hurt | to hurt | *Mir tut der Kopf weh.* — My head hurts. |

Because the thing is the subject, the verb agrees with the thing, not with you:

- *Die Ohrringe gefallen mir.* — I like the earrings. (plural thing → *gefallen*)
- *Gefallen dir meine Schuhe?* — Do you like my shoes?
- *Du fehlst mir.* — I miss you. (literally "you are missing to me")
- *Ihr fehlt mir.* — I miss you all.

*fehlen* is the hardest one for English speakers, because the roles are reversed: *Ich fehle dir* means "you miss me". Read it as "I am missing *for you*". Without a person, *fehlen* simply means "to be missing": *Hier fehlt eine Seite.* — There's a page missing here.

*gefallen* or *mögen*? Both mean "like". *gefallen* is mostly about how something looks or seems, often the first impression: *Wie gefällt dir Berlin?* — How do you like Berlin? *mögen* is for general, lasting likes: *Ich mag Berlin.* For food, use *schmecken* or *mögen*: *Das schmeckt mir.* Note the stem change: *es gefällt*, perfect *hat gefallen*.

*passen* has three common uses: size (*Die Jacke passt mir nicht, sie ist zu klein*), matching (*Der Schal passt gut zur Jacke* — goes well with) and time (*Passt dir Montag?* — Does Monday suit you?).

## Verbs with two objects

Verbs of giving, showing and telling often have two objects: a thing (accusative, the **[[direct object]]**) and a person who receives it (dative, the **[[indirect object]]**).

*Ich gebe dem Mann den Schlüssel.* — I give the man the key.

| verb | example |
|---|---|
| *geben* | *Gib mir bitte das Salz.* — Pass me the salt, please. |
| *schenken* | *Wir schenken unserer Tochter ein Fahrrad.* — We're giving our daughter a bike. |
| *zeigen* | *Zeigst du mir deine Fotos?* — Will you show me your photos? |
| *bringen* | *Ich bringe dir einen Tee.* — I'll bring you a tea. |
| *schicken* | *Sie hat ihrer Oma ein Päckchen geschickt.* — She sent her grandma a small parcel. |
| *erklären* | *Kannst du mir das erklären?* — Can you explain that to me? |
| *leihen* | *Leihst du mir dein Fahrrad?* — Will you lend me your bike? |
| *empfehlen* | *Ich empfehle Ihnen den Fisch.* — I recommend the fish (to you). |
| *wünschen* | *Ich wünsche dir viel Glück!* — I wish you lots of luck! |
| *erzählen* | *Erzähl mir alles!* — Tell me everything! |

*empfehlen* changes its vowel: *du empfiehlst, er empfiehlt*, perfect *hat empfohlen*. *leihen* is strong: *hat geliehen*. *leihen* and *borgen* both mean "to lend" with a dative person (*Ich leihe/borge dir das Geld*) and "to borrow" with a reflexive dative (*Ich leihe/borge mir das Geld von meinem Bruder* — I borrow the money from my brother).

## Word order: who comes first?

When a sentence has a dative and an accusative object, the order depends on whether they are nouns or pronouns. There are three rules, and you can check every sentence against them.

1. Two nouns: dative before accusative. Person, then thing.
- *Ich schenke meinem Vater ein Buch.* — I'm giving my father a book.

2. A pronoun comes before a noun, whichever one it is.
- *Ich schenke ihm ein Buch.* — I'm giving him a book.
- *Ich schenke es meinem Vater.* — I'm giving it to my father.

3. Two pronouns: accusative before dative. Thing, then person.
- *Ich schenke es ihm.* — I'm giving it to him.

| | dative noun | dative pronoun |
|---|---|---|
| accusative noun | *Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball.* | *Ich gebe ihm den Ball.* |
| accusative pronoun | *Ich gebe ihn dem Kind.* | *Ich gebe ihn ihm.* |

The same three rules as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Ordering a dative and an accusative object
  accDescr: Look at the two objects. If both are nouns, the dative comes first: Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball. If one is a pronoun and one a noun, the pronoun comes first: Ich gebe ihm den Ball, or Ich gebe ihn dem Kind. If both are pronouns, the accusative comes first: Ich gebe ihn ihm.
  A{"Two objects: nouns or pronouns?"} -- two nouns --> B["Dative first: dem Kind den Ball"]
  A -- "one pronoun, one noun" --> C["Pronoun first: ihm den Ball / ihn dem Kind"]
  A -- two pronouns --> D["Accusative first: ihn ihm"]
```

A memory hook: short words go first. Pronouns are short, so they jump ahead of nouns; and of two pronouns, the accusative (*es, ihn, sie*) is usually the shorter, quick one. Rule 3 also gives you the very common *Gib es mir!* (Give it to me!) and *Ich zeige es dir* (I'll show you).

These rules apply in every sentence type: *Hast du ihm das Geld schon gegeben?* — Have you given him the money yet? *…, weil ich es ihr gezeigt habe.* — … because I showed it to her.

## Reading: Ein Geschenk für Opa

> Nächste Woche hat mein Opa Geburtstag. Er wird achtzig, und wir wollen ihm etwas Besonderes schenken. Aber was? Er hat schon alles. Meine Schwester wollte ihm ein Parfüm kaufen, aber das gefällt ihm bestimmt nicht. Er benutzt seit vierzig Jahren dieselbe Seife.
>
> Dann hatte meine Mutter eine Idee: Opa fehlt das Meer. Früher sind wir jeden Sommer mit ihm an die Ostsee gefahren. Also schenken wir ihm einen Gutschein für ein Wochenende in Warnemünde, und wir fahren alle mit. Ein Freund hat uns ein kleines Hotel empfohlen, direkt am Strand.
>
> Wir haben den Gutschein schön eingepackt und ihn Oma gezeigt. Sie hat gelacht: „Das passt perfekt zu ihm!" Am Sonntag geben wir ihn ihm beim Kaffee. Hoffentlich ist die Überraschung groß. Und ich habe schon eine Frage für Opa: Kannst du mir am Strand deinen Regenschirm leihen? Er nimmt ihn nämlich überallhin mit, auch im Sommer.

In English:

> Next week it's my grandpa's birthday. He's turning eighty, and we want to give him something special. But what? He already has everything. My sister wanted to buy him a perfume, but he certainly won't like that. He has used the same soap for forty years.
>
> Then my mother had an idea: Grandpa misses the sea. In the past we went to the Baltic every summer with him. So we're giving him a voucher for a weekend in Warnemünde, and we're all going with him. A friend recommended a small hotel to us, right on the beach.
>
> We wrapped the voucher nicely and showed it to Grandma. She laughed: "That's perfect for him!" On Sunday we'll give it to him over coffee. Hopefully the surprise will be big. And I've already got a question for Grandpa: can you lend me your umbrella on the beach? You see, he takes it everywhere, even in summer.

Notes: *Er wird achtzig* uses *werden* (to become), which is lesson 8; *etwas Besonderes* (something special) is also explained there. *dieselbe* means "the same", *nämlich* "you see, namely", *überallhin* "everywhere". *ein kleines Hotel* has an adjective ending (module 3). Look at the order: *wir wollen ihm etwas Besonderes schenken* (the short personal pronoun *ihm* first), *Wir haben ... ihn Oma gezeigt* (pronoun before noun), *geben wir ihn ihm* (two pronouns: accusative *ihn* before dative *ihm*).

## Things you give, lend and lose

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *der Gutschein* | voucher, gift card |
| *das Paket / das Päckchen* | parcel / small parcel |
| *die Überraschung*, *überraschen* | surprise, to surprise |
| *der Wunsch* | wish |
| *die Empfehlung* | recommendation |
| *einpacken* | to wrap (up), pack |
| *der Schmuck* | jewellery |
| *die Kette*, *der Ring*, *das Armband* | necklace, ring, bracelet |
| *das Parfüm* | perfume |
| *das Portemonnaie* | wallet, purse |
| *der Regenschirm* | umbrella |
| *die Sonnenbrille* | sunglasses (one pair, singular) |

![Six things, each labeled in German: die Kette (necklace), der Ring, der Regenschirm (umbrella), die Sonnenbrille (sunglasses), das Portemonnaie (wallet) and das Paket (parcel).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*die Sonnenbrille* is singular like *die Brille*: *Wo ist meine Sonnenbrille? Sie gehört mir!* In southern Germany you'll hear *der Geldbeutel* for *das Portemonnaie*; *die Geldbörse* is a more formal word.

## Pronunciation

- *Portemonnaie*: French spelling, German sound: port-mo-NEE, stress on the last syllable.
- *Parfüm*: par-FÜM, stress at the end. *Päckchen*: short *ä*, soft *ch*.
- *gratulieren*: -ie- stressed, gra-tu-LIE-ren. *empfehlen*: emp-FEH-len, long *e*.
- *ihm* and *ihn* sound almost the same; listen for the final *m* or *n*.

## Common mistakes

- Accusative after a dative verb: ~~Ich helfe dich.~~ ~~Ich danke dich.~~ → *Ich helfe dir. Ich danke dir.*
- Using *gefallen* like *like*: ~~Ich gefalle die Kette.~~ → *Die Kette gefällt mir.* (The thing is the subject.)
- Wrong verb form: ~~Die Schuhe gefällt mir.~~ → *Die Schuhe gefallen mir.* (plural subject)
- *fehlen* backwards: "I miss you" is *Du fehlst mir*, not ~~Ich fehle dir~~ (that means "you miss me").
- English order with pronouns: ~~Ich gebe ihm es.~~ → *Ich gebe es ihm.*
- Forgetting the plural *-n*: ~~Ich schenke den Kinder Bücher.~~ → *den Kindern*.
- *gratulieren* with *für*: ~~Ich gratuliere dir für den Geburtstag.~~ → *zum Geburtstag*.

## Key points

- Dative verbs: *helfen, danken, antworten, gratulieren, vertrauen, verzeihen, glauben* + dative person.
- *gefallen, schmecken, gehören, passen, stehen, fehlen, wehtun*: the thing is the subject, the person is dative. *Die Kette gefällt mir. Du fehlst mir.*
- Giving verbs have a dative person and an accusative thing: *Ich schenke meinem Vater ein Buch.*
- Order: two nouns → dative first; pronoun before noun; two pronouns → accusative first (*es ihm*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Describing people; werden; jeder, alle, etwas, niemand
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson closes the module about people by describing them: what they look like, what they are like, and how they change. You will learn the words for appearance and character, the verb *werden* (to become) in all its forms, and a group of small words that talk about people and things in general: *jeder* (every), *alle* (all), *einige* (some), *etwas* (something), *niemand* (nobody) and their friends.

You know many of these words from A1 as single items. Here you put them together to say things like *Jeder kennt ihn*, *Ich habe nichts Neues gehört* and *Mein Bruder ist ruhiger geworden*. That last one has a comparative, which comes in lesson 12; just enjoy it for now.

## What do they look like?

The question is *Wie sieht er/sie aus?* — What does he/she look like? *aussehen* is separable: *Sie sieht ihrer Mutter ähnlich* (she looks like her mother), perfect *hat ausgesehen*. The noun is *das Aussehen* (appearance).

| | German | English |
|---|---|---|
| height and build | *groß, klein, mittelgroß* | tall, short, medium height |
| | *schlank, dünn, dick* | slim, thin, fat |
| face and hair | *das Gesicht* | face |
| | *das Haar / die Haare* | hair |
| | *blond, braun, schwarz, grau, rot* | blond, brown, black, grey, red |
| | *lang, kurz, lockig, glatt* | long, short, curly, straight |
| | *der Bart* | beard |
| | *eine Brille tragen* | to wear glasses |
| overall | *hübsch, schön, hässlich* | pretty, beautiful, ugly |

![Head and shoulders of a man, labeled in German: die Haare (hair), die Brille (glasses), die Nase (nose), der Mund (mouth), der Bart (beard) and das Ohr (ear).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

German usually talks about hair in the plural: *Seine Haare sind kurz.* — His hair is short. *Ihre Haare sind lockig.* — Her hair is curly. The singular *das Haar* is a single hair, or the hair as a whole in a more formal style: *Ihr Haar ist sehr schön.*

Two patterns describe a person:

- *sein* + adjective: *Er ist groß und schlank. Ihre Haare sind blond.*
- *haben* + noun: *Er hat einen Bart. Sie hat eine Brille.* With a describing word before a plural noun you'll hear *Sie hat lange Haare* and *Er hat blaue Augen*. The *-e* is an adjective ending, which module 3 explains; for now learn *lange Haare, kurze Haare, blaue Augen* as chunks.

A word of tact: *dick* is direct and can be rude about a person, as "fat" is in English. *hässlich* (ugly) is fine for things and the weather, but almost never polite about people.

## What are they like?

For character, the question is *Wie ist er/sie?* — What is he/she like? *der Charakter* is someone's character, and *die Eigenschaft* is a quality or trait: *Welche Eigenschaften findest du wichtig?* — Which qualities do you think are important?

| positive | | negative or neutral | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *freundlich* | friendly | *unfreundlich* | unfriendly |
| *nett* | nice, kind | *ernst* | serious |
| *sympathisch* | likeable | *faul* | lazy |
| *lustig* | funny, fun | *neugierig* | curious, nosy |
| *ehrlich* | honest | | |
| *fleißig* | hard-working | | |
| *höflich* | polite | | |
| *klug* | clever | | |

The prefix *un-* makes many adjectives negative, as in English: *freundlich → unfreundlich, höflich → unhöflich, ehrlich → unehrlich, sympathisch → unsympathisch.*

Watch three false friends. *sympathisch* is not "sympathetic" (understanding your problems); it means likeable, someone you take to: *Der neue Nachbar ist sehr sympathisch.* *lustig* means funny or fun, not "lusty". And *neugierig* can be positive (curious, keen to learn) or negative (nosy), depending on the tone.

To say someone is similar to someone else, use *ähnlich* + dative: *Du bist deinem Vater sehr ähnlich.* — You're very like your father. *Die Schwestern sehen sich ähnlich.* — The sisters look alike.

## werden: to become

*werden* is one of the most important verbs in German. In this lesson it means "to become, to get, to turn". It is irregular:

| | *werden* |
|---|---|
| *ich* | *werde* |
| *du* | *wirst* |
| *er / sie / es* | *wird* |
| *wir* | *werden* |
| *ihr* | *werdet* |
| *sie / Sie* | *werden* |

Look at *du wirst* (no *d*) and *er wird* (no extra *-t*). Simple past: *wurde* (*ich wurde, du wurdest, er wurde*); perfect: *ist geworden*, with *sein* because it describes a change.

*werden* has three common uses:

- With an adjective, for a change of state: *Es wird kalt.* — It's getting cold. *Ich werde müde.* — I'm getting tired. *Er ist ganz rot geworden.* — He went bright red.
- With a job or role, without an article: *Ich möchte Krankenpfleger werden.* — I'd like to become a nurse. *Sie ist Mutter geworden.* — She has become a mother.
- With an age, for birthdays: *Meine Tochter wird nächste Woche zehn.* — My daughter turns ten next week.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Three uses of werden, to become
  accDescr: werden means to become. With an adjective it describes a change of state, as in Es wird kalt. With a job or role it takes no article, as in Sie wird Ärztin. With an age it means to turn, as in Er wird zehn. In all three uses the perfect is ist geworden.
  W["werden = to become"] --> A["+ adjective, a change: Es wird kalt."]
  W --> B["+ job or role, no article: Sie wird Ärztin."]
  W --> C["+ age, to turn: Er wird zehn."]
  A --> P["Perfect with sein: ist geworden"]
  B --> P
  C --> P
```

Don't confuse *werden* with *wollen*. *Ich will Ärztin werden* means "I want to become a doctor": *will* is from *wollen* (to want), not English "will". You will also see *werden* used for the future (*Es wird regnen* — It will rain); that is lesson 14.

## jeder, alle, einige

*jeder* means "every, each". It takes the same endings as *der*: *jeder* (masculine), *jede* (feminine), *jedes* (neuter), and it is singular only.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter |
|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | *jeder Tag* | *jede Woche* | *jedes Jahr* |
| accusative | *jeden Tag* | *jede Woche* | *jedes Jahr* |
| dative | *jedem Tag* | *jeder Woche* | *jedem Jahr* |

- *Jedes Kind bekommt ein Geschenk.* — Every child gets a present.
- *Ich jogge jeden Morgen.* — I go jogging every morning. (accusative for time: *jeden Tag, jede Woche*)
- *Er hilft jedem Nachbarn.* — He helps every neighbour.

On its own, *jeder* means "everyone": *Jeder kennt ihn.* — Everyone knows him. *Das kann jeder.* — Anyone can do that.

For the plural, use *alle* (all): *Alle Kinder bekommen ein Geschenk.* *alle* alone means everybody, with a plural verb: *Alle sind da.* — Everyone's here. Compare *Jeder ist da* (singular verb) and *Alle sind da* (plural verb): same meaning, different verb.

*einige* means "some, a few", *viele* "many", *manche* "some (but not all)"; all three are plural: *Einige Kollegen sind krank.* — Some colleagues are ill. *Viele Leute finden ihn sympathisch, manche nicht.*

*dieser* (this) and *welcher* (which) from A1 work the same way as *jeder*: *Welches Kleid meinst du? — Dieses.*

## etwas, nichts, jemand, niemand, alles, man

These **[[indefinite pronouns]]** don't point to a particular person or thing. You know them from A1; here they are together:

| things | | people | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *etwas* | something, anything | *jemand* | someone, anyone |
| *nichts* | nothing | *niemand* | no one, nobody |
| *alles* | everything | *jeder*, *alle* | everyone |
| | | *man* | one, you, people |

*etwas, nichts* and *alles* never change. *jemand* and *niemand* can take case endings, *jemanden* (Akk) and *jemandem* (Dat), especially in writing; in speech the plain form is common: *Ich habe niemand(en) gesehen.* — I didn't see anyone. *Kannst du jemandem helfen?*

In everyday German, *etwas* is often shortened to *was*: *Ich muss dir was erzählen.* — I have to tell you something.

### etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes *(preview)*

After *etwas, nichts, viel* and *wenig*, an adjective becomes a noun: it gets a capital letter and the ending *-es*.

- *Gibt es etwas Neues?* — Is there anything new?
- *Nichts Besonderes.* — Nothing special.
- *Ich wünsche dir alles Gute!* — I wish you all the best! (after *alles*, the ending is *-e*)
- *Ich habe heute viel Interessantes gelernt.* — I learned a lot of interesting things today.

For now, learn these as useful phrases. *Was gibt's Neues? — Nichts Besonderes* is a very common little exchange between friends.

## Reading: Die neue WG

Elif has moved into a *WG* (*Wohngemeinschaft*, a shared flat). She writes to her friend Marie.

> Liebe Marie,
>
> seit einer Woche wohne ich jetzt in der WG, und ich fühle mich schon richtig wohl! Ich muss dir unbedingt von meinen Mitbewohnern erzählen.
>
> Jonas ist Student, sehr groß und dünn, mit langen, lockigen Haaren und einem Bart. Er sieht ein bisschen aus wie ein Musiker, und das ist er auch: Er spielt jeden Abend Gitarre. Er ist lustig und sehr sympathisch, aber leider auch ziemlich faul. Das Bad putzt er nie.
>
> Frau Brandt ist sechzig und die Älteste in der WG. Sie ist klein und schlank, hat graue Haare und trägt eine rote Brille. Am Anfang war sie ein bisschen ernst, aber jetzt ist sie richtig nett. Sie ist ehrlich, höflich und fleißig – sie arbeitet noch, und am Wochenende backt sie für alle Kuchen. Sie wird im Mai Oma! Sie hat sich so gefreut.
>
> Und dann ist da noch Kater Felix. Er gehört niemandem, sagt Jonas, aber er bekommt jeden Morgen etwas von jedem. Er wird langsam richtig dick.
>
> Was gibt's Neues bei dir? Schreib mir bald!
>
> Liebe Grüße
>
> Elif

In English:

> Dear Marie,
>
> I've been living in the shared flat for a week now, and I already feel really at home! I absolutely have to tell you about my flatmates.
>
> Jonas is a student, very tall and thin, with long curly hair and a beard. He looks a bit like a musician, and he is one: he plays the guitar every evening. He's funny and very likeable, but unfortunately also pretty lazy. He never cleans the bathroom.
>
> Mrs Brandt is sixty and the oldest in the flat. She's short and slim, has grey hair and wears red glasses. At first she was a bit serious, but now she's really nice. She's honest, polite and hard-working – she still works, and at the weekend she bakes cake for everyone. She's going to be a grandma in May! She was so pleased.
>
> And then there's Felix the tomcat. He belongs to nobody, Jonas says, but he gets something from everyone every morning. He's slowly getting really fat.
>
> What's new with you? Write soon!
>
> Love,
>
> Elif

Notes: *der Mitbewohner* is a flatmate, *der Kater* a tomcat, *die Älteste* "the oldest one" (lesson 12). *mit langen, lockigen Haaren* and *eine rote Brille* contain adjective endings from module 3. Look at *werden* twice: *Sie wird Oma* (role, no article) and *Er wird dick* (change of state). *Er gehört niemandem* uses the dative verb *gehören*, so *niemand* takes the dative ending; in speech you'll also hear plain *niemand*.

## Pronunciation

- *sympathisch*: süm-PA-tisch; *y* sounds like *ü*. *Charakter*: ka-RAK-ter, with a *k* sound and the stress in the middle; plural *Charaktere*: ka-rak-TE-re.
- *wirst* and *wird*: short *i*; the final *d* in *wird* sounds like *t*.
- *ähnlich*: long *ä*; *höflich*: long *ö*; *fleißig*: *ei* as in "eye", then a sharp *ss* sound.
- *Gesicht*: soft *ch* as in *ich*, ge-SICHT.

## Common mistakes

- ~~Er ist sympathisch mit mir.~~ *sympathisch* means likeable. "He's sympathetic" is *Er hat Verständnis.*
- ~~Ich will morgen kommen~~ for "I will come tomorrow". *will* means "want". Use the present (*Ich komme morgen*) or *werden* (lesson 14).
- ~~Du wirdst~~ / ~~er werdet~~ → *du wirst, er wird.*
- Perfect with *haben*: ~~Er hat dick geworden.~~ → *Er ist dick geworden.*
- An article with a job: ~~Sie wird eine Ärztin.~~ → *Sie wird Ärztin.*
- *jeder* with a plural: ~~jede Leute, jeder Kinder~~ → *alle Leute, jedes Kind.*
- ~~etwas neu~~ / ~~nichts besonders~~ → *etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes* (capital, *-es*).
- Treating hair as one thing: *Seine Haare sind kurz* is more natural than *Sein Haar ist kurz*, and ~~Seine Haare ist kurz~~ is wrong (plural subject, plural verb).

## Key points

- Appearance: *Wie sieht er aus? Er ist groß und schlank, hat kurze Haare und einen Bart.* Character: *Wie ist sie? Sie ist nett, ehrlich und fleißig.*
- *un-* makes the opposite: *unfreundlich, unhöflich.* *sympathisch* = likeable.
- *werden* = to become: *werde, wirst, wird, werden, werdet, werden*; perfect *ist geworden*. With jobs no article; with ages = turn.
- *jeder/jede/jedes* (singular, *der*-endings) vs *alle* (plural).
- *etwas, nichts, alles, jemand, niemand, man* are indefinite pronouns; *etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes, alles Gute*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Imagine, remember, treat yourself: verbs with mir and dir
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module gave you two separate tools. In lesson 5 you met the dative reflexive pronoun with body parts and clothes: *Ich putze mir die Zähne. Ich ziehe mir eine Jacke an.* In lesson 7 you learned verbs with two objects, a dative person and an accusative thing: *Ich kaufe meiner Schwester ein Buch.* This honors lesson puts the two together. What happens when the person who gets the thing is the subject itself? *Ich kaufe mir ein Buch.* — I'm buying myself a book.

That small *mir* is everywhere in everyday German, and some very useful verbs only work with it: *sich etwas vorstellen* (to imagine something), *sich etwas merken* (to remember something), *sich etwas ansehen* (to have a look at something), *sich etwas leisten* (to afford something). You will also learn to tell *Darf ich mich vorstellen?* from *Stell dir vor!*, and to say "each other" clearly with *einander*.

## The pattern: a thing for yourself

A **[[dative reflexive]]** is a reflexive pronoun in the dative case. You use it mainly when the sentence already has an accusative object (the thing) and the person who receives, wants or experiences that thing is the subject. The sentence has the same shape as a giving sentence from lesson 7, only the dative points back to the subject:

| sentence | who gets the book? |
|---|---|
| *Ich kaufe meinem Bruder ein Buch.* | my brother (dative noun) |
| *Ich kaufe ihm ein Buch.* | him (dative pronoun) |
| *Ich kaufe mir ein Buch.* | me, the subject (dative reflexive) |

A verb that always takes the dative, like *helfen*, has a dative reflexive even without a thing: *Ich helfe mir selbst* (I help myself). The "each other" section below comes back to this.

The forms are the ones from lesson 5. Only *ich* and *du* have their own dative forms; all the others look like the accusative:

| subject | dative reflexive | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ich* | *mir* | *Ich mache mir einen Tee.* — I'm making myself a tea. |
| *du* | *dir* | *Nimm dir ein Stück Kuchen!* — Help yourself to a piece of cake! |
| *er / sie / es* | *sich* | *Sie kauft sich ein Fahrrad.* — She's buying herself a bike. |
| *wir* | *uns* | *Wir bestellen uns eine Pizza.* — We're ordering (ourselves) a pizza. |
| *ihr* | *euch* | *Holt euch etwas zu trinken!* — Get yourselves something to drink! |
| *sie / Sie* | *sich* | *Nehmen Sie sich bitte einen Stuhl.* — Please take a chair. |

With *kaufen, machen, bestellen, holen, nehmen* the *mir* is optional: *Ich mache einen Tee* is complete, and *Ich mache mir einen Tee* adds "for myself". Germans use it all the time, so copy it.

## Verbs that need mir and dir

For a second group of verbs the dative reflexive is not optional. The meaning lives in the pronoun, and without it the verb means something else or sounds wrong. Learn them as chunks with *sich (Dat) etwas*:

| verb | English | example |
|---|---|---|
| *sich etwas ansehen* | to have a look at | *Ich sehe mir die Wohnung morgen an.* |
| *sich etwas anschauen* | to take a look at (southern, Austrian) | *Schau dir das an!* |
| *sich etwas merken* | to remember, make a note of | *Merk dir die Adresse!* |
| *sich etwas vorstellen* | to imagine | *Ich kann mir das gut vorstellen.* |
| *sich etwas überlegen* | to think something over | *Ich überlege es mir.* |
| *sich etwas wünschen* | to wish for, want (as a present) | *Was wünschst du dir zum Geburtstag?* |
| *sich etwas leisten* | to afford | *Wir können uns kein Auto leisten.* |
| *sich etwas ausdenken* | to make up, invent | *Die Ausrede hat er sich ausgedacht.* |
| *sich etwas gönnen* | to treat yourself to | *Gönn dir mal eine Pause!* |

*sich etwas ansehen* is looking at something on purpose: a flat before you rent it, a film you sit down to watch. *sich etwas merken* keeps something in your memory (*das Gedächtnis*); someone who often forgets is *vergesslich*. *sich etwas leisten* usually comes with *können*: *Das kann ich mir nicht leisten.*

The "something" can also be a whole clause, which you know from lesson 3 and 4. The dative pronoun stays in the main clause:

- *Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen, dass er das gesagt hat.* — I can't imagine that he said that.
- *Hast du dir gemerkt, wann der Zug fährt?* — Did you remember when the train leaves?
- *Ich überlege mir noch, ob ich mitkomme.* — I'm still thinking about whether I'll come along.

## One verb, two meanings: mich or mir?

Some verbs can take either reflexive pronoun, and the case changes the meaning. The most important is *vorstellen*:

- *Darf ich mich vorstellen? Ich heiße Jonas.* — May I introduce myself? My name is Jonas. (accusative: I present myself)
- *Ich kann mir das nicht vorstellen.* — I can't imagine that. (dative: I put a picture in front of myself)

Without a reflexive pronoun, *vorstellen* means to introduce someone else: *Ich stelle dir meine Freundin vor.* — Let me introduce my girlfriend to you. The rule from lesson 5 decides between *mich* and *mir* every time: is there another accusative object? In *Ich stelle mir das vor*, *das* is the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun must be dative.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing mich or mir with vorstellen
  accDescr: Start with the verb vorstellen and ask whether there is another accusative object. If there is none, use the accusative mich, which means to introduce yourself: Darf ich mich vorstellen? If there is one, such as das or a dass clause, use the dative mir, which means to imagine: Ich kann mir das vorstellen.
  A["vorstellen with a reflexive pronoun"] --> B{"Another accusative object? (das, ein Haus, a dass clause)"}
  B -- no --> C["mich: introduce yourself"]
  B -- yes --> D["mir: imagine"]
  C --> E["Darf ich mich vorstellen?"]
  D --> F["Ich kann mir das vorstellen."]
```

A very common exclamation uses the dative: *Stell dir vor!* — Guess what! (literally "imagine"). Friends start news with it: *Stell dir vor, Lena bekommt ein Baby!*

## Word order and the perfect

Everything you learned about two objects in lesson 7 still works, because the dative reflexive is a pronoun.

1. A pronoun comes before a noun: *Ich sehe mir den Film an.*
2. Two pronouns: accusative before dative: *Ich sehe ihn mir an.* — I'll watch it. *Merk es dir!* — Remember it! *Ich überlege es mir.* — I'll think it over.
3. *das* often moves to position 1 for emphasis, and then the rest follows: *Das kann ich mir nicht vorstellen.*

In the perfect, these verbs use *haben* like every reflexive verb, and the pronoun stays straight after *haben*:

- *Ich habe mir ein neues Handy gekauft.* — I've bought myself a new phone.
- *Hast du dir die Wohnung schon angesehen?* — Have you had a look at the flat yet?
- *Das habe ich mir gemerkt.* — I've made a note of that.

Watch the participles: *angesehen, angeschaut, ausgedacht* (separable, *ge* in the middle; *ausgedacht* is a mixed verb like *denken – gedacht*), *gemerkt, gewünscht, geleistet, gegönnt* (regular), *überlegt* (inseparable *über-*, so no *ge-*) and *vorgestellt*.

### Body parts again: accidents

Lesson 5 used the dative reflexive for washing and brushing. It is the same for accidents to your own body. The body part is the accusative object, so the pronoun is dative:

- *Ich habe mir den Arm gebrochen.* — I broke my arm. (*brechen: bricht, hat gebrochen*)
- *Sie hat sich beim Joggen den Fuß verstaucht.* — She sprained her ankle jogging.

Compare *Ich habe mich verletzt* (I hurt myself: no other object, accusative) with *Ich habe mir die Hand verletzt* (I hurt my hand: dative).

## Each other: sich, einander, gegenseitig

In lesson 5 you saw that plural *uns, euch, sich* can mean "each other": *Wir sehen uns morgen.* This works with dative verbs too: *Wir schreiben uns jeden Tag* (we write to each other every day), *Sie helfen sich* (they help each other).

But *sich* can be ambiguous. *Anna und Ben helfen sich* could mean that each one helps himself or herself, or that they help each other. When context doesn't decide, make "each other" clear with:

- *einander* (each other), which never changes: *Sie helfen einander.*
- *sich gegenseitig* (mutually): *Sie helfen sich gegenseitig.*

![Two panels. On the left, reflexive: Anna and Ben each have an arrow looping back to themselves, with the sentence Sie waschen sich selbst (they wash themselves). On the right, reciprocal: one arrow goes from Anna to Ben and one from Ben to Anna, with the sentence Sie helfen einander (they help each other).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To stress the reflexive meaning instead, add *selbst*: *Sie waschen sich selbst* (they wash themselves). With a preposition, *einander* joins it as one word, which is very common: *miteinander* (with each other), *voneinander* (from or about each other), *aneinander* (of each other): *Wir sprechen jeden Abend miteinander. Die Zwillinge denken oft aneinander.*

### Example 1: Building a sentence step by step

Task: say "I'm having a look at the new flat tomorrow", then replace the flat with a pronoun.

1. The verb is *sich etwas ansehen*: separable, with a dative reflexive and an accusative thing.
2. Subject *ich*, so the dative reflexive is *mir*. The thing is *die neue Wohnung* (accusative feminine, so the article stays *die*; *neue* is a chunk for now).
3. Position 2 is the conjugated verb *sehe*; the prefix *an* goes to the end; the pronoun *mir* comes before the noun object: *Ich sehe mir morgen die neue Wohnung an.* (The time word *morgen* goes after the short pronoun and before the noun.)
4. Replace *die neue Wohnung* with *sie*. Now there are two pronouns, so the accusative comes first: *Ich sehe sie mir morgen an.*

### Example 2: mich or mir?

Task: complete *Ich habe ___ gestern beim Chef vorgestellt* and *Ich kann ___ gut vorstellen, dass er Erfolg hat.*

1. First sentence: is there another accusative object? *beim Chef* is a preposition phrase, not an object, so no. The pronoun is accusative: *mich*. Meaning: I introduced myself to the boss yesterday.
2. Second sentence: the *dass* clause is what I imagine, so it is the object. The pronoun is dative: *mir*. Meaning: I can well imagine that he'll be successful.
3. Check with the meaning: introducing yourself goes with *mich*; imagining goes with *mir*.

## Reading: Ein Wunsch für Lissabon

> Stell dir vor, nächsten Monat werde ich dreißig! Meine Familie fragt mich schon seit Wochen: „Was wünschst du dir?" Ehrlich gesagt wünsche ich mir nichts für die Wohnung. Ich habe genug Sachen. Ich wünsche mir eine Reise nach Lissabon.
>
> Leider kann ich mir im Moment keine teure Reise leisten. Aber dann hatte mein Bruder Tim eine Idee. „Wir schenken dir den Flug zusammen", hat er gesagt, „und das Hotel suchst du dir selbst aus." Ich konnte es mir zuerst gar nicht vorstellen.
>
> Gestern Abend habe ich mir im Internet Fotos von der Stadt angesehen: die alten gelben Straßenbahnen, die Aussicht über die Dächer, die Cafés. Ich habe mir sofort drei Restaurants gemerkt, oder besser: aufgeschrieben, denn ich bin ziemlich vergesslich.
>
> Nur eine Sache muss ich mir noch überlegen: Fahre ich allein oder mit meiner besten Freundin Sara? Wir kennen uns seit dem Kindergarten und verstehen uns super. Wir haben schon oft miteinander Urlaub gemacht. Vielleicht gönne ich mir einfach beides: zuerst drei Tage allein, dann vier Tage mit Sara.

In English:

> Guess what, next month I'm turning thirty! My family has been asking me for weeks: "What would you like (as a present)?" To be honest, I don't want anything for the flat. I have enough things. What I want is a trip to Lisbon.
>
> Unfortunately I can't afford an expensive trip at the moment. But then my brother Tim had an idea. "We'll all give you the flight together," he said, "and you can choose the hotel yourself." At first I couldn't imagine it at all.
>
> Yesterday evening I looked at photos of the city online: the old yellow trams, the view over the roofs, the cafés. I made a note of three restaurants straight away, or rather: wrote them down, because I'm pretty forgetful.
>
> There's just one thing I still have to think about: do I go alone or with my best friend Sara? We've known each other since kindergarten and get on really well. We've often been on holiday together. Maybe I'll simply treat myself to both: three days alone first, then four days with Sara.

Notes: *ehrlich gesagt* means "to be honest", *aussuchen* "to choose", *die Aussicht* "the view"; *teure, gelben, besten* have adjective endings (module 3). The dative reflexives: *wünschst du dir, wünsche ich mir, kann ich mir … leisten, konnte es mir … vorstellen* (two pronouns: *es* before *mir*), *habe ich mir … angesehen, gemerkt, muss ich mir … überlegen, gönne ich mir*. And the reciprocal ones: *wir kennen uns, verstehen uns, miteinander*.

## Pronunciation

- *merken*: short *e*; the *r* after a vowel is soft, close to "MAIR-ken". *Gedächtnis*: ge-DÄCHT-nis, with the soft *ch* of *ich* (after *ä* the *ch* is always soft).
- *einander*: ein-AN-der, stress on the second syllable; *miteinander*: mit-ein-AN-der.
- *sich verstauchen*: ver-STAU-chen; the *ch* after *au* is the throaty *ch* of *Bauch*.
- *gönnen*: short *ö*; don't confuse it with *können* (to be able to).

## Common mistakes

- Accusative instead of dative: ~~Ich kann mich das nicht vorstellen.~~ → *Ich kann mir das nicht vorstellen.* With another object, the pronoun is dative.
- Leaving out the pronoun: ~~Ich merke die Nummer.~~ → *Ich merke mir die Nummer.* ~~Ich kann kein Auto leisten.~~ → *Ich kann mir kein Auto leisten.*
- English order with two pronouns: ~~Ich sehe mir ihn an.~~ → *Ich sehe ihn mir an.* (accusative first)
- Possessive with body parts: ~~Ich habe meinen Arm gebrochen.~~ is understood, but *Ich habe mir den Arm gebrochen* is what Germans say.
- *sein* in the perfect: ~~Ich bin mir das Bein gebrochen.~~ → *Ich habe mir das Bein gebrochen.*
- *einander* with a pronoun: ~~Sie helfen sich einander.~~ → *Sie helfen einander* or *Sie helfen sich gegenseitig*. Use one or the other, not both.

## Key points

- A dative reflexive (*mir, dir, sich, uns, euch, sich*) points back to the subject when the sentence also has an accusative object: *Ich kaufe mir ein Buch.*
- With *kaufen, machen, bestellen, nehmen* it adds "for myself"; with *sich etwas ansehen, merken, vorstellen, überlegen, wünschen, leisten, ausdenken, gönnen* it is part of the verb.
- *mich* or *mir*: no other accusative object → *mich*; another object → *mir*. *Ich stelle mich vor* (introduce) / *Ich stelle mir das vor* (imagine).
- Two pronouns: accusative first: *Ich sehe ihn mir an. Merk es dir!* Perfect with *haben*: *Ich habe mir das gemerkt.*
- "Each other": *uns, euch, sich*; to make it clear, *einander* or *sich gegenseitig*; with a preposition, *miteinander, voneinander*.

lessons.title: Mir ist kalt, du fehlst mir: feelings with the dative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 7 you met the "upside-down" verbs: *Die Kette gefällt mir*, *Du fehlst mir*. The thing or person that causes the feeling is the subject, and the person who has the feeling is in the dative. In German A1 you also learned the chunk *Mir ist kalt* (I'm cold). This honors lesson shows that these are not odd exceptions but one big pattern, and one of the most German things about German: feelings, sensations and impressions very often put the person in the dative.

You will learn to say how you feel physically (*Mir ist schlecht, mir ist schwindlig*), what matters to you (*Das ist mir wichtig*), what occurs to you, strikes you or seems strange to you (*Mir fällt etwas ein, mir fällt etwas auf, das kommt mir komisch vor*), what is easy or hard for you (*Deutsch fällt mir leicht*), and who you feel sorry for (*Du tust mir leid*). The last part of the lesson is about people again: the many shades between *Ich mag dich* and *Ich liebe dich*.

## The experiencer in the dative

The person who feels or experiences something is called the **[[experiencer]]**. In English the experiencer is usually the subject: *I* am cold, *I* like it, *I* miss you. In German the experiencer of many feelings is in the dative, and the subject is either the thing that causes the feeling or nothing at all.

| German | literally | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Mir ist kalt.* | to me is cold | I'm cold. |
| *Die Suppe schmeckt mir.* | the soup tastes good to me | I like the soup. |
| *Du fehlst mir.* | you are missing to me | I miss you. |
| *Das ist mir egal.* | that is all the same to me | I don't mind. |
| *Mir fällt nichts ein.* | to me falls nothing in | I can't think of anything. |

## Mir ist …: how you feel

With adjectives for body sensations, German uses *sein* + dative person, with no subject at all:

| *Mir ist …* | English |
|---|---|
| *Mir ist kalt / warm / heiß.* | I'm cold / warm / hot. |
| *Mir ist schlecht.* | I feel sick. |
| *Mir ist übel.* | I feel sick (a little more formal). |
| *Mir ist schwindlig.* | I feel dizzy. |
| *Mir ist langweilig.* | I'm bored. (informal) |

Change the person by changing the dative: *Ist dir kalt?* (Are you cold?) *Ihm ist schlecht.* (He feels sick.) *Uns ist langweilig.* (We're bored.) The verb is always *ist*, because there is no real subject to agree with.

Why not *Ich bin kalt*? Because with *ich* as the subject, the adjective describes you as a person: *Ich bin kalt* means "I'm a cold person", and *Ich bin langweilig* means "I'm boring". Compare the three ways to talk about boredom: *Ich langweile mich* (lesson 5), *Mir ist langweilig* (everyday, especially with children) and *Der Film ist langweilig* (the film is boring).

### Das ist mir wichtig: what matters to you

A second group has a real subject, usually *das*, *es* or a *dass*-clause, and gives your attitude to it:

- *Das ist mir egal.* — I don't care. / I don't mind.
- *Du bist mir wichtig.* — You matter to me.
- *Ist es dir recht, wenn ich später komme?* — Is it all right with you if I come later?
- *Das ist mir unangenehm.* — That makes me uncomfortable. / I feel awkward about that.
- *Die Wohnung ist uns zu teuer.* — The flat is too expensive for us.

When a *dass*- or *wenn*-clause is the real subject, *es* holds position 1 and the clause follows: *Es ist mir wichtig, dass du ehrlich bist.* — It's important to me that you're honest. If something else comes first, *es* is usually left out: *Mir ist wichtig, dass du ehrlich bist.* (*Mir ist es wichtig, dass …* is also correct.)

## Verbs of feeling and thinking with the dative

Here are the most useful dative verbs of this kind beyond lesson 7. In all of them the thing is the subject and the person is dative, so the verb agrees with the thing.

| verb | example | English |
|---|---|---|
| *leidtun* | *Es tut mir leid.* / *Du tust mir leid.* | I'm sorry. / I feel sorry for you. |
| *einfallen* | *Mir fällt sein Name nicht ein.* | I can't think of his name. |
| *auffallen* | *Mir fällt auf, dass du müde bist.* | I notice that you're tired. |
| *vorkommen* | *Das kommt mir komisch vor.* | That seems strange to me. |
| *leichtfallen* | *Deutsch fällt mir leicht.* | I find German easy. |
| *schwerfallen* | *Die Aussprache fällt mir schwer.* | I find the pronunciation hard. |

*leidtun* is the verb inside the phrase *Es tut mir leid*. With a person as the subject it means pity: *Der arme Hund tut mir leid* (I feel sorry for the poor dog). Be careful: *Du tust mir leid* is sympathy, not an apology. To apologise, say *Es tut mir leid* or *Entschuldigung*.

*einfallen* is for an idea or memory that comes into your head (or doesn't): *Mir ist eine Idee eingefallen.* *auffallen* is for something you notice: *Ist dir etwas aufgefallen?* *vorkommen* gives an impression and usually comes with an adjective: *Die Zeit kommt mir sehr lang vor* (the time seems very long to me). *komisch* means "strange, funny-odd" here, not "comic".

All five *-fallen* and *-kommen* verbs are separable, and because *fallen* and *kommen* form the perfect with *sein*, so do they: *Mir ist nichts eingefallen. Das ist mir gleich aufgefallen. Die Prüfung ist mir leichtgefallen.* *leidtun* takes *haben*: *Es hat mir leidgetan.*

Because the thing is the subject, the verb must be plural for a plural thing:

- *Mir fällt das Wort nicht ein.* — I can't think of the word.
- *Mir fallen die Wörter nicht ein.* — I can't think of the words.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Who is the subject in a feeling sentence?
  accDescr: Start with an English feeling sentence such as I am cold, I like it or I can't think of the word. If it is a body sensation such as cold, hot, sick or dizzy, use Mir ist with no subject: Mir ist kalt. If not, ask whether the verb or phrase is one that takes the dative, such as gefallen, fehlen, einfallen or egal sein. If it is, the thing or person that causes the feeling is the subject and the person who feels is in the dative, with the verb agreeing with the thing: Die Wörter fallen mir nicht ein. Otherwise use a normal verb with ich as the subject, such as Ich mag dich.
  A["English: I am cold / I can't think of the words"] --> B{"A body sensation? (cold, hot, sick, dizzy)"}
  B -- yes --> C["Mir ist + adjective, no subject: Mir ist kalt."]
  B -- no --> D{"A dative verb or phrase? (gefallen, fehlen, einfallen, egal sein)"}
  D -- yes --> E["Thing = subject, person = dative: Die Wörter fallen mir nicht ein."]
  D -- no --> F["Normal verb with ich: Ich mag dich."]
```

### Example 1: Choosing the structure

Task: say "I'm hot", "I don't care" and "I find maths hard".

1. "I'm hot" is a body sensation. No subject, person in the dative, verb *ist*: *Mir ist heiß.* Not *Ich bin heiß*, which in slang means something quite different.
2. "I don't care": the thing I don't care about is the subject, *das*: *Das ist mir egal.*
3. "I find maths hard": *schwerfallen* with the subject *Mathe* (singular): *Mathe fällt mir schwer.* Starting with the person is also fine, as long as the verb still agrees with *Mathe*: *Mir fällt Mathe schwer.*

### Example 2: The perfect, with a plural subject

Task: put *Mir fallen die Namen nicht ein* into the perfect.

1. The subject is *die Namen* (plural), so the auxiliary is plural too.
2. *einfallen* is built on *fallen*, which takes *sein*: so *sind*, not *haben*.
3. The participle of *einfallen* is *eingefallen* (separable, *ge* in the middle), and it goes to the end.
4. Result: *Mir sind die Namen nicht eingefallen.* — I couldn't think of the names. A common slip is ~~Mir habe die Namen nicht eingefallen~~: both the auxiliary and the person are wrong there.

## From Ich mag dich to Ich liebe dich

German has a whole scale for liking people, and the steps matter more than in English, where "I love you" is used quite freely.

![A scale of six ways to say you like someone, from weakest at the bottom to strongest at the top: Ich finde dich nett (I think you're nice), Ich mag dich (I like you), Ich hab dich gern (I'm fond of you), Ich hab dich lieb (I love you, not romantic: family and close friends), Ich bin in dich verliebt (I'm in love with you), Ich liebe dich (I love you: partners, also family).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The scale is a rough guide, not a rule: families and regions differ. Some points that are fairly safe:

- *Ich hab dich lieb* (from *lieb haben*, also written *liebhaben*) is warm but not romantic: parents and children, grandparents, close friends. In messages it is often shortened to *hdl*.
- *Ich liebe dich* is a big sentence, mostly kept for partners and close family. Saying it to a friend can sound odd.
- *Du gefällst mir* usually means that someone attracts you; *Du bist mir sympathisch* means you find them likeable.
- *Du fehlst mir* (lesson 7) is the warm everyday way to say "I miss you".

Relationships have their own phrases: *Wir sind zusammen* (we're a couple), *Sie hat Schluss gemacht* (she broke up), *mein Schwarm* (my crush), and when you are far from home you have *Heimweh* (homesickness).

## Reading: Die erste Woche in Kanada

Jana, 17, is spending a school year in Canada. She writes to her best friend Melli.

> Liebe Melli,
>
> jetzt bin ich schon eine Woche in Halifax. Meine Gastfamilie ist total nett, und ich mag meine Gastschwester Emily sehr. Trotzdem habe ich manchmal Heimweh. Du fehlst mir, und Mama und Papa fehlen mir auch, aber sag ihnen das bitte nicht!
>
> Die Schule ist anders als bei uns. Mir ist sofort aufgefallen, dass hier alle Schüler zum Mittagessen bleiben. Englisch fällt mir zum Glück leicht, aber in Mathe fallen mir oft die Wörter nicht ein. Gestern hat mich der Lehrer etwas gefragt, und mir ist nichts eingefallen. Das war mir so unangenehm!
>
> Und das Wetter! Mir ist ständig kalt, obwohl es erst September ist. Die Leute hier finden es warm. Das kommt mir echt komisch vor.
>
> Am Wochenende fahren wir ans Meer. Emily sagt, auf dem Boot wird einem schnell schlecht. Mir ist das egal, ich will unbedingt Wale sehen!
>
> Ich hab dich lieb! Schreib mir bald.
>
> Deine Jana

In English:

> Dear Melli,
>
> I've been in Halifax for a week now. My host family is really nice, and I like my host sister Emily a lot. Still, I'm sometimes homesick. I miss you, and I miss Mum and Dad too, but please don't tell them that!
>
> School is different from ours. I noticed straight away that all the students stay for lunch here. Luckily I find English easy, but in maths I often can't think of the words. Yesterday the teacher asked me something and my mind went blank. That was so embarrassing!
>
> And the weather! I'm cold all the time, even though it's only September. People here think it's warm. That seems really strange to me.
>
> At the weekend we're going to the sea. Emily says you get seasick quickly on the boat. I don't care, I really want to see whales!
>
> Love you! Write soon.
>
> Your Jana

Notes: *die Gastfamilie* is the host family; *ständig* means "all the time"; *obwohl* (although) sends the verb to the end like *weil*. *wird einem schlecht* uses *werden* (to become) with *einem*, the dative of *man*: "one gets sick". Count the dative experiencers: *fehlst mir, fehlen mir, mir ist aufgefallen, fällt mir leicht, fallen mir nicht ein, mir ist nichts eingefallen, war mir unangenehm, mir ist kalt, kommt mir komisch vor, mir ist egal*.

## Pronunciation

- *schwindlig*: SCHWIND-lich; the final *-ig* sounds like *ich*. *komisch*: KOH-misch, with a long *o*.
- *übel*: long *ü*, Ü-bel. *Heimweh*: HEIM-weh, the *h* in *weh* is silent.
- *leidtun*: the *d* sounds like *t*: LEIT-tuun.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich bin kalt* for "I'm cold": say *Mir ist kalt*. ~~Ich bin langweilig~~ for "I'm bored": *Mir ist langweilig* or *Ich langweile mich*.
- A subject where there is none: ~~Ich ist kalt~~, ~~Mir bin kalt~~ → *Mir ist kalt.*
- The verb agreeing with the person: ~~Mir fällt die Wörter nicht ein~~ → *Mir fallen die Wörter nicht ein.*
- *haben* with the *-fallen* verbs: ~~Mir hat nichts eingefallen~~ → *Mir ist nichts eingefallen.*
- *Du tust mir leid* as an apology: it means "I feel sorry for you". Apologise with *Es tut mir leid*.
- *Ich liebe dich* to a friend: *Ich hab dich lieb* or *Ich mag dich sehr* fits better.

## Key points

- Many feelings put the person who feels (the experiencer) in the dative.
- Body sensations: *Mir ist kalt / warm / heiß / schlecht / übel / schwindlig / langweilig*, no subject, always *ist*.
- Attitudes: *Das ist mir egal / wichtig / recht / unangenehm*; with a clause, *Es ist mir wichtig, dass …*
- Dative verbs: *leidtun, einfallen, auffallen, vorkommen, leichtfallen, schwerfallen*; the thing is the subject and the verb agrees with it; the *-fallen* and *-kommen* verbs take *sein* in the perfect.
- Liking people: *nett finden → mögen → gern haben → lieb haben → verliebt sein → lieben*, as a rough scale.

lessons.title: Adjective endings after ein, kein and mein
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 your adjectives always came after *sein*: *Die Jacke ist neu. Der Rock ist zu kurz.* That's safe, but real descriptions put the adjective right in front of the noun: "a new jacket", "my old shoes", "a short skirt". German can do that too, but then the adjective needs an ending. This module is about those endings, and it's the part of A2 grammar that learners worry about most.

The good news: the endings follow a small, logical system, and you already know its building blocks, because they are the same letters you see on *der, die, das, dem* and *den*. This lesson covers adjectives after *ein*, *kein* and the possessives (*mein, dein, sein, unser …*). Lesson 10 adds *der, dieser* and *welcher*, lesson 11 covers adjectives with no article at all, and lesson 12 compares things (*bigger, the biggest*).

The theme is clothes, because nothing makes you describe things as much as shopping for something to wear.

## Clothes

| der (masculine) | die (feminine) | das (neuter) |
|---|---|---|
| der Rock — skirt | die Kleidung — clothes, clothing | das Kleid — dress |
| der Pullover — jumper, sweater | die Hose — trousers | das Hemd — shirt |
| der Mantel — coat | die Jeans — jeans | das T-Shirt — T-shirt |
| der Anzug — suit | die Bluse — blouse | |
| der Schuh — shoe | die Jacke — jacket | |
| der Stiefel — boot | die Socke — sock | |
| der Hut — hat (with a brim) | die Mütze — woolly hat, cap | |
| der Schal — scarf | die Größe — size | |
| der Handschuh — glove | die Mode — fashion | |
| der Gürtel — belt | | |

A few things to notice:

- *die Hose* is singular in German: one pair of trousers is *eine Hose*. Two pairs are *zwei Hosen*. *die Jeans* can be singular or plural: *Die Jeans ist neu* and *Die Jeans sind neu* are both fine.
- *die Kleidung* is a collective word, like English "clothing": *Ich kaufe neue Kleidung* (I'm buying new clothes).
- A *Hut* has a brim; a *Mütze* is a soft woolly hat or a cap. In winter you wear a *Mütze*.
- *der Handschuh* is literally a "hand shoe".

Here is a winter outfit with the words in place:

![A person dressed for winter. Labels: die Mütze (woolly hat with a bobble) on the head, der Schal (scarf) round the neck, die Jacke (jacket) on the body, die Handschuhe (gloves) on the hands, die Hose (trousers) on the legs and die Stiefel (boots) on the feet.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The verb for wearing clothes is *tragen*, which also means "to carry". It changes its vowel like *fahren*: *ich trage, du trägst, er trägt*. To try something on in a shop, use the separable verb *anprobieren*: *Kann ich die Jacke anprobieren?* (Can I try the jacket on?) Three useful adjectives: *eng* (tight), *bequem* (comfortable) and *modisch* (fashionable). *weit*, which you know as "far", also means "loose, wide" for clothes: *Die Hose ist zu weit.* Patterns are *gestreift* (striped), *kariert* (checked) and *bunt* (colourful).

From lesson 7 you know that *passen* and *stehen* take the dative: *Die Hose passt mir* (the trousers fit me), *Das Kleid steht dir* (the dress suits you).

## Before the noun, an adjective needs an ending

Compare these two sentences:

- *Der Pullover ist warm.* — The jumper is warm.
- *Ich habe einen warmen Pullover.* — I have a warm jumper.

In the first, *warm* comes after *sein* and has no ending. This is a **[[predicative adjective]]**, and it never changes, exactly as in A1. In the second, *warm* stands between the article and the noun. This is an **[[attributive adjective]]**, and in German it always takes an **[[adjective ending]]**: *warmen*.

The ending depends on three things you already think about for articles: the gender of the noun, the case (nominative, accusative, dative), and whether it's singular or plural. It also depends on which article comes before it. That sounds like a lot, but there are only two possible endings in most places: *-e* and *-en*. The other three (*-er, -es, -em*) appear only where they are needed as signals.

## The signal idea

German likes every noun phrase to show its gender and case somewhere, once. Usually the article does this job: *der* shouts "masculine, nominative", *dem* shouts "masculine or neuter, dative". When the article already gives the signal, the adjective can relax and take a plain *-e* or *-en*.

But *ein* is a weak signal. *ein* can be masculine nominative (*ein Rock*), neuter nominative (*ein Kleid*) or neuter accusative (*ein Kleid*). Looking at *ein* alone, you can't tell. So in exactly those three places, the adjective takes over the job and shows the ending that *der* or *das* would have had:

- *der Rock* → *ein kurzer Rock* (the *-er* of *der*)
- *das Kleid* → *ein rotes Kleid* (the *-es* of *das*)

This is the **[[signal ending]]** rule: if the article doesn't show gender and case, the adjective does. Remember it, and the table below stops being something to memorise and becomes something you can work out.

## The endings after ein, kein and mein

*ein, kein* and the possessives *mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr* all take the same endings, so grammars call them **[[ein-words]]**. Here are their adjective endings in the nominative and accusative:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | ein neuer Rock | eine neue Jacke | ein neues Kleid | meine neuen Schuhe |
| accusative | einen neuen Rock | eine neue Jacke | ein neues Kleid | meine neuen Schuhe |

Read the table with the signal idea:

- Masculine nominative: *ein* gives no signal, so the adjective takes *-er* (from *der*).
- Masculine accusative: *einen* already shows the accusative, so the adjective takes *-en*.
- Feminine: *eine* is clear, and the adjective takes *-e* in both cases.
- Neuter: *ein* gives no signal in either case, so the adjective takes *-es* (from *das*) in both.
- Plural: *meine, keine, unsere* are clear, so the adjective takes *-en*. (There is no plural of *ein*; lesson 11 deals with adjectives that have no article.)

Examples:

- *Das ist ein schöner Mantel.* — That's a lovely coat.
- *Ich suche einen warmen Mantel.* — I'm looking for a warm coat.
- *Sie trägt eine gestreifte Bluse.* — She's wearing a striped blouse.
- *Er hat ein kariertes Hemd an.* — He's got a checked shirt on.
- *Das sind keine bequemen Schuhe.* — Those aren't comfortable shoes.
- *Wo sind meine alten Stiefel?* — Where are my old boots?

## The dative: always -en

The dative is the easiest case of all. After *einem, einer, keinem, meinen* and the rest, every adjective ending is *-en*:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dative | einem neuen Rock | einer neuen Jacke | einem neuen Kleid | meinen neuen Schuhen |

The dative article (*einem, einer*) is a strong, clear signal, so the adjective just adds *-en*. Remember that plural nouns add *-n* in the dative too: *mit meinen neuen Schuhen*.

- *Ich gehe mit meiner besten Freundin einkaufen.* — I'm going shopping with my best friend.
- *Was trägst du zu einem schwarzen Anzug?* — What do you wear with a black suit?
- *Er spricht mit einem netten Verkäufer.* — He's talking to a nice sales assistant.

## Putting it together

All the ein-word endings in one table:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | -er | -e | -es | -en |
| accusative | -en | -e | -es | -en |
| dative | -en | -en | -en | -en |

A memory hook: draw a line around the five boxes in the top left (masculine nominative, feminine nominative and accusative, neuter nominative and accusative). Those are the only places that aren't *-en*. Everything else is *-en*.

To choose an ending, ask three questions: What gender is the noun (or is it plural)? What case is it in? Does the article already show that? Then:

1. *Ich kaufe (ein) (blau) Pullover.* — masculine, accusative (object of *kaufen*), and *einen* shows it → *einen blauen Pullover*.
2. *(Ein) (gelb) Mütze liegt auf dem Tisch.* — feminine, nominative → *Eine gelbe Mütze*.
3. *Sie kommt mit (ein) (rot) Kleid.* — neuter, dative (after *mit*) → *mit einem roten Kleid*.

The same questions as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing an adjective ending after ein, kein or mein
  accDescr: Start with an adjective before a noun after an ein-word. If the noun is plural or the case is dative, the ending is -en. Otherwise look at the gender. Feminine nominative or accusative takes -e. Neuter nominative or accusative takes -es. Masculine nominative takes -er, and masculine accusative takes -en.
  A["Adjective after ein, kein, mein …"] --> B{"Plural or dative?"}
  B -- yes --> EN1["-en: meinen neuen Schuhen"]
  B -- no --> C{"Gender of the noun?"}
  C -- feminine --> E["-e: eine neue Jacke"]
  C -- neuter --> ES["-es: ein neues Kleid"]
  C -- masculine --> D{"Nominative or accusative?"}
  D -- nominative --> ER["-er: ein neuer Rock"]
  D -- accusative --> EN2["-en: einen neuen Rock"]
```

## Small spelling changes

- Adjectives ending in *-el* drop the *e* before an ending: *dunkel* → *eine dunkle Hose*.
- Adjectives ending in *-er* after *au* or *eu* drop that *e* too: *teuer* → *ein teures Hemd*.
- Two or more adjectives take the same ending: *ein langer, warmer Mantel*.
- A few colours borrowed from other languages, like *lila* (purple) and *rosa* (pink), take no ending at all in standard German: *ein rosa Hemd*.

## Dialogue: In the shop

> Verkäuferin: Guten Tag! Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
>
> Lena: Ja, gern. Ich suche einen warmen Mantel für den Winter. Mein alter Mantel ist leider kaputt.
>
> Verkäuferin: Welche Größe haben Sie?
>
> Lena: Achtunddreißig, glaube ich. Haben Sie auch einen langen Mantel in Dunkelblau?
>
> Verkäuferin: Ja, hier. Das ist ein sehr modischer Mantel, und er ist aus Wolle. Möchten Sie ihn anprobieren?
>
> Lena: Gern … Hm, er ist ein bisschen eng. Haben Sie ihn eine Nummer größer?
>
> Verkäuferin: Moment … Ja, hier ist er in Größe 40. Der ist bequemer.
>
> Lena: Ja, der passt mir gut. Und haben Sie vielleicht auch einen karierten Schal dazu?
>
> Verkäuferin: Natürlich. Zu einem dunkelblauen Mantel passt ein grauer oder ein roter Schal sehr gut.
>
> Lena: Dann nehme ich den roten. Meine Mutter sagt immer, ich trage zu wenig Farbe!

In English:

> Sales assistant: Hello! Can I help you?
>
> Lena: Yes, please. I'm looking for a warm coat for the winter. Unfortunately my old coat is broken.
>
> Sales assistant: What size are you?
>
> Lena: Thirty-eight, I think. Do you also have a long coat in dark blue?
>
> Sales assistant: Yes, here. This is a very fashionable coat, and it's made of wool. Would you like to try it on?
>
> Lena: I'd love to … Hm, it's a bit tight. Do you have it one size bigger?
>
> Sales assistant: One moment … Yes, here it is in size 40. This one's more comfortable.
>
> Lena: Yes, this one fits me well. And do you maybe have a checked scarf to go with it?
>
> Sales assistant: Of course. A grey or a red scarf goes very well with a dark blue coat.
>
> Lena: Then I'll take the red one. My mother always says I wear too little colour!

Look at the endings: *einen warmen Mantel* and *einen langen Mantel* (masculine accusative, *-en*); *mein alter Mantel* and *ein sehr modischer Mantel* (masculine nominative, *-er*); *zu einem dunkelblauen Mantel* (dative, *-en*); *ein grauer oder ein roter Schal* (subject of *passt*, so nominative, *-er*). *aus Wolle* means "made of wool"; lesson 10 has more materials. *bequemer* and *größer* are comparatives, which lesson 12 explains. *Dann nehme ich den roten* uses the article *den* and leaves out the noun; lesson 10 shows how that works.

## Pronunciation

- *Hemd*: the *d* at the end sounds like *t*: "hemt".
- *Bluse*: the *s* before a vowel is a soft "z": BLOO-ze.
- *Mütze*: short *ü*, then a sharp *tz*: MÜT-se.
- *Jeans* and *T-Shirt* are said roughly as in English, but *T-Shirt* is often "tee-shirt" with a German *t*.
- *anprobieren*: stress on the separable prefix and on *-ie-*: AN-pro-bee-ren.
- Adjective endings are never stressed: *ein KURzer Rock*, *einen WARmen Mantel*. Don't swallow them, though: the ending is the whole point.

## Common mistakes

- *Das ist ein neu Kleid.* — Before a noun, the adjective needs an ending: *ein neues Kleid*.
- *Der Pullover ist warmer.* — After *sein*, no ending: *Der Pullover ist warm.* (*wärmer* means "warmer", which is a comparison.)
- *Ich trage ein schwarzer Pullover.* — The object is accusative: *einen schwarzen Pullover*.
- *Sie hat eine neues Bluse.* — *Bluse* is feminine, so *-e*: *eine neue Bluse*. Check the gender first.
- *mit einem roter Schal* — after any dative article the ending is *-en*: *mit einem roten Schal*.
- *eine dunkele Jacke* — drop the *e* of *-el*: *eine dunkle Jacke*.
- *Ich trage eine Hosen.* — *Hose* is singular in German: *eine Hose*.

## Key points

- An adjective after *sein* never has an ending; an adjective before a noun always does.
- After *ein, kein* and possessives: masculine nominative *-er*, neuter nominative and accusative *-es*, feminine nominative and accusative *-e*, everything else *-en*.
- Every adjective in the dative and every plural after *keine/meine* ends in *-en*.
- The signal rule: when *ein* doesn't show the gender, the adjective shows it with the ending of *der* or *das*.
- *dunkel → dunkle*, *teuer → teure*; *lila* and *rosa* never change.
- *tragen* (du trägst, er trägt) means to wear and to carry; *anprobieren* is separable.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Adjective endings after der, dieser and welcher
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you put adjectives after *ein, kein* and *mein*: *ein warmer Mantel, meine neuen Schuhe*. Now you'll put them after *der, die, das* and the words that behave like them: *dieser* (this), *welcher* (which), *jeder* (every) and *alle* (all). This table is the easiest of the three, because after these articles the adjective almost never has to signal anything.

You'll also learn to leave the noun out (*Welchen nehmen Sie? – Den blauen.*), to say what something is made of, and to deal with a department store: finding the right floor, paying, and taking something back.

## In the department store

A *Kaufhaus* is a big shop with many *Abteilungen* (departments) on several floors. The ground floor is *das Erdgeschoss*; the floors above it are *der erste Stock, der zweite Stock* and so on, as you know from A1. You go up on the *Rolltreppe* (escalator) or in the *Aufzug* (lift).

| German | English |
|---|---|
| das Kaufhaus | department store |
| die Abteilung | department |
| das Erdgeschoss | ground floor |
| die Rolltreppe | escalator |
| der Aufzug | lift, elevator |
| die Umkleidekabine | changing room |
| der Kunde / die Kundin | customer |
| die Marke | brand |
| der Rabatt | discount |
| reduziert | reduced, on sale |
| günstig | good value, cheap |
| die Tüte | (paper or plastic) bag |
| die Quittung | receipt |
| der Kassenzettel | till receipt |

*günstig* is the polite, positive way to say something is cheap; *billig* (A1) can sound like "cheap and nasty". *Die Jacke ist sehr günstig* is a compliment; *Die Jacke sieht billig aus* is not.

The picture shows a small *Kaufhaus* in cross-section: the *Aufzug* on the left goes to every floor, and the *Rolltreppe* takes you up from the *Erdgeschoss* to the first floor (*der erste Stock*) and on to the second (*der zweite Stock*).

![A department store in cross-section with three floors: Erdgeschoss at the bottom, 1. Stock and 2. Stock above. Labels: der Aufzug (a lift shaft on the left, with the lift car on the ground floor), die Rolltreppe (an escalator from the ground floor to the first floor, and another up to the second), die Umkleidekabine (a changing room with a curtain on the first floor) and die Kasse (the till, a counter with a cash register on the ground floor). A clothes rail stands on the second floor.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At the till you'll hear *Brauchen Sie eine Tüte?* (Do you need a bag?). Bags cost extra, so many people bring their own.

## Materials: aus + dative

To say what something is made of, use *aus* (from, out of) and the material with no article:

| | |
|---|---|
| das Material — material | das Leder — leather |
| die Baumwolle — cotton | das Holz — wood |
| die Wolle — wool | das Metall — metal |
| das Glas — glass | das Plastik — plastic |

- *Die Tasche ist aus Leder.* — The bag is made of leather.
- *Ich suche einen Pullover aus Baumwolle.* — I'm looking for a cotton jumper.
- *Das Spielzeug ist aus Holz, nicht aus Plastik.* — The toy is made of wood, not plastic.

*Baumwolle* is literally "tree wool". *das Glas* is both the material and a drinking glass: *ein Glas Wasser*.

## The endings after der-words

*der, die, das* and the words that take the same endings — *dieser, jeder, welcher* and, in the plural, *alle* — are called **[[der-words]]**. They show gender and case very clearly: in *dieser Rock* the article can only be masculine nominative, and *diesem* can only be masculine or neuter dative. Because the article always gives the signal, the adjective never needs to: it takes only *-e* or *-en*.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | der neue Rock | die neue Jacke | das neue Kleid | die neuen Schuhe |
| accusative | den neuen Rock | die neue Jacke | das neue Kleid | die neuen Schuhe |
| dative | dem neuen Rock | der neuen Jacke | dem neuen Kleid | den neuen Schuhen |

Look at the five *-e* boxes: masculine nominative, feminine nominative and accusative, neuter nominative and accusative. They are exactly the five boxes that weren't *-en* in lesson 9. Everywhere else, the ending is *-en* again. So the shape is the same in both tables; only the five special boxes differ:

| | masculine nom. | neuter nom./acc. | feminine nom./acc. |
|---|---|---|---|
| after ein-words | ein neuer Rock | ein neues Kleid | eine neue Jacke |
| after der-words | der neue Rock | das neue Kleid | die neue Jacke |

After *ein* the adjective has to show *-er* or *-es*; after *der* and *das* it doesn't, because the article already did.

Examples:

- *Der blaue Pullover ist reduziert.* — The blue jumper is reduced.
- *Ich nehme die schwarze Hose.* — I'll take the black trousers.
- *Kann ich dieses gestreifte Hemd umtauschen?* — Can I exchange this striped shirt?
- *Wir fahren mit dem neuen Aufzug.* — We're taking the new lift.
- *Die Umkleidekabine ist neben der großen Rolltreppe.* — The changing room is next to the big escalator.
- *Jeder neue Kunde bekommt zehn Prozent Rabatt.* — Every new customer gets ten per cent off.
- *Alle reduzierten Jacken sind im zweiten Stock.* — All the reduced jackets are on the second floor.

Note *im zweiten Stock*: *im* is *in dem*, so *zweiten* has the dative ending *-en*. Ordinal numbers like *erste, zweite, dritte* take endings just like any other adjective.

## Asking which one: welcher

*welcher* (which) takes the same endings as *der*: *welcher Rock, welche Jacke, welches Kleid, welche Schuhe*, accusative *welchen Rock*. Any adjective after it takes the der-word endings:

- *Welche rote Jacke meinst du?* — Which red jacket do you mean?
- *In welchem großen Kaufhaus warst du?* — Which big department store were you in?

## Leaving out the noun

When it's clear what you're talking about, German simply drops the noun and keeps the article and the adjective, with the ending unchanged. English adds "one":

- *Welchen Pullover nehmen Sie? – Den blauen.* — Which jumper are you taking? – The blue one.
- *Ich habe zwei Hemden. Das weiße ist neu.* — I have two shirts. The white one is new.
- *Gefällt dir die kurze Hose? – Nein, die lange gefällt mir besser.* — Do you like the short trousers? – No, I like the long ones better.

German goes one step further and makes some adjectives into real nouns, written with a capital letter. These are **[[adjectival nouns]]**: they keep their adjective endings.

- *der Kleine / die Kleine* — the little one (a small boy or girl)
- *das Neue* — the new thing, what's new: *Das Neue an dem Laden ist …* — What's new about the shop is …
- *der Bekannte / ein Bekannter* — an acquaintance (you met this in lesson 6)

At A2 you only need to recognise these. Notice that *der Bekannte* but *ein Bekannter* follow the two tables you know.

## Taking things back

Shops in Germany don't have to take back goods that are fine, but most will exchange them if you have the receipt. If something is faulty, you have a right to complain.

| German | English |
|---|---|
| umtauschen | to exchange (for something else) |
| zurückgeben | to give back, to return |
| reklamieren | to complain about (a faulty product) |
| die Garantie | guarantee, warranty |

*umtauschen* and *zurückgeben* are separable: *Ich tausche die Hose um. Ich gebe die Schuhe zurück.* *zurückgeben* has the stem change of *geben*: *er gibt zurück*. *reklamieren* is not separable and has no *ge-* in the perfect: *Ich habe den Toaster reklamiert.*

Which word you need depends on the situation:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Taking something back to a shop in Germany
  accDescr: If the product is faulty, you reklamieren it: by law the seller must put it right (the legal warranty, usually two years in Germany), whether or not there is also a guarantee. If it is not faulty, the shop does not have to take it back, but with the receipt most shops will let you umtauschen it for something else or zurückgeben it for your money. Without a receipt it is usually hard.
  A["You want to take something back"] --> B{"Is it faulty?"}
  B -- yes --> R["reklamieren: the legal warranty covers it"]
  B -- no --> C{"Do you have the Kassenzettel?"}
  C -- yes --> U["Most shops let you umtauschen or zurückgeben"]
  C -- no --> H["Usually difficult: the shop decides"]
```

## Dialogue: At the customer service desk

> Kundin: Guten Tag. Ich möchte diese graue Jacke umtauschen. Ich habe sie letzte Woche hier gekauft.
>
> Verkäufer: Haben Sie den Kassenzettel noch?
>
> Kundin: Ja, hier ist die Quittung.
>
> Verkäufer: Danke. Was ist denn das Problem mit der Jacke?
>
> Kundin: Der linke Ärmel ist kaputt, sehen Sie? Und die Jacke war nicht billig. Das ist doch eine teure Marke!
>
> Verkäufer: Oh, das tut mir leid. Auf die Jacke haben Sie natürlich Garantie. Möchten Sie das Geld zurück oder eine neue Jacke?
>
> Kundin: Lieber eine neue. Aber haben Sie die Jacke auch in Dunkelgrün? Die graue gefällt meinem Mann nicht so gut.
>
> Verkäufer: Die dunkelgrünen Jacken hängen in der Damenabteilung im ersten Stock, direkt neben der Rolltreppe. Und heute sind alle grünen Modelle reduziert.
>
> Kundin: Super! Dann bekomme ich vielleicht sogar Geld zurück.

In English:

> Customer: Hello. I'd like to exchange this grey jacket. I bought it here last week.
>
> Sales assistant: Do you still have the receipt?
>
> Customer: Yes, here's the receipt.
>
> Sales assistant: Thanks. So what's the problem with the jacket?
>
> Customer: The left sleeve is broken, see? And the jacket wasn't cheap. It's an expensive brand!
>
> Sales assistant: Oh, I'm sorry. The jacket is under guarantee, of course. Would you like your money back or a new jacket?
>
> Customer: A new one, please. But do you have the jacket in dark green as well? My husband doesn't like the grey one so much.
>
> Sales assistant: The dark green jackets are hanging in the women's department on the first floor, right next to the escalator. And today all the green styles are reduced.
>
> Customer: Great! Then maybe I'll even get some money back.

Find the der-word endings: *diese graue Jacke* (feminine accusative, *-e*), *der linke Ärmel* (masculine nominative, *-e*), *die graue* with no noun, *die dunkelgrünen Jacken* (plural, *-en*), *im ersten Stock* (dative, *-en*), *alle grünen Modelle* (plural, *-en*). Compare *eine teure Marke* and *eine neue Jacke*, which follow lesson 9. (*der Ärmel* = sleeve, *die Damenabteilung* = women's department, *das Modell* = model, style, *sogar* = even.)

## Pronunciation

- *Erdgeschoss*: stress on the first part, ERD-ge-schoss; the *o* is short.
- *Rolltreppe*: ROLL-trep-pe, with two short vowels.
- *Umkleidekabine*: UM-klei-de-ka-bi-ne; *ei* as in English "eye".
- *Garantie*: stress on the last syllable, ga-ran-TIE, with a long *ie*.
- *reklamieren*: re-kla-MIE-ren, like all *-ieren* verbs.
- *Leder* has a long *e*: LAY-der. *Wolle* has a short *o*.

## Common mistakes

- *der neuer Rock* — after *der*, no *-er*: *der neue Rock*. The *-er* belongs after *ein*.
- *das schwarzes Kleid* — after *das*, just *-e*: *das schwarze Kleid*.
- *die neue Schuhe* — in the plural after *die*, the ending is *-en*: *die neuen Schuhe*.
- *Ich nehme den blau.* — Keep the ending when you drop the noun: *den blauen*.
- *eine Tasche von Leder* — for materials, use *aus*: *eine Tasche aus Leder*.
- *Ich tausche um die Hose.* — The prefix goes to the end: *Ich tausche die Hose um.*
- *Ich habe den Mantel gereklamiert.* — No *ge-* with *-ieren* verbs: *reklamiert*.

## Key points

- After *der, dieser, jeder, welcher* and *alle*, the adjective ends in *-e* in the five "special" boxes (masculine nominative, feminine and neuter nominative and accusative) and *-en* everywhere else.
- The five special boxes are the same as in lesson 9: there they show *-er/-e/-es*, here only *-e*.
- When the noun is clear, drop it and keep the ending: *Den blauen, bitte.*
- Adjectival nouns keep adjective endings: *der Kleine, ein Bekannter, das Neue*.
- Materials: *aus* + material, no article: *aus Holz, aus Baumwolle*.
- *umtauschen* and *zurückgeben* are separable; *reklamieren* has no *ge-*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Adjectives without an article; food and cooking
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for
