You can now put an adjective after *ein* (lesson 9) and after *der* (lesson 10). But a lot of the time there's no article at all. You say "fresh bread", "hot water", "with cold milk", not "a fresh bread". In German that's when the adjective has the most work to do: with no article to show gender and case, the adjective shows it alone.

This lesson teaches that third and last table, shows how *viele, einige* and *ein paar* fit in, and then puts all three tables side by side. The theme is food: cooking at home, following a recipe and eating out.

## In the kitchen

| German | English |
|---|---|
| das Rezept | recipe |
| die Zutat | ingredient |
| der Topf | pot, saucepan |
| die Pfanne | frying pan |
| der Teller | plate |
| die Tasse | cup |
| der Löffel | spoon |
| die Gabel | fork |
| das Messer | knife |
| das Salz | salt |
| der Pfeffer | pepper |
| der Zucker | sugar |
| das Öl | oil |

![Kitchen things on a worktop, from left to right: der Topf (a saucepan with a lid and two handles), die Pfanne (a frying pan with a long handle), der Teller (a plate), and standing upright die Gabel (fork), das Messer (knife) and der Löffel (spoon).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The verbs of cooking are mostly regular, but *braten*, *backen* and *schneiden* change their vowel or have an irregular perfect:

| | present (du / er) | perfect |
|---|---|---|
| braten — to fry, to roast | du brätst, er brät | hat gebraten |
| backen — to bake | du backst, er backt (also bäckst, bäckt) | hat gebacken |
| schneiden — to cut | du schneidest, er schneidet | hat geschnitten |
| schälen — to peel | regular | hat geschält |
| probieren — to taste, to try | regular | hat probiert |

*probieren* is "try" in the sense of tasting: *Probier mal die Suppe!* (Try the soup!). For clothes you use *anprobieren* from lesson 9. Two more cooking verbs are worth recognising: *mischen* (to mix) and *rühren* (to stir).

Food is *süß* (sweet), *sauer* (sour), *salzig* (salty) or *scharf* (spicy, hot). *scharf* also means "sharp", so *ein scharfes Messer* is a sharp knife and *eine scharfe Soße* a spicy sauce. *heiß* is only about temperature. *frisch* means fresh.

## Endings with no article

When there's no article, the adjective takes the ending that *der, die, das* would have had. It's the signal rule from lesson 9 at full strength: nothing else is there to show the case, so the adjective shows it.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | frischer Fisch | frische Milch | frisches Brot | frische Eier |
| accusative | frischen Fisch | frische Milch | frisches Brot | frische Eier |
| dative | frischem Fisch | frischer Milch | frischem Brot | frischen Eiern |

Compare each box with the definite article:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | der → -er | die → -e | das → -es | die → -e |
| accusative | den → -en | die → -e | das → -es | die → -e |
| dative | dem → -em | der → -er | dem → -em | den → -en |

So you don't need to learn a new table: you need the last letters of the article you already know. A memory hook: *der* gives *-er*, *das* gives *-es*, *dem* gives *-em*, *die* gives *-e*. The one place where English speakers slip is the plural: after *die* it's *-en* (*die frischen Eier*), but with no article it's *-e* (*frische Eier*).

Examples:

- *Frischer Fisch schmeckt am besten.* — Fresh fish tastes best.
- *Ich trinke gern kaltes Wasser.* — I like drinking cold water.
- *Wir brauchen braunen Zucker.* — We need brown sugar.
- *Sie trinkt Kaffee mit warmer Milch.* — She drinks coffee with warm milk.
- *Brot mit frischem Käse ist lecker.* — Bread with fresh cheese is delicious.
- *Kleine Kinder essen nicht gern scharfe Sachen.* — Small children don't like eating spicy things.

This happens most with mass nouns (*Wasser, Zucker, Milch*), with plurals, after *mit* and *aus*, and in signs and menus: *Frische Brötchen! Heißer Kaffee!*

## Numbers, viele, einige and ein paar

Numbers have no endings and don't count as an article, so the adjective after them takes the no-article ending:

- *zwei große Töpfe* — two big pots
- *mit drei kleinen Löffeln* — with three small spoons (dative plural, *-en*)

The same goes for *viele* (many), *einige* (some, a few) and *wenige* (few). They take the same endings as the adjective, and so does every adjective after them:

- *viele frische Zutaten* — lots of fresh ingredients
- *Einige alte Rezepte sind sehr einfach.* — Some old recipes are very simple.
- *mit vielen guten Freunden* — with lots of good friends

*ein paar* (a few, a couple of) never changes, and the adjective after it takes the no-article ending: *ein paar frische Eier*, *mit ein paar guten Ideen*.

Be careful with *alle*: it's a der-word, so the adjective after it ends in *-en*: *alle frischen Eier*. And *etwas* (some) and *viel* (a lot of) before a singular mass noun don't change either, so the adjective shows the ending: *mit etwas warmer Butter*, *viel kaltes Wasser*.

## A recipe: Grandma's pancakes

German recipes use the polite imperative (*Schneiden Sie …*) or, more often, just the infinitive at the end (*Die Eier aufschlagen*). Here is a family recipe written as a note.

> Omas Pfannkuchen (für 4 Personen)
>
> Zutaten: 250 Gramm Mehl, 3 frische Eier, ein halber Liter kalte Milch, eine Prise Salz, ein Löffel Zucker, etwas Öl für die Pfanne.
>
> Mehl, Salz und Zucker in eine große Schüssel geben. Die Eier und die Milch dazugeben und alles gut mischen. Den Teig zehn Minuten stehen lassen.
>
> Etwas Öl in einer schweren Pfanne heiß machen. Eine kleine Kelle Teig in die Pfanne geben und den Pfannkuchen auf beiden Seiten goldbraun braten.
>
> Mit frischem Obst oder mit Zucker und Zimt servieren. Mein Opa isst sie lieber herzhaft, mit gebratenem Speck. Probieren Sie beides!

In English:

> Grandma's pancakes (serves 4)
>
> Ingredients: 250 grams of flour, 3 fresh eggs, half a litre of cold milk, a pinch of salt, a spoonful of sugar, a little oil for the pan.
>
> Put the flour, salt and sugar in a large bowl. Add the eggs and the milk and mix everything well. Leave the batter to stand for ten minutes.
>
> Heat a little oil in a heavy frying pan. Put a small ladle of batter in the pan and fry the pancake on both sides until golden brown.
>
> Serve with fresh fruit or with sugar and cinnamon. My grandad prefers them savoury, with fried bacon. Try both!

Find the no-article endings: *frische Eier* (plural), *kalte Milch* (feminine), *mit frischem Obst* and *mit gebratenem Speck* (dative, *-em*). Compare *in einer schweren Pfanne* (lesson 9) and *eine große Schüssel*. *ein halber Liter* shows that *halb* is an adjective too. (*das Mehl* = flour, *die Schüssel* = bowl, *der Teig* = batter, dough, *die Kelle* = ladle, *der Zimt* = cinnamon, *der Speck* = bacon, *eine Prise* = a pinch, *herzhaft* = savoury, not sweet.)

## In a restaurant

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Speisekarte | menu |
| die Vorspeise | starter |
| die Hauptspeise | main course |
| der Nachtisch | dessert (also *die Nachspeise*) |
| bestellen | to order |
| die Rechnung | bill |
| das Trinkgeld | tip |

*bestellen* is inseparable: *Ich habe eine Suppe bestellt.* When you want to pay, say *Die Rechnung, bitte* or *Wir möchten bitte zahlen*. The waiter often asks *Zusammen oder getrennt?* (Together or separately?). In Germany you tip about five to ten per cent, and you say the total out loud as you pay: if the bill is 27 Euro, you give 30 and say *Dreißig, bitte* or *Stimmt so* (keep the change).

> Kellner: Haben Sie schon gewählt?
>
> Jana: Ja. Als Vorspeise nehme ich die Tomatensuppe. Ist sie scharf?
>
> Kellner: Nein, nur ein bisschen Pfeffer. Und als Hauptspeise?
>
> Jana: Den gebratenen Fisch mit grünem Salat, bitte.
>
> Tom: Für mich das Schnitzel mit Pommes. Und ein großes Glas kaltes Wasser, bitte.
>
> Kellner: Gern. Möchten Sie danach auch einen Nachtisch?
>
> Tom: Vielleicht später. Der Apfelkuchen mit warmer Vanillesoße klingt gut!

In English:

> Waiter: Have you decided?
>
> Jana: Yes. As a starter I'll have the tomato soup. Is it spicy?
>
> Waiter: No, just a bit of pepper. And for the main course?
>
> Jana: The fried fish with green salad, please.
>
> Tom: For me the schnitzel with chips. And a large glass of cold water, please.
>
> Waiter: Certainly. Would you like a dessert afterwards too?
>
> Tom: Maybe later. The apple cake with warm vanilla sauce sounds good!

*ein großes Glas kaltes Wasser*: *großes* follows *ein* (neuter, *-es*), and *kaltes Wasser* has no article (also *-es*). *mit grünem Salat* and *mit warmer Vanillesoße* are dative with no article. *den gebratenen Fisch* follows *den*. *gebraten* is the participle of *braten*, used as an adjective: participles take endings like any other adjective.

## All three tables side by side

| | masc. nom. | masc. acc. | fem. nom./acc. | neut. nom./acc. | dative (all) | plural nom./acc. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| after der-words | der gute | den guten | die gute | das gute | dem/der guten | die guten |
| after ein-words | ein guter | einen guten | eine gute | ein gutes | einem/einer guten | keine guten |
| no article | guter | guten | gute | gutes | gutem / guter, plural guten | gute |

Three questions decide every ending: Is there an article? Does the article show gender and case? If not, which letter would *der/die/das* end in? If the article shows it, the adjective ends in *-e* or *-en*. If the article doesn't, or there is none, the adjective shows it.

As a chart (the "five special boxes" are masculine nominative and feminine and neuter nominative and accusative):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which adjective ending? All three tables in one chart
  accDescr: If the adjective is not before a noun, it has no ending. If it is before a noun, look at the word in front. After a der-word, use -e in the five special boxes and -en everywhere else. After an ein-word, use -er, -e or -es in the five special boxes and -en everywhere else. With no article, or after a number, ein paar, viele or einige, use the ending of der, die, das, dem or den, except -e in the plural nominative and accusative.
  A{"Is the adjective before a noun?"} -- no --> N["No ending: Der Fisch ist frisch."]
  A -- yes --> B{"What comes before it?"}
  B -- "der, dieser, alle" --> D{"One of the five special boxes?"}
  D -- yes --> D1["-e: der frische Fisch"]
  D -- no --> D2["-en: mit dem frischen Fisch"]
  B -- "ein, kein, mein" --> E{"One of the five special boxes?"}
  E -- yes --> E1["-er / -e / -es: ein frischer Fisch"]
  E -- no --> E2["-en: mit einem frischen Fisch"]
  B -- "nothing, a number, viele" --> F["Ending of der/die/das/dem: frischer Fisch, mit frischem Fisch"]
```

## Pronunciation

- *Löffel*: short *ö*, double *f*: LÖF-fel.
- *Zutat*: stress on the first part, TSOO-taht; *z* is always "ts".
- *Pfanne, Pfeffer*: say the *p* and the *f* together, a quick "pf". Don't drop the *p*.
- *Messer, Teller*: short *e*, as in English "mess" and "tell".
- *Rechnung*: the *ch* is the soft *ch* of *ich*.
- *Öl*: a long *ö*, made by saying "ay" with rounded lips.

## Common mistakes

- *mit warm Milch* — with no article the adjective must show the case: *mit warmer Milch*.
- *Ich trinke kalten Wasser.* — *Wasser* is neuter, and neuter accusative takes *-es*: *kaltes Wasser*.
- *frischen Eier* (as subject or object) — plural with no article is *-e*: *frische Eier*. It's *-en* only after *die* or in the dative.
- *alle frische Zutaten* — *alle* is a der-word: *alle frischen Zutaten*.
- *Die Suppe ist heiß* when you mean spicy — say *scharf*.
- *Ich habe die Kartoffeln geschneidet.* — The perfect of *schneiden* is *geschnitten*.
- *Er bratet den Fisch.* — *braten* has a vowel change: *er brät*.

## Key points

- With no article, the adjective takes the last letter(s) of *der/die/das/dem/den*: *-er, -e, -es, -em, -en*.
- Plural with no article: *-e* in the nominative and accusative, *-en* in the dative.
- Numbers and *ein paar* don't change; *viele, einige, wenige* take the same endings as the adjective after them; *alle* is a der-word.
- *braten* (er brät), *backen* (hat gebacken), *schneiden* (hat geschnitten).
- *scharf* = spicy or sharp; *probieren* = to taste; *Die Rechnung, bitte* and *Stimmt so*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Comparing: bigger, the biggest
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Describing something often means comparing it: the city is louder than the village, the lake is deeper than the river, this is the most beautiful valley in the area. In this lesson you'll learn the **[[comparative]]** (*größer* — bigger) and the **[[superlative]]** (*am größten, der größte* — the biggest), the short adjectives that add an umlaut, the irregular ones, and the two little words you need to compare: *als* (than) and *wie* (as).

In A1 you met one comparison already: *gern, lieber, am liebsten* (to like, to prefer, to like most). Now you'll see that it belongs to a pattern. And because comparatives and superlatives in front of a noun take the adjective endings from lessons 9 to 11, this lesson is also a review of the whole module.

The theme is town and country: landscapes, regions and where people prefer to live.

## Town and country

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Großstadt | big city |
| die Hauptstadt | capital (city) |
| der Einwohner | inhabitant, resident |
| die Gegend | area, region |
| die Umgebung | surroundings, the area around a place |
| die Landschaft | landscape, countryside |
| die Grenze | border |
| der Wald | forest, woods |
| die Wiese | meadow |
| das Feld | field |
| der Bauernhof | farm |
| der Hügel | hill |
| das Tal | valley |
| das Ufer | bank, shore |
| die Küste | coast |

The points of the compass are all masculine: *der Norden, der Süden, der Osten, der Westen*. "In the north" is *im Norden*; "to the north" is *nach Norden*. Compound words are common: *Norddeutschland* (northern Germany), *Süddeutschland*, *die Nordsee*.

*die Gegend* and *die Umgebung* are close. *die Gegend* is any area or region: *Das ist eine schöne Gegend.* *die Umgebung* is what surrounds a particular place: *Hamburg und Umgebung* (Hamburg and the surrounding area). *das Ufer* is the edge of a river or lake; the edge of the sea is *die Küste* or, where you swim, *der Strand* (A1).

![A landscape. On the left, der Hügel (a hill) with der Wald (a group of trees) on it, and die Wiese (a meadow with flowers) in front. In the middle, der Fluss (a river) runs through the valley, and das Ufer is its bank. On the right, der Bauernhof (a farmhouse and a barn), das Feld (a striped field) in front, and der Berg (a mountain with snow on top) behind.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

New adjectives for describing places: *hoch* (high, tall), *tief* (deep), *breit* (wide, broad), *schmal* (narrow), *flach* (flat, shallow), *gefährlich* (dangerous), *sauber* (clean) and *schmutzig* (dirty). *hoch* loses its *c* before an ending: *ein hoher Berg*, *die hohen Häuser*.

## The comparative: -er

To say "bigger", "older", "more interesting", German adds *-er* to the adjective. There is never a separate word for "more", even with long adjectives:

| adjective | comparative |
|---|---|
| klein — small | kleiner — smaller |
| schön — beautiful | schöner — more beautiful |
| schnell — fast | schneller — faster |
| interessant — interesting | interessanter — more interesting |
| gefährlich — dangerous | gefährlicher — more dangerous |

The thing you compare with comes after *als* (than):

- *Das Dorf ist ruhiger als die Stadt.* — The village is quieter than the town.
- *Der Wald ist schöner als der Park.* — The woods are more beautiful than the park.
- *Mein Bruder fährt schneller als ich.* — My brother drives faster than I do.

Adjectives in *-el* and *-er* drop their *e*: *dunkel → dunkler*, *teuer → teurer*.

## Short adjectives add an umlaut

Many common one-syllable adjectives with *a, o* or *u* add an **[[umlaut]]** in the comparative and superlative:

| adjective | comparative | superlative |
|---|---|---|
| alt | älter | am ältesten |
| jung | jünger | am jüngsten |
| groß | größer | am größten |
| kurz | kürzer | am kürzesten |
| lang | länger | am längsten |
| warm | wärmer | am wärmsten |
| kalt | kälter | am kältesten |
| arm — poor | ärmer | am ärmsten |
| oft | öfter | am häufigsten (*am öftesten* is rare) |

Not every short adjective does it: *flach → flacher*, *klar → klarer*, *voll → voller*. Adjectives with *au* never do (*laut → lauter*), and neither do longer ones (*sauber → sauberer*). If you aren't sure, the dictionary shows it, and the vocabulary notes in this course do too.

## The superlative: am -sten

The superlative has two forms. After a verb, use *am* + adjective + *-sten*:

- *Im Sommer ist es hier am schönsten.* — It's nicest here in summer.
- *Hier ist der Fluss am breitesten.* — The river is at its widest here.

If the adjective ends in *-d, -t, -s, -ß, -z* or *-sch*, add an *e* so that you can say it: *am ältesten, am breitesten, am kürzesten, am heißesten*. The one big exception is *groß*: *am größten*.

Before a noun, the superlative is an adjective like any other, with *-st-* and then the normal ending. Since a superlative is always "the" one, it almost always follows *der, die, das*, so it uses the der-word endings from lesson 10:

- *der höchste Berg* — the highest mountain
- *die schönste Landschaft* — the most beautiful landscape
- *in der größten Stadt* — in the biggest city (dative, *-en*)
- *die ältesten Einwohner* — the oldest inhabitants (plural, *-en*)

## Comparatives before a noun

A comparative before a noun also takes the normal endings, on top of the *-er*. That gives forms that look strange at first:

- *Wir suchen eine größere Wohnung.* — We're looking for a bigger flat. (*größer* + *-e*)
- *Ich möchte in einem kleineren Dorf wohnen.* — I'd like to live in a smaller village. (*kleiner* + *-en*)
- *Das ist ein schönerer Weg.* — That's a nicer path. (*schöner* + *-er*)

The first *-er* says "more"; the second is the ending from lesson 9. Both are needed.

## The irregular ones

A few very common adjectives have irregular forms. You know the first from A1.

| adjective / adverb | comparative | superlative |
|---|---|---|
| gern — gladly | lieber | am liebsten |
| gut — good | besser | am besten |
| viel — much, a lot | mehr | am meisten |
| hoch — high | höher | am höchsten |
| nah — near | näher | am nächsten |

*mehr* never takes an ending: *mehr Einwohner, mit mehr Zeit*. Its opposite is *weniger* (less, fewer). *am nächsten* also gives you *nächste* (next): *die nächste Stadt* is the nearest town, and *nächste Woche* is next week.

- *Hier ist die Luft besser als in der Stadt.* — The air is better here than in the city.
- *Berlin hat mehr Einwohner als Hamburg.* — Berlin has more inhabitants than Hamburg.
- *Die Zugspitze ist der höchste Berg in Deutschland.* — The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.

## als and wie

- *als* follows a comparative: *größer als*, *mehr als*, *lieber als*.
- *so … wie* means "as … as", with the plain adjective: *Mein Bruder ist so groß wie ich.* — My brother is as tall as me.
- *genauso … wie* means "just as … as": *Die Luft ist hier genauso sauber wie in den Bergen.* — The air here is just as clean as in the mountains.
- *nicht so … wie* means "not as … as": *Unser Dorf ist nicht so laut wie die Stadt.* — Our village isn't as noisy as the town.

A short way to remember: different → *als*; the same → *wie*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: als or wie?
  accDescr: When you compare two things, ask whether they are different or the same. If they are different, use the comparative and als, as in größer als. If they are the same, use so or genauso with the plain adjective and wie, as in so groß wie. Not the same is nicht so plus the plain adjective plus wie.
  A{"Are the two things different or the same?"} -- different --> B["comparative + als: größer als"]
  A -- the same --> C["so / genauso + adjective + wie: so groß wie"]
  A -- "not the same (not as …)" --> D["nicht so + adjective + wie: nicht so groß wie"]
```

*immer* + comparative means that something keeps growing: *Die Stadt wird immer größer* (the city keeps getting bigger), *immer mehr Leute* (more and more people). *werden* (to become) is from lesson 8.

## A text: City or country?

> Seit drei Jahren wohnen Miriam und Daniel nicht mehr in der Großstadt, sondern in einem kleinen Dorf im Süden, fünfzig Kilometer von der Grenze zur Schweiz.
>
> „Am Anfang war alles schwieriger“, sagt Miriam. „Der nächste Supermarkt ist acht Kilometer entfernt, und der Bus fährt nur dreimal am Tag. In der Stadt war das Leben bequemer. Aber hier ist die Luft viel sauberer, und die Landschaft ist schöner als auf jeder Postkarte.“
>
> Hinter ihrem Haus beginnt eine große Wiese, dann kommt der Wald. Im Tal fließt ein schmaler Fluss. „Er ist nicht so tief, wie er aussieht“, sagt Daniel, „aber im Frühling ist er gefährlich, wenn der Schnee schmilzt.“
>
> Daniel arbeitet jetzt zu Hause und fährt nur noch einmal pro Woche ins Büro. „Ich verdiene weniger als früher, aber ich habe mehr Zeit. Das ist mir wichtiger.“
>
> Ist das Dorf also der beste Ort zum Leben? „Für uns ja“, lacht Miriam. „Aber unsere Kinder sehen das anders. Sie finden die Stadt am interessantesten.“

In English:

> For three years Miriam and Daniel haven't lived in the big city any more, but in a small village in the south, fifty kilometres from the border with Switzerland.
>
> "At first everything was harder," says Miriam. "The nearest supermarket is eight kilometres away, and the bus only runs three times a day. Life was more comfortable in the city. But here the air is much cleaner, and the countryside is more beautiful than on any postcard."
>
> Behind their house there's a big meadow, then the woods. A narrow river flows through the valley. "It isn't as deep as it looks," says Daniel, "but in spring it's dangerous, when the snow melts."
>
> Daniel works from home now and only goes into the office once a week. "I earn less than before, but I have more time. That's more important to me."
>
> So is the village the best place to live? "For us, yes," laughs Miriam. "But our children see it differently. They find the city the most interesting."

Find the comparisons: *schwieriger, bequemer, sauberer, schöner als, wichtiger* (comparatives); *nicht so tief wie* (equal → *wie*); *weniger als, mehr* (irregular); *der nächste Supermarkt, der beste Ort* (superlative + der-word ending); *am interessantesten* (superlative after the verb). *viel* before a comparative means "much": *viel sauberer*. (*entfernt* = away, *fließen* = to flow, *schmelzen* = to melt, *verdienen* = to earn, *der Ort* = place.)

## Pronunciation

- *höher*: the *h* in the middle is silent; it just keeps the *ö* long: HÖ-er.
- *am nächsten*: soft *ch*, as in *ich*. *näher* has no *ch* at all.
- *Wiese*: long *ie*, soft *s*: VEE-ze.
- *Tal* has a long *a*; *Täler* (valleys) a long *ä*.
- *Ufer*: long *u*, OO-fer. *Hügel*: long *ü*, HÜ-gel.
- *Landschaft, Grenze, Gegend*: the stress is on the first syllable.

## Common mistakes

- *mehr schön* — German adds *-er* even to long adjectives: *schöner*, *interessanter*.
- *größer wie* — after a comparative use *als*: *größer als*. (You'll hear *wie* in casual speech, but it's not standard.)
- *so groß als* — for equality use *wie*: *so groß wie*.
- *gooder / am guten* — *gut, besser, am besten*.
- *der höher Berg* — *hoch* becomes *hoh-* before a noun: *der hohe Berg*, comparative *der höhere Berg*.
- *Wir suchen eine größer Wohnung.* — Comparatives before a noun still need an ending: *eine größere Wohnung*.
- *am ältsten* — after *t*, add an *e*: *am ältesten*.

## Key points

- Comparative: adjective + *-er* (*schneller*), followed by *als*. Equal: *so … wie*.
- Superlative after a verb: *am* + *-sten* (*am schnellsten*); *-esten* after *d, t, s, ß, z, sch*, but *am größten*.
- Many short adjectives add an umlaut: *alt – älter – am ältesten*.
- Irregular: *gut – besser – am besten*, *viel – mehr – am meisten*, *gern – lieber – am liebsten*, *hoch – höher – am höchsten*, *nah – näher – am nächsten*.
- Before a noun, comparatives and superlatives take normal endings: *eine größere Stadt*, *der höchste Berg*.
- *immer* + comparative: *immer mehr, immer größer*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Beyond the three tables: participles, place names and adjectives as nouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 9 to 11 you learned the three tables of adjective endings and the one idea behind them: a noun phrase shows its gender and case once, either on the article or on the adjective. That system covers far more than words like *neu* and *rot*. Walk through a German market or read a menu, and you'll see three more kinds of word using the same endings: verbs turned into adjectives (*frisch gepresster Saft, kochendes Wasser*), city names turned into adjectives (*Wiener Schnitzel, Schweizer Käse*), and adjectives turned into nouns (*zwei Erwachsene, ein Deutscher*).

This honors lesson shows how each of them works. You won't need a new table: everything here runs on the tables you already know, plus one surprising exception. You'll also learn the names grammar books use for the three tables, so that you can use any German grammar or dictionary on your own.

## The three tables have names

Most grammar books, in English and in German, call the three tables "declensions":

| the adjective comes after … | what the article does | name | German name |
|---|---|---|---|
| a der-word (*der, dieser, jeder, welcher, alle*) | always gives the signal | **[[weak declension]]** | schwache Deklination |
| an ein-word (*ein, kein, mein …*) | sometimes gives the signal | **[[mixed declension]]** | gemischte Deklination |
| no article (or a number, *viele, ein paar*) | gives no signal | **[[strong declension]]** | starke Deklination |

The names fit the signal idea. "Strong" endings do all the work themselves (*-er, -es, -em*, the letters of *der, das, dem*). "Weak" endings only ever say *-e* or *-en*, because the article has done the work. "Mixed" is a bit of both: strong in the three places where *ein* says nothing, weak everywhere else.

So when a dictionary or grammar says "the adjective takes the strong ending here", it means "use the no-article table". The words have nothing to do with **[[strong verbs]]** like *fahren, fuhr, gefahren*: it's the same word used for a different idea.

## Verbs as adjectives: participles

### The past participle: done to it

You know the **[[past participle]]** from the perfect tense: *gekocht, gebraten, geöffnet, reduziert*. Put one in front of a noun and it becomes an adjective with ordinary endings:

- *ein gekochtes Ei* — a boiled egg
- *der gebratene Fisch* — the fried fish
- *mit frisch gepresstem Saft* — with freshly squeezed juice
- *alle reduzierten Jacken* — all the reduced jackets

A past participle used like this usually means that something has been done to the noun: the egg has been boiled, the jackets have been reduced. An adverb in front of it, like *frisch* (freshly) or *selbst* (yourself), never takes an ending, because it describes the participle, not the noun: *frisch gebackenes Brot, selbst gemachte Marmelade*.

After *sein*, the participle has no ending, like any adjective: *Das Geschäft ist geöffnet. Die Suppe ist hausgemacht.* You see this on many signs: *Geöffnet* (open), *Geschlossen* (closed), *Frisch gestrichen* (wet paint, literally "freshly painted").

### The present participle: doing it

German has a second participle that English speakers often don't notice. The **[[present participle]]** is the infinitive plus *-d*:

| infinitive | present participle | example |
|---|---|---|
| kochen | kochend | *kochendes Wasser* — boiling water |
| lachen | lachend | *die lachenden Kinder* — the laughing children |
| schlafen | schlafend | *ein schlafendes Baby* — a sleeping baby |
| fließen | fließend | *fließendes Wasser* — running water |
| passen | passend | *ein passendes Geschenk* — a suitable present |
| folgen | folgend | *die folgenden Fragen* — the following questions |

It means that the noun is doing something at that moment, like English "-ing". Compare:

- *kochendes Wasser* — boiling water (it is boiling now)
- *gekochtes Wasser* — boiled water (it has been boiled; it may be cold by now)

Unlike English, German does **not** use the present participle to make the progressive tenses: "The water is boiling" is *Das Wasser kocht*, never ~~*Das Wasser ist kochend*~~. In everyday German the present participle mostly stands before a noun. A few have become ordinary words: *fließend* also means "fluent" (*Sie spricht fließend Deutsch*), *passend* means "suitable" or "matching", and *folgend* means "following".

### Example 1: a menu line

A café menu says: *Frisch gepresster Orangensaft*. Why *-er*?

1. Find the noun: *Orangensaft*, which is *der Saft*, masculine.
2. Find the case: on a menu the item stands alone, like a subject, so nominative.
3. Look in front: no article at all, so the strong (no-article) ending: the *-er* of *der*.
4. *frisch* is an adverb describing *gepresst*, so it takes no ending.

On the order you'd say *Ich nehme einen frisch gepressten Orangensaft*: now *einen* gives the signal (masculine accusative), and the participle takes *-en*.

## City names as adjectives: no ending at all

Here is the exception. Take the name of a town and add *-er*, and you get an adjective meaning "from that place": *Berlin → Berliner, Wien → Wiener, Frankfurt → Frankfurter, Köln → Kölner, die Schweiz → Schweizer*. These **[[place-name adjectives]]** are special in two ways:

1. They are written with a capital letter.
2. They never take an ending, in any case or gender.

| | example |
|---|---|
| nominative | *Der Kölner Dom ist sehr alt.* — Cologne Cathedral is very old. |
| accusative | *Ich esse ein Wiener Schnitzel.* — I'm eating a Wiener schnitzel. |
| dative | *in der Berliner U-Bahn* — on the Berlin underground |
| no article | *mit Schweizer Käse* — with Swiss cheese |
| plural | *die Frankfurter Würstchen* — the frankfurters |

Compare a normal adjective in the same place: *mit Schweizer Käse* but *mit frischem Käse*; *ein Wiener Schnitzel* but *ein großes Schnitzel*. Some names change a little: *der Schwarzwald → Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte* (Black Forest gateau), *Nürnberg → Nürnberger Würstchen*.

The same *-er* word is also the noun for a person from that place: *Er ist Berliner* (he's from Berlin), *die Wiener* (the people of Vienna). And sometimes it's a food. In much of Germany a jam doughnut is called *ein Berliner*, while in Berlin itself people usually call it *ein Pfannkuchen*, and in the south and in Austria *ein Krapfen*. That's why a popular story says that John F. Kennedy told Berlin "I am a doughnut" when he said *Ich bin ein Berliner* in 1963. The story is a myth: the sentence is correct German, and his audience understood exactly what he meant.

Country adjectives that don't end in *-er* behave normally: *das deutsche Brot, österreichischer Wein, die schweizerische Regierung*. Only the *-er* form is frozen.

## Adjectives as nouns, in all three tables

In lesson 10 you met **[[adjectival nouns]]** like *der Bekannte* and *ein Bekannter*. Several very common words for people work the same way. Each one is an adjective with a capital letter, and it takes exactly the ending an adjective would take before an invisible noun such as *Mann*, *Frau* or *Leute*:

| | after a der-word (weak) | after an ein-word (mixed) | no article (strong) |
|---|---|---|---|
| man | der Erwachsene | ein Erwachsener | als Erwachsener (as an adult) |
| woman | die Erwachsene | eine Erwachsene | als Erwachsene |
| plural | die Erwachsenen | meine Verwandten | zwei Erwachsene, viele Deutsche |
| dative plural | mit den Erwachsenen | mit meinen Verwandten | mit zwei Erwachsenen |

The words worth learning now: *der/die Erwachsene* (adult, from *erwachsen*, grown up), *der/die Jugendliche* (young person, teenager), *der/die Verwandte* (relative) and *der/die Deutsche* (German person).

Notice the trap with nationalities. *Deutsche* is an adjectival noun, so it changes: *der Deutsche, ein Deutscher, zwei Deutsche*. But *Österreicher* and *Schweizer* are ordinary nouns: *der Österreicher, ein Österreicher, zwei Österreicher*, with no adjective endings at all. You say *Er ist Deutscher* but *Er ist Österreicher*, and *Sie ist Deutsche* but *Sie ist Österreicherin*.

### Example 2: a ticket price list

A museum sign reads: *Erwachsene 12 €, Jugendliche 8 €, Kinder bis 6 Jahre frei*. Then a family at the desk says: *Zwei Erwachsene und ein Jugendlicher, bitte.*

- *Erwachsene, Jugendliche* on the sign: plural, no article → strong ending *-e*.
- *zwei Erwachsene*: a number doesn't count as an article → still *-e*.
- *ein Jugendlicher*: after *ein*, masculine nominative → mixed ending *-er*. (A teenage girl would be *eine Jugendliche*.)
- The cashier answers: *Das macht 32 Euro für die Erwachsenen und den Jugendlichen.* After *die* and *den*, the weak ending *-en*.

### Example 3: putting all three together

*In der Kölner Altstadt gibt es eine kleine Bäckerei mit frisch gebackenen Brötchen.* (In Cologne's old town there's a little bakery with freshly baked rolls.)

- *Kölner*: place-name adjective, no ending, even in the dative.
- *kleine*: after *eine*, feminine accusative (object of *es gibt*) → *-e*.
- *frisch gebackenen*: *frisch* is an adverb (no ending); *gebacken* is a past participle after *mit* with no article, dative plural → strong *-en*.

## Dialogue: Am Marktstand

![A market stall sign for Marktstand Huber. Frisch gepresster Orangensaft 3,50 €; Hausgemachte Kartoffelsuppe 4,90 €; Gefüllte Paprika mit Reis 6,50 €; Nürnberger Würstchen (6 Stück) 4,20 €; Schweizer Käse, 100 g 2,80 €. Below: Kaffee für Erwachsene 2,00 €, Kakao für Kinder gratis. Samstags geöffnet von 7 bis 14 Uhr.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Herr Huber: Guten Morgen! Was darf es sein?
>
> Frau Aydın: Zwei frisch gepresste Orangensäfte, bitte. Und ist die Kartoffelsuppe wirklich hausgemacht?
>
> Herr Huber: Natürlich! Meine Frau kocht sie jeden Freitag nach einem alten Rezept von ihrer Oma.
>
> Frau Aydın: Dann nehme ich eine Suppe. Und für meinen Sohn die gefüllte Paprika.
>
> Herr Huber: Gern. Möchten Sie noch etwas Käse? Der Schweizer Käse ist heute besonders gut.
>
> Frau Aydın: Gern, zweihundert Gramm. Wir haben am Sonntag Besuch, meine Verwandten aus Wien kommen.
>
> Herr Huber: Ah, Wiener! Dann brauchen Sie auch Würstchen. Die Nürnberger sind ganz frisch.
>
> Frau Aydın: Gute Idee. Die Kinder lieben Würstchen. Und die Erwachsenen auch!

In English:

> Mr Huber: Good morning! What can I get you?
>
> Mrs Aydın: Two freshly squeezed orange juices, please. And is the potato soup really homemade?
>
> Mr Huber: Of course! My wife makes it every Friday from an old recipe of her grandma's.
>
> Mrs Aydın: Then I'll have a soup. And the stuffed pepper for my son.
>
> Mr Huber: Certainly. Would you like some cheese too? The Swiss cheese is especially good today.
>
> Mrs Aydın: Yes please, two hundred grams. We've got visitors on Sunday, my relatives from Vienna are coming.
>
> Mr Huber: Ah, Viennese! Then you'll need sausages too. The Nürnberger ones are really fresh.
>
> Mrs Aydın: Good idea. The children love sausages. And so do the adults!

Look at the forms: *zwei frisch gepresste Orangensäfte* (number + strong plural *-e*), *die gefüllte Paprika* (weak *-e*), *der Schweizer Käse* (no ending), *meine Verwandten* (mixed plural *-en*), *die Erwachsenen* (weak plural *-en*). *Wiener* on its own here means people from Vienna. (*hausgemacht* = homemade, *gefüllt* = stuffed, filled, *die Paprika* = pepper, the vegetable.)

## How to work out any ending

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Is it a normal adjective ending or not?
  accDescr: First ask whether the word is a place-name adjective in -er such as Kölner or Schweizer. If it is, it never takes an ending. Otherwise it takes a normal adjective ending, even if it is a participle like gekocht or kochend, or an adjectival noun like Erwachsene. Then look at the word in front. After a der-word use the weak endings -e or -en. After an ein-word use the mixed endings. With no article, a number or viele use the strong endings.
  A{"Is it a place name + -er, like Kölner?"} -- yes --> Z["No ending ever: mit Schweizer Käse"]
  A -- no --> B["Normal adjective endings, also for participles and adjectival nouns"]
  B --> C{"What comes before it?"}
  C -- "der-word" --> W["weak: -e / -en"]
  C -- "ein-word" --> M["mixed: -er / -e / -es / -en"]
  C -- "nothing, a number, viele" --> S["strong: -er / -e / -es / -em / -en"]
```

## Common mistakes

- *mit Schweizerem Käse* — place-name adjectives never change: *mit Schweizer Käse*.
- *ein schweizer Käse* — they're written with a capital letter: *ein Schweizer Käse*.
- *frischer gepresster Saft* — *frisch* describes the participle, so no ending: *frisch gepresster Saft*.
- *Das Wasser ist kochend.* — for "is boiling" use the verb: *Das Wasser kocht.*
- *zwei Erwachsenen* (as subject or object) — after a number the strong plural is *-e*: *zwei Erwachsene*. It's *-en* only in the dative or after *die, meine*: *mit zwei Erwachsenen, die Erwachsenen*.
- *Er ist ein Deutsche.* — after *ein*, masculine nominative takes *-er*: *Er ist Deutscher* or *ein Deutscher*.
- *zwei Österreichern* as a subject — *Österreicher* is an ordinary noun, plural *die Österreicher*, *-n* only in the dative.
- *gekochtes Wasser* when you mean water that is boiling now — that's *kochendes Wasser*.

## Key points

- Grammar books call the three tables the weak (after der-words), mixed (after ein-words) and strong (no article) declensions.
- Past participles before a noun take normal endings and usually mean "has been done": *ein gekochtes Ei, die reduzierten Jacken*.
- Present participle = infinitive + *-d*, meaning "-ing": *kochendes Wasser, die folgenden Fragen*. It is not used for "is doing".
- An adverb in front of a participle has no ending: *frisch gebackenes Brot*.
- Place-name adjectives in *-er* are capitalized and never change: *der Kölner Dom, mit Schweizer Käse*.
- *Erwachsene, Jugendliche, Verwandte, Deutsche* are adjectival nouns: *ein Erwachsener, zwei Erwachsene, die Erwachsenen*. *Österreicher* and *Schweizer* are ordinary nouns.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Highest, biggest, longest: comparing the German-speaking countries
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 12 you learned to say that one thing is *größer als* another, *so groß wie* another, or *am größten*. That's enough for a simple comparison, but real descriptions are more precise. Is the city a little bigger or much bigger? Twice as big? The second-biggest? One of the biggest? This honors lesson gives you the tools for that, and uses them on a real subject: the geography of Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the three main countries where German is spoken.

The numbers in this lesson are real, rounded figures. Areas and heights hardly change; population figures change every year, so treat them as "about" (they're estimates for the mid-2020s).

## Three degrees

Grammar books call the plain form of an adjective the **[[positive]]**: *groß, hoch, lang*. With the comparative (*größer*) and the superlative (*am größten*), these are the three degrees of comparison:

| positive | comparative | superlative |
|---|---|---|
| groß | größer | am größten / der größte |
| hoch | höher | am höchsten / der höchste |
| lang | länger | am längsten / der längste |

Everything in this lesson builds on those three forms.

## Much bigger, a little bigger, even bigger

To say how big a difference is, put a word in front of the comparative. These words are **[[intensifiers]]**:

| intensifier | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| viel | much, far | *Die Schweiz ist viel kleiner als Deutschland.* |
| etwas, ein bisschen, ein wenig | a little, slightly | *Österreich hat etwas mehr Einwohner als die Schweiz.* |
| noch | even | *Der Großglockner ist hoch, aber die Dufourspitze ist noch höher.* |
| immer | more and more | *Die Städte werden immer größer.* |

Two things English speakers get wrong. First, "much" is *viel*, never *sehr*: ~~*sehr größer*~~. *sehr* goes only with the positive: *sehr groß*. Second, *noch* (even) suggests that the first thing is already big: *noch höher* means "higher still".

To give the exact difference, use *um* + the amount: *Der Großglockner ist um 836 Meter höher als die Zugspitze.* (In speech the *um* is often left out.)

With a superlative, *mit Abstand* or *bei Weitem* means "by far": *Berlin ist mit Abstand die größte Stadt Deutschlands.*

## Twice as big, half as big

To multiply, use the *so … wie* pattern from lesson 12 and put the number in front:

- *doppelt so groß wie* — twice as big as (also *zweimal so groß wie*)
- *dreimal so lang wie* — three times as long as
- *halb so groß wie* — half as big as
- *ungefähr neunmal so viele Einwohner wie* — about nine times as many inhabitants as

Note *so viele … wie* for countable things (*Einwohner, Seen*) and *so viel … wie* for amounts (*Wasser, Zeit*).

### Example 1: comparing two countries

Austria has an area of about 83,900 km² and Switzerland about 41,300 km². How do you compare them?

1. Divide: 83,900 ÷ 41,300 ≈ 2.0.
2. Twice as big → *doppelt so groß wie*.
3. The subject is Austria: ***Österreich ist ungefähr doppelt so groß wie die Schweiz.***
4. Turned round: *Die Schweiz ist ungefähr halb so groß wie Österreich.*

But the two countries have almost the same population, about 9.2 million against 9.1 million: *Österreich hat fast genauso viele Einwohner wie die Schweiz* or *Österreich hat nur etwas mehr Einwohner als die Schweiz.* Both sentences are true; they put the weight in different places.

## The second-biggest and one of the biggest

### Ranking with ordinals

To say "the second-biggest" or "the third-longest", join the ordinal number (from A1: *zweite, dritte*) to the superlative as one word, without its ending: *zweit-, dritt-, viert-*:

- *die zweitgrößte Stadt* — the second-biggest city
- *der dritthöchste Berg* — the third-highest mountain
- *Wien ist die zweitgrößte Stadt im deutschsprachigen Raum.* — Vienna is the second-biggest city in the German-speaking world (after Berlin).

The superlative part takes its normal ending: *in der zweitgrößten Stadt*.

### "One of the …"

"One of the biggest cities" is *eine der größten Städte*. Learn it as a chunk:

| the noun is … | "one of the …" |
|---|---|
| masculine | *einer der höchsten Berge* |
| feminine | *eine der größten Städte* |
| neuter | *eines der schönsten Länder* |

*einer/eine/eines* matches the gender of the noun (one mountain, one city), and the noun itself is plural, because you pick one from a group. The *der* in the middle is the genitive plural ("of the"), and the adjective after it ends in *-en*. Lesson 18 gives a first look at the genitive, and you'll learn it properly at B1; for now, the chunk is enough:

- *Der Bodensee ist einer der größten Seen in Mitteleuropa.* — Lake Constance is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe.
- *Zürich ist eine der teuersten Städte der Welt.* — Zurich is one of the most expensive cities in the world.

## Most, at least, at most

- *die meisten* + plural noun means "most (of the)": *Die meisten Schweizer sprechen Deutsch.* — Most Swiss people speak German. Don't confuse it with *am meisten* after a verb: *Wer hat am meisten gegessen?* — Who ate the most?
- *mindestens* (at least) and *höchstens* (at most) come from superlatives too: *Die Fahrt dauert mindestens drei Stunden. Der Fluss ist hier höchstens einen Meter tief.*
- *so … wie möglich* means "as … as possible": *Wir fahren so früh wie möglich los.* — We'll set off as early as possible.

## The German-speaking countries in numbers

The chart compares the highest mountain in each of the three countries.

```plot
{"x": [0.3, 3.7], "y": [-800, 5400], "grid": false, "bars": [{"x": 1, "height": 2962, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 2, "height": 3798, "width": 0.6}, {"x": 3, "height": 4634, "width": 0.6}], "segments": [{"from": [0.4, 0], "to": [3.6, 0]}], "labels": [{"at": [1, 3200], "text": "2962 m"}, {"at": [2, 4036], "text": "3798 m"}, {"at": [3, 4872], "text": "4634 m"}, {"at": [1, -500], "text": "Zugspitze"}, {"at": [2, -500], "text": "Großglockner"}, {"at": [3, -500], "text": "Dufourspitze"}], "caption": "Height in metres of the highest mountain in Germany (Zugspitze), Austria (Großglockner) and Switzerland (Dufourspitze)"}
```

| | Deutschland | Österreich | die Schweiz |
|---|---|---|---|
| area (*die Fläche*) | about 357,600 km² | about 83,900 km² | about 41,300 km² |
| population (*die Bevölkerung*) | about 83 million | about 9.2 million | about 9.1 million |
| highest mountain | Zugspitze, 2,962 m | Großglockner, 3,798 m | Dufourspitze, 4,634 m |
| biggest city | Berlin | Wien | Zürich |

### Example 2: from a table to sentences

Use the table to compare Germany with Austria.

- Area: 357,600 ÷ 83,900 ≈ 4.3 → *Deutschland ist mehr als viermal so groß wie Österreich.*
- Population: 83 ÷ 9.2 ≈ 9 → *Deutschland hat ungefähr neunmal so viele Einwohner wie Österreich.*
- Mountains: 3,798 − 2,962 = 836 → *Der höchste Berg Österreichs ist um 836 Meter höher als der höchste Berg Deutschlands.*

Notice *mehr als viermal*: the exact figure is about 4.3, so "more than four times" is accurate, and "five times" would be wrong.

## A text: Drei Länder, drei Rekorde

> Deutschland ist das größte deutschsprachige Land: Es ist mehr als viermal so groß wie Österreich und hat ungefähr neunmal so viele Einwohner. Berlin ist mit Abstand die größte Stadt, Wien die zweitgrößte.
>
> Aber bei den Bergen gewinnt Deutschland nicht. Die Zugspitze an der Grenze zu Österreich ist knapp 3000 Meter hoch. Der Großglockner in Österreich ist viel höher, und die Dufourspitze in der Schweiz ist noch höher: Sie ist über 4600 Meter hoch. Die Schweiz ist zwar das kleinste der drei Länder, aber sie hat die höchsten Berge.
>
> Und das Wasser? Der Rhein ist der längste Fluss in Deutschland. Die Donau ist insgesamt mehr als doppelt so lang wie der Rhein, aber nur ein kürzerer Teil von ihr fließt durch Deutschland. Der Bodensee ist einer der größten Seen in Mitteleuropa, und er gehört drei Ländern: Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz. Der Genfer See ist noch etwas größer, aber dort spricht man Französisch.
>
> Übrigens: Viele Menschen denken, dass Bern die Hauptstadt der Schweiz ist. Offiziell hat die Schweiz aber keine Hauptstadt. Bern heißt „Bundesstadt“, und dort arbeiten die Regierung und das Parlament.

In English:

> Germany is the biggest German-speaking country: it's more than four times as big as Austria and has about nine times as many inhabitants. Berlin is by far the biggest city, Vienna the second-biggest.
>
> But with mountains, Germany doesn't win. The Zugspitze, on the border with Austria, is just under 3,000 metres high. The Großglockner in Austria is much higher, and the Dufourspitze in Switzerland is higher still: it's over 4,600 metres high. Switzerland may be the smallest of the three countries, but it has the highest mountains.
>
> And the water? The Rhine is the longest river in Germany. The Danube is more than twice as long as the Rhine in total, but only a shorter part of it flows through Germany. Lake Constance is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe, and it belongs to three countries: Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Lake Geneva is a little bigger still, but there people speak French.
>
> By the way: many people think that Bern is the capital of Switzerland. Officially, though, Switzerland has no capital. Bern is called the "federal city", and that's where the government and parliament work.

Find the tools: *mehr als viermal so groß wie, neunmal so viele* (multiples); *mit Abstand die größte, die zweitgrößte* (ranking); *viel höher, noch höher, noch etwas größer* (intensifiers); *einer der größten Seen* (one of the …); *das kleinste der drei Länder* (superlative with a group). (*knapp* = just under, *insgesamt* = in total, *zwar … aber* = admittedly … but, *übrigens* = by the way, *deutschsprachig* = German-speaking.)

A note on simplification: "the biggest lake in Germany" is a tricky title. Lake Constance is by far the largest lake that Germany has a share in, but because it is shared, the largest lake lying entirely inside Germany is the Müritz in Mecklenburg, which is much smaller. And the borders inside Lake Constance have never been fully agreed between the three countries.

## How to choose the right tool

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a comparison pattern
  accDescr: To compare, first ask whether the things are the same or different. The same takes genauso plus adjective plus wie. If they are different, ask whether you want to say by how much. A rough amount takes viel, etwas or noch plus the comparative plus als. An exact amount takes um plus the amount plus the comparative plus als. A multiple takes doppelt, dreimal or halb so plus adjective plus wie. To place something at the top of a group, use the superlative; for second or third place use zweit- or dritt- plus the superlative; for one of the top few use einer, eine or eines der plus the superlative plus a plural noun.
  A{"What do you want to say?"} -- "the same" --> S["genauso + adjective + wie"]
  A -- "different" --> B{"How different?"}
  B -- roughly --> R["viel / etwas / noch + comparative + als"]
  B -- exactly --> E["um 836 Meter + comparative + als"]
  B -- "a multiple" --> M["doppelt / dreimal / halb so + adjective + wie"]
  A -- "top of a group" --> T{"Which place?"}
  T -- first --> T1["der größte, am größten"]
  T -- "second, third" --> T2["der zweitgrößte, der drittgrößte"]
  T -- "one of the top" --> T3["einer der größten Seen"]
```

## Common mistakes

- *sehr größer* — with a comparative, "much" is *viel*: *viel größer*.
- *zweimal größer als* for "twice as big" — standard German uses *doppelt (zweimal) so groß wie*. You'll hear *zweimal größer*, but it's ambiguous and best avoided.
- *die zweite größte Stadt* — write it as one word with no ending on the ordinal: *die zweitgrößte Stadt*.
- *einer der größte See* — the noun is plural and the adjective ends in *-en*: *einer der größten Seen*.
- *eine der höchsten Berge* — *Berg* is masculine, so *einer der höchsten Berge*.
- *am meisten Schweizer* — before a noun, "most" is *die meisten*: *die meisten Schweizer*.
- *so viel Einwohner wie* — for things you count, *so viele*: *so viele Einwohner wie*.

## Key points

- The three degrees: positive (*groß*), comparative (*größer*), superlative (*am größten*).
- Intensifiers: *viel* (much), *etwas / ein bisschen* (a little), *noch* (even) + comparative; never *sehr* + comparative. Exact difference: *um* + amount.
- Multiples: *doppelt / dreimal / halb so* + adjective + *wie*.
- Ranking: *die zweitgrößte, der dritthöchste* (one word). "One of the": *einer/eine/eines der* + superlative in *-en* + plural noun.
- *die meisten* + noun = most; *mindestens* = at least; *höchstens* = at most; *so … wie möglich* = as … as possible.
- Germany is the biggest German-speaking country; Switzerland has the highest mountains; Bern is the Swiss "federal city", not officially a capital.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Where is it, where does it go? Two-way prepositions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In German A1 (lesson 19) you described a room: *Das Sofa ist im Wohnzimmer. Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch.* You learned that nine prepositions take the dative when they answer *Wo?* (where?). That covers a room that is already finished. But real life is messier: you move into a new flat, carry boxes, put the sofa somewhere, hang pictures on the wall and look for the keys you put down somewhere yesterday.

This lesson adds the second half of the picture. The same nine prepositions take the accusative when something moves to a new place, answering *Wohin?* (where to?). You'll also learn the five pairs of verbs German uses for "put" and "be somewhere" (*stellen/stehen, legen/liegen, setzen/sitzen, hängen/hängen, stecken/stecken*), their perfect forms, and the words you need when you move house: the landlord, the deposit, the boxes and the washing machine.

## Wo? or Wohin? The one question that decides the case

The **[[two-way prepositions]]** are *in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen*. They are called two-way because they can take two cases. Which one you use depends on a single question:

| Question | Situation | Case | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Wo?* — where? | a position; nothing moves to a new place | **[[dative]]** | *Der Karton steht im Flur.* — The box is (standing) in the hall (*der Flur*). |
| *Wohin?* — where to? | movement or a change of place towards a goal | **[[accusative]]** | *Ich stelle den Karton in den Flur.* — I'm putting the box into the hall. |

The movement has to be from one place to another. Walking around inside the kitchen is still *Wo?*: *Er läuft in der Küche hin und her* (He walks up and down in the kitchen). Walking into the kitchen is *Wohin?*: *Er läuft in die Küche.*

A memory hook: Accusative = Arrow (both start with A). If you could draw an arrow to a new spot, use the accusative. If you could draw a dot, use the dative.

![Two panels. Left, green, headed "Wo? → Dativ": a book lies on a table with a black dot above it, labeled Punkt (dot), and the sentence Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. Right, pink, headed "Wohin? → Akkusativ": a book in the air with a curved arrow down onto the table, labeled Pfeil (arrow), and the sentence Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The articles

After a two-way preposition, the article simply takes the normal dative or accusative form:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Wo?* (dative) | *auf dem Tisch* | *an der Wand* | *im (in dem) Regal* | *in den Kisten* |
| *Wohin?* (accusative) | *auf den Tisch* | *an die Wand* | *ins (in das) Regal* | *in die Kisten* |

Notice that the feminine changes from *der* to *die*, the masculine from *dem* to *den*, and the neuter from *dem* to *das*. Only the plural noun loses the extra dative *-n*: *in den Kisten* (dative) but *in die Kisten* (accusative).

- *Die Bücher liegen auf dem Boden.* — The books are lying on the floor.
- *Leg die Bücher bitte nicht auf den Boden!* — Please don't put the books on the floor!
- *Das Bild hängt über dem Sofa.* — The picture is hanging above the sofa.
- *Wir hängen das Bild über das Sofa.* — We're hanging the picture above the sofa.
- *Die Katze schläft unter dem Bett.* — The cat is sleeping under the bed.
- *Die Katze läuft unter das Bett.* — The cat runs under the bed.

### Contractions

You already know *im* (in dem) and *am* (an dem) for the dative. The accusative has its own short forms with *das*:

| Long form | Short form | Case | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *in dem* | *im* | dative | *im Keller* — in the cellar |
| *an dem* | *am* | dative | *am Fenster* — at the window |
| *in das* | *ins* | accusative | *ins Schlafzimmer* — into the bedroom |
| *an das* | *ans* | accusative | *ans Fenster* — to the window |

You will also meet *aufs* (auf das): *aufs Sofa*. It is correct in writing too, just less frequent than *ins* and *ans*.

## Put and be: five verb pairs

English uses "put" for almost everything and "is" for almost every position. German is more precise. It has pairs of verbs: one describes the action of putting something somewhere (*Wohin?* + accusative), the other describes the result, where it now is (*Wo?* + dative).

| Putting (*Wohin?* + accusative) | Being there (*Wo?* + dative) | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| *stellen* — to put (upright) | *stehen* — to stand, be (upright) | things that stand on a base: bottles, furniture, a lamp, books in a row |
| *legen* — to put (flat), lay | *liegen* — to lie, be (flat) | things lying flat: keys, a phone, a carpet, a person in bed |
| *setzen* — to sit (someone) down | *sitzen* — to sit, be sitting | people and animals; *sich setzen* = to sit down |
| *hängen* — to hang (something up) | *hängen* — to hang, be hanging | pictures, curtains, coats, lamps from the ceiling |
| *stecken* — to put (into), stick | *stecken* — to be (inside), be stuck | something inside something tight: a key in a lock, a phone in a pocket |

- *Ich stelle die Flasche in den Kühlschrank.* — I put the bottle in the fridge.
  *Die Flasche steht im Kühlschrank.* — The bottle is in the fridge.
- *Er legt den Teppich ins Wohnzimmer.* — He puts the rug in the living room.
  *Der Teppich liegt im Wohnzimmer.* — The rug is in the living room.
- *Die Mutter setzt das Baby auf den Stuhl.* — The mother sits the baby on the chair.
  *Das Baby sitzt auf dem Stuhl.* — The baby is sitting on the chair.
- *Wir hängen den Vorhang ans Fenster.* — We're hanging the curtain at the window.
  *Der Vorhang hängt am Fenster.* — The curtain is hanging at the window.
- *Sie steckt den Schlüssel in die Tasche.* — She puts the key in her bag.
  *Der Schlüssel steckt in der Tasche.* — The key is in the bag.

How do you know whether something *steht* or *liegt*? Ask how it rests. A book standing on a shelf *steht*; the same book lying flat on the table *liegt*. A plate on the table usually *steht* in German (it rests on its base), and so do cups and glasses. Cities also "lie": *Wien liegt an der Donau* (Vienna lies on the Danube).

### Why there are two verbs: a memory hook

Look at the pairs again. The putting verbs (*stellen, legen, setzen*) all have an *e* and are regular, like *machen*. They always have a **[[direct object]]**: you put *something*. The being verbs (*stehen, liegen, sitzen*) have other vowels, are irregular, and never take an object. So: *e* for effort (you do something to an object, and the object goes into the accusative).

*hängen* and *stecken* look the same in both meanings. Only the object, the case after the preposition and the perfect of *hängen* tell them apart. (*stecken* is regular in both meanings: *hat gesteckt*.)

This chart sums up the choice:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the verb and the case with a two-way preposition
  accDescr: Ask whether someone moves something to a new place. If yes, the question is Wohin, the preposition takes the accusative, and you use a putting verb with an object: stellen for upright things, legen for flat things, setzen for people, hängen with the perfect gehängt, or stecken. If no, the question is Wo, the preposition takes the dative, and you use a being verb with no object: stehen, liegen, sitzen, hängen with the perfect gehangen, or stecken.
  A{"Does someone move something to a new place?"} -- yes --> B["Wohin? + accusative"]
  A -- no --> C["Wo? + dative"]
  B --> D["Putting verb + object: stellen, legen, setzen, hängen (gehängt), stecken"]
  C --> E["Being verb, no object: stehen, liegen, sitzen, hängen (gehangen), stecken"]
  D --> F["Ich stelle die Lampe neben das Sofa."]
  E --> G["Die Lampe steht neben dem Sofa."]
```

### The perfect forms

| Putting (regular) | Perfect | Being (irregular) | Perfect |
|---|---|---|---|
| *stellen* | *hat gestellt* | *stehen* | *hat gestanden* |
| *legen* | *hat gelegt* | *liegen* | *hat gelegen* |
| *setzen* | *hat gesetzt* | *sitzen* | *hat gesessen* |
| *hängen* | *hat gehängt* | *hängen* | *hat gehangen* |
| *stecken* | *hat gesteckt* | *stecken* | *hat gesteckt* |

- *Wohin hast du meine Brille gelegt?* — Where did you put my glasses?
- *Sie hat den ganzen Tag auf dem Balkon gesessen.* — She sat on the balcony all day.
- *Ich habe die Jacke an die Tür gehängt.* — I hung the jacket on the door.
- *Die Jacke hat an der Tür gehangen.* — The jacket was hanging on the door.

In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, *stehen, liegen* and *sitzen* form the perfect with *sein*: *Ich bin lange gesessen.* That is correct there; in the rest of Germany people use *haben*, and this course does too.

### Other verbs with Wo? and Wohin?

The same logic works for every verb. Verbs of movement (*gehen, fahren, kommen, laufen, bringen, tragen*) usually answer *Wohin?*; verbs of being or staying (*sein, wohnen, arbeiten, bleiben, warten, schlafen*) answer *Wo?*

- *Wir fahren in die Stadt.* — We're driving into town. / *Wir wohnen in der Stadt.* — We live in town.
- *Bring die Kiste bitte in den Keller.* — Please take the crate down to the cellar. / *Die Kiste bleibt im Keller.* — The crate stays in the cellar.
- *Ich gehe ins Bett.* — I'm going to bed. / *Ich liege im Bett.* — I'm lying in bed.

## Moving house

Moving is a big topic in German everyday life, because most people rent. You know *umziehen* (to move house) from A1. Two new verbs show the direction:

- *einziehen* — to move in: *Wir sind am Samstag in die neue Wohnung eingezogen.* — We moved into the new flat on Saturday. (in + accusative: the arrow goes in)
- *ausziehen* — to move out: *Mein Bruder ist aus der WG ausgezogen.* — My brother has moved out of the shared flat. (aus + dative)

Both are separable and form the perfect with *sein*, like *umziehen*. (*die WG*, short for *Wohngemeinschaft*, is a flat shared by several people.)

The people and the money:

- *der Vermieter* (landlord) rents the flat to *der Mieter* (tenant). You know *mieten* (to rent) and *die Miete* (rent).
- *die Kaution* — the deposit, by law at most three months' rent (without the extra costs): *Die Kaution bekommen Sie zurück, wenn Sie ausziehen.*
- *die Nebenkosten* — the extra costs for heating, water and rubbish collection, paid on top of the rent. An advert might say: *Miete 650 € plus 180 € Nebenkosten.*

Most of the things appear in the dialogue below. A few more: *die Möbel* (furniture) is a plural word: *Die Möbel kommen morgen.* *Die Decke* is both a blanket and the ceiling: *Die Lampe hängt an der Decke.* The dishwasher (*die Spülmaschine*) stands in the kitchen, and *der Müll* (rubbish) goes into the bin outside.

Here is Lena's living room on moving day, with some of the new words:

![A living room on moving day. A lamp, labeled die Lampe, hangs from the ceiling. A picture of mountains, das Bild, hangs on the wall above a sofa with two cushions, die Kissen. On the right is a window with a curtain on each side, der Vorhang. An oval rug, der Teppich, lies on the floor in front of the sofa, and a cardboard box marked Küche, der Karton, stands on the floor on the right.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Describe the picture with *Wo?*: *Die Lampe hängt an der Decke. Der Teppich liegt vor dem Sofa. Der Karton steht unter dem Fenster.*

The jobs: *sauber machen* (to clean), *abwaschen* (to wash up), *staubsaugen* (to vacuum) and, from A1, *aufräumen* (to tidy up) and *putzen* (to clean). *Wenn man auszieht, muss man die Wohnung sauber machen* — When you move out, you have to clean the flat.

## Dialogue: Moving day

Lena is moving into her first flat. Her friend Tarek is helping.

> Tarek: So, das ist der letzte Karton. Wohin soll ich ihn stellen?
>
> Lena: Was steht denn drauf? Ah, „Küche“. Stell ihn bitte neben den Herd.
>
> Tarek: Und die große Kiste mit den Büchern? Die ist wirklich schwer!
>
> Lena: Die kommt ins Wohnzimmer, zwischen das Sofa und den Schreibtisch. Die Bücher stelle ich später ins Regal.
>
> Tarek: Okay. Sag mal, wo ist eigentlich der Teppich? Gestern hat er noch im Flur gelegen.
>
> Lena: Den habe ich schon ins Schlafzimmer gelegt. Und die Vorhänge hängen auch schon am Fenster. Schau!
>
> Tarek: Sehr schön. Und wo sind die Kissen?
>
> Lena: Die liegen in dem blauen Sack auf dem Balkon. Leg sie einfach aufs Sofa.
>
> Tarek: Puh. Darf ich mich jetzt mal kurz setzen?
>
> Lena: Natürlich! Setz dich! Ich hole uns etwas zu trinken. Das Bier steht schon im Kühlschrank.
>
> Tarek: Und wann kommt die Waschmaschine?
>
> Lena: Morgen. Mein Vermieter sagt, sie muss in den Keller. Da unten stehen alle Waschmaschinen.

In English:

> Tarek: Right, that's the last box. Where should I put it?
>
> Lena: What does it say on it? Ah, "kitchen". Put it next to the cooker, please.
>
> Tarek: And the big crate with the books? It's really heavy!
>
> Lena: That goes in the living room, between the sofa and the desk. I'll put the books on the shelf later.
>
> Tarek: OK. Tell me, where's the rug actually? Yesterday it was lying in the hall.
>
> Lena: I've already put it in the bedroom. And the curtains are already hanging at the window. Look!
>
> Tarek: Very nice. And where are the cushions?
>
> Lena: They're in the blue bag on the balcony. Just put them on the sofa.
>
> Tarek: Phew. Can I sit down for a moment now?
>
> Lena: Of course! Sit down! I'll get us something to drink. The beer is already in the fridge.
>
> Tarek: And when is the washing machine coming?
>
> Lena: Tomorrow. My landlord says it has to go in the cellar. All the washing machines are down there.

Look at the pairs: *stell ihn neben den Herd* (accusative, putting) against *Das Bier steht im Kühlschrank* (dative, position). *Er hat im Flur gelegen* is the perfect of *liegen*; *Den habe ich ins Schlafzimmer gelegt* is the perfect of *legen*. (*drauf* = on it, *der Sack* = bag or sack, *Setz dich!* = sit down, *da unten* = down there.)

## Pronunciation

- *Vorhang*: the *v* sounds like *f*: FOR-hang.
- *Teppich* ends in the soft *ch* of *ich*, not in "k".
- *Kaution*: *-tion* is pronounced "tsee-ohn", stressed at the end: kau-TSION.
- *Spülmaschine*: *sch* as in "shoe", stress on the first part: SPÜL-ma-schi-ne.
- *liegen* (long *ie*) and *legen* (long *e*) sound different; so do *sitzen* (short *i*) and *setzen* (short *e*). Say them slowly in pairs.
- *staubsaugen*: *au* twice, like English "ow": STAUB-sau-gen.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich lege das Buch auf dem Tisch.* — Putting is movement: *auf den Tisch*.
- *Das Buch liegt auf den Tisch.* — Lying is position: *auf dem Tisch*.
- *Ich stehe die Flasche in den Kühlschrank.* — *stehen* has no object. For putting, use *stellen*: *Ich stelle die Flasche …*
- *Ich sitze mich.* — To sit down is *sich setzen*: *Ich setze mich.*
- *Ich habe das Bild an die Wand gehangen.* — When you hang something, use the regular perfect: *gehängt*. *gehangen* is only for "was hanging".
- *Ich gehe in das Kino* sounds stiff; Germans say *ins Kino*.
- Using *Wohin?* logic with *aus*, *bei*, *zu* or *nach*. These are dative-only prepositions: *Ich gehe zum Arzt* (not *zu den Arzt*) even though you move.

## Key points

- *in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen* take the dative for *Wo?* (position) and the accusative for *Wohin?* (movement to a new place).
- Accusative = arrow, dative = dot.
- Contractions: *im, am* (dative), *ins, ans* (accusative).
- Putting verbs are regular and take an object: *stellen, legen, setzen, hängen (gehängt), stecken* + accusative.
- Being verbs have no object: *stehen (gestanden), liegen (gelegen), sitzen (gesessen), hängen (gehangen)* are irregular; *stecken (gesteckt)* is regular in both meanings. They take the dative.
- *stehen* for things upright, *liegen* for things flat; *sich setzen* = to sit down.
- *einziehen in* + accusative, *ausziehen aus* + dative; both use *sein* in the perfect.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Planning a trip
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you bought train tickets and talked about a holiday you had already taken. Now you plan one: you book a room, ask about breakfast, say how long you're staying and from when, and talk about what you will do there. Two pieces of grammar help. The first is a set of **[[time prepositions]]** that answer "when?" and "how long?": *vor, seit, ab, bis, in, für*. The second is a group of small words that show direction (*hin, her, oben, unten, draußen, drinnen*). At the end you'll get a first look at the **[[future tense]]** with *werden*.

## Time prepositions

You know some of these from A1. Here they are side by side:

| Preposition | Case | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *vor* | dative | … ago (looking back from now) | *vor einem Jahr* — a year ago |
| *seit* | dative | since, for (started in the past and still going on) | *seit zwei Wochen* — for two weeks (and still) |
| *ab* | dative | from … on, starting | *ab Montag, ab dem ersten Mai* — from Monday, from the first of May |
| *bis* | (accusative) | until, by | *bis Freitag, bis zum Wochenende* — until Friday, until the weekend |
| *in* | dative | in (from now into the future) | *in drei Tagen* — in three days |
| *für* | accusative | for (a planned length of time) | *für eine Woche* — for a week |
| *nach* | dative | after | *nach dem Frühstück* — after breakfast |

### vor and in: the past and the future seen from today

*vor* points back from now, *in* points forward from now. English puts "ago" after the noun; German puts *vor* in front, with the dative:

- *Ich war vor zwei Jahren in Wien.* — I was in Vienna two years ago.
- *Vor einer Woche habe ich das Hotel gebucht.* — I booked the hotel a week ago.
- *In drei Wochen fliegen wir nach Portugal.* — We're flying to Portugal in three weeks.
- *Der Zug fährt in zehn Minuten ab.* — The train leaves in ten minutes.

Plural nouns in the dative end in *-n*: *Tage → vor zwei Tagen*, *Monate → vor zwei Monaten*, *Jahre → in fünf Jahren*. Plurals that already end in *-n* don't change: *in drei Wochen, vor zwei Stunden*.

### seit or für?

Both can be "for" in English, and this is a classic trap.

- *seit* + dative: something started in the past and is still true now. German uses the **[[present tense]]**: *Ich wohne seit drei Jahren in Hamburg.* — I have lived in Hamburg for three years (and still do).
- *für* + accusative: a planned or limited length of time, often in the future: *Wir fahren für eine Woche an die Ostsee.* — We're going to the Baltic for a week.

Very often German simply leaves *für* out: *Wir bleiben zwei Nächte.* — We're staying (for) two nights.

### ab and bis: from and until

*ab* marks a starting point: *Das Frühstück gibt es ab sieben Uhr.* — Breakfast is from seven. *Ab nächster Woche habe ich Urlaub.* — From next week I'm on holiday. *bis* marks the end: *Das Zimmer ist bis Sonntag frei.* With an article, *bis* almost always joins with *zu*: *bis zum Montag, bis zur Abfahrt*. Put both together for a range: *von Montag bis Freitag* or *ab Montag bis Freitag*.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| *Wann?* — when? | *vor einem Monat, in zwei Tagen, nach dem Essen* |
| *Seit wann?* — since when? | *seit Montag, seit einem Jahr* |
| *Ab wann?* — from when? | *ab dem 3. Juli* (*ab dem dritten Juli*) |
| *Bis wann?* — until when? | *bis Sonntag, bis zum 10. Juli* |
| *Wie lange?* — how long? | *eine Woche, für zwei Nächte, drei Tage lang* |

On a timeline, with "now" (*jetzt*) in the middle:

![A timeline with jetzt in the middle, the past on the left and the future on the right. vor einem Jahr (ago): an arrow from now back to a point in the past. seit drei Jahren (since, for, still true): a bar from a point in the past up to now, continuing a little past now. in drei Tagen (in, from now): an arrow from now forward to a point in the future. ab Montag (from … on): a bar starting at a future point and running on to the right with an arrowhead. bis Freitag (until): a bar from now that stops at a point in the future. für eine Woche (for, planned): a bar with a clear start and end in the future.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Booking a room

Some useful words before the dialogue. A hotel, guesthouse or campsite is *eine Unterkunft* (accommodation). You can stay in *ein Einzelzimmer* (single room) or *ein Doppelzimmer* (double room), and you pay per *Übernachtung* (night's stay). *Halbpension* means breakfast and dinner are included. You *buchen* (book) online, or *reservieren* (reserve) a room or a table by phone; you then have *eine Buchung* or *eine Reservierung*. When you arrive you go to *die Rezeption* (reception), where you are *der Gast* (guest). Travelling abroad you need *den Pass* (passport), sometimes *ein Visum* (visa), and you pass through *den Zoll* (customs) with your *Gepäck* (luggage).

## Dialogue: On the phone to a guesthouse

Jonas wants to book a room for a trip to the Black Forest (*der Schwarzwald*).

> Rezeption: Pension Waldblick, guten Tag. Was kann ich für Sie tun?
>
> Jonas: Guten Tag. Ich möchte ein Doppelzimmer reservieren, ab dem 14. August, für fünf Nächte.
>
> Rezeption: Also vom 14. bis zum 19. August. Einen Moment … Ja, da haben wir noch ein Zimmer frei, mit Balkon.
>
> Jonas: Super. Was kostet die Übernachtung?
>
> Rezeption: 95 Euro pro Nacht mit Frühstück. Mit Halbpension sind es 125 Euro.
>
> Jonas: Nur Frühstück, bitte. Mittags sind wir sowieso unterwegs. Ab wann gibt es Frühstück?
>
> Rezeption: Ab halb sieben, bis zehn Uhr. Möchten Sie gleich buchen?
>
> Jonas: Ja, gern. Kann man bei Ihnen auch parken?
>
> Rezeption: Natürlich, direkt hinter dem Haus. Wann kommen Sie denn an?
>
> Jonas: Wahrscheinlich gegen fünf. Wir fahren in Köln um elf los.
>
> Rezeption: Kein Problem, die Rezeption ist bis acht Uhr abends offen. Ich schicke Ihnen die Buchung per E-Mail.

In English:

> Reception: Pension Waldblick, good afternoon. What can I do for you?
>
> Jonas: Good afternoon. I'd like to reserve a double room from the 14th of August, for five nights.
>
> Reception: So from the 14th to the 19th of August. One moment … Yes, we still have a room free, with a balcony.
>
> Jonas: Great. How much is a night?
>
> Reception: 95 euros a night with breakfast. With half board it's 125 euros.
>
> Jonas: Just breakfast, please. We'll be out and about at lunchtime anyway. From what time is breakfast?
>
> Reception: From half past six until ten. Would you like to book straight away?
>
> Jonas: Yes, please. Can you park at your place too?
>
> Reception: Of course, right behind the house. When will you arrive?
>
> Jonas: Probably around five. We're leaving Cologne at eleven.
>
> Reception: No problem, reception is open until eight in the evening. I'll send you the booking by e-mail.

*Die Pension* is a small guesthouse. (*sowieso* = anyway, *wahrscheinlich* = probably, *gegen fünf* = around five, *losfahren* = to set off.) Notice *ab dem 14. August* (dative: *ab dem vierzehnten*) and *für fünf Nächte* (accusative plural).

## Where to and where from: hin and her

German shows the direction of movement relative to the speaker. *hin* means away from the speaker, *her* means towards the speaker. You know *wohin* (where to) and *woher* (where from); they are built the same way.

![Three figures on a line. In the middle is the speaker, labeled ich. A person on the left walks towards the speaker along an arrow labeled her, with the example Komm her! (towards me). From the speaker another arrow points away to a lake on the right, labeled hin, with the example Ich fahre hin. (away from me). Below: woher? = where from (towards me); wohin? = where to (away from me).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Wo gehst du hin?* — Where are you going? (= *Wohin gehst du?*, very common in speech)
- *Komm her!* — Come here!
- *Wo kommst du her?* — Where do you come from?
- *Wir fahren morgen zum See. Fährst du auch hin?* — We're driving to the lake tomorrow. Are you going there too?

The two little words combine with direction words: *hinauf* (up, away from me), *herunter* (down, towards me), *hinein* (in), *heraus* (out). In everyday speech they shrink to *rauf, runter, rein, raus*, and Germans often don't care about *hin* or *her* any more: *Komm rein!* — Come in! *Ich gehe kurz raus.* — I'm just popping out.

### oben, unten, draußen, drinnen

These words describe a place (*Wo?*). For a direction (*Wohin?*), put *nach* in front:

| Where? (place) | Where to? (direction) |
|---|---|
| *oben* — upstairs, at the top | *nach oben* — upstairs, up |
| *unten* — downstairs, below | *nach unten* — downstairs, down |
| *draußen* — outside | *nach draußen* (or *raus*) — outside, out |
| *drinnen* — inside, indoors | *nach drinnen* (or *rein*) — inside, in |

- *Das Zimmer ist oben, im zweiten Stock.* — The room is upstairs, on the second floor.
- *Bringen Sie das Gepäck bitte nach oben?* — Will you take the luggage upstairs, please?
- *Bei schönem Wetter frühstücken wir draußen.* — In nice weather we have breakfast outside.
- *Es regnet, lass uns drinnen bleiben.* — It's raining, let's stay inside.

*unterwegs* means "on the way, out and about": *Wir sind den ganzen Tag unterwegs.*

## Talking about the future

German usually talks about the future with the present tense and a time word, as you have done since A1: *Morgen fahren wir nach Freiburg. In zwei Wochen fliege ich nach Rom.* That's normal and correct.

There is also a future tense with *werden*: a form of *werden* in position 2, the infinitive at the end. You know *werden* as "to become"; here it works like English "will".

| | werden | + infinitive at the end |
|---|---|---|
| ich | *werde* | *… viel wandern* |
| du | *wirst* | *… den Pass brauchen* |
| er / sie / es | *wird* | *… schön werden* |
| wir | *werden* | *… im Zelt schlafen* |
| ihr | *werdet* | *… viel sehen* |
| sie / Sie | *werden* | *… pünktlich ankommen* |

Use it mainly for:

- predictions: *Morgen wird es regnen.* — It will rain tomorrow. *Das wird teuer.* — That will be expensive.
- promises and firm plans: *Ich werde dich jeden Tag anrufen.* — I will call you every day.

When the time is clear from a time word, the present tense is more natural: *Nächstes Jahr machen wir eine Reise nach Kanada* sounds better than a sentence full of *werden*.

## A text: A postcard from a campsite

> Liebe Oma, seit vier Tagen sind wir jetzt am Bodensee. Wir schlafen im Zelt auf einem Campingplatz direkt am Wasser. Morgens ist es draußen noch kalt, aber mittags scheint die Sonne. Gestern haben wir mit dem Schiff eine Stadt in der Schweiz besichtigt. Mein Pass war natürlich im Auto, aber am Zoll hat niemand gefragt! Der Reiseführer sagt, es gibt hier viele Sehenswürdigkeiten, aber die Kinder wollen nur baden. In drei Tagen packen wir unsere Reisetaschen und fahren nach Hause. Ich werde dir viele Fotos zeigen! Liebe Grüße, Miriam

Dear Grandma, we've been at Lake Constance for four days now. We're sleeping in a tent on a campsite right by the water. In the mornings it's still cold outside, but at midday the sun shines. Yesterday we took a boat to visit a town in Switzerland. My passport was in the car, of course, but nobody asked at customs! The guidebook says there are lots of sights here, but the children only want to swim. In three days we'll pack our travel bags and drive home. I'll show you lots of photos! Love, Miriam

(*das Schiff* = ship, boat; *baden* = to swim, bathe.)

## Pronunciation

- *Sehenswürdigkeit*: long, but regular: SEH-ens-wür-dig-keit; the *h* is silent, the *-ig-* sounds like "ich".
- *Rezeption*: re-tsep-TSION; both *z* and *-tion* have a "ts" sound.
- *Visum*: the *v* is pronounced like English *v* here (a Latin word): VEE-zoom.
- *Gepäck*: stress on the second syllable: ge-PÄCK.
- *draußen*: *au* as in "ow", *ß* as a sharp *s*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich war in Wien zwei Jahre vor.* — *vor* goes in front: *vor zwei Jahren*.
- *vor zwei Jahre* — dative plural needs *-n*: *vor zwei Jahren*.
