lessons.title: School, courses and learning; whose is it?
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 17 you talked about work. Before work comes learning, and in German-speaking countries learning never quite stops: school, vocational training, university, then evening classes and further training for adults. This lesson gives you the words to talk about schools, subjects, courses and exams, and to sign up for a course yourself.

The grammar answers a small but constant question: whose is it? You'll learn two everyday ways to show possession, *Annas Buch* and *das Buch von meiner Schwester*, and you'll learn to recognize a third, more formal one, the **[[genitive]]**: *das Buch meiner Schwester*. Finally, we review separable and inseparable verbs, because the language of learning is full of them: *sich anmelden, durchfallen, bestehen, wiederholen, verbessern*.

## Schools in Germany

Every German state (*Bundesland*) runs its own schools, so details differ, but the outline is similar everywhere. (Austria and Switzerland have their own systems; in both, the final exam at a Gymnasium is called *die Matura*.)

| Stage | School | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| age 6–10 | *die Grundschule* (lesson 2) | primary school, four years (six in Berlin and Brandenburg) |
| from about 10 | *das Gymnasium* | academic secondary school; ends with *das Abitur*, the exam you need for university |
| from about 10 | *die Realschule* | secondary school up to grade 10 |
| from about 10 | *die Gesamtschule* and others | comprehensive schools that combine the types |
| after school | *die Berufsschule* | vocational school, one or two days a week during an *Ausbildung* (apprenticeship) |
| after the Abitur | *die Universität* (A1), *die Hochschule* | university, college |

The usual routes, simplified (there are more, for example from the *Realschule* on to the *Abitur*):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The main routes through German schools, simplified
  accDescr: Everyone starts at the Grundschule, from about age 6 to 10. Then pupils go to a Gymnasium, a Realschule or a Gesamtschule. The Gymnasium and the Gesamtschule can lead to the Abitur, which opens the way to a university or Hochschule, or to an Ausbildung. The Realschule and the Gesamtschule usually lead to an Ausbildung with the Berufsschule.
  G["Grundschule, age 6 to 10"] --> Gy["Gymnasium"]
  G --> R["Realschule"]
  G --> Ge["Gesamtschule"]
  Gy --> Abi["Abitur"]
  Ge --> Abi
  R --> Aus["Ausbildung and Berufsschule"]
  Ge --> Aus
  Abi --> Uni["Universität or Hochschule"]
  Abi --> Aus
```

A *Gymnasium* is not a sports hall: that false friend is *die Turnhalle*. The plural is *die Gymnasien*. And *das Abitur* (often just *Abi*) is a school-leaving exam, not a university degree: *Ich habe 2015 Abitur gemacht.* — I did my Abitur in 2015.

In an *Ausbildung*, young people work in a company and go to the *Berufsschule* at the same time. Many well-paid jobs, from electrician to bank clerk, start this way.

## School subjects

| Subject | German |
|---|---|
| maths | *die Mathematik*, usually *Mathe* |
| biology, chemistry, physics | *die Biologie, die Chemie, die Physik* |
| geography | *die Erdkunde* (also *Geografie*) |
| history | *die Geschichte* |
| art, music, PE | *die Kunst, die Musik, der Sport* |
| German, English, French | *Deutsch, Englisch, Französisch* |
| foreign language | *die Fremdsprache* |

![Six school subjects as pictures: a board with sums for Mathe, a globe for Erdkunde, musical notes for Musik, a paint palette for Kunst, a football for Sport and a flask for Chemie](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*die Geschichte* is the word you know for "story"; it also means history. *Physik* (phü-SIK) and *Chemie* (che-MIE) are both stressed on the last syllable. In Germany *Chemie* starts with a *ch* like in *ich*; in Austria and the south you'll hear a *k*.

Talk about subjects without an article: *Ich habe heute Mathe und Chemie.* — I have maths and chemistry today. *Mein Lieblingsfach war Erdkunde.* — My favourite subject was geography.

The lessons themselves are *der Unterricht* (no plural): *Der Unterricht beginnt um acht.* — Lessons start at eight. The verb is *unterrichten*, to teach: *Sie unterrichtet Kunst an einem Gymnasium.* — She teaches art at a Gymnasium.

## Courses for adults

Adults learn at a *Volkshochschule* (VHS), a public adult education centre found in almost every town, or at private schools and online. Learning for your job is *die Weiterbildung* — further training.

- *Ich möchte mich für den Spanischkurs anmelden.* — I'd like to sign up for the Spanish course.
- *Die Anmeldung ist bis zum 15. September möglich.* — Registration is possible until 15 September.
- *Die Gebühr beträgt 120 Euro.* — The fee is 120 euros. (*betragen* = to amount to)
- *Der Kurs hat zwölf Teilnehmer.* — The course has twelve participants. (One woman is *eine Teilnehmerin*.)
- *Am Ende bekommen Sie ein Zertifikat.* — At the end you get a certificate.

And the exam: *Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden!* — I passed the exam! The opposite is *durchfallen*: *Er ist bei der Prüfung durchgefallen.* — He failed the exam. (You'll also hear *durch die Prüfung gefallen*.) For small tests in class Germans say *der Test* (plural *die Tests*). *das Ergebnis* is the result: *Wann bekommen wir die Ergebnisse?*

If you have no idea, say so: *Keine Ahnung!* — No idea! (*die Ahnung* = idea, notion; mostly used in *keine Ahnung haben*: *Ich habe keine Ahnung von Physik.* — I know nothing about physics.)

## Whose is it? Name + s

With a name, German adds *-s* to the name and puts it in front of the thing, like English, but without an apostrophe:

- *Annas Buch* — Anna's book
- *Peters Lehrerin* — Peter's teacher
- *Frau Wagners Kurs* — Ms Wagner's course
- *Deutschlands Schulen* — Germany's schools

The thing has no article: not *das Annas Buch*, just *Annas Buch*.

When the name already ends in an *s*-sound (*s, ß, x, z*), you write an apostrophe instead of the *-s*: *Hans' Zeugnis, Max' Fahrrad*. These are awkward to say, so in speech people prefer *von*: *das Fahrrad von Max*.

## Whose is it? von + dative

For everything that isn't a name, everyday German uses *von* + dative after the thing:

| Possessor | Example |
|---|---|
| masculine | *das Auto von meinem Bruder* — my brother's car |
| feminine | *der Laptop von der Lehrerin* — the teacher's laptop |
| neuter | *das Zimmer von dem Kind* → *vom Kind* — the child's room |
| plural | *die Hefte von den Schülern* — the pupils' notebooks |

*von* always takes the **[[dative]]**, so remember the dative endings: *dem/einem/meinem* (masculine and neuter), *der/einer/meiner* (feminine), *den … -n* (plural). *von dem* contracts to *vom*.

*von* also works with names, and it's the natural choice in conversation: *Das ist die Tasche von Lisa.* — That's Lisa's bag. The question is *Von wem ist das?* — Whose is that? (Or, from lesson 7, *Wem gehört das?*)

Which way to choose? This chart puts the three patterns of this lesson side by side:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Three ways to say whose something is
  accDescr: If the owner is a name, add s to the name and put it first, as in Annas Buch. If the owner is anyone else, use von plus the dative in everyday speech, as in das Auto von meinem Bruder. In written German you will also read the genitive, as in das Auto meines Bruders; at this level you only need to recognize it.
  A{"Who owns it?"} -- "a name" --> B["name + s: Annas Buch"]
  A -- "anyone else, in speech" --> C["von + dative: das Auto von meinem Bruder"]
  A -- "anyone else, in writing" --> D["genitive, recognize it: das Auto meines Bruders"]
```

## The genitive: recognize it

Written German, and careful speech, have a fourth case for possession: the genitive. It comes after the noun, like *von*, but has its own articles:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| definite | *des Lehrers* | *der Lehrerin* | *des Kindes* | *der Kinder* |
| indefinite / my | *eines / meines Bruders* | *einer / meiner Schwester* | *eines / meines Kindes* | *meiner Kinder* |

Masculine and neuter nouns add *-s* or *-es*. You don't need to produce these yet; you need to recognize them in fixed expressions and texts:

- *am Anfang des Kurses* — at the beginning of the course
- *am Ende der Woche* — at the end of the week
- *die Hälfte der Teilnehmer* — half of the participants
- *der Name des Lehrers* — the teacher's name
- *die Hauptstadt Österreichs* — the capital of Austria (a name just adds *-s*, as in *Annas*)

The question word is *wessen?* — whose? *Wessen Heft ist das?* You'll read it more than you'll say it; in speech, *Von wem …?* is normal.

## Review: separable and inseparable verbs in learning

Many verbs about learning have prefixes. Remember the rule: stressed prefixes separate, unstressed ones don't.

| Verb | Present | Perfect | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| *sich ANmelden* | *Ich melde mich an.* | *Ich habe mich angemeldet.* | separable |
| *DURCHfallen* | *Er fällt durch.* | *Er ist durchgefallen.* | separable, *sein* |
| *MITschreiben* | *Sie schreibt mit.* | *Sie hat mitgeschrieben.* | separable |
| *beSTEHen* | *Du bestehst bestimmt.* | *Du hast bestanden.* | inseparable |
| *verBESSern* | *Ich verbessere meine Aussprache.* | *Ich habe sie verbessert.* | inseparable |
| *unterRICHten* | *Er unterrichtet Mathe.* | *Er hat Mathe unterrichtet.* | inseparable |
| *wiederHOLen* | *Wir wiederholen die Wörter.* | *Wir haben sie wiederholt.* | inseparable (repeat, revise) |

Inseparable verbs never get *ge-* in the perfect: *verbessert*, not *geverbessert*. *-ieren* verbs don't either: *Ich habe Biologie studiert.* (*mitschreiben* = to take notes.)

With zu + infinitive from lesson 17: *Ich habe vergessen, mich anzumelden.* — I forgot to sign up. *Ich versuche, meine Noten zu verbessern.* — I'm trying to improve my grades.

## Dialogue: at the Volkshochschule

Lukas wants to sign up for an English course and talks to the woman at the registration desk.

> Lukas: Guten Tag. Ich möchte mich für einen Englischkurs anmelden. Ich brauche Englisch für meine Arbeit.
>
> Frau Haas: Gern. Haben Sie schon Englisch gelernt?
>
> Lukas: Ja, in der Schule, aber das ist lange her. Ich habe die Realschule besucht, und Englisch war nie mein Lieblingsfach. Ich hatte immer Angst, Fehler zu machen.
>
> Frau Haas: Kein Problem. Am Anfang des Kurses machen alle Teilnehmer einen kleinen Test. Dann wissen wir, welches Niveau für Sie richtig ist.
>
> Lukas: Und was passiert, wenn ich beim Test durchfalle?
>
> Frau Haas: Keine Sorge! Bei diesem Test kann man nicht durchfallen. Er zeigt nur, was Sie schon können. Der Unterricht ist dienstags und donnerstags von 18 bis 19.30 Uhr.
>
> Lukas: Das passt gut. Wie hoch ist die Gebühr?
>
> Frau Haas: 145 Euro für zwölf Wochen. Manche Firmen bezahlen die Weiterbildung ihrer Mitarbeiter. Fragen Sie doch mal Ihren Chef.
>
> Lukas: Gute Idee. Bekomme ich am Ende ein Zertifikat?
>
> Frau Haas: Ja, wenn Sie die Prüfung bestehen. Hier ist das Anmeldeformular. Füllen Sie es bitte aus und unterschreiben Sie hier unten.

In English:

> Lukas: Hello. I'd like to sign up for an English course. I need English for my work.
>
> Ms Haas: Certainly. Have you learned English before?
>
> Lukas: Yes, at school, but that was a long time ago. I went to a Realschule, and English was never my favourite subject. I was always afraid of making mistakes.
>
> Ms Haas: No problem. At the beginning of the course all participants take a little test. Then we know which level is right for you.
>
> Lukas: And what happens if I fail the test?
>
> Ms Haas: Don't worry! You can't fail this test. It only shows what you can already do. Lessons are on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6 to 7.30 p.m.
>
> Lukas: That suits me. How much is the fee?
>
> Ms Haas: 145 euros for twelve weeks. Some companies pay for their employees' further training. Why don't you ask your boss?
>
> Lukas: Good idea. Do I get a certificate at the end?
>
> Ms Haas: Yes, if you pass the exam. Here's the registration form. Please fill it in and sign down here.

Find the genitives: *am Anfang des Kurses* and *die Weiterbildung ihrer Mitarbeiter* (their employees' further training). In speech, Frau Haas could also say *die Weiterbildung von ihren Mitarbeitern*. *das ist lange her* = that was long ago; *das Niveau* = level (pronounced the French way, "nee-VOH").

## A short text: Mias Weg

> Mia ist in Leipzig aufgewachsen. Nach der Grundschule ist sie aufs Gymnasium gegangen. Mathe und Physik fand sie schwer, aber in Kunst hatte sie immer gute Noten. Nach dem Abitur hat sie keinen Studienplatz bekommen und eine Ausbildung als Fotografin gemacht. Heute hat sie ein eigenes Studio. Am Wochenende besucht sie einen Kurs an der Volkshochschule, denn sie will ihr Italienisch verbessern. Das Studio von Mias Mutter ist gleich nebenan.

Mia grew up in Leipzig. After primary school she went to the Gymnasium. She found maths and physics hard, but she always had good grades in art. After the Abitur she didn't get a university place and did an apprenticeship as a photographer. Today she has her own studio. At the weekend she takes a course at the Volkshochschule, because she wants to improve her Italian. Mia's mother's studio is right next door.

Notice *das Studio von Mias Mutter*: *von* for the studio, name + *s* for the mother. (*eigen* = own; *nebenan* = next door; *der Studienplatz* = a place at university.)

## Common mistakes

- *Anna's Buch* — No apostrophe in German after an ordinary name: *Annas Buch*.
- *das Annas Buch* — No article before the name + s form: *Annas Buch*.
- *das Auto von mein Bruder* — *von* takes the dative: *von meinem Bruder*.
- *Ich bin in der Prüfung durchgefallen* is fine in speech, but the verb takes *sein*, not *haben*: *Ich habe durchgefallen* is wrong.
- *Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht* means "I took the exam", not that you passed it. "Passed" is *bestanden*.
- *Er hat Englisch geunterrichtet.* — *unterrichten* is inseparable: *hat unterrichtet*.
- Using *Gymnasium* for "gym" — a *Gymnasium* is a school. The gym where you work out is *das Fitnessstudio*; the one at school is *die Turnhalle*.

## Key points

- Schools: *Grundschule*, then *Gymnasium* (to the *Abitur*), *Realschule* or *Gesamtschule*; *Berufsschule* alongside an *Ausbildung*.
- Subjects take no article: *Ich habe Mathe.* *Geschichte* = story and history.
- Courses: *sich für einen Kurs anmelden*, *die Anmeldung*, *die Gebühr*, *die Teilnehmer*; exams: *bestehen* (pass), *durchfallen* (fail, with *sein*).
- Possession with names: *Annas Buch* (no apostrophe, no article). Everything else in speech: *von* + dative, *das Auto von meinem Bruder*.
- The genitive (*des Lehrers, der Lehrerin*) is mainly written; recognize it in phrases like *am Ende der Woche*.
- Stressed prefixes separate (*anmelden, durchfallen*); unstressed ones don't and take no *ge-* (*bestanden, verbessert, unterrichtet*).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Banks, offices and phone calls
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Sooner or later everyone living in a German-speaking country has to open a bank account, register an address, deal with insurance or get something repaired. These conversations are polite, a little formal and full of fixed phrases, and many of them happen on the phone. This lesson gives you the words and the scripts.

The grammar builds on lessons 3, 4 and 15. You'll practise the polite **[[indirect question]]** (*Können Sie mir sagen, wo das Bürgeramt ist?*), which is the most useful sentence in any office, and you'll meet a verb that lets other people do the work: *lassen*. *Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren* means you're having your bike repaired, not repairing it yourself.

## At the bank

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *das Konto, die Konten* | account |
| *das Girokonto* | current account, checking account |
| *ein Konto eröffnen* | to open an account |
| *die EC-Karte / die Kreditkarte* | debit card / credit card |
| *der Geldautomat* | cash machine, ATM |
| *Geld abheben* | to withdraw money |
| *Geld einzahlen* | to pay money in |
| *überweisen / die Überweisung* | to transfer / bank transfer |

German life runs on the *Girokonto*: your salary arrives there, and your rent goes out by *Überweisung*. Many Germans still pay cash, so you'll often hear *Ich muss noch schnell Geld abheben.* — I just need to get some cash. The card most people use is still called *EC-Karte* in everyday speech, although its official name has been *Girocard* since 2007 (and many banks now issue Visa or Mastercard debit cards instead).

Watch the verbs:

- *abheben* and *einzahlen* are separable: *Ich hebe 100 Euro ab. Er zahlt das Geld ein.* *abheben* is irregular: *hat abgehoben*.
- *überweisen* is inseparable: *Ich überweise dir das Geld morgen.* — I'll transfer the money to you tomorrow. Perfect: *hat überwiesen*.

## At the office: Amt and Behörde

*die Behörde* is any public authority; *das Amt* (plural *die Ämter*) is a specific office: *das Finanzamt* (tax office), *das Standesamt* (registry office, where civil weddings happen). In big cities, the office for passports and addresses is *das Bürgeramt* (in some towns *Bürgerbüro*).

In Germany, when you move into a new flat you must register your address there within two weeks of moving in: *Sie müssen sich beim Bürgeramt anmelden.* (Austria is stricter: three days.) You met *sich anmelden* in lesson 18 for courses; here it means to register an address. You get a written confirmation on the spot (*die Meldebestätigung*), and if you later need official proof of your address, you can ask for a *Meldebescheinigung*. *die Bescheinigung* is any official certificate or confirmation on paper.

To get anything from an authority, you fill in and submit (*stellen*) *einen Antrag* — an application form, a request: *Ich möchte einen neuen Pass beantragen.* — I'd like to apply for a new passport. *beantragen* is inseparable: *Ich habe einen Pass beantragt.* Compare *sich bewerben* (lesson 17), which is for jobs and places, never for documents.

## Insurance, damage and the police

*die Versicherung* means both insurance and the insurance company. *versichern* is to insure: *Ist das Fahrrad versichert?* — Is the bike insured? Most households in Germany (about 85 percent) have *eine Haftpflichtversicherung*, which pays if you damage someone else's things.

If something happens, you *melden* it — report it: *Ich möchte einen Schaden melden.* — I'd like to report some damage. *der Schaden* (plural *die Schäden*) is damage or a loss. A theft goes to *die Polizei*: *Wir haben den Diebstahl bei der Polizei gemeldet.* — We reported the theft to the police. (*der Diebstahl* = theft.)

Things that are broken go to a repair shop: *die Werkstatt* (plural *die Werkstätten*), for cars and bikes. The repair is *die Reparatur*, and the verb is *reparieren*: *Die Reparatur kostet 80 Euro.*

## Polite indirect questions

A direct question can sound abrupt to a stranger: *Wo ist das Bürgeramt?* Put a polite frame in front and it turns into an indirect question, with the verb at the end, just as you learned in lesson 4:

| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| *Wo ist der Geldautomat?* | *Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Geldautomat ist?* |
| *Wann hat das Amt geöffnet?* | *Wissen Sie, wann das Amt geöffnet hat?* |
| *Wie lange dauert die Reparatur?* | *Könnten Sie mir sagen, wie lange die Reparatur dauert?* |
| *Kann ich hier Geld einzahlen?* | *Ich möchte wissen, ob ich hier Geld einzahlen kann.* |
| *Brauche ich einen Termin?* | *Wissen Sie, ob ich einen Termin brauche?* |

The rules in one list:

- W-questions keep their question word: *wo, wann, wie lange, was, warum…*
- Yes/no questions use *ob* (whether).
- The conjugated verb goes to the end; a separable verb joins up again: *ob ich hier Geld einzahlen kann*, *wann der Zug ankommt*.
- The question mark belongs to the frame: *Wissen Sie, …?* gets one; *Ich möchte wissen, …* gets a full stop.

Here are the same rules as a procedure you can follow every time:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Turning a direct question into a polite indirect question
  accDescr: Start with a polite frame such as Können Sie mir sagen or Wissen Sie. If the question has a question word like wo or wann, keep it; if it is a yes/no question, use ob. Then move the conjugated verb to the end, joining a separable verb back together. Finally, end with a question mark if the frame is a question, or a full stop after Ich möchte wissen.
  A["1. Polite frame: Können Sie mir sagen, ... / Wissen Sie, ..."] --> B{"2. Does the question have a question word?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["keep it: wo, wann, wie lange ..."]
  B -- "no, yes/no question" --> D["use ob"]
  C --> E["3. Conjugated verb to the end: wo das Amt ist"]
  D --> E
  E --> F["4. ? after a question frame, . after Ich möchte wissen"]
```

*Könnten Sie …?* from lesson 15 is the most polite frame of all: *Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, welche Unterlagen ich mitbringen muss?* — Could you please tell me which documents I need to bring?

## lassen: having something done

*lassen* + infinitive means you get someone else to do something. Like a modal verb, it sends a second verb to the end without *zu*:

- *Ich lasse mein Auto in der Werkstatt reparieren.* — I'm having my car repaired at the garage.
- *Wir lassen die Wohnung streichen.* — We're having the flat painted.
- *Sie lässt sich die Haare schneiden.* — She's having her hair cut.

The picture shows the difference between doing it yourself and having it done:

![Two pictures. Left: a woman repairs her own bike with a spanner, captioned Ich repariere mein Fahrrad. Right: a mechanic in a workshop repairs her bike while she watches, captioned Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*lassen* changes its stem: *ich lasse, du lässt, er/sie/es lässt, wir lassen, ihr lasst, sie lassen*.

It has two other everyday meanings:

- to let, allow: *Lass mich bitte ausreden!* — Please let me finish (speaking)! *Meine Eltern lassen mich nicht allein reisen.* — My parents don't let me travel alone.
- to leave something somewhere: *Ich habe meinen Schirm im Bus gelassen.* — I left my umbrella on the bus.

In the perfect, when *lassen* has a second verb, you'll see two infinitives at the end: *Ich habe das Fahrrad reparieren lassen.* — I had the bike repaired. Recognize this for now; it's the same pattern modal verbs use in the perfect (*Ich habe arbeiten müssen*).

## On the phone

| Situation | German | English |
|---|---|---|
| Line busy | *Es ist besetzt.* | It's engaged / busy. |
| Being put through | *Einen Moment, ich verbinde Sie.* | One moment, I'll put you through. |
| Wrong department | *Da sind Sie bei mir falsch.* | You've got the wrong person. |
| Calling back | *Kann ich Sie zurückrufen?* | Can I call you back? |
| Answering machine | *Bitte sprechen Sie nach dem Signalton.* | Please speak after the tone. |
| Not hearing well | *Die Verbindung ist schlecht.* | The line is bad. |

*verbinden* (to connect, put through; *hat verbunden*) and *zurückrufen* (separable; *hat zurückgerufen*) are the key verbs. A voicemail box is *die Mailbox* on a mobile; the machine on a landline is *der Anrufbeantworter*, literally "call answerer", often shortened to *AB* (ah-BEH).

### Spelling and numbers

Offices always want your name spelled. You can spell with words: *M wie Martha*. The traditional German spelling alphabet uses first names (*A wie Anton, B wie Berta, C wie Cäsar*) and is still what most people use; since 2022 the official standard (DIN 5009) uses city names instead (*A wie Aachen, B wie Berlin, C wie Chemnitz*). Either is understood.

Phone numbers are read in single digits or in pairs: *0 30 – 45 67 89* is *null drei null, vier fünf, sechs sieben, acht neun* or *null dreißig, fünfundvierzig, siebenundsechzig, neunundachtzig*. On the phone, many people say *zwo* for *zwei* so it isn't confused with *drei*.

### Formal and informal

Everything in this lesson uses *Sie*. Offices, banks and insurance companies write *Sehr geehrte Frau Becker* or *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren* and end with *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*. Only friends and family get *Liebe Anna* and *Viele Grüße*. Lesson 23 covers letters and e-mails in detail.

## Dialogue: a lost wallet

Sara's wallet was stolen on the tram. She calls her bank.

> Bank: Rheintalbank Freiburg, guten Tag, Sie sprechen mit Herrn Yilmaz.
>
> Sara: Guten Tag, mein Name ist Sara Lindqvist. Man hat mir heute Morgen in der Straßenbahn das Portemonnaie gestohlen. Meine EC-Karte und meine Kreditkarte waren darin.
>
> Bank: Oh, das tut mir leid. Wie schreibt man Ihren Nachnamen?
>
> Sara: L wie Ludwig, I, N wie Nordpol, D wie Dora, Q, V, I, S, T.
>
> Bank: Danke. Ich sperre die Karten sofort. Haben Sie den Diebstahl schon bei der Polizei gemeldet?
>
> Sara: Nein, noch nicht. Können Sie mir sagen, ob ich das unbedingt machen muss?
>
> Bank: Ja, bitte melden Sie ihn. Sie brauchen eine Bescheinigung von der Polizei für Ihre Versicherung.
>
> Sara: Gut. Und wie bekomme ich jetzt Geld? Ich muss morgen die Miete überweisen.
>
> Bank: Überweisungen können Sie online machen. Und mit Ihrem Ausweis können Sie in jeder Filiale Geld abheben. Die neuen Karten schicken wir Ihnen in einer Woche.
>
> Sara: Wissen Sie, was die neuen Karten kosten?
>
> Bank: Das kann ich Ihnen leider nicht sagen. Da verbinde ich Sie mit meiner Kollegin. Einen Moment, bitte … Hm, es ist besetzt. Soll sie Sie zurückrufen?
>
> Sara: Ja, gern. Meine Nummer ist null eins sieben sechs, zwo drei, vier fünf, sechs sieben, acht neun.

In English:

> Bank: Rheintalbank Freiburg, hello, you're speaking to Mr Yilmaz.
>
> Sara: Hello, my name is Sara Lindqvist. Someone stole my wallet on the tram this morning. My debit card and my credit card were in it.
>
> Bank: Oh, I'm sorry. How do you spell your surname?
>
> Sara: L as in Ludwig, I, N as in Nordpol, D as in Dora, Q, V, I, S, T.
>
> Bank: Thank you. I'm blocking the cards immediately. Have you already reported the theft to the police?
>
> Sara: No, not yet. Can you tell me whether I really have to do that?
>
> Bank: Yes, please report it. You need a confirmation from the police for your insurance.
>
> Sara: All right. And how do I get money now? I have to transfer the rent tomorrow.
>
> Bank: You can do transfers online. And with your ID card you can withdraw money at any branch. We'll send you the new cards in a week.
>
> Sara: Do you know what the new cards cost?
>
> Bank: I'm afraid I can't tell you that. I'll put you through to my colleague. One moment, please … Hm, it's busy. Shall she call you back?
>
> Sara: Yes, please. My number is 0176 23 45 67 89.

*sperren* = to block (a card; in Germany you can also block cards at any time on *116 116*); *stehlen* = to steal (*hat gestohlen*); *die Filiale* = branch. *Man hat mir das Portemonnaie gestohlen* is how Germans report a theft when they don't know who did it.

## A message on the answering machine

> Guten Tag, hier ist die Fahrradwerkstatt Kessler. Das ist eine Nachricht für Herrn Becker. Ihr Fahrrad ist fertig, die Reparatur hat 65 Euro gekostet. Sie können es ab morgen um neun Uhr abholen. Wenn Sie Fragen haben, rufen Sie uns bitte unter 0761 – 33 82 14 zurück. Auf Wiederhören!

Hello, this is Kessler bicycle repairs. This is a message for Mr Becker. Your bike is ready; the repair cost 65 euros. You can pick it up from nine o'clock tomorrow. If you have any questions, please call us back on 0761 33 82 14. Goodbye!

*Auf Wiederhören* ("until we hear each other again") is the phone version of *Auf Wiedersehen*.

## Common mistakes

- *Können Sie mir sagen, wo ist die Bank?* — In an indirect question the verb goes to the end: *wo die Bank ist*.
- *Wissen Sie, wenn das Amt offen ist?* — "When" as a question word is *wann*; and "whether" is *ob*, not *wenn*: *Wissen Sie, ob das Amt heute offen ist?*
- *Ich lasse mein Auto zu reparieren.* — No *zu* after *lassen*.
- *Ich habe mein Auto repariert* means you did it yourself. If the garage did it: *Ich habe mein Auto reparieren lassen.*
- *Ich hebe Geld aus.* — The verb is *abheben*: *Ich hebe Geld ab.*
- *Ich bewerbe mich um einen Pass.* — For documents use *beantragen*: *Ich beantrage einen Pass.*
- *Er lasst …* — Stem change: *er lässt*.

## Key points

- Bank: *das Konto, das Girokonto*, *Geld abheben / einzahlen*, *überweisen* (inseparable).
- Offices: *die Behörde, das Amt, das Bürgeramt*; *einen Antrag stellen, etwas beantragen*; *die Bescheinigung*. Register your address with *sich anmelden*.
- *die Versicherung, einen Schaden melden, die Polizei*; *die Werkstatt, die Reparatur*.
- Polite indirect questions: *Können/Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo/wann/ob …* + verb at the end.
- *lassen* + infinitive (no *zu*) = have something done: *Ich lasse das Fahrrad reparieren.* Also: let, and leave behind. *du/er lässt*.
- Phone: *Es ist besetzt. Ich verbinde Sie. Kann ich Sie zurückrufen? Auf Wiederhören!*

lessons.title: Health and the doctor's office
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you learned the body and how to say *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen*. This lesson takes you through a whole visit to the doctor: calling for an appointment, describing what's wrong and for how long, understanding the doctor's questions and instructions, and getting your medicine at the pharmacy. You'll also learn what to do in an emergency.

Three pieces of grammar make this possible:

- *seit* + dative for how long something has been going on: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Fieber.*
- *sollte* and *müsste* for advice: *Sie sollten ein paar Tage im Bett bleiben.*
- the **[[imperative]]** in instructions: *Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal täglich.*

## Illnesses and injuries

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *die Gesundheit* | health |
| *die Krankheit* | illness, disease |
| *die Erkältung* | cold |
| *der Husten* / *husten* | cough / to cough |
| *der Schnupfen* | runny nose, head cold |
| *die Grippe* | flu |
| *die Allergie* | allergy |
| *die Verletzung* / *verletzt* | injury / injured, hurt |
| *die Wunde* / *bluten* | wound / to bleed |
| *niesen* | to sneeze |
| *schwanger* | pregnant |

You *have* most illnesses, with or without an article: *Ich habe eine Erkältung. Ich habe Husten und Schnupfen. Sie hat Grippe.* An allergy is *gegen* something: *Ich habe eine Allergie gegen Nüsse.* — I'm allergic to nuts.

*verletzt* is an adjective: *Mein Knie ist verletzt.* — My knee is hurt. (In lesson 5 you learned the reflexive verb: *Ich habe mich verletzt.*)

When someone sneezes, Germans say *Gesundheit!* — literally "health!" — and the answer is *Danke!*

## At the doctor's

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *der Zahnarzt / die Zahnärztin* | dentist |
| *die Krankenkasse* | health insurance fund |
| *die Versichertenkarte* | health insurance card |
| *untersuchen / die Untersuchung* | to examine / examination |
| *das Pflaster* | plaster, Band-Aid |
| *der Verband* | bandage, dressing |
| *die Spritze* | injection, shot |
| *operieren / die Operation* | to operate / operation |
| *der Notfall* | emergency |
| *der Krankenwagen* | ambulance |

![Five things from the doctor's office with their German names: das Pflaster, der Verband, die Spritze, die Versichertenkarte and die Tabletten](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In Germany almost everyone belongs to a *Krankenkasse*. At the reception desk of a *Praxis* you're asked: *Haben Sie Ihre Versichertenkarte dabei?* — Do you have your insurance card with you? (Its official name is *elektronische Gesundheitskarte*, but *Versichertenkarte* and *Krankenkassenkarte* are what people say.)

The doctor gives you *ein Rezept*. You know this word from lesson 11 as a recipe; at the doctor's it means a prescription. You take it to the *Apotheke*. If you can't work, the doctor writes you off sick: *Der Arzt hat mich für drei Tage krankgeschrieben.* That connects to lesson 17: you *melden dich krank* with your boss, and the doctor's note confirms it.

### Emergencies

The emergency number in Germany and Austria and across the EU is *112* (*eins eins zwei*): *Rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen!* — Call an ambulance! When your practice is closed (at night, at the weekend) and it isn't life-threatening but can't wait, Germany has the medical on-call service, *116 117*, which answers around the clock. Hospitals have *die Notaufnahme*, the emergency department.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Who to call when you are ill in Germany
  accDescr: If it is life-threatening, call 112 for an ambulance. If it is not life-threatening but cannot wait and your practice is closed, call the medical on-call service on 116 117. Otherwise, call your practice and make an appointment.
  A{"Is it life-threatening?"} -- "yes" --> B["112: Rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen!"]
  A -- "no" --> C{"Can it wait until the practice opens?"}
  C -- "no" --> D["116 117: medical on-call service"]
  C -- "yes" --> E["Call the Praxis and make a Termin"]
```

## seit: how long so far

To say how long something has been going on and still is, German uses *seit* + dative and the **[[present tense]]**:

- *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Husten.* — I've had a cough for three days.
- *Sie ist seit einer Woche krank.* — She's been ill for a week.
- *Wir warten seit einer Stunde.* — We've been waiting for an hour.
- *Er wohnt seit 2019 in Wien.* — He has lived in Vienna since 2019.

English uses "have had / have been … for / since"; German keeps the present tense, because the cough is still there. A memory hook: *seit* means it isn't over yet, so the verb stays in the present.

*seit* covers both "for" and "since": *seit drei Tagen* (for three days), *seit Montag, seit gestern, seit dem Unfall* (since Monday, since yesterday, since the accident). The noun after it is dative, so plural nouns add *-n*: *seit zwei Wochen, seit drei Monaten, seit vielen Jahren*.

The questions are *Seit wann …?* (since when) and *Wie lange schon …?* (how long already):

- *Seit wann haben Sie die Schmerzen?* — *Seit gestern Abend.*
- *Wie lange haben Sie schon Fieber?* — *Seit zwei Tagen.*

Compare *vor* (lesson 14), which points to a moment in the past: *Ich habe mich vor drei Tagen erkältet.* — I caught a cold three days ago.

The time line shows the difference: *vor* points back to one finished moment, *seit* covers the whole stretch up to now.

![A time line from Monday to Thursday. On Monday: Ich habe mich erkältet. A bar from Monday up to today is labeled seit drei Tagen: Ich habe Husten, in the present tense. An arrow from Thursday back to Monday is labeled vor drei Tagen: Ich habe mich erkältet, in the past.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Advice: sollte and müsste

You met *sollte* in lesson 15. It's the standard way to give advice, from a friend or a doctor:

| | sollen → sollte | müssen → müsste |
|---|---|---|
| ich | sollte | müsste |
| du | solltest | müsstest |
| er / sie / es | sollte | müsste |
| wir | sollten | müssten |
| ihr | solltet | müsstet |
| sie / Sie | sollten | müssten |

- *Du solltest zum Arzt gehen.* — You should go to the doctor.
- *Sie sollten nicht so viel arbeiten.* — You shouldn't work so much.
- *Ihr solltet mehr Wasser trinken.* — You should all drink more water.

*müsste* is the **[[Konjunktiv II]]** of *müssen*. It is a little stronger than *sollte* ("really ought to") and often comes with *eigentlich* (actually, really): *Ich müsste eigentlich mehr Sport machen.* — I really ought to do more sport. People use it about themselves to admit something they don't do.

Notice the umlaut: *müsste* has one, *sollte* never does.

## Instructions: the imperative

Doctors, pharmacists and package inserts give instructions in the imperative, usually the *Sie* form with the verb first:

- *Machen Sie bitte den Oberkörper frei.* — Please take off your top. (*der Oberkörper* = upper body)
- *Atmen Sie tief ein. Und wieder aus.* — Breathe in deeply. And out again.
- *Legen Sie sich bitte hier hin.* — Please lie down here.
- *Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal täglich nach dem Essen.* — Take the tablets three times a day after meals.
- *Kommen Sie in einer Woche wieder.* — Come back in a week.

Between friends and in the family, use the *du* form (no *-st*, no *du*): *Bleib im Bett! Trink viel Tee! Nimm eine Tablette! Iss etwas!* Remember the stem-changing verbs: *nehmen → nimm*, *essen → iss*.

## How often?

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *täglich* | daily |
| *wöchentlich* | weekly |
| *monatlich* | monthly |
| *einmal / zweimal / dreimal täglich* | once / twice / three times a day |
| *morgens, mittags, abends* | in the morning(s), at midday, in the evening(s) |
| *alle vier Stunden* | every four hours |
| *vor / nach dem Essen* | before / after meals |

*täglich* and *wöchentlich* are adjectives too: *eine tägliche Tablette*, *die wöchentliche Untersuchung*. *alle* + time + plural means "every": *alle zwei Tage*.

## Dialogue: at the doctor's

Tom has been feeling ill for a few days. He sees Dr. Lehmann.

> Dr. Lehmann: Guten Tag, Herr Fischer. Was fehlt Ihnen denn?
>
> Tom: Ich habe seit vier Tagen Husten und Schnupfen, und seit gestern habe ich auch Fieber. Ich bin total müde.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Wie hoch ist das Fieber?
>
> Tom: Heute Morgen hatte ich 38,5.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Hm. Machen Sie bitte den Oberkörper frei, ich möchte Sie untersuchen … Atmen Sie tief ein … und aus. Husten Sie bitte einmal.
>
> Tom: Ist es eine Grippe?
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Nein, zum Glück nicht. Es ist eine starke Erkältung. Haben Sie Allergien gegen Medikamente?
>
> Tom: Nein, ich habe keine Allergien.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Gut. Ich gebe Ihnen ein Rezept für einen Hustensaft. Nehmen Sie ihn dreimal täglich nach dem Essen. Sie sollten viel trinken und ein paar Tage im Bett bleiben.
>
> Tom: Ich müsste eigentlich morgen arbeiten …
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Das geht nicht. Ich schreibe Sie bis Freitag krank. Wenn das Fieber nicht besser wird, kommen Sie bitte wieder.
>
> Tom: Vielen Dank, Frau Doktor.

In English:

> Dr Lehmann: Hello, Mr Fischer. So what's the matter?
>
> Tom: I've had a cough and a runny nose for four days, and since yesterday I've also had a temperature. I'm completely exhausted.
>
> Dr Lehmann: How high is the temperature?
>
> Tom: This morning it was 38.5.
>
> Dr Lehmann: Hm. Please take off your top, I'd like to examine you … Breathe in deeply … and out. Please cough once.
>
> Tom: Is it flu?
>
> Dr Lehmann: No, luckily not. It's a bad cold. Are you allergic to any medicines?
>
> Tom: No, I don't have any allergies.
>
> Dr Lehmann: Good. I'll give you a prescription for cough syrup. Take it three times a day after meals. You should drink a lot and stay in bed for a few days.
>
> Tom: I'm actually supposed to work tomorrow …
>
> Dr Lehmann: That's not possible. I'm signing you off sick until Friday. If the fever doesn't get better, please come back.
>
> Tom: Thank you very much, doctor.

*Was fehlt Ihnen?* (literally "What is missing to you?") is the classic doctor's question, with the dative verb *fehlen* from lesson 7. Germans give their temperature in degrees Celsius and say *achtunddreißig fünf*. A woman doctor is addressed as *Frau Doktor*, a man as *Herr Doktor*.

## A notice in the waiting room

> Liebe Patientinnen und Patienten, bitte bringen Sie zu jedem Termin Ihre Versichertenkarte mit. Wenn Sie Fieber oder starken Husten haben, melden Sie sich bitte vorher telefonisch an. Bei einem Notfall rufen Sie die 112. Die Praxis ist mittwochs nachmittags geschlossen.

Dear patients, please bring your insurance card to every appointment. If you have a temperature or a bad cough, please let us know by phone in advance. In an emergency, call 112. The practice is closed on Wednesday afternoons.

## Pronunciation

- *Husten*: long *u*, HUU-sten. *husten* (the verb) sounds the same.
- *Schnupfen*: the *pf* is one quick sound, lips closed, then *f*: SCHNUP-fen.
- *Allergie*: stress on the last syllable, al-ler-GIE. The *g* is hard, as in "go".
- *Operation*: o-pe-ra-TSION, the *-tion* is "tsion".
- *niesen*: long *ie*, and the *s* between vowels is voiced like English *z*: NEE-zen.
- *müsste*: short *ü*; don't confuse it with *musste* (had to, past).

## Common mistakes

- *Ich habe Husten seit drei Tagen gehabt.* — German uses the present with *seit*: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Husten.*
- *seit drei Tage* — Dative plural adds *-n*: *seit drei Tagen*.
- *Ich bin krank für eine Woche* to mean "I've been ill for a week" — use *seit*: *Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.* (*für* is for a planned period: *Ich bin für eine Woche in Berlin.*)
- *Du sollst zum Arzt gehen* is an order someone gave ("you're supposed to"). Advice is *Du solltest zum Arzt gehen.*
- *Nimmst die Tablette!* — The *du* imperative drops *-st*: *Nimm die Tablette!*
- *Ich habe eine Allergie für Katzen.* — Use *gegen*: *eine Allergie gegen Katzen*.
- *Mein Arm ist verletzen.* — After *sein* use the adjective: *Mein Arm ist verletzt.*

## Key points

- *seit* + dative + present tense for something that started in the past and is still going on: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Fieber.* Questions: *Seit wann …? Wie lange schon …?*
- Advice: *Du solltest / Sie sollten …*; stronger or self-critical: *Ich müsste eigentlich …*
- Instructions use the imperative: *Nehmen Sie …*, *Atmen Sie ein*; with friends *Bleib im Bett! Nimm …!*
- Frequency: *täglich, wöchentlich, dreimal täglich, alle vier Stunden*.
- *Was fehlt Ihnen? Ich habe eine Erkältung / Husten / Schnupfen / Grippe.* *Gesundheit!* after a sneeze.
- Bring the *Versichertenkarte*; the doctor writes *ein Rezept* and may sign you off sick. Emergency: *112*.

lessons.title: Applying for a job: CV, cover letter and the Arbeitszeugnis
lessons.body:
## From the interview back to the paperwork

In lesson 17 Jonas sat in a job interview, *das Vorstellungsgespräch*. But before anyone in Germany, Austria or Switzerland gets that invitation, they send a set of documents, and those documents follow rules that surprise many newcomers. A German CV looks different from an American résumé. The cover letter has a fixed shape. And when you leave a job, your employer writes you a reference, *das Arbeitszeugnis*, in a polite, positive language whose real meaning sits between the lines.

This honors lesson walks you through all three. Along the way you'll learn a new way of writing that German uses everywhere in work and official life: packing information into nouns instead of verbs, the **[[nominal style]]**.

## What goes into an application

A complete application (*die Bewerbung*, from lesson 17) is usually sent by e-mail as one PDF file or uploaded to a company's website. Traditionally it contains:

- *das Anschreiben* — the cover letter, one page;
- *der Lebenslauf* — the CV (lesson 1), one or two pages;
- *die Zeugnisse* — copies of certificates: your last school certificate, your final exam from an *Ausbildung* or university, and the *Arbeitszeugnisse* from earlier jobs.

German employers expect these papers (*die Unterlagen*). An application with a CV only can look incomplete, although more and more companies, especially large ones and start-ups, now accept a CV alone or an online form.

The process then runs like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The path of a job application in Germany
  accDescr: You read a job advertisement and send your application with cover letter, CV and certificates. The company replies with either a rejection or an invitation to a job interview. After the interview you get either a rejection or an offer. With an offer you sign the employment contract, and the job starts with a probation period of up to six months.
  A["Stellenanzeige: job advert"] --> B["Bewerbung: Anschreiben, Lebenslauf, Zeugnisse"]
  B --> C{"Answer from the company"}
  C -- "Absage" --> X["try the next advert"]
  C -- "Einladung" --> D["Vorstellungsgespräch"]
  D --> E{"Answer"}
  E -- "Absage" --> X
  E -- "Zusage" --> F["Arbeitsvertrag unterschreiben"]
  F --> G["Probezeit: up to 6 months"]
```

Two answers you hope for and fear: *die Zusage* (yes, the job is yours) and *die Absage*. You know *die Absage* from A1 as a cancellation; in applications it's the rejection: *Leider müssen wir Ihnen eine Absage erteilen.* — Unfortunately we have to turn you down. If the company hires you, it *stellt dich ein*: *Die Firma hat drei neue Mitarbeiter eingestellt.* — The company has hired three new employees. *einstellen* is separable. The contract is *der Arbeitsvertrag*, and most jobs start with *die Probezeit*, a probation period of up to six months during which either side can end the job with two weeks' notice.

## The German CV

![A one-page German CV for Lena Hoffmann with a photo top right and the headings Persönliche Daten, Berufserfahrung, Ausbildung and Sprachkenntnisse, then place, date and signature at the bottom](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A German *Lebenslauf* is a table: dates on the left, facts on the right, no full sentences. The usual sections are:

| Section | What goes there |
|---|---|
| *Persönliche Daten* | name, address, phone, e-mail; often date of birth |
| *Berufserfahrung* | jobs, newest first |
| *Ausbildung* | school, apprenticeship, university, newest first |
| *Kenntnisse* | *Sprachkenntnisse* (languages), computer skills |
| *Ort, Datum, Unterschrift* | place, date and signature at the bottom |

Three things that are different from an English-language résumé:

- **The photo.** Many Germans still put a professional photo in the top right corner. Since the General Equal Treatment Act of 2006 (*AGG*), which forbids discrimination in hiring, many employers no longer ask for one, and many applicants leave it out. Both are normal; a holiday snapshot is not.
- **Gaps.** Germans expect a CV without unexplained gaps. If you spent a year travelling or looking after a child, write it in: *2022–2023 Elternzeit* (parental leave).
- **Signature.** The handwritten signature with place and date is traditional; in an e-mail application it's now optional.

*die Berufserfahrung* is work experience (*der Beruf* + *die Erfahrung*); *die Sprachkenntnisse* (plural) are language skills. Levels are often given with the CEFR letters you know: *Englisch: gut (B2)*.

## The nominal style

Look at the right-hand column of a CV: *Kundenbetreuung, Erstellung von Angeboten, Organisation von Besprechungen*. There are no verbs, only nouns. This is the nominal style: the action is turned into a noun, and the object follows with *von* (or in the genitive).

| Verb style (how you'd say it) | Nominal style (how a CV says it) |
|---|---|
| *Ich habe Kunden betreut.* | *Betreuung von Kunden* / *Kundenbetreuung* |
| *Ich habe Angebote geschrieben.* | *Erstellung von Angeboten* |
| *Ich habe Besprechungen organisiert.* | *Organisation von Besprechungen* |
| *Ich habe die Post erledigt.* | *Bearbeitung der Post* |

Most of these nouns end in *-ung* and are feminine: *betreuen → die Betreuung, bearbeiten → die Bearbeitung, erstellen → die Erstellung* (*erstellen* = to draw up, produce). Verbs in *-ieren* make nouns in *-ation*: *organisieren → die Organisation, präsentieren → die Präsentation*. They are feminine too.

In a CV the nominal style saves space and sounds professional. In a conversation it sounds stiff: in the interview you say *Ich habe die Kunden betreut*, not *Meine Tätigkeit war die Betreuung der Kunden*. You'll meet the nominal style again in official letters (honors lesson 3 of this module).

### Example 1: from your own words to a CV line

Jonas (lesson 17) wants to describe his current job in his CV. He writes down what he does, then turns each verb into a noun:

1. *Ich bin für die Kunden zuständig.* → the key verb is *betreuen* (to look after): *Betreuung der Kunden*, shorter *Kundenbetreuung*.
2. *Ich schreibe Angebote.* → "write" becomes the more formal *erstellen*: *Erstellung von Angeboten*.
3. *Ich bereite Verträge vor.* → *vorbereiten → die Vorbereitung*: *Vorbereitung von Verträgen*.

His CV line: *seit 03/2023 · Kaufmännischer Mitarbeiter, Druckerei Krause, Kassel · Kundenbetreuung, Erstellung von Angeboten, Vorbereitung von Verträgen*. Notice *von* + dative plural: *von Angeboten, von Verträgen*, with the plural dative *-n*.

## The cover letter

The *Anschreiben* is a formal letter of one page. Its parts always come in the same order: your address, the company's address, the date, a bold subject line (*Bewerbung als …*), the greeting, three or four short paragraphs, the closing, your signature, and a list of what's enclosed (*Anlagen*). The text answers three questions: why this job, why you, and when you can start.

Here is a model. Lena, whose CV you saw above, applies for a new job.

> Bewerbung als Kauffrau für Büromanagement – Ihre Stellenanzeige vom 2. Februar 2026
>
> Sehr geehrte Frau Albers,
>
> hiermit bewerbe ich mich um die Stelle als Kauffrau für Büromanagement in Ihrem Team.
>
> Seit 2019 arbeite ich bei der Druckerei Weber in Leipzig. Zu meinen Aufgaben gehören die Betreuung von Kunden, die Erstellung von Angeboten und die Organisation von Terminen. Ich arbeite sorgfältig und gern im Team.
>
> Ihre Firma arbeitet international, und ich möchte meine Englischkenntnisse im Beruf verbessern. Deshalb interessiert mich diese Stelle besonders.
>
> Ich kann ab dem 1. Mai bei Ihnen anfangen. Über eine Einladung zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch würde ich mich sehr freuen.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> Lena Hoffmann
>
> Anlagen: Lebenslauf, Zeugnisse

In English:

> Application for the position of office management clerk – your job advertisement of 2 February 2026
>
> Dear Ms Albers,
>
> I am hereby applying for the position of office management clerk in your team.
>
> Since 2019 I have been working at the Weber printing company in Leipzig. My tasks include looking after customers, preparing quotes and organizing appointments. I work carefully and enjoy working in a team.
>
> Your company works internationally, and I would like to improve my English at work. That's why this job interests me in particular.
>
> I can start with you from 1 May. I would be very pleased to be invited to an interview.
>
> Yours sincerely,
>
> Lena Hoffmann
>
> Enclosures: CV, certificates

Notes on the language:

- *hiermit* = hereby. *Hiermit bewerbe ich mich um …* is the classic first line. Many advisers now recommend a more personal opening, but it's never wrong.
- *Seit 2019 arbeite ich …*: *seit* + present tense, as in lesson 20.
- *Zu meinen Aufgaben gehören …* lists tasks in the nominal style. The verb *gehören* is plural because the subject is the list.
- *sorgfältig* = careful, thorough. Other qualities employers like: *zuverlässig* (reliable), *motiviert*, *pünktlich*, *teamfähig* (good at teamwork).
- *Über eine Einladung … würde ich mich sehr freuen* is the standard closing line: *sich freuen über* (lesson 6) + Konjunktiv II (lesson 15) for politeness.
- No comma after *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*, and the text after *Sehr geehrte Frau Albers,* starts with a small letter (lesson 23).

### Example 2: building the last paragraph

Say you want to write: "I'm looking forward to meeting you." The verb is *sich freuen auf* + accusative. The thing you look forward to is an action, so you use a da-word that points forward to a zu-infinitive (lessons 6 and 17):

1. *Ich freue mich auf* + something → the something is "meeting you", an action.
2. Replace *auf* + action with *darauf* and put the action after a comma: *Ich freue mich darauf, …*
3. The action as zu + infinitive at the end: *Sie kennenzulernen* (*kennenlernen* is separable, so *zu* goes in the middle).

Result: *Ich freue mich darauf, Sie kennenzulernen.* With a noun instead, you don't need *darauf*: *Ich freue mich auf das Gespräch mit Ihnen.*

## The Arbeitszeugnis: reading between the lines

In Germany every employee who leaves a job has a legal right to a written reference, *das Arbeitszeugnis*. A simple one only states the job and how long it lasted; on request, the employer must write a qualified one that also judges performance and behaviour. Austria (*Dienstzeugnis*) and Switzerland have similar rules.

German courts say a reference must be true but also benevolent, so it shouldn't make it harder for you to find a new job. The result is a style in which almost every sentence sounds positive, and the real grade is shown by small differences. The law forbids secret codes, but some fixed formulas are so widely known that HR departments read them like school grades. The most famous is the sentence about satisfaction (*die Zufriedenheit*). This scale is the one usually quoted in advice books; it's a convention, not a law, and individual writers vary:

| Formula | Usually read as |
|---|---|
| *stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit* | sehr gut (1) |
| *stets zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit* | gut (2) |
| *zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit* | befriedigend (3) |
| *zu unserer Zufriedenheit* | ausreichend (4) |
| *im Großen und Ganzen zu unserer Zufriedenheit* | mangelhaft (5) |

*stets* means always (a formal *immer*). Two small words carry the grade: *stets* and the form of *voll*. The top form *vollsten* is a superlative of *voll*, which logically can't be "fuller than full"; style guides call it illogical, yet in references it's the standard top grade. It's a good example of how a convention can be stronger than a rule.

Other phrases that sound kind but aren't:

- *Er war stets bemüht, die Aufgaben zu erledigen.* — He always made an effort to get the tasks done. Read: he tried, but didn't succeed.
- *Sie hat sich im Rahmen ihrer Fähigkeiten eingesetzt.* — She did her best within her abilities. Read: her abilities were limited.

The last sentence matters too. A good reference ends with thanks, regret and good wishes: *Wir bedauern ihr Ausscheiden sehr, danken ihr für die stets sehr gute Zusammenarbeit und wünschen ihr für die Zukunft alles Gute.* (*bedauern* = to regret; *das Ausscheiden* = leaving). In 2012 Germany's Federal Labour Court ruled that employees have no legal right to this closing sentence, but readers still notice when it's missing.

### Example 3: grading a reference

Read the sentence: *Frau Neumann erledigte die ihr übertragenen Aufgaben zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit.* (*übertragen* = assigned; *erledigte* is the simple past of *erledigen*.)

1. Find the formula: *zu unserer vollen Zufriedenheit*.
2. Check for *stets*: it's missing.
3. Check the form of *voll*: *vollen*, not *vollsten*.
4. Compare with the table: no *stets* + *vollen* = befriedigend (3), a solid but average grade.

If the sentence had been *stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit*, the grade would be the top one.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich bewerbe mich für die Stelle.* — Use *um*: *Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle* (lesson 17); *als* + job title: *als Kauffrau*.
- Writing the CV in full sentences (*Ich habe drei Jahre bei Weber gearbeitet.*) — a German CV uses dates and noun phrases: *2019–2022 Druckerei Weber*.
- Mixing up *die Zusage* (a yes) and *die Absage* (a no). *zu* agrees, *ab* says no.
- *Die Betreuung von Kunde* — after *von* the noun is dative, and plurals add *-n*: *von Kunden, von Verträgen*.
- *Ich freue mich, Sie kennenzulernen* is mostly said when you actually meet ("I'm pleased to meet you"). In a letter, about a meeting still to come, *darauf* makes the future clear: *Ich freue mich darauf, Sie kennenzulernen.*
- Taking every friendly reference sentence at face value. *Er war stets bemüht* sounds nice and is a bad grade.

## Key points

- An application: *Anschreiben* (one page), *Lebenslauf* (table, newest first, no gaps), *Zeugnisse*. The answer is a *Zusage* or an *Absage*; a company *stellt* new staff *ein*.
- The nominal style turns actions into nouns: *Kunden betreuen → Kundenbetreuung, Angebote erstellen → Erstellung von Angeboten*. *-ung* and *-ation* nouns are feminine. Use it in CVs and formal writing, not in conversation.
- Cover letter phrases: *Hiermit bewerbe ich mich um …*, *Zu meinen Aufgaben gehören …*, *Über eine Einladung zu einem Vorstellungsgespräch würde ich mich sehr freuen.*
- The *Arbeitszeugnis* sounds positive throughout; the grade hides in formulas: *stets zu unserer vollsten Zufriedenheit* is the best, *stets bemüht* is a warning sign. This scale is a widely used convention, not law.

lessons.title: At the pharmacy: prescriptions and the package insert
lessons.body:
## After the doctor's office

In lesson 20 Tom left Dr. Lehmann's practice with *ein Rezept* for cough syrup and the instruction *Nehmen Sie ihn dreimal täglich nach dem Essen.* Then what? He goes to the *Apotheke*, and the medicine comes in a box with a folded sheet of paper inside: *die Packungsbeilage*, in everyday speech *der Beipackzettel*. It's one of the most important texts you'll ever read in German, and one of the hardest, because it's written in a dense, formal style.

This honors lesson explains how medicines are sold in Germany, how a package insert is built, and the two grammar patterns that fill it: the **[[passive]]** (*Die Tabletten werden … eingenommen*) and long **[[compound nouns]]** (*die Packungsbeilage, das Schmerzmittel*). Everything here is about understanding; you don't need to write a package insert.

One rule comes first: this lesson teaches language, not medicine. The medicine in it, *Musterin*, is made up. For a real medicine, follow your own package insert and ask the doctor or the pharmacist (*der Apotheker, die Apothekerin*).

## Three kinds of medicine

German law sorts medicines (*die Arzneimittel*, the official word; *das Medikament* from A1 is the everyday one) into three groups:

| Group | Where you get it | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *verschreibungspflichtig* (prescription only) | at the pharmacy, with a prescription | antibiotics, most heart medicines |
| *apothekenpflichtig* (pharmacy only) | at the pharmacy, no prescription needed | many painkillers, cough syrups |
| *freiverkäuflich* (on general sale) | also in supermarkets and drugstores | some herbal teas and other mild remedies |

Medicines from the last two groups are *rezeptfrei*: you don't need a prescription. Notice that in Germany even a simple painkiller (*das Schmerzmittel*) is often sold only in a pharmacy, not next to the shampoo; the pharmacist can advise you.

The doctor *verschreibt* a medicine (*verschreiben* = to prescribe; *hat verschrieben*). Since 2024, prescriptions for people with statutory health insurance (*Krankenkasse*, lesson 20) are electronic: the *E-Rezept*. You redeem it at any pharmacy with your *Versichertenkarte*, with an app, or with a printed code. For prescription medicines, adults with statutory insurance usually pay a share (*die Zuzahlung*) of 10 percent of the price, at least 5 and at most 10 euros per pack (never more than the medicine costs); children don't pay it.

At night and on Sundays, one pharmacy in each area stays open by rota: *die Notdienst-Apotheke*. Every pharmacy door shows which one is on duty.

### At the pharmacy

> Apothekerin: Guten Tag, was kann ich für Sie tun?
>
> Tom: Ich habe hier ein Rezept für einen Hustensaft. Und haben Sie auch etwas gegen Halsschmerzen?
>
> Apothekerin: Ja, diese Lutschtabletten sind rezeptfrei. Nehmen Sie alle drei Stunden eine, höchstens sechs am Tag. Nehmen Sie noch andere Medikamente?
>
> Tom: Nein, nur den Hustensaft.
>
> Apothekerin: Gut. Die Zuzahlung für den Saft beträgt fünf Euro, die Lutschtabletten kosten 7,95 Euro. Die genaue Dosierung steht in der Packungsbeilage.
>
> Tom: Vielen Dank.

In English:

> Pharmacist: Hello, what can I do for you?
>
> Tom: I have a prescription here for cough syrup. And do you also have something for a sore throat?
>
> Pharmacist: Yes, these lozenges don't need a prescription. Take one every three hours, at most six a day. Are you taking any other medicines?
>
> Tom: No, only the cough syrup.
>
> Pharmacist: Good. The prescription charge for the syrup is five euros, the lozenges cost 7.95 euros. The exact dosage is in the package insert.
>
> Tom: Thank you very much.

*die Lutschtablette* = lozenge (*lutschen* = to suck); *höchstens* = at most; *die Dosierung* = dosage. *Nehmen Sie noch andere Medikamente?* is a question every pharmacist asks, because medicines can affect each other.

## How a package insert is built

Every package insert in the European Union follows the same template, so once you know it in German you can find your way in any of them:

![The first page of a package insert for the made-up medicine Musterin 200 mg: a title, a box telling you to read the whole leaflet before taking the medicine and to keep it, the six numbered section headings, and the start of section 3 with the dosage](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Section heading | What you find there |
|---|---|
| 1. *Was ist … und wofür wird es angewendet?* | what the medicine is and what it's for |
| 2. *Was sollten Sie vor der Einnahme … beachten?* | when not to take it, warnings, pregnancy, other medicines |
| 3. *Wie ist … einzunehmen?* | how much, how often, how long |
| 4. *Welche Nebenwirkungen sind möglich?* | side effects |
| 5. *Wie ist … aufzubewahren?* | how to store it, expiry date |
| 6. *Inhalt der Packung und weitere Informationen* | the ingredients, the maker |

Key words: *der Wirkstoff* (active ingredient), *die Anwendung* (use), *anwenden* (to use, apply: *angewendet*), *die Einnahme* (taking it), *einnehmen* (to take a medicine; separable: *Nehmen Sie die Tablette ein*), *wirken* (to work, have an effect: *Das Mittel wirkt schnell*), *die Schwangerschaft* (pregnancy; *schwanger* is from lesson 20). Medicines come as *Tabletten*, *Kapseln* (*die Kapsel*), *Tropfen* (*der Tropfen*, drops), *Saft* (syrup) or *Salbe* (*die Salbe*, ointment). *schlucken* means to swallow.

Headings 3 and 5 use *ist … einzunehmen*, *ist … aufzubewahren*: "how is it to be taken, how is it to be stored". *sein* + *zu* + infinitive expresses what must or can be done, and you'll meet it often in official letters (next honors lesson). Here simply read *Wie ist Musterin einzunehmen?* as "How should I take Musterin?"

### Side effects and what "rare" means

Section 4 lists side effects (*die Nebenwirkungen*) by how often they occur, and the words have exact meanings:

| Word | Meaning in a package insert |
|---|---|
| *sehr häufig* | more than 1 in 10 people treated |
| *häufig* | 1 to 10 in 100 |
| *gelegentlich* | 1 to 10 in 1,000 |
| *selten* | 1 to 10 in 10,000 |
| *sehr selten* | fewer than 1 in 10,000 |

So *häufig* (frequent) here means "up to one person in ten", which is less than many readers think, and *selten* (rare) means at most one in a thousand. Writing numbers, German uses a point where English uses a comma: *10.000* is ten thousand.

## The passive: who does it doesn't matter

Section 3 of the Musterin leaflet says:

*Die Tabletten werden unzerkaut mit einem Glas Wasser nach dem Essen eingenommen.* — The tablets are taken whole (unchewed) with a glass of water after meals.

The sentence doesn't say who takes the tablets; that's the point. This is the passive: **werden** (in its normal present forms) + the past participle at the end.

| Active (who does it is named) | Passive (the action is what counts) |
|---|---|
| *Man nimmt die Tabletten nach dem Essen ein.* | *Die Tabletten werden nach dem Essen eingenommen.* |
| *Der Arzt verschreibt das Mittel.* | *Das Mittel wird (vom Arzt) verschrieben.* |
| *Man bewahrt die Salbe im Kühlschrank auf.* | *Die Salbe wird im Kühlschrank aufbewahrt.* |

How to recognize it:

- a form of *werden* in position 2 (*wird, werden*);
- a past participle at the end (*eingenommen, verschrieben, aufbewahrt*);
- the thing being acted on is the subject.

You already know *werden* in two other jobs: "to become" with an adjective or noun (*Er wird Arzt.*, lesson 8) and the future with an infinitive (*Ich werde anrufen.*, lesson 14). With a past participle it's the passive. At A2 you only need to understand it; German B1 teaches you to build it.

The passive is everywhere in instructions, rules and news: *Hier wird nicht geraucht.* (No smoking here.) *Die Praxis wird um 18 Uhr geschlossen.* (The practice closes at 6 p.m.)

### Example 1: reading the dosage

The Musterin leaflet says: *Erwachsene: 1 Tablette bis zu dreimal täglich. Nehmen Sie nicht mehr als 3 Tabletten pro Tag ein.* What's the most a man may take in two days?

1. *bis zu dreimal täglich* = up to three times a day, one tablet each time.
2. *nicht mehr als 3 Tabletten pro Tag* confirms the daily maximum: 3.
3. Two days: 2 × 3 = 6 tablets at most.

Then check the other conditions in the same section: *unzerkaut* (don't chew), *mit einem Glas Wasser*, *nach dem Essen*.

### Example 2: turning passive into active

Make these leaflet sentences into everyday active sentences with *man* or *Sie*:

1. *Die Kapseln werden morgens eingenommen.* → subject *die Kapseln*, participle *eingenommen* from *einnehmen*. Active: *Man nimmt die Kapseln morgens ein.* or *Nehmen Sie die Kapseln morgens ein.*
2. *Die Salbe wird zweimal täglich dünn aufgetragen.* (*auftragen* = to apply, spread) → *Man trägt die Salbe zweimal täglich dünn auf.*
3. *Das Arzneimittel wird bei Kindern unter 12 Jahren nicht angewendet.* → *Man wendet das Arzneimittel bei Kindern unter 12 Jahren nicht an.* (*bei* + dative here means "in the case of".)

## Compound nouns: read them from the back

A compound noun joins two or more nouns into one word, and the package insert is full of them. Two rules unlock nearly all of them:

- The **last** part says what the thing is, and gives the gender: *die Packung* + *die Beilage* = *die Packungsbeilage*, a kind of *Beilage* (enclosure). *der Schmerz* + *das Mittel* = *das Schmerzmittel*, a kind of *Mittel* (remedy).
- Read the parts from the back to the front: *der Hustensaft* = *Saft* for *Husten* (cough syrup); *die Lutschtablette* = a tablet for sucking.

Often a linking *-s-* or *-n-* sits between the parts: *die Packung-s-beilage, die Schwangerschaft-s-woche, der Schmerz-en-s-geld* (compensation for pain). You can't always predict it, but you can always see it.

### Example 3: a long word step by step

*die Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung* is the doctor's note that says you can't work (lesson 20: *krankschreiben*). Take it apart from the back:

1. *die Bescheinigung* — certificate (lesson 19). So the word is feminine and is a certificate.
2. *Unfähigkeit* — inability (*un-* + *fähig*, able, + *-keit*).
3. *Arbeit-s-* — work, with a linking *s*.

So: a certificate of inability to work. People shorten it to *die AU* or *die Krankschreibung*, and since 2023 doctors send it electronically to the *Krankenkasse*; employers then call it up there. In Germany, if you're ill for more than three calendar days, you need one by the next working day, and your employer may ask for it from the first day.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *werden* + participle as the future. *Die Tabletten werden eingenommen* is "are taken", not "will take". Future has an infinitive: *Ich werde die Tabletten nehmen.*
- *Ich nehme die Tablette.* is fine in speech, but in instructions the verb is separable *einnehmen*: *Nehmen Sie die Tablette nach dem Essen ein.* Don't forget the *ein* at the end.
- Thinking *häufig* means "most people". In a package insert it means up to one in ten.
- Getting the gender of a compound from the first part: *der Schmerz* but *das Schmerzmittel*.
- Asking at the supermarket for *Kopfschmerztabletten*: in Germany most painkillers are only at the *Apotheke*.
- Treating an online translation of a package insert as enough. If anything is unclear, ask the pharmacist: *Können Sie mir sagen, wie ich das einnehmen muss?*

## Key points

- Medicines are *verschreibungspflichtig*, *apothekenpflichtig* or *freiverkäuflich*; the last two are *rezeptfrei*. Prescriptions are now usually *E-Rezepte*; adults pay a *Zuzahlung* of 5 to 10 euros.
- Every package insert has the same six sections: what it's for, warnings, dosage, side effects, storage, contents.
- *häufig* = up to 1 in 10, *gelegentlich* = up to 1 in 100, *selten* = up to 1 in 1,000.
- The passive is *werden* + past participle: *Die Tabletten werden nach dem Essen eingenommen.* The action matters, not who does it. Recognize it; you'll build it in B1.
- Compound nouns: the last part gives the meaning and the gender; read from the back. *die Packungsbeilage, das Schmerzmittel, der Hustensaft.*
