lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat A2 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of German A2. Like the last lesson of A1, it does three things: it explains what A2 means, describes the best-known exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat A2, with strategies for each part, and reviews the grammar of the whole course with pointers back to the lessons. The questions at the end cover the whole course, so use them as a final check. You don't have to take the exam, but the free official practice tests are the best way to find out whether you have really reached A2.

## What A2 means

A2 is the second level of the **[[CEFR]]**, the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. In plain words, someone at A2:

- can follow short, clear sentences about the everyday things that matter to them: family, shopping, home, work, the local area;
- can get through simple everyday situations where people swap information directly: buying, booking, arranging a time, asking the way;
- can say in simple words where they come from, what their life is like and what they need.

The biggest difference (*der Unterschied*) from A1: you no longer depend on the other person speaking slowly and helping all the time. You can tell a short story in the past (lessons 1–2), give reasons and opinions (lesson 3), describe people and things in detail (lessons 8–12), and handle shops, offices, doctors and messages (lessons 10–11 and 17–23). Conversations on unfamiliar or abstract topics are still hard, and that is normal: that is B1.

## The Goethe-Zertifikat A2

The adult version of the exam has four parts. Lesen, Hören and Schreiben are taken in writing, one after the other; Sprechen is a separate oral exam, usually taken in pairs.

| part | time | parts | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lesen (reading) | 30 minutes | 4 | a short newspaper or magazine text; an information board (for example in a building or a shop); a personal e-mail; matching people to small ads |
| Hören (listening) | about 30 minutes | 4 | short announcements, radio items and phone messages; a conversation whose details you match to pictures; short everyday conversations; a radio interview |
| Schreiben (writing) | 30 minutes | 2 | an informal SMS of 20–30 words; a semi-formal e-mail of 30–40 words; each covers three content points |
| Sprechen (speaking) | about 15 minutes | 3 | in pairs, with no preparation time: asking and answering questions with word cards; talking about your own life; planning an appointment together |

There are 100 points: 75 for the written parts and 25 for speaking. To pass you need 60 points overall, and at least 45 of the 75 written points and 15 of the 25 speaking points. All three conditions must be met:

![Three bars. The written exam (Lesen, Hören, Schreiben) has 75 points, with a mark at 45: at least 45. Speaking has 25 points, with a mark at 15: at least 15. The total has 100 points, with a mark at 60: at least 60 to pass.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Did I pass the Goethe-Zertifikat A2?
  accDescr: Three checks, all needed. First, at least 45 of the 75 written points. If not, the exam is not passed. Second, at least 15 of the 25 speaking points. If not, not passed. Third, at least 60 of 100 points overall. If not, not passed. If all three are yes, you have passed.
  A{"Written part: at least 45 of 75?"} -- no --> X["Not passed"]
  A -- yes --> B{"Speaking: at least 15 of 25?"}
  B -- no --> X
  B -- yes --> C{"Total: at least 60 of 100?"}
  C -- no --> X
  C -- yes --> P["Passed"]
```

So 70 points in all is not a pass if only 12 of them come from Sprechen. (If you reach both minimums, 45 + 15, your total is automatically at least 60, so in practice the two part minimums decide.) The grades:

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut (very good) |
| 80–89 | gut (good) |
| 70–79 | befriedigend (satisfactory) |
| 60–69 | ausreichend (sufficient, a pass) |

The Goethe-Institut offers free official practice material: a complete model test with audio and answers, a second practice test, and an interactive online version.

- [Model test for adults (Modellsatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/A2/A2_Modellsatz_Erwachsene.pdf)
- [Practice test for adults (Übungssatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/A2/A2_Uebungssatz_Erwachsene.pdf)
- [Interactive online practice](https://bfu.goethe.de/a2_mod_2MX5/)
- [Official exam rules (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/resources/files/pdf325/durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_a2.pdf)

Dates, fees and details can change, so check with the exam centre where you register. Other A2 exams (telc, ÖSD) test the same level, though the tasks are a little different (*unterschiedlich*).

## Strategies for each part

### Lesen

- Read the task and the questions first, then the text. You are looking for specific information, not translating every word.
- In matching tasks (people and ads), underline the key need of each person: a time, a price, an age, a place. Then look for an ad that fits all of it, not just one word. Watch out: one person may have no matching ad.
- If you don't know the meaning (*die Bedeutung*) of a word, guess it from the context and move on.
- Information boards are lists of floors, departments or offices: scan, don't read. The vocabulary of lessons 10, 14 and 19 helps.
- Read the small words carefully (*genau lesen*): *nur, nicht, kein, schon, noch nicht, erst*. They often decide the answer. A *Hinweis* (note) in small print may be important too.

### Hören

- Before each audio, read the questions and think about which words you will hear: a time? a place? a price?
- In announcements (*Durchsagen* at the station, *Ansagen* on the phone), listen for numbers: platforms, times, phone numbers. Note them on paper while you listen.
- People often correct themselves: *Wir treffen uns um sieben, nein, um halb acht.* The last information counts.
- Don't be put off by one word you missed. Keep listening; the answer often comes a moment later.

### Schreiben

- Lesson 23 is your preparation. Number the three points and write at least one sentence for each.
- Choose the register from the person: a friend → *du*, informal; a teacher, colleague or neighbour → *Sie*, semi-formal.
- Use one or two linking words (*weil, deshalb, trotzdem, dass*) and a polite form (*Könnten Sie …? Ich würde gern …*).
- Keep to the length. A few words more are fine; double the length means double the room for mistakes.
- Save three minutes at the end to check verb positions, capitals and endings.

### Sprechen

- The speaking test is a conversation (*ein Gespräch*), and the examiners want to see that you can react to your partner, not just recite.
- Questions with word cards: you get a topic and a word, and you make a question. Make it simple and complete: topic *Freizeit*, word *Wochenende* → *Was machst du am Wochenende?* Then answer your partner's question with two or three sentences, not one word.
- Talking about your life: you get a card with a question about your everyday life (*Wohnen, Essen, Reisen, Arbeit* …). Prepare at home: for each common topic, have four or five sentences ready, including the past (*Letztes Jahr bin ich …*), a reason (*weil …*) and an opinion (*Ich finde, dass …*).
- Planning together: you and your partner each have a calendar with appointments and must find a time for something you want to do together. Suggest, react, and agree. The phrases are below.
- If you don't understand: *Wie bitte? Kannst du das noch einmal sagen? Was bedeutet …?* Asking is part of the conversation; silence is not.

### Planning an appointment: phrases

| suggesting | reacting | agreeing |
|---|---|---|
| *Hast du am Samstag Zeit?* | *Am Samstag passt es mir leider nicht.* | *Gut, dann machen wir das so.* |
| *Wie wäre es mit Sonntag um zehn?* | *Da kann ich leider nicht, da habe ich …* | *Einverstanden!* |
| *Wollen wir uns nach dem Kurs treffen?* | *Um zehn ist es mir zu früh. Geht es auch später?* | *Super, das passt.* |
| *Sollen wir zusammen ein Geschenk kaufen?* | *Gute Idee! Aber wann?* | *Also treffen wir uns um drei am Bahnhof.* |

*Einverstanden* means "agreed, OK". *vereinbaren* is to arrange or agree on (*einen Termin vereinbaren*), and *der Zeitpunkt* is the point in time: *Ist das ein guter Zeitpunkt?*

## Exam language

Instructions are in German. These words come up often:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Anzeige | small ad, advertisement |
| die Durchsage / die Ansage | announcement (loudspeaker / recorded) |
| der Hinweis | note, tip, notice |
| das Thema | topic |
| beachten | to pay attention to, to note |
| verwechseln | to mix up, to confuse |
| zusammenfassen, die Zusammenfassung | to summarize, summary |
| die Lücke | gap (in a text) |
| die Reihenfolge | order, sequence |
| passend | suitable, matching |
| korrigieren | to correct |

- *Beachten Sie die Uhrzeit.* — Pay attention to the time.
- *Verwechseln Sie nicht Montag und Mittwoch!* — Don't mix up Monday and Wednesday!
- *Finden Sie die passende Anzeige.* — Find the matching ad.
- *Wann bekomme ich mein Ergebnis?* — When will I get my result?

## Review of the course

| topic | core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| perfect and simple past | *habe verstanden, ist umgezogen*; *war, hatte, konnte, musste* | 1, 2 |
| subordinate clauses | verb at the end after *weil, dass, wenn, als, ob* | 3, 4 |
| reflexive verbs | *Ich freue mich. Ich wasche mir die Hände.* | 5 |
| verbs with prepositions | *warten auf, sich freuen über; Worauf? Darauf.* | 6 |
| dative verbs, two objects | *Das gefällt mir. Ich gebe es ihm.* | 7, 22 |
| werden, indefinite pronouns | *Sie wird Ärztin. Jemand, niemand, etwas Neues* | 8 |
| adjective endings | *ein neuer Laptop, der neue Laptop, neuer Laptop* | 9, 10, 11 |
| comparison | *größer als, so groß wie, am größten* | 12 |
| two-way prepositions | *Wo? im Regal (dative). Wohin? ins Regal (accusative).* | 13 |
| time prepositions | *vor einem Jahr, seit zwei Wochen, ab Montag* | 14, 20 |
| Konjunktiv II | *Ich hätte gern … Könnten Sie …? Du solltest …* | 15 |
| linking adverbs | *deshalb, trotzdem, sonst*: verb right after | 16 |
| zu + infinitive | *Ich habe keine Zeit, anzurufen.* | 17 |
| possession | *Annas Buch, das Auto von meinem Bruder* | 18 |
| lassen, indirect questions | *Ich lasse das Auto reparieren. Wissen Sie, wo …?* | 19 |
| relative clauses | *der Mann, der …; das Buch, das ich …* | 21 |
| ordinals, ein-pronouns | *am dritten Mai; Ich habe einen. Das ist meins.* | 22 |
| messages | register, three points, *Es tut mir leid, dass …* | 23 |

If you remember only three things from A2, make them these: in a subordinate clause, the verb goes to the end; adjective endings show gender and case when the article doesn't; and polite German lives in *würde, hätte, könnte*.

## Dialogue: planning together

Two learners, Marta and Dev, practise the third speaking task. They want to visit their friend Paula, who is in hospital.

> Marta: Dev, wir wollen Paula im Krankenhaus besuchen. Wann hast du Zeit?
>
> Dev: Hm, ich schaue mal in meinen Kalender. Am Montag arbeite ich bis 18 Uhr. Wie wäre es mit Dienstagvormittag?
>
> Marta: Da kann ich leider nicht, da habe ich um zehn einen Termin beim Zahnarzt. Geht es bei dir am Dienstagnachmittag?
>
> Dev: Nachmittags habe ich meinen Deutschkurs, der dauert bis vier. Aber danach habe ich frei.
>
> Marta: Gut, um halb fünf passt es mir auch. Und wir sollten vorher ein Geschenk kaufen. Was meinst du, Blumen?
>
> Dev: Ich glaube, Blumen sind im Krankenhaus nicht so praktisch. Wir könnten ihr eine Zeitschrift kaufen, die sie gern liest.
>
> Marta: Gute Idee! Ich kenne eine, die sie toll findet. Also: Wir treffen uns am Dienstag um halb fünf am Kiosk vor dem Krankenhaus?
>
> Dev: Einverstanden. Aber nicht verwechseln: der Kiosk am Haupteingang, nicht der am Parkplatz!

Translation:

> Marta: Dev, we want to visit Paula in hospital. When are you free?
>
> Dev: Hm, let me look in my calendar. On Monday I'm working until 6 pm. How about Tuesday morning?
>
> Marta: I'm afraid I can't then, I've got a dentist's appointment at ten. Does Tuesday afternoon work for you?
>
> Dev: In the afternoon I have my German course, which lasts until four. But after that I'm free.
>
> Marta: Good, half past four suits me too. And we should buy a present first. What do you think, flowers?
>
> Dev: I don't think flowers are very practical in hospital. We could buy her a magazine she likes reading.
>
> Marta: Good idea! I know one she thinks is great. So: we'll meet on Tuesday at half past four at the kiosk in front of the hospital?
>
> Dev: Agreed. But don't mix them up: the kiosk at the main entrance, not the one at the car park!

The dialogue uses a suggestion (*Wie wäre es mit …?*), a refusal with a reason, *sollten* and *könnten*, a relative clause (*eine Zeitschrift, die sie gern liest*; *der dauert bis vier* is spoken style) and the pronoun *eine*. Dev's last line avoids a *Missverständnis* (misunderstanding).

## Pronunciation

- *Missverständnis*: MISS-ver-ständ-nis, stress on the first syllable.
- *Thema*: TEH-ma; the *th* is a plain *t*.
- *Zusammenfassung*: zu-SAM-men-fas-sung.
- *korrigieren*: kor-ri-GIE-ren, stress on *-gie-*, like all *-ieren* verbs.

## Common mistakes

- Answering a card with one word. *Wochenende? — Fußball.* Say a full sentence and add a detail: *Am Wochenende spiele ich meistens Fußball, weil …*
- Ignoring your partner in the planning task. React to what they say: *Ah, am Montag arbeitest du. Und am Dienstag?*
- In Schreiben, writing *du* to a teacher, or forgetting the opening and closing.
- Thinking 45 written points are enough. You also need 15 in Sprechen, and 60 overall.
- *Ich habe eine Missverständnis* → *ein Missverständnis* (neuter).

## What comes next: B1

At B1 you will talk about experiences, plans and opinions in more detail and follow the main points of clear speech on familiar topics. The grammar adds the simple past of all verbs, the passive and the genitive in full. The Goethe-Zertifikat B1 is a common requirement for work, study and citizenship in Germany.

Until then, keep your vocabulary reviews going every day, read graded readers from the reading list, and find German you enjoy: podcasts for learners, series with German subtitles, a tandem partner.

## Key points

- A2: you handle routine everyday situations and simple exchanges about familiar things, and describe your background and needs.
- Goethe A2: Lesen 30 min, Hören about 30 min, Schreiben 30 min (SMS 20–30 words, e-mail 30–40 words), Sprechen about 15 min in pairs. Pass with 60/100 and at least 45/75 written and 15/25 speaking.
- Practise with the free official model test, practice test and interactive version.
- Planning: *Hast du … Zeit? Wie wäre es mit …? Da kann ich leider nicht. Einverstanden!*
- Exam language: *die Anzeige, die Durchsage, der Hinweis, die Lücke, beachten, verwechseln, passend*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson. Herzlichen Glückwunsch: you have finished German A2!

lessons.title: Die Nachrichten: reading German news
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you learned the words for screens and media (*die Nachrichten, der Artikel, der Bericht, die Sendung*) and how to build relative clauses. This honors lesson puts both to work on the kind of German you meet every day once you start reading real texts: the news. News German has its own habits. Headlines leave out verbs and articles, reports are written in the simple past, journalists say where every fact comes from, and long relative clauses pack in details. None of this needs new grammar beyond A2, but it does need a few keys. With them, a short news report (*die Meldung*) stops being a wall of words and becomes something you can read for its facts.

You will learn the parts of a news page, how to turn a headline into a normal sentence, the simple past forms reports use, three ways to say who says so (*laut*, *sollen* and quotes), relative clauses with prepositions, and how to check a story before you believe it.

## Where the news comes from

In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, most people get their news from a mix of television, radio, newspapers and the internet. Some names you will see:

- *die Tagesschau* is the main evening news of ARD, the association of German public broadcasters, every day at 20 Uhr. It has been on air since 1952 and is the best-known news programme in Germany. ZDF, the second public channel, has *heute*. Austria's public broadcaster is ORF, Switzerland's German-language one is SRF.
- A broadcaster or channel is *der Sender*; the people watching are *die Zuschauer*; the people reading a paper are *die Leser* (*der Leser, die Leserin*).
- A daily paper comes out (*erscheint*) every morning; most also have a website with current (*aktuelle*) news all day.

For learners there are news services in simpler German. Deutsche Welle publishes *Langsam gesprochene Nachrichten*, real news read slowly, with the text to read along. Deutschlandfunk's *nachrichtenleicht* gives the week's news in short, simple sentences. Both are free online.

The journalists (*der Journalist, die Journalistin*) who write the news report (*berichten*) on a few big areas: politics (*die Politik*) and the government (*die Regierung*), the economy (*die Wirtschaft*), local events, sport, culture and the weather forecast (*die Wettervorhersage*).

## The parts of a news page

Every article in a paper or on a news website has the same parts:

![The front page of an invented local paper, the Neckar-Bote. Under the paper's name and date is a large headline, Neue Brücke: Stadt plant Eröffnung im Mai, then two bold sentences, then a photo of a bridge with a caption, and columns of text. Labels name die Schlagzeile, der Vorspann, das Foto, die Bildunterschrift and der Text.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *die Schlagzeile*: the headline, the news in a few words, in big letters.
- *der Vorspann*: the lead, one or two bold sentences under the headline that give the main facts.
- *das Foto* and *die Bildunterschrift*: the photo and its caption.
- *der Text*: the body of the article, with details, background and quotes.

News reports are built so that you can stop reading at any point and still have the most important facts. Journalists call the key facts the W-questions: *wer? was? wann? wo?* come first, *wie? warum?* follow, and background comes last.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a news report is built
  accDescr: A news report starts with the headline, a short summary in a few words. Then comes the lead, one or two sentences that answer the main W-questions: who, what, when and where. Then the text gives details: how and why. At the end come background and quotes, the least important part, which an editor can cut first.
  A["Headline: the news in a few words"] --> B["Lead: who? what? when? where?"]
  B --> C["Details: how? why?"]
  C --> D["Background and quotes (cut first if space is short)"]
```

## Headline German: the nominal style

Headlines save space. They use the **[[nominal style]]**: instead of a verb, they use the noun made from it, and they leave out articles and the verb *sein*. Many German nouns come from verbs, and you can often see the verb inside:

| verb | noun | in a headline |
|---|---|---|
| eröffnen (to open) | die Eröffnung | *Eröffnung im Mai* |
| streiken (to strike) | der Streik | *Streik bei der Bahn* |
| wählen (to elect, to vote) | die Wahl | *Wahl in Hamburg: Ergebnis am Abend* |
| verletzen (to injure) | die Verletzung (injury); der/die Verletzte (injured person) | *Unfall auf der A8: zwei Verletzte* |

Typical headline habits:

- No article, no *sein*: *Neue Brücke fertig* means *Die neue Brücke ist fertig.*
- A colon instead of a sentence. The part before the colon is the topic, the part after it is the news: *Unfall auf der A8: zwei Verletzte* — Accident on the A8: two injured.
- Present tense for the past. *Feuerwehr rettet Katze vom Dach* reports something that already happened: the fire brigade rescued a cat from a roof.
- Numbers as figures: *12 Millionen für neue Brücke*.

### Example 1: from headline to sentence

Headline: *Streik bei der Bahn: Tausende Pendler warten*

1. Find the topic before the colon: *Streik bei der Bahn*. *der Streik* is the noun from *streiken*, so the full idea is *Die Bahn streikt* or *Es gibt einen Streik bei der Bahn* (*die Bahn* = the railway).
2. The news after the colon has a verb already: *Tausende Pendler warten* — thousands of commuters are waiting (*der Pendler* = commuter).
3. Put it together, adding articles and a link: *Es gibt einen Streik bei der Bahn, deshalb warten Tausende Pendler.* — There's a rail strike, so thousands of commuters are waiting.

## Reports are written in the simple past

Spoken German tells the past with the perfect (lesson 1). Written reports use the **[[simple past]]** for most verbs (lesson 2), so a news text is full of forms you have learned to recognize:

| infinitive | simple past (er/sie/es) | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| sein | war | was |
| haben | hatte | had |
| geben (es gibt) | gab (es gab) | there was / were |
| kommen | kam | came |
| sagen | sagte | said |
| berichten | berichtete | reported |
| mitteilen | teilte … mit | announced, informed |
| stattfinden | fand … statt | took place |
| beginnen | begann | began |

Two patterns cover almost everything: weak verbs add *-te* (*sagte, berichtete, plante*), strong verbs change their vowel (*kommen – kam, finden – fand, beginnen – begann*). Separable verbs split as in the present: *Die Polizei teilte am Montag mit, dass …* — The police announced on Monday that …

You will also meet the **[[passive]]**, which B1 teaches in full: *werden* + a past participle, used when it doesn't matter who did something. For now, just recognize it: *Zwei Menschen wurden verletzt.* — Two people were injured. *Die Brücke wurde 1950 gebaut.* — The bridge was built in 1950.

## Who says so? laut, sollen and quotes

Good journalists tell you where each fact comes from: the source (*die Quelle*). Three tools do this.

*laut* + dative means "according to": *laut einer Umfrage* — according to a survey (*die Umfrage*); *laut dem Wetterdienst* — according to the weather service. A name or a noun without an article stays as it is: *laut Polizei*, *laut Tagesschau*. (In formal writing you will also see *laut* with the genitive, *laut eines Berichts*; both are used.) This *laut* is a preposition and has nothing to do with the adjective *laut* (loud).

The **[[hearsay]]** use of *sollen* means "is said to, is supposed to": the writer passes on what others say without promising it is true. *Das neue Handy soll 900 Euro kosten.* — The new phone is said to cost 900 euros. *Der Fahrer soll zu schnell gewesen sein* is the same idea about the past (just recognize it). Compare *Du sollst um acht Uhr hier sein* (you are supposed to be here at eight: an instruction). In news, *soll* almost always means "reportedly".

Quotes go in German quotation marks, low at the start and high at the end: „Wir sind sehr zufrieden“, sagte die Bürgermeisterin. After the quote, the verb comes first and then the speaker, because the quote fills position 1: *„…“, sagte sie* (not *sie sagte*).

## Relative clauses with prepositions

News sentences describe a lot in one go, and lesson 21's relative clauses help. Two extra patterns are very common in reports.

First, a preposition before the relative pronoun. The preposition decides the case, and the noun before the comma decides the gender, so: gender looks back, case comes from the preposition.

- *die Brücke, über die täglich 8.000 Autos fahren* — the bridge over which 8,000 cars drive every day (*über* + accusative: movement across).
- *die Firma, bei der er seit zehn Jahren arbeitet* — the company he has worked for for ten years (*bei* + dative, feminine: *der*).
- *der Streik, über den alle sprechen* — the strike everybody is talking about (*sprechen über* + accusative, masculine: *den*).
- *die Kinder, mit denen die Polizei sprach* — the children the police spoke with (*mit* + dative plural: *denen*).

English often puts the preposition at the end ("the company he works for"). German never does: the preposition always comes first, right after the comma.

Second, *wo* for places. For a place, you can use *in dem / in der* or simply *wo*: *die Stadt, in der der Unfall passierte* = *die Stadt, wo der Unfall passierte* — the town where the accident happened. Used like this, *wo* is a **[[relative adverb]]**. With a city or country name, *wo* is the normal choice: *in Hamburg, wo die Wahl stattfand*.

### Example 2: joining two sentences with a preposition

Sentences: *Das ist die Brücke. Über die Brücke fahren täglich 8.000 Autos.*

1. Which noun is repeated? *die Brücke* — feminine.
2. What is its job in the second sentence? It follows *über*, which here takes the accusative (movement across). Feminine accusative: *die*.
3. Move the preposition and pronoun to the front of the second clause: *über die*.
4. Send the verb to the end: *über die täglich 8.000 Autos fahren*.
5. Result: *Das ist die Brücke, über die täglich 8.000 Autos fahren.*

Sentences: *Herr Kaya ist der Mann. Die Polizei hat mit dem Mann gesprochen.*

1. Repeated noun: *der Mann* — masculine.
2. Job: after *mit*, always dative. Masculine dative: *dem*.
3. *mit dem*, verb to the end (auxiliary last): *mit dem die Polizei gesprochen hat*.
4. Result: *Herr Kaya ist der Mann, mit dem die Polizei gesprochen hat.*

## Reading: a short report

> Feuer in Bäckerei: Feuerwehr rettet zwei Menschen
>
> *Am Sonntagmorgen brannte es in einer Bäckerei in der Altstadt von Tübingen. Zwei Menschen wurden leicht verletzt.*
>
> Das Feuer begann laut Feuerwehr gegen 5 Uhr in der Backstube, wo zu dieser Zeit schon zwei Mitarbeiter arbeiteten. Eine Nachbarin, die den Rauch sah, rief sofort die Feuerwehr. Die Feuerwehrleute holten die beiden Männer aus dem Haus und brachten sie ins Krankenhaus. Ein Kabel, das zu heiß war, soll das Feuer verursacht haben. Die Polizei prüft das noch. Die Bäckerei, in der es seit 1890 Brot und Brezeln gibt, bleibt mindestens zwei Wochen geschlossen. „Wir sind froh, dass niemand schwer verletzt ist“, sagte die Besitzerin.

Translation: Fire in bakery: fire brigade rescues two people. *On Sunday morning a fire broke out in a bakery in Tübingen's old town. Two people were slightly injured.* According to the fire brigade, the fire started at about 5 am in the bakehouse, where two employees were already working at that time. A neighbour who saw the smoke called the fire brigade at once. The firefighters got the two men out of the building and took them to hospital. A cable that got too hot is said to have caused the fire. The police are still checking this. The bakery, which has sold bread and pretzels since 1890, will stay closed for at least two weeks. "We're glad that nobody was badly hurt," said the owner.

Words: *brennen – brannte* = to burn (*es brannte* = there was a fire), *die Backstube* = bakehouse, *der Rauch* = smoke, *verursachen* = to cause, *der Besitzer, die Besitzerin* = owner, *die Feuerwehr* = fire brigade, *die Feuerwehrleute* = firefighters. The text is invented, but it is written the way local news really is.

### Example 3: reading for the W-questions

Read the lead and the first sentences, and answer the W-questions in short notes:

- *Was?* Ein Feuer in einer Bäckerei (*Feuer in Bäckerei*, *brannte es*).
- *Wann?* Am Sonntagmorgen, gegen 5 Uhr.
- *Wo?* In der Altstadt von Tübingen, in der Backstube.
- *Wer?* Zwei Mitarbeiter, leicht verletzt; eine Nachbarin rief die Feuerwehr.
- *Warum?* Vielleicht ein heißes Kabel. *soll … verursacht haben* is hearsay: it isn't certain yet, and *Die Polizei prüft das noch* confirms it.

The quote at the end adds feeling, not facts: the pyramid at work.

## Checking the news

Not everything that looks like news is true. Before you share a story, check it (*prüfen*): Who is the source? Is it current (*aktuell*), or an old story shared again? Do other papers and broadcasters report it too? Does the headline match the text? And watch the hearsay words: *soll*, *angeblich* (allegedly) and *laut* + an unnamed source tell you that a fact has not been confirmed.

## Pronunciation

- *Schlagzeile*: SCHLAG-zei-le, with *ei* as in "eye".
- *Journalist*: jour-na-LIST. The *J* is said like the *s* in "measure", as in French; the stress is at the end.
- *Regierung*: re-GIE-rung, long *ie*.
- *Feuerwehr*: FEU-er-wehr; *eu* sounds like "oy".

## Common mistakes

- Reading *soll* in a report as an order. *Der Minister soll krank sein* means he is said to be ill, not that he should be.
- Taking *laut* as "loud": *laut Polizei* is "according to the police".
- Putting the preposition at the end, as in English: *die Firma, die er bei arbeitet* → *die Firma, bei der er arbeitet*.
- Taking the case from the noun instead of the preposition: *mit die Kinder* → *mit denen*: *mit* always takes the dative.
- *„…“, sie sagte* → *„…“, sagte sie*: after a quote, the verb comes first.
- Translating a headline word for word. Rebuild it as a sentence: add the article and turn the noun back into a verb.

## Key points

- News pages have *die Schlagzeile*, *der Vorspann*, *das Foto*, *die Bildunterschrift* and *der Text*; the most important facts come first.
- Headlines use the nominal style: nouns instead of verbs, no articles, no *sein*, a colon, present tense for past events.
- Reports use the simple past: *war, hatte, gab, kam, sagte, teilte mit, fand statt*. Recognize the passive: *wurden verletzt*.
- Sources: *laut* + dative (*laut einer Umfrage, laut Polizei*); hearsay *soll* (*soll 900 Euro kosten*); quotes with *„…“, sagte sie*.
- Relative clauses with a preposition: the preposition goes first and decides the case (*über die, bei der, mit denen*); for places, *wo*.
- Before you share a story: source, date, other media, headline vs text.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 22 followed the festive year: Advent, Christmas, Silvester, Karneval, Easter. This honors lesson follows a life instead. Families in the German-speaking countries mark its big steps with their own customs: a paper cone of sweets on the first school day, smashed plates before a wedding, cake that the birthday person brings to work. Knowing them helps you understand what people are doing, and saying the right thing at the right moment is a big part of sounding at home in a language.

You will also learn why so many wishes end in *-en* or *-es* (*Herzlichen Glückwunsch, Herzliches Beileid*): it is the grammar of lesson 11 hiding inside a set phrase. And you will practise writing short cards, happy and sad.

The customs below are common, not universal: they vary by region, religion and family, and many people skip them. Where something is mainly found in one region, the lesson says so.

## Celebrations through a life

```mermaid
timeline
  accTitle: Family celebrations through a life
  accDescr: A timeline of family celebrations in German-speaking countries. In childhood, a baby may be christened at a Taufe, and at about six children start school with an Einschulung and a Schultüte. In youth, between about 9 and 14, many celebrate an Erstkommunion, a Konfirmation or a Jugendweihe. In adult life come the Polterabend and the Hochzeit, and round birthdays. Later come wedding anniversaries: the Silberhochzeit after 25 years and the Goldene Hochzeit after 50.
  Childhood : Taufe (christening) : Einschulung with a Schultüte (about 6)
  Youth (about 9 to 14) : Erstkommunion, Konfirmation or Jugendweihe
  Adult life : Polterabend and Hochzeit : runde Geburtstage (30, 40, 50 ...)
  Later : Silberhochzeit (25 years) : Goldene Hochzeit (50 years)
```

- *die Taufe* is a christening (baptism), usually a church service followed by a family lunch.
- Catholic children celebrate their *Erstkommunion* at about nine; Protestant teenagers their *Konfirmation* at about fourteen. The *Jugendweihe* is a non-religious coming-of-age ceremony at about fourteen, mostly in eastern Germany. All three come with a family party and presents, often money.

## The first day of school: Einschulung

In Germany children usually start school at about six. The first day, *die Einschulung*, is a family occasion: there is often a short ceremony at the school, photos, and lunch or cake with grandparents afterwards. Every new pupil carries *eine Schultüte*, a large decorated paper cone filled with sweets, small toys and school things such as pens. The custom began in Saxony and Thuringia in the early 1800s; in parts of eastern Germany the cone is still called *Zuckertüte*. Parents or grandparents usually prepare it, and some families make it together with the child.

## Birthdays: three rules

Birthdays (lesson 22 gave you *Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!*) come with some unwritten rules that surprise visitors:

1. Don't congratulate early. Many Germans think it brings bad luck to wish someone a happy birthday before the day. Afterwards is fine: *Alles Gute nachträglich!* — Belated happy birthday! Some people *feiern rein*: they start the party the evening before and celebrate into the birthday at midnight.
2. The birthday person invites. If you celebrate with friends in a restaurant, the person whose birthday it is often pays, and at work it is common to bring a cake for colleagues.
3. Round birthdays matter. A *runder Geburtstag* (30, 40, 50 …) gets a bigger party. In Bremen there is a well-known custom for people who turn 30 and are not married: men sweep the steps of the cathedral and women clean door handles at the town hall until someone sets them free with a kiss.

## Weddings: Standesamt, Polterabend and more

In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, only a civil ceremony makes a marriage legally valid. The couple marry at *das Standesamt*, the registry office, in a short ceremony (*die Trauung*) with family and witnesses. A church wedding is optional and usually comes after the civil one, on the same day or later. On the day, the couple are *das Brautpaar*: *die Braut* (bride) and *der Bräutigam* (groom).

Before the wedding come two parties:

- *der Junggesellenabschied* (often just *JGA*): the hen or stag party. Friends of the bride or groom take them through town, often in costumes, sometimes selling small things to strangers for fun.
- *der Polterabend*: an evening party, a few days or the night before the wedding, at the couple's or their parents' home. Guests bring old plates, cups and other china and smash it on the ground. The pieces (*die Scherben*, singular *die Scherbe*) bring luck, as the saying goes: *Scherben bringen Glück.* Then the couple sweep everything up together, a first test of working as a team. Glass and mirrors are traditionally left out, because broken glass is said to bring bad luck.

Marriage (*die Ehe*) has its anniversaries (*das Jubiläum*, plural *die Jubiläen*): *die Silberhochzeit* after 25 years, *die Goldene Hochzeit* after 50. Firms and clubs celebrate a *Jubiläum* too: *Unsere Firma hat 100-jähriges Jubiläum.*

When people move into a new flat, they may hold *eine Einweihungsparty* (a housewarming). A traditional present is bread and salt, *Brot und Salz*, so that the household never lacks the basics.

## Sad occasions

When someone dies (*der Tod*), there is *eine Beerdigung* (a funeral), and people write cards with a black border. The key phrase is *Herzliches Beileid* (sincere condolences), or more formally *Mein aufrichtiges Beileid*. A condolence card is short and calm:

![Two cards side by side. The birthday card has a colourful border and dots and says Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum 40. Geburtstag! Alles Gute, viel Glück und Gesundheit! The condolence card has a plain black border and says In stiller Anteilnahme, Herzliches Beileid, Wir denken an euch.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*In stiller Anteilnahme* (in silent sympathy) is a usual closing for condolences. *Wir denken an euch* — we're thinking of you.

## Why wishes end in -en: the hidden verb

Look at the endings: *Herzlichen Glückwunsch!*, *Guten Rutsch!*, *Schönes Wochenende!*, *Gute Besserung!*, *Frohe Ostern!*, *Herzliches Beileid!* Each wish is an **[[ellipsis]]**: a sentence with words left out because everyone knows them. The missing part is *Ich wünsche dir / Ihnen …*, and what you wish someone is the direct object, so the wish is accusative. There is no article, so the adjective takes the strong (signal) ending, as in lesson 11:

| wish | noun | full sentence (rarely said) |
|---|---|---|
| *Herzlichen Glückwunsch!* | der Glückwunsch (masc.) | *Ich spreche dir meinen herzlichen Glückwunsch aus.* |
| *Guten Rutsch!* | der Rutsch (masc.) | *Ich wünsche dir einen guten Rutsch.* |
| *Gute Besserung!* | die Besserung (fem.) | *Ich wünsche Ihnen gute Besserung.* |
| *Schönes Wochenende!* | das Wochenende (neut.) | *Ich wünsche euch ein schönes Wochenende.* |
| *Herzliches Beileid!* | das Beileid (neut.) | *Ich spreche Ihnen mein herzliches Beileid aus.* |
| *Frohe Ostern!* | Ostern (here plural) | *Wir wünschen euch frohe Ostern.* |

Only the masculine shows the accusative clearly: *-en*, not *-er*. That is why *Herzlicher Glückwunsch* is wrong as a wish, though you can see it in a sentence where it is the subject: *Ein herzlicher Glückwunsch kam von der Chefin.*

Two more patterns: *Alles Gute!* has *-e* because after *alles* an adjective-noun takes *-e* (like *alles Neue*), and *Viel Glück! Viel Spaß! Viel Erfolg!* use *viel* without an ending before a singular noun.

The occasion follows with *zu* + dative: *zum Geburtstag, zur Hochzeit, zum Jubiläum*. With an ordinal or adjective, add the ending after *zum* (lesson 22): *zum 40. Geburtstag* (read *zum vierzigsten Geburtstag*), *zum neuen Job*, *zur Goldenen Hochzeit*.

### Example 1: a birthday card for a colleague

Situation: your colleague Herr Schulz turns 50. You say *Sie* to him.

1. Opening: semi-formal, *Lieber Herr Schulz,* (lesson 23).
2. Wish: *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum 50. Geburtstag!* (masculine accusative *-en*; *zum fünfzigsten*).
3. A personal line: *Vielen Dank für die gute Zusammenarbeit!* (*die Zusammenarbeit* = cooperation.)
4. A second wish: *Alles Gute, viel Glück und vor allem Gesundheit!*
5. Closing: *Herzliche Grüße, Ihre Mia Berger.*

### Example 2: congratulations to a couple

Situation: your friends Lena and Tom are getting married. You say *ihr* to them.

1. *Liebe Lena, lieber Tom,* — one adjective per name, *Liebe* for her, *lieber* for him (small *l* after the comma).
2. *Herzliche Glückwünsche zur Hochzeit!* — plural *Glückwünsche*, so *-e*; *zur* because *die Hochzeit* is feminine.
3. *Wir wünschen euch alles Liebe für eure gemeinsame Zukunft.* — *euch* (dative, to you two), *eure* (your).
4. *Eure Sara und Jan*

### Example 3: a condolence card

Situation: the father of your neighbour, Frau Öztürk, has died.

1. *Liebe Frau Öztürk,*
2. *es tut uns sehr leid, dass Ihr Vater gestorben ist.* — the *dass*-clause from lesson 23, verb at the end.
3. *Wir sind in Gedanken bei Ihnen und Ihrer Familie.* — We are thinking of you and your family.
4. *In stiller Anteilnahme, Familie Becker*

Keep it short, avoid jokes and exclamation marks, and don't say *Herzlichen Glückwunsch* by mistake: *Herzliches Beileid* is the phrase.

## Reading: a wedding weekend

Mara writes to her English friend Kate about her cousin's wedding.

> Liebe Kate,
>
> letztes Wochenende hat meine Cousine Julia geheiratet, und es war wunderbar! Am Freitag war der Polterabend im Garten von Julias Eltern. Fast hundert Gäste kamen, und jeder hatte alte Teller oder Tassen dabei. Wir haben alles auf den Boden geworfen, und am Ende mussten Julia und Max die Scherben zusammen wegfegen. Das hat zwei Stunden gedauert!
>
> Am Samstagvormittag war die Trauung auf dem Standesamt. Das ging ganz schnell, nur zwanzig Minuten. Danach gab es Sekt vor dem Rathaus, und alle haben das Brautpaar mit Reis beworfen. Am Nachmittag waren wir in der Kirche, und am Abend haben wir bis drei Uhr morgens gefeiert. Julias Opa hat eine Rede gehalten, bei der alle geweint haben. Er und Oma feiern nächstes Jahr übrigens Goldene Hochzeit!
>
> Wie war die Hochzeit deiner Schwester? Schreib mir bald!
>
> Liebe Grüße
>
> Mara

Translation: Dear Kate, last weekend my cousin Julia got married, and it was wonderful! On Friday the Polterabend was in the garden of Julia's parents. Almost a hundred guests came, and everyone had brought old plates or cups. We threw everything on the ground, and at the end Julia and Max had to sweep up the pieces together. It took two hours! On Saturday morning the ceremony was at the registry office. That was very quick, only twenty minutes. Afterwards there was sparkling wine in front of the town hall, and everyone threw rice at the bride and groom. In the afternoon we were in church, and in the evening we partied until three in the morning. Julia's grandpa gave a speech during which everyone cried. By the way, he and Grandma are celebrating their golden wedding next year! How was your sister's wedding? Write soon! Love, Mara

Notice the mix of tenses: Mara writes the perfect (*hat geheiratet, haben geworfen*) as in speech, but uses the simple past for *war, kamen, hatte, mussten, gab* (lessons 1 and 2). *Julias Eltern* and *Julias Opa* are names with *-s* (lesson 18). *bei der alle geweint haben* is a relative clause with a preposition: during which. New words: *wegfegen* = to sweep away, *bewerfen* = to throw at, *die Rede* = speech, *weinen* = to cry.

## Pronunciation

- *Bräutigam*: BRÄU-ti-gam; *äu* sounds like "oy".
- *Polterabend*: POL-ter-a-bend, stress on the first syllable.
- *Jubiläum*: ju-bi-LÄ-um, four syllables; the *J* is like English "y".
- *Beileid*: BEI-leid; both *ei* like "eye".
- *Schultüte*: SCHUL-tü-te, long *u* and long *ü*.

## Common mistakes

- *Herzlicher Glückwunsch!* → *Herzlichen Glückwunsch!* The wish is accusative.
- *Frohe Geburtstag!* → *Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!* or *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!* (*Geburtstag* is masculine; *Frohen Geburtstag!* exists but is less common.)
- Congratulating before the birthday. Wait for the day, or say *nachträglich* afterwards.
- *zum vierzigste Geburtstag* → *zum vierzigsten Geburtstag*.
- Thinking a church wedding alone is legally valid. In all three countries, the Standesamt is what counts.
- *Herzlichen Glückwunsch* on a condolence card. The phrase for a death is *Herzliches Beileid*.

## Key points

- Life events: *die Taufe, die Einschulung* (with *die Schultüte*), *die Konfirmation, die Hochzeit, die Beerdigung*; anniversaries are *Jubiläen*: *Silberhochzeit* (25), *Goldene Hochzeit* (50).
- Weddings: legally only at *das Standesamt*; *der Polterabend* with *Scherben* for luck; *der Junggesellenabschied*; *das Brautpaar* = *die Braut* + *der Bräutigam*.
- Birthdays: never early; the birthday person often invites or brings cake; *runde Geburtstage* are big.
- Wishes are an ellipsis of *Ich wünsche dir …*: accusative, no article, strong endings: *Herzlichen Glückwunsch, Guten Rutsch, Schönes Wochenende, Herzliches Beileid*; *Alles Gute*; *Viel Glück*.
- Occasion with *zu* + dative: *zum 50. Geburtstag, zur Hochzeit*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading strategies: skim, scan and read closely
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 24 you met the Lesen part of the Goethe-Zertifikat A2 and a few tips: read the task first, guess unknown words, watch the small words. This honors module turns those tips into real skills, because reading and listening are how you'll keep learning German after this course, from notices and newspapers to stories and poems.

This first lesson is about *how* you read. A good reader doesn't read a timetable the way they read a letter from a friend. You'll learn three ways of reading, how to recognise the type of a text in a second, how small words like *erst* and *außer* can turn an answer upside down, and how a short newspaper report is built. All the texts are everyday German at A2 level, with a few new words glossed as you go.

## Three ways to read

Before you read anything, ask: what do I need from this text? The answer decides how you read it.

| way of reading | German name | question it answers | speed | typical text |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[[skimming]]** | *globales Lesen* | What is this about? Who is it for? | very fast | a newspaper page, a notice board, a website |
| **[[scanning]]** | *selektives Lesen* | When? Where? How much? | fast, eyes jump | a timetable, an ad, an information board |
| **[[detailed reading]]** | *detailliertes Lesen* | What exactly does it say? | slow, every word | rules, instructions, a contract, an e-mail with a request |

Skimming (*überfliegen*, literally "to fly over") means letting your eyes run over the headline (*die Überschrift*), the first sentence of each paragraph and anything in large or bold print. You don't stop at unknown words. After ten seconds you should know the topic and the **[[text type]]**: notice, ad, e-mail, report.

Scanning means hunting for one piece of information. You know what it looks like before you find it: a time has a colon or the word *Uhr*, a price has *Euro* or €, a date has a month or a dot (*14.5.*). Your eyes jump until they see the shape, and then you read only that sentence.

Detailed reading means reading every word of the part that matters, including the small ones, so that you catch every detail (*die Einzelheit*). You do this last, and only where the task needs it. Most exam questions need one or two sentences read in detail, not the whole text.

The main idea (*die Hauptsache*) is this: switch between the three. (In an exam, read the task and the questions first, as lesson 24 said, so you know what you need; then start the chart.) Skim first to know what you have, scan to find the right place, and read that place in detail. Here is the decision as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing how to read a text
  accDescr: First skim every text for its type and topic. Then ask what you need. If you need one fact, such as a time, price or place, scan for its shape and then read that one sentence in detail. If you need the general idea, skimming is enough. If you need to follow rules or instructions exactly, read the whole relevant part in detail, including small words like nur, erst and außer.
  A["Skim: text type and topic"] --> B{"What do I need?"}
  B -- "one fact" --> C["Scan for its shape: Uhr, Euro, a date"]
  C --> D["Read that sentence in detail"]
  B -- "the general idea" --> E["Skimming is enough"]
  B -- "exact rules or steps" --> F["Read the relevant part in detail"]
  F --> G["Check the small words: nur, erst, außer"]
```

## Text types and their clues

Every text type has a typical look and typical phrases. If you know them, you can skim much faster. These are the short texts you'll see most often in German-speaking countries:

| text type | where you see it | typical clues |
|---|---|---|
| *der Aushang* (notice) | in a block of flats, at work, at school | a sender at the top (*Hausverwaltung*, *die Schulleitung*), *An alle …*, a date and time |
| *das Plakat* (poster) | on walls, at bus stops | large letters, an event, a date, *Eintritt frei* |
| *die Anzeige* (small ad) | on a notice board, in a newspaper, online | *Zu verkaufen*, *Suche …*, *Biete …*, a price, a contact |
| *der Zettel* (note, slip of paper) | on a door, a car, a fridge | handwritten style, short sentences, often a request |
| *die Infotafel* (information board) | in a department store, hospital, office building | floors or rooms and what's there, few full sentences |
| *die Meldung* (short news report) | in a newspaper or news app | a headline, a place name at the start, the past tense |

A **[[text type]]** is a kind of text with its own purpose and form. Knowing the type tells you what to expect: a notice from the building management contains a rule or a change, a small ad contains something offered or wanted, a lost-pet note asks for help and often offers a reward (*die Belohnung*).

Here is a notice board (*das Schwarze Brett*, literally "the black board") in the entrance of a block of flats in Germany:

![A notice board in a block of flats with four texts. Top left, a notice: Hausverwaltung Berger. An alle Mieterinnen und Mieter: Am Dienstag, 14. Mai, gibt es von 8 bis 12 Uhr kein Wasser. Grund: Reparatur im Keller. Vielen Dank! Top right, a poster: Sommerfest im Hof, Samstag, 18. Mai, ab 16 Uhr, Musik, Grill, Spiele für Kinder, Salat oder Kuchen mitbringen! Bottom left, a small ad with tear-off strips: Zu verkaufen: Kinderfahrrad, blau, gut erhalten, 40 Euro, Familie Yilmaz, 2. Stock. Bottom right, a note: Katze entlaufen! Mia, grau mit weißen Pfoten, seit Montag nicht zu Hause. Wer hat sie gesehen? Belohnung: 50 Euro. Bitte bei Jonas klingeln, Erdgeschoss links.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

New words on the board: *der Hof* (courtyard), *gut erhalten* (in good condition), *entlaufen* (run away, of an animal), *die Pfote* (paw), *klingeln* (to ring the bell), *das Erdgeschoss* (ground floor).

### Example 1: Skimming the board

Give yourself ten seconds. What are the four texts, and who wrote them?

1. Top left: a sender at the top (*Hausverwaltung Berger*) and *An alle Mieterinnen und Mieter*. It's an *Aushang* from the property management to all tenants. Topic: water.
2. Top right: huge letters, an event, a day and a time. It's a *Plakat* for a summer party.
3. Bottom left: *Zu verkaufen*, a price and strips to tear off. It's an *Anzeige*: someone is selling something.
4. Bottom right: an exclamation, a description of an animal and *Belohnung*. It's a *Zettel* about a lost cat.

Notice that you didn't need *Keller* or *Pfoten* to answer. Skimming works with the words you know.

### Example 2: Scanning for facts

Now find the answers as fast as you can. For each one, decide first what shape the answer has.

1. *Wann gibt es kein Wasser?* You're looking for a day and times. Scan the notice for a date: *Am Dienstag, 14. Mai, von 8 bis 12 Uhr.*
2. *Was soll man zum Fest mitbringen?* Look for *mitbringen*: *Salat oder Kuchen.*
3. *Wie viel kostet das Fahrrad?* Look for *Euro*: *40 Euro.*
4. *Wo kann man sich melden, wenn man die Katze findet?* Look for a place in the building: *bei Jonas, Erdgeschoss links.*

Each answer needed one line. The rest of the text was the haystack around the needle.

## Detailed reading: the small words

In the exam and in life, the trap is rarely a difficult word. It's a small one that changes the meaning. When a question is about rules, times or conditions, read these words slowly:

| word | meaning | example | what it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| *nur* | only | *Nur mit Termin.* | without an appointment: no |
| *erst* | not until, only (later than you'd expect) | *Der Laden öffnet erst um 10.* | at 9 it's still closed |
| *schon* | already | *Wir öffnen schon um 7.* | earlier than you'd expect |
| *noch nicht* | not yet | *Die Tickets gibt es noch nicht.* | they'll come later |
| *nicht mehr* | no longer | *Es gibt keine Tickets mehr.* | sold out (*ausverkauft*) |
| *außer* | except | *täglich außer sonntags* | Sunday is closed |
| *ab* | from (onwards) | *ab 18 Jahren* | 17-year-olds can't |
| *bis spätestens* | by … at the latest | *bis spätestens Freitag* | Saturday is too late |
| *ohne* | without | *Eintritt ohne Anmeldung* | you can just come |

*erst* and *nur* both sometimes translate as "only", which is why learners confuse them. *nur* limits an amount (*nur zwei Tickets*: no more than two). *erst* says something happens later than expected (*erst um 10*: not before 10). *Ich habe erst zwei Kapitel gelesen* means "I've only read two chapters so far", and more will come.

## Reading a news report

Newspaper reports have a fixed shape. The headline gives the topic in a few words, often without a verb. The **[[lead]]**, the first sentence or paragraph, answers the most important W-questions: *Wer? Was? Wann? Wo?* The later paragraphs add details, quotes and the *Warum?* So if you only have time for one paragraph, read the first one. Reports tell past events mostly in the simple past (*sagte*, *erklärte*, *kam*); the first sentence often uses the perfect, and anything that is still true now is in the present, as in the report below.

> Neustadt: Bibliothek verleiht jetzt auch Werkzeug
>
> Eine Bohrmaschine, ein Zelt oder eine Nähmaschine: In der Stadtbibliothek Neustadt kann man seit Montag nicht nur Bücher leihen, sondern auch Dinge für den Alltag. Die neue „Bibliothek der Dinge“ hat schon 120 Gegenstände. Bald sollen es 200 sein.
>
> Die Idee hatte die Bibliothekarin Sabine Roth. „Viele Leute kaufen eine Bohrmaschine und benutzen sie nur zehn Minuten im Jahr“, sagte sie bei der Eröffnung. „Das kostet Geld und ist schlecht für die Umwelt.“
>
> Das Leihen ist kostenlos. Man braucht nur einen Bibliotheksausweis. Er kostet für Erwachsene 12 Euro im Jahr, für Kinder und Jugendliche unter 18 nichts. Die Dinge darf man zwei Wochen behalten. Elektrische Geräte bekommt man aber erst ab 18 Jahren.
>
> Die Bibliothek sucht noch Spenden: Wer gut erhaltene Dinge zu Hause hat, kann sie montags bis freitags von 10 bis 18 Uhr vorbeibringen. Kleidung und Möbel nimmt sie nicht an.

Neustadt: Library now lends tools too. A drill, a tent or a sewing machine: since Monday you can borrow not only books but also things for everyday life at Neustadt city library. The new "Library of Things" already has 120 items. Soon there are to be 200. The idea came from the librarian Sabine Roth. "Many people buy a drill and use it for only ten minutes a year," she said at the opening. "That costs money and is bad for the environment." Borrowing is free. All you need is a library card. It costs adults 12 euros a year and nothing for children and young people under 18. You may keep the things for two weeks. But you only get electrical appliances from the age of 18. The library is still looking for donations: anyone who has things in good condition at home can drop them off Monday to Friday from 10 am to 6 pm. It doesn't accept clothes or furniture.

(*verleihen* to lend out, *das Werkzeug* tools, *die Bohrmaschine* drill, *der Gegenstand* object, item, *die Eröffnung* opening, *der Bibliotheksausweis* library card, *das Gerät* appliance, device, *die Spende* donation, *vorbeibringen* to drop off.)

The lead answers *Was?* (you can borrow things), *Wo?* (Neustadt city library) and *Wann?* (since Monday). The second paragraph gives *Wer?* and *Warum?*; the third and fourth give the rules, and that's where the small words live: *nur*, *erst ab 18*, *nicht*.

### Example 3: True or false?

Read the report in detail and decide: *richtig* or *falsch*?

1. *Ein 16-jähriger Schüler kann eine elektrische Bohrmaschine leihen.* The third paragraph says *Elektrische Geräte bekommt man aber erst ab 18 Jahren.* He's 16: *falsch*. A reader who only saw *kostenlos* and *unter 18 nichts* would say *richtig*.
2. *Ein Bibliotheksausweis ist für alle kostenlos.* Only for under-18s; adults pay 12 Euro: *falsch*.
3. *Man kann ein altes Sofa spenden.* *Möbel nimmt sie nicht an*, and a sofa is furniture: *falsch*.
4. *Die Bibliothek hat im Moment mehr als 100 Gegenstände.* *schon 120*: *richtig*. The 200 is a plan (*Bald sollen es 200 sein*), not a fact yet.

Every answer came from one sentence, and in three of the four a small word decided it.

## Common mistakes

- Reading every text from the first word to the last at the same speed. Skim first; you'll often find you need only one line.
- Stopping at the first unknown word. Mark it and read on; the next sentence often explains it.
- Matching words instead of meaning. If the question says *Bohrmaschine* and the text says *Bohrmaschine*, check the sentence around it: it may say *erst ab 18*.
- Confusing *erst* and *nur*: *erst um 10* is a time limit (not before 10), *nur zehn Minuten* is an amount.
- Ignoring *außer*: *täglich außer montags* means closed on Mondays, not open on Mondays.
- Taking a plan for a fact. *sollen*, *bald* and *geplant* describe the future.

## Key points

- Three ways to read: **[[skimming]]** for the topic and type, **[[scanning]]** for one fact, **[[detailed reading]]** for exact rules.
- Skim, scan, then read the right place in detail.
- Know the text types: *Aushang*, *Plakat*, *Anzeige*, *Zettel*, *Infotafel*, *Meldung*; each has typical clues.
- Small words decide answers: *nur, erst, schon, noch nicht, nicht mehr, außer, ab, bis spätestens, ohne*.
- A news report puts the most important facts in the **[[lead]]**; quotes and details follow.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Unknown words: compounds, word families and context
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you learned to read past unknown words. But sometimes the unknown word *is* the answer, and you have no dictionary in the exam. The good news: German is a building-block language. Most long words are made of short words you already know, and the same endings and beginnings come back again and again. Once you see the blocks, a word like *Wohnungsschlüssel* stops being scary.

This lesson gives you four tools for working out what a word means: taking compounds apart, recognising word families and their endings, spotting international words (and the false friends among them), and using the context. At the end you'll see how to find the right form in a dictionary (*das Wörterbuch*) when you do look a word up. In A1 lesson 5 you learned that endings like *-ung* and *-heit* tell you a noun's gender; here they help you with its meaning.

## Tool 1: take compounds apart

German writes compound nouns as one word, where English often uses two (*die Haustür*, front door) or a phrase (*der Wohnungsschlüssel*, the key to the flat). The trick is to read them from the back. The last part, the **[[head word]]**, says what the thing is. Everything in front of it is a **[[modifier]]**: it says what kind.

![The compound der Wohnungsschlüssel split into its parts: the article der, which comes from the head word; the modifier Wohnung, meaning flat; a linking s; and the head word Schlüssel, meaning key. Together: the key to the flat.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *der Schlüssel* is a key, so *der Wohnungsschlüssel* is a key, the one for the flat (*die Wohnung*).
- *der Hausschuh*: a shoe (*Schuh*) for the house, a slipper, not a kind of house.
- *das Schuhhaus*: a house for shoes, a shoe shop. Same blocks, opposite order, different thing.

Three rules follow from this:

1. The head word gives the gender. *die Wohnung* + *der Schlüssel* = *der Wohnungsschlüssel*. *das Haus* + *die Tür* = *die Haustür*.
2. The head word gives the plural. *die Wohnungsschlüssel*, *die Haustüren*. Only the last part changes.
3. Modifiers can be nouns, verbs or adjectives. A verb drops its infinitive ending, sometimes keeping an *-e-*: *der Schreibtisch* (a table for writing: desk), *das Wartezimmer* (waiting room). An adjective keeps its plain form: *die Großstadt* (big city), *das Kleingeld* (small change).

Between the parts you'll often see a small linking sound: *-s-* (*Wohnungsschlüssel*, *Geburtstag*), *-n-* or *-en-* (*Sonnenbrille*, *Straßenbahn*), *-e-* (*Hundeleine*, dog lead). It carries no meaning; just ignore it when you take the word apart. After *-ung*, *-heit* and *-keit* it's practically always *-s-*.

Long compounds work the same way, one block at a time, from the back: *der Haustürschlüssel* → *Schlüssel* for the *Haustür* → the key to the front door. *die Kinderarztpraxis* → *Praxis* (practice, surgery) of the *Kinderarzt* (children's doctor) → a paediatric practice.

### Example 1: Decoding compounds

Work out the meaning and the article of each word.

1. *Fahrradschloss*. Head: *Schloss*, here a lock (*das Schloss*). Modifier: *das Fahrrad*. A bike lock: *das Fahrradschloss*.
2. *Wochenmarkt*. Head: *der Markt*. Modifier: *die Woche*, with *-n-*. A market held every week: *der Wochenmarkt*.
3. *Mülltrennung*. Head: *die Trennung* (from *trennen*, to separate). Modifier: *der Müll*. Separating rubbish for recycling: *die Mülltrennung*. You met *trennen* in lesson 16.
4. *Esszimmer*. Head: *das Zimmer*. Modifier: the verb *essen* without *-en*. A room for eating, a dining room: *das Esszimmer*.

## Tool 2: word families and endings

A **[[word family]]** is a group of words built on the same root. If you know one member, you can often guess the others:

| root | family members |
|---|---|
| *fahren* (to go, drive) | *die Fahrt* (journey), *der Fahrer* (driver), *die Abfahrt* (departure), *das Fahrrad* (bicycle), *die Fahrkarte* (ticket) |
| *sicher* (safe, sure) | *die Sicherheit* (safety, security), *unsicher* (unsure, unsafe), *versichern* (to insure), *die Versicherung* (insurance) |
| *bekannt* (known) | *unbekannt* (unknown), *der/die Bekannte* (acquaintance), *kennen* (to know a person) |

The building blocks at the front and back of words are a **[[prefix]]** and a **[[suffix]]**. Each one adds a fairly regular meaning:

| block | meaning | examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-er* | a person or a machine that does it | *der Fahrer*, *der Drucker* (printer), *der Lautsprecher* (loudspeaker) |
| *-ung* | the action or its result | *die Lösung* (solution), *die Trennung*, *die Wohnung* |
| *-heit*, *-keit* | a quality, from an adjective | *die Sicherheit*, *die Sauberkeit* (cleanliness), *die Freundlichkeit* (friendliness) |
| *-lich*, *-ig* | makes adjectives | *freundlich*, *sonnig*, *wolkig* |
| *-bar* | can be done | *essbar* (edible), *trinkbar*, *machbar* (doable) |
| *-los* | without | *arbeitslos*, *kostenlos* (free of charge), *sprachlos* (speechless) |
| *un-* | the opposite (*das Gegenteil*) | *unbekannt*, *unfreundlich*, *unmöglich* |

These are tendencies, not laws. *die Kleinigkeit* comes from *klein* and means "a small thing, a trifle", which fits the pattern. But *unheimlich* doesn't mean "not homely": it means "creepy", and in speech also "incredibly" (*unheimlich nett*). Use the blocks to make a guess, then check the guess against the sentence.

### Example 2: Guessing from the blocks

A hotel review: *Die Sauberkeit im Zimmer war super, aber die Freundlichkeit an der Rezeption war leider nicht so groß. Das Frühstück war fast unbezahlbar.*

1. *Sauberkeit*: *sauber* (clean) + *-keit* (the quality) = cleanliness. The room was very clean.
2. *Freundlichkeit*: *freundlich* + *-keit* = friendliness. The staff weren't very friendly.
3. *unbezahlbar*: *un-* (not) + *bezahlen* (to pay) + *-bar* (can be done) = "not payable", unaffordable. Breakfast was very expensive.

You knew none of the three words, and you understood the whole review.

## Tool 3: international words and false friends

Many German words look like English ones because they *are* related or borrowed: *das Hotel*, *die Information*, *der Computer*, *die Musik*, *der Garten*. Trust them, usually. But a **[[false friend]]** is a German word that looks like an English word and means something different. These are worth learning by heart:

| German | means | not |
|---|---|---|
| *das Gift* | poison | a gift (that's *das Geschenk*) |
| *bekommen* | to get, receive | to become (that's *werden*) |
| *also* | so, therefore | also (that's *auch*) |
| *aktuell* | current, up to date | actual (that's *tatsächlich*) |
| *eventuell* | possibly, maybe | eventually (that's *irgendwann*, *schließlich*) |
| *der Chef* | the boss | a chef (that's *der Koch*) |
| *sensibel* | sensitive | sensible (that's *vernünftig*) |
| *das Handy* | mobile phone | handy (that's *praktisch*) |

*das Handy* is a German invention that sounds English; English speakers don't use it for a phone.

## Tool 4: the context

When the blocks don't help, the sentences around a word usually do. Ask: what kind of word is it (noun, verb, adjective)? What would make sense here? Is there an example, a contrast or an explanation nearby?

> *Im Flur steht eine alte Kommode. Sie hat vier Schubladen. In der obersten liegen unsere Mützen und Schals, in der untersten die Schuhcreme.*

*Schublade* has an article and a plural, so it's a noun. A *Kommode* has four of them, and things lie *in* them, at the top and at the bottom. A *Kommode* is a chest of drawers; *die Schublade* is a drawer. The **[[context]]** (*der Zusammenhang*), the text around a word, often gives you more than any one block. A word you can guess (*erraten*) from the context is one you'll remember, too.

Here is the whole method as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What to do with an unknown word
  accDescr: First ask whether you need the word for your task. If not, read on. If you do, check whether it is a compound and take it apart from the back. If not, look for a known root, prefix or suffix. If that doesn't help, check whether it looks like an English word, keeping false friends in mind. If it still isn't clear, use the context. Finally, check your guess against the whole sentence.
  A["Unknown word"] --> B{"Do I need it for my task?"}
  B -- "no" --> C["Read on"]
  B -- "yes" --> D{"Is it a compound?"}
  D -- "yes" --> E["Take it apart from the back"]
  D -- "no" --> F{"Known root, prefix or suffix?"}
  F -- "yes" --> G["Build the meaning from the blocks"]
  F -- "no" --> H["Looks English? Watch for false friends"]
  H --> I["Use the context"]
  E --> J["Check the guess against the sentence"]
  G --> J
  I --> J
```

### Example 3: Context in a notice

*Achtung: Der Aufzug ist defekt. Bitte benutzen Sie die Treppe. Die Reparatur dauert voraussichtlich bis Freitag.*

1. *defekt*: an international word (defective). The lift doesn't work; that's why you should take the stairs.
2. *voraussichtlich* is long, but it sits before *bis Freitag* in a sentence about how long a repair will take. A good guess: "probably, expected". That's right: it means "expected, according to current plans". You didn't need it to understand the notice, and that's the point of the first question in the chart: often you can skip it.

## When you do look a word up

A dictionary lists the basic form, not the form you see in the text. Work back to it first:

- Verbs: find the infinitive. *Er kauft heute ein* → *einkaufen* (put the separable prefix back). *gefunden* → *finden*. *fand* → *finden* (look in the list of strong verbs).
- Nouns: find the singular. *Bäume* → *der Baum*; *Häuser* → *das Haus*. A plural with an umlaut may have none in the singular.
- Adjectives: drop the ending. *mit einem neuen Rad* → *neu*. *größer, am größten* → *groß*.
- Compounds: if the whole word isn't there, look up the head word, then the modifier.

## Common mistakes

- Reading a compound from the front. *der Hausschuh* is a shoe, *das Schuhhaus* is a shop.
- Taking the gender from the first part: *das Haus* + *die Tür* is *die Haustür*, not *das*.
- Trusting every English look-alike. *Gift*, *also*, *eventuell* and *bekommen* mean something else.
- Treating *-bar* or *un-* as automatic. Check the guess: *unheimlich* isn't "not homely".
- Looking up a verb in the form you saw. *kauft … ein* is under *einkaufen*; *ging* is under *gehen*.
- Looking up every word. Ask first whether you need it.

## Key points

- Read compounds from the back: the **[[head word]]** says what it is and gives the gender and plural; the **[[modifier]]** says what kind. Ignore linking *-s-*, *-n-*, *-e-*.
- A **[[word family]]** shares a root: *fahren, die Fahrt, der Fahrer, die Abfahrt*.
- Common blocks: *-er* (person, machine), *-ung* (action), *-heit/-keit* (quality), *-bar* (can be done), *-los* (without), *un-* (opposite).
- Learn the **[[false friends]]**: *Gift, bekommen, also, aktuell, eventuell, Chef, sensibel, Handy*.
- Use the **[[context]]**, and check every guess against the sentence.
- Before you use a dictionary, find the infinitive, the singular or the plain adjective.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Listening: announcements, voice messages and real spoken German
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Reading lets you go back; listening doesn't. In lesson 19 you learned phone phrases and read a message from a bike workshop, and lesson 24 gave you first tips for the Hören part of the exam. This lesson goes further: it shows how spoken German differs from the German in your textbook, how announcements at stations and in shops are built, and how to take quick notes so you don't lose a time or a number.

You can't hear sound in this lesson, so the listening texts are written as transcripts, the way people actually speak them. Read them aloud, or let the app read them to you, and try to hear them in your head. The questions at the end use transcripts too.

## Spoken German is not written German

In relaxed speech, Germans shorten and swallow sounds, just as English speakers say "gonna" and "wanna". These **[[reductions]]** are normal, not lazy or wrong, and you'll hear them from teachers, news presenters off air and your neighbours alike. In writing they appear only in chat messages and in dialogue in books.

| written | spoken | example |
|---|---|---|
| *ich habe* | *ich hab* | *Ich hab keine Zeit.* |
| *haben wir* | *ham wir* | *Ham wir noch Milch?* |
| *es gibt*, *gibt es* | *'s gibt*, *gibt's* | *Was gibt's heute?* |
| *ist* | *is* | *Das is nich so schlimm.* |
| *nicht* | *nich*; in the south and Austria *net* | *Ich weiß nich.* |
| *ein, eine, einen* | *'n, 'ne, 'nen* | *Hast du 'nen Stift?* |
| *einmal* | *mal* | *Komm mal her!* |
| *gerade* | *grad* | *Ich bin grad im Bus.* |
| *etwas*, *so etwas* | *was*, *so was* | *Ich hab was vergessen.* |
| *vor dem*, *für das* | *vorm*, *fürs* | *Wir treffen uns vorm Kino.* |
| *nein* | *nee* | *Nee, lieber morgen.* |

Two tips. First, reductions mostly hit the small, predictable words: pronouns, articles, *haben*, *sein*, *nicht*. The nouns and numbers, which carry the information, stay clear. Second, don't copy reductions into your exam writing; use them in speech when they come naturally.

## The little words that fill speech

Spoken German is full of short words that add a feeling, not a fact. A **[[modal particle]]** is a small unstressed word like *ja*, *doch*, *mal*, *halt* or *eben* that shows the speaker's attitude:

- *ja*: as we both know. *Das ist ja teuer!* — Wow, that's expensive (as you can see).
- *doch*: contradiction or urging. *Komm doch mit!* — Oh, come on, come along!
- *mal*: softens a request. *Kannst du mal helfen?* — Could you give me a hand?
- *halt*, *eben*: that's just how it is. *Der Bus fährt halt nur stündlich.* — The bus only runs once an hour, there's nothing you can do. *halt* is more southern, *eben* more northern; both are common everywhere.
- *denn*: friendly interest in a question. *Was machst du denn hier?* — So what are you doing here?

A **[[filler word]]** gives the speaker time to think: *also* (well, so), *na ja* (well…, oh well), *ähm*, *tja*, *sozusagen* (so to speak). And a **[[tag question]]** at the end asks for agreement, like English "right?": *ne?* in the north, *gell?* or *gelt?* in the south and Austria, *oder?* almost everywhere and especially in Switzerland, *nicht wahr?* in careful speech.

When you listen, you can usually let these words fly past. *Na ja, also, das war halt so, ne?* contains no information at all. When you speak, one or two (*mal*, *halt*, *na ja*) make you sound natural.

## Changes and corrections

Speakers change their minds while talking, and the exam loves this. The rule: the last version counts.

- *Wir treffen uns um sieben, nee, warte, um halb acht.* → 7:30.
- *Der Zug fährt nicht von Gleis 4, sondern von Gleis 6.* → platform 6.
- *Ich komme am Dienstag, ach nein, am Mittwoch hab ich ja Zeit.* → Wednesday.

Listen for the signal words *nein*, *nee*, *ach*, *warte*, *Moment*, *also doch*, *sondern*, *nicht … sondern*.

## Announcements: a fixed pattern

Announcements over the loudspeaker (*der Lautsprecher*) at stations, airports and in shops follow a pattern. If you know it, you know when to listen hardest.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How a station announcement is built
  accDescr: An announcement starts with something to get attention, such as Achtung or a platform number. Then it names the train, with its number, destination and planned time. Then it says what is different today: a delay, a new platform or a cancellation. Then it says what passengers should do, and it often ends with an apology or a repetition.
  A["Attention: Achtung, Gleis 7"] --> B["Which train: number, destination, planned time"]
  B --> C["What's different: delay, platform, cancelled"]
  C --> D["What to do: other platform, next train"]
  D --> E["Apology or repetition"]
```

Here is a departures board (*die Abfahrtstafel*) and three announcements that go with it.

![A departures board headed Abfahrt with columns Zeit, Zug, Nach, Gleis and Hinweis. 14:05, RE 7 to Köln Hbf, platform 3. 14:12, ICE 578 to Hamburg-Altona, platform 7, note: about 15 minutes later. 14:20, S 2 to Flughafen, platform 1, note: today platform 2. 14:31, RB 48 to Bonn, platform 5, note: cancelled.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Achtung an Gleis 7: Der ICE 578 nach Hamburg-Altona, planmäßige Abfahrt 14 Uhr 12, hat heute circa 15 Minuten Verspätung. Wir bitten um Entschuldigung.
>
> Information zur S 2 in Richtung Flughafen, Abfahrt 14 Uhr 20: Die S-Bahn fährt heute von Gleis 2. Ich wiederhole: Die S 2 fährt heute von Gleis 2.
>
> Eine Information für Reisende nach Bonn: Die RB 48, Abfahrt 14 Uhr 31, fällt heute aus. Die nächste Verbindung nach Bonn ist um 15 Uhr 31.

Attention, platform 7: The ICE 578 to Hamburg-Altona, scheduled departure 14:12, is running about 15 minutes late today. We apologise. — Information about the S 2 towards the airport, departure 14:20: The S-Bahn leaves from platform 2 today. I repeat: the S 2 leaves from platform 2 today. — Information for passengers to Bonn: The RB 48, departure 14:31, is cancelled today. The next connection to Bonn is at 15:31.

New words: *planmäßig* (scheduled, as planned), *circa* or *ca.* (about), *die Richtung* (direction), *Reisende* (travellers), *ausfallen* (to be cancelled; *fällt aus*), *die Verbindung* (connection). The trains: *der ICE* (high-speed train), *der RE* (regional express), *die RB* (regional train), *die S-Bahn* (suburban train). Notice *die RB* and *die S 2*: the gender comes from *die Bahn*.

On the platform and at the train doors you'll also hear *Vorsicht bei der Einfahrt* (careful, a train is coming in), *Bitte einsteigen!* (please get on) and, in Berlin's U-Bahn, *Zurückbleiben, bitte!* (please stand back: the doors are closing). In a supermarket ten minutes before closing: *Liebe Kundinnen und Kunden, unser Markt schließt in zehn Minuten. Bitte kommen Sie zu den Kassen.*

### Example 1: Matching announcements to the board

What changes for each traveller?

1. Anna wants the ICE to Hamburg. The announcement starts with her platform (*Gleis 7*) and her train. What's different: *15 Minuten Verspätung*. She stays at platform 7 and leaves at about 14:27.
2. Ben is going to the airport. *S 2 … fährt heute von Gleis 2*: he must go from platform 1 to platform 2. The announcement repeats it, which tells you it's important.
3. Clara is going to Bonn on the 14:31. *fällt heute aus*: her train is cancelled; the next one is at 15:31. She has an hour to wait.

Each time, the useful part came after the train was named. That's when to listen hardest.

## Voice messages and notes

A voice message (*die Sprachnachricht*, or on the phone *die Mailbox*) is fast and informal, and you may hear it only once or twice. Don't try to write sentences. Listen (*zuhören*) and note (*notieren*) only keywords, *Stichworte*: nouns, numbers, times, places. Before you listen, write the questions *wer? was? wann? wo?* on your paper and fill them in.

> Hey Sara, ich bin's, Timo. Du, wegen Samstag: Wir treffen uns um sieben, nee, warte, um halb acht, weil Lena erst um sieben von der Arbeit kommt. Treffpunkt ist vorm Kino, nicht am Bahnhof, ja? Und kannst du vielleicht 'n bisschen Geld fürs Essen mitbringen? Ich hab grad keins. Na ja, ruf mich einfach zurück, ne? Tschüss!

Hi Sara, it's me, Timo. About Saturday: we're meeting at seven, no, wait, at half past seven, because Lena doesn't get back from work until seven. The meeting point is in front of the cinema, not at the station, OK? And could you maybe bring a bit of money for food? I haven't got any right now. Well, just call me back, OK? Bye!

### Example 2: Taking notes

Sara's notes, in *Stichworte*:

| question | note |
|---|---|
| wer? | Timo, Lena, ich |
| wann? | Sa, 19:30 (nicht 19:00!) |
| wo? | vor Kino (nicht Bahnhof) |
| was mitbringen? | Geld fürs Essen |
| was tun? | Timo zurückrufen |

Notice what she left out: *Du, wegen*, *na ja*, *ne?*, *einfach*, the reason why Lena is late. And notice the two traps she marked: a correction (*sieben, nee … halb acht*) and a contrast (*vorm Kino, nicht am Bahnhof*).

## Numbers when you listen

Numbers are where listeners lose points. Three traps:

- German says the units before the tens: *vierundsechzig* is 64. Write the 4 first, leave a space in front of it, then write the 6 into the space.
- *-zehn* or *-zig*? *siebzehn* is 17, *siebzig* is 70; *fünfzehn* 15, *fünfzig* 50. Listen for the end of the word.
- Times: announcements use the 24-hour clock (*vierzehn Uhr zwölf* = 14:12). In conversation, *halb drei* means 2:30, half *to* three, not half past.

### Example 3: Writing numbers as you hear them

1. *Die Telefonnummer ist null eins fünf zwo, achtundvierzig, dreiundsiebzig.* Digits first: 0 1 5 2, then pairs, units first: *acht-und-vierzig* → 48, *drei-und-siebzig* → 73. Note: 0152 48 73. *zwo* is *zwei*, said on the phone so it isn't confused with *drei*.
2. *Der Bus fährt um Viertel vor fünf.* A quarter to five: 4:45, or 16:45 in the afternoon.
3. *Das kostet siebzehn fünfzig.* Prices are said like this without *Euro*: 17,50 €. Listen for *-zehn*: not 70,50.

## Practising on your own

Listening improves only by listening. Some ways that work at A2:

- Listen twice: first without the text, for the gist, then with the transcript to check what you missed. Then listen once more without it.
- Read transcripts aloud, including the reductions. Saying *ham wir* yourself makes it easier to hear.
- Use learner material with transcripts, for example Deutsche Welle's free courses such as *Nicos Weg* (on the reading list) or its slowly spoken news. Offers change, so check what's currently available.
- Put the radio or a podcast on while you cook. Understanding only the topic is a good start.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to understand every word. Listen for nouns, numbers and the signal words for changes.
- Writing down the first time you hear. *um sieben, nee, um halb acht*: the last version counts.
- Hearing *siebzig* for *siebzehn*, or writing 64 for *sechsundvierzig*. Units come first.
- Reading *halb drei* as 3:30. It's 2:30.
- Mistaking a modal particle for information. *Das ist halt so* adds no new fact.
- Stopping when you miss a word. The answer often comes a moment later, so keep listening.

## Key points

- Spoken German uses **[[reductions]]**: *hab, ham, is, nich, 'n, 'nen, mal, grad, vorm, fürs*.
