questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden!" What happened?
choices: She signed up for the exam.
questions.explanation: bestehen means to pass an exam. "Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht" would only mean she took it; failing is durchfallen, and signing up is sich anmelden.

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Spanisch für Anfänger. Volkshochschule Bremen. Dienstags, 18.30 bis 20 Uhr, ab 7. Oktober, zehn Abende. Gebühr: 98 Euro. Anmeldung bis 30. September online oder im Büro. Am Ende bekommen alle Teilnehmer ein Zertifikat." Which statement is true?
choices: You have to register by 30 September.
The course takes place on Tuesday mornings.
Only participants who pass a test get a certificate.
questions.explanation: "Anmeldung bis 30. September" means registration is open until 30 September. The course starts on 7 October (ab 7. Oktober), it runs in the evening (18.30 bis 20 Uhr), and all participants get a certificate.

questions.stem: Mia says: "Ich habe Geschichte studiert." What did she study?
questions.explanation: die Geschichte means both story and history; as a subject you study, it is history. Geography is Erdkunde and art is Kunst.

questions.stem: What is a "Gymnasium" in Germany?
questions.explanation: A Gymnasium is the academic secondary school that ends with the Abitur. It is a false friend: a gym is das Fitnessstudio or, at school, die Turnhalle. Vocational school is die Berufsschule.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte ___ für den Englischkurs anmelden."
questions.explanation: sich anmelden is reflexive with an accusative pronoun that matches the subject: ich möchte mich anmelden. "sich" is only for er/sie/es and sie/Sie, and "mir" is dative.

questions.stem: "Weißt du, wann wir den Test schreiben?" – "___ Frag doch Frau Haas."
questions.explanation: Keine Ahnung! means "No idea!", which fits because the speaker then suggests asking the teacher. Kein Problem answers a request, Gute Besserung is said to someone who is ill, and Herzlichen Glückwunsch congratulates.

questions.stem: Complete politely: "Können Sie mir sagen, wo ___?"
questions.explanation: In an indirect question the conjugated verb goes to the end: wo der Geldautomat ist. "wo ist der Geldautomat" keeps the word order of a direct question, the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wissen Sie, ___ ich für den Antrag einen Termin brauche?"
questions.explanation: The direct question is a yes/no question (Brauche ich einen Termin?), so the indirect question uses ob, "whether". "wenn" means if/when and is a typical mistake from English "if"; dass doesn't ask anything.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich lasse mein Fahrrad in der Werkstatt ___."
questions.explanation: lassen works like a modal verb: the second verb goes to the end as a plain infinitive without zu: reparieren lassen. "zu reparieren" adds a zu that lassen never takes.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe mein Auto reparieren lassen" mean?
choices: I let my car get damaged.
I left my car at the garage.
questions.explanation: lassen + infinitive means getting someone else to do the job: I had my car repaired. If you did it yourself, you'd say Ich habe mein Auto repariert. Leaving something somewhere is lassen without a second verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "Meine Schwester ___ sich die Haare schneiden."
questions.explanation: lassen changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: sie lässt. "lasst" is the ihr form, and "lass" is the du imperative.

questions.stem: You need cash from your account. What do you do at the cash machine?
questions.explanation: Geld abheben means to withdraw money. einzahlen is to pay money in, überweisen is to transfer it to another account, and sparen is to save.

questions.stem: A message on your answering machine: "Hallo Frau Schulz, hier ist die Autowerkstatt Brenner. Ihr Auto ist leider noch nicht fertig, wir warten noch auf ein Teil. Sie können es am Donnerstag ab 14 Uhr abholen." When can Frau Schulz collect her car?
questions.explanation: "am Donnerstag ab 14 Uhr" means on Thursday from 2 p.m., so in the afternoon. The car isn't ready today (noch nicht fertig), and the message doesn't ask her to call back.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte einen neuen Reisepass ___."
questions.explanation: You apply for a document with beantragen. sich bewerben is for jobs and places, anmelden is for registering (yourself or an address), and melden means to report something.

questions.stem: You call the Bürgeramt and hear a short beeping sound again and again. Your friend says: "Es ist besetzt." What does that mean?
questions.explanation: besetzt means engaged or busy: someone else is on the line. A closed office is geschlossen, and a wrong number is eine falsche Nummer.

questions.stem: The bank employee says: "Einen Moment bitte, ich verbinde Sie mit meiner Kollegin." What is happening?
choices: You are being put through to her colleague.
Her colleague will call you back later.
Her colleague is busy at the moment.
You should call her colleague directly.
questions.explanation: verbinden on the phone means to connect or put through: she is transferring your call. Calling back would be zurückrufen, and busy would be besetzt.

questions.stem: You have just moved into a flat in Germany. "Wo muss ich meine neue Adresse anmelden?" – "Beim ___."
questions.explanation: You register your address at the Bürgeramt (citizens' office) within two weeks of moving in. The Finanzamt deals with taxes and the Standesamt with births and marriages.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Können Sie mir sagen, wann das Amt öffnet?
Ich möchte wissen, ob ich hier parken darf.
Könnten Sie mir sagen, wie viel das kostet?
Wissen Sie, wo ist die Post?
questions.explanation: In an indirect question the verb goes to the end: Wissen Sie, wo die Post ist? The other three sentences all put the verb last correctly (öffnet, darf, kostet).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ drei Tagen Fieber." (The fever started three days ago and I still have it.)
questions.explanation: For something that started in the past and is still going on, German uses seit + dative with the present tense: seit drei Tagen. "vor drei Tagen" means three days ago, and "für" is the English pattern ("for three days").

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I've been ill for a week" (and still am)?
choices: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.
Ich war für eine Woche krank.
Ich bin vor einer Woche krank gewesen.
questions.explanation: German uses the present tense with seit: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank. The other sentences use a past tense, which says the illness is over, or use haben where krank needs sein.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie hat seit drei ___ Rückenschmerzen."
questions.explanation: seit takes the dative, and dative plural nouns add -n: seit drei Monaten. "Monate" is the nominative and accusative plural, the form learners often forget to change.

questions.stem: Give your friend advice: "Du ___ zum Arzt gehen."
questions.explanation: Advice uses the Konjunktiv II form sollte, and the du form is solltest. "Du sollst" means someone has told you to (an order, not advice), and "sollte" is the ich and er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Tell a friend to take the tablet: "___ die Tablette mit viel Wasser!"
questions.explanation: The du imperative is the du form without du and without -st, keeping the e→i change: du nimmst → Nimm! "Nimmst" keeps the ending, and "Nehmen" without Sie isn't a polite command.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correct instruction from a doctor to a patient?
questions.explanation: The Sie imperative puts the verb first with Sie after it, and a separable prefix goes to the end: Atmen Sie tief ein. "Einatmen Sie" forgets to split the verb, and a doctor uses Sie, not du.

questions.stem: From a package insert: "Nehmen Sie dreimal täglich zwei Tabletten nach dem Essen. Nehmen Sie nicht mehr als sechs Tabletten pro Tag. Schwangere sollten vorher mit dem Arzt sprechen." How many tablets a day is the normal dose?
questions.explanation: dreimal täglich zwei Tabletten is three times a day two tablets, so six a day, which is also the maximum. "two" is one dose, and "three" is how many times a day.

questions.stem: The doctor asks: "Was fehlt Ihnen denn?" What is a good answer?
choices: Ich fehle heute bei der Arbeit.
Nein, mir fehlt nichts, ich bin krank.
Ich habe seit gestern Halsschmerzen und Fieber.
questions.explanation: "Was fehlt Ihnen?" is the doctor's way of asking "What's the matter?", so you describe your symptoms. The other answers take fehlen literally (to be missing or absent), and "mir fehlt nichts" would mean you're fine.

questions.stem: Someone sneezes next to you. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Germans say Gesundheit! (health) after a sneeze, like "Bless you!". Gute Besserung is for someone who is ill, Prost is a toast, and Entschuldigung is what the person who sneezed might say.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe eine Allergie ___ Katzen."
questions.explanation: An allergy in German is "against" something: eine Allergie gegen Katzen. "für" and "von" are guesses from English ("allergy for", "allergic to"); German always uses gegen.

questions.stem: How do you say "I really ought to do more sport"? "Ich ___ eigentlich mehr Sport machen."
questions.explanation: müsste (with umlaut) is the Konjunktiv II of müssen: "really ought to, would have to". "musste" without the umlaut is the simple past (had to), and "muss" is a plain "must".

questions.stem: What is "der Krankenwagen"?
questions.explanation: der Krankenwagen (literally "sick car") is an ambulance. A hospital is das Krankenhaus, the waiting room das Wartezimmer, and a sick note die Krankschreibung.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist der Kollege, ___ unsere Webseite macht."
questions.explanation: Kollege is masculine, and inside the relative clause he is the subject (he makes the website), so the nominative "der" is right. "den" would be correct only if he were the object, as in "den ich kenne".

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Laptop, ___ ich gekauft habe, war nicht teuer."
questions.explanation: Laptop is masculine, and in the relative clause "ich" is the subject: I bought the laptop, so the laptop is the direct object and takes the accusative "den". "der" is the tempting choice if you take the case from "Der Laptop" at the start of the sentence, but case comes from inside the relative clause.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wo sind die Fotos, ___ wir im Urlaub gemacht haben?"
questions.explanation: Fotos is plural, and the plural relative pronoun is "die" in both nominative and accusative. "das" agrees with the singular "das Foto", but here the antecedent is plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Die Sendung, die um acht Uhr anfängt, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung, die fängt um acht Uhr an, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung, die um acht Uhr fängt an, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung die um acht Uhr anfängt ist sehr gut.
questions.explanation: A relative clause sends the verb to the end, and a separable verb joins up again there: "die um acht Uhr anfängt". The relative clause also needs a comma on both sides. The second choice keeps main-clause order; the third splits the verb; the fourth has no commas.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kennst du die Frau, ___ das Video hochgeladen hat?"
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun agrees with the antecedent "die Frau" (feminine), and the woman is the subject of the relative clause, so "die". "das" is the tempting mistake of agreeing with "das Video", which is only the object inside the clause.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist der Freund, mit ___ ich das Programm installiert habe."
questions.explanation: "mit" always takes the dative, and Freund is masculine, so the relative pronoun is "dem". The preposition comes first, before the relative pronoun. "den" is accusative; "denen" is the dative plural.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist alles, ___ ich über das Programm weiß."
questions.explanation: After alles, etwas and nichts German uses "was" as the relative pronoun: "alles, was ich weiß". "das" follows a neuter noun, but "alles" is not a noun; "wer" asks about people.

questions.stem: What does "Ich lade die App herunter" mean?
questions.explanation: "herunterladen" (separable: ich lade … herunter) means to download. To upload is "hochladen", to delete "löschen", to save "speichern".

questions.stem: Which word completes the sentence? "Ich habe mein ___ vergessen und kann mich nicht einloggen."
questions.explanation: You need a password to log in: "Ich habe mein Passwort vergessen" means I've forgotten my password. "mein" also fits only a masculine or neuter noun, but a screen, a comment or a radio make no sense here.

questions.stem: Read: "Morgens höre ich im Auto Radio. Eine Zeitung kaufe ich nicht mehr; die Artikel, die mich interessieren, lese ich online. Die Sendungen, die ich mag, kommen sehr spät, deshalb nehme ich sie auf." How does the writer watch the late programmes?
choices: In the car, on the radio.
Later, because the writer records them.
questions.explanation: "deshalb nehme ich sie auf" means "so I record them": "aufnehmen" is to record. The radio in the car is for the mornings, and the writer no longer buys a newspaper.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ich kenne einen Mann, den in Wien wohnt und Videos macht."
choices: "wohnt" should be at the start of the clause.
There should be no comma before "den".
questions.explanation: The man is the one who lives in Vienna, so inside the relative clause he is the subject and the pronoun is nominative "der". "einen" is correct in the main clause (Ich kenne einen Mann), but its case doesn't carry over into the relative clause.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to join: "Ich habe eine App. Ich benutze die App jeden Tag."
choices: Ich habe eine App, die benutze ich jeden Tag.
Ich habe eine App, die ich jeden Tag benutze.
Ich habe eine App, was ich jeden Tag benutze.
Ich habe eine App, ich jeden Tag benutze.
questions.explanation: "die App" is feminine and the object of "benutze", so the relative pronoun is "die" (feminine accusative = nominative), and the verb goes to the end. The first choice keeps main-clause order, "was" can't follow a noun in correct German, and the last drops the relative pronoun as English does.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich gratuliere ___ zum Geburtstag!"
questions.explanation: gratulieren takes a dative object: "Ich gratuliere dir". "dich" is the accusative, the most common mistake, because English "congratulate you" has a direct object.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir laden ___ herzlich zu unserer Feier ein."
questions.explanation: einladen takes an accusative object (the guest), and "euch" is the accusative of "ihr". "dir" is dative, which is right after gratulieren but not after einladen. "ihnen" (small i) means them, in the dative.

questions.stem: How do you say "on 24 December" aloud?
questions.explanation: Dates use ordinal numbers. From 20 the ordinal ends in -ste, and after "am" it takes the ending -en: "am vierundzwanzigsten". The cardinal "vierundzwanzig" and the ending -e are wrong after am; "im" is for months, not days.

questions.stem: Which ordinal is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: The irregular ordinals are erste, dritte, siebte and achte. "dreite", "einste" and "achtte" don't exist: achte has only one t. (You may also see the longer variant "siebente".)

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du schon einen Weihnachtsbaum?" – "Ja, wir haben gestern ___ gekauft."
questions.explanation: The pronoun replaces "einen Weihnachtsbaum" (masculine, accusative object), so it is "einen". "ein" is the article without its ending, and "eins" is the neuter pronoun.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ist das dein Glas?" – "Nein, das ist nicht ___."
questions.explanation: Standing alone for "das Glas" (neuter), the possessive needs the neuter ending: "meins". "mein" is the article form used before a noun ("mein Glas"); "meiner" would replace a masculine noun.

questions.stem: It is 30 December. You say goodbye to a colleague until next year. What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Guten Rutsch!" is the wish for the change to the new year, said before 1 January. On 30 December it's too late for Frohe Weihnachten, Ostern is in spring, and Gute Besserung is for someone who is ill.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ich ein Kind war, haben wir jedes Jahr bei meiner Oma gefeiert."
questions.explanation: One period in the past (when I was a child) takes "als". "wenn" is for repeated events or the present and future; "wann" is a question word; "ob" means whether.

questions.stem: What do people in the Rhineland usually do at Karneval?
choices: They dress up in costumes and watch parades.
They paint eggs for the children.
They let off fireworks at midnight.
questions.explanation: At Karneval (Fasching in Bavaria and Austria) people "verkleiden sich": they dress up in costumes, and there are parades. Advent candles belong to December, painted eggs to Easter, and midnight fireworks to Silvester.

questions.stem: Read: "Am Samstag, dem 31. Dezember, feiern wir Silvester bei uns. Wir fangen um 20 Uhr mit einem Buffet an. Wer möchte, kann gern ein Kostüm tragen. Könnt ihr mir bis zum 20. Bescheid sagen?" What must the guests do?
choices: Let the host know by the 20th.
questions.explanation: "Könnt ihr mir bis zum 20. Bescheid sagen?" asks the guests to let the host know by the 20th. A costume is optional ("Wer möchte, kann …"), and the buffet is provided by the hosts.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Wir wünschen Sie und Ihre Familie frohe Weihnachten."
choices: "Sie und Ihre Familie" should be "Ihnen und Ihrer Familie".
questions.explanation: wünschen takes a dative person and an accusative thing: you wish something TO someone. So the people must be dative: "Ihnen und Ihrer Familie". "frohe Weihnachten" is correct with no article.

questions.stem: In Germany, when are Christmas presents usually opened?
questions.explanation: In Germany the presents are given on Heiligabend, the evening of 24 December. The morning of the 25th is the British and American custom.

questions.stem: You write to your course teacher, Ms Brandt, whom you call "Sie". Which opening and closing fit best?
choices: Lieber Frau Brandt, … Mit freundlichen Grüßen
Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, … Bis bald!
questions.explanation: This is semi-formal: you know her but say Sie, so "Liebe Frau Brandt" with "Viele Grüße" is ideal. "Lieber" is for a man; "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren" is for an unknown reader and doesn't match "Bis bald".

questions.stem: Complete the formal opening: "Sehr ___ Herr Wagner,"
questions.explanation: For a man the opening is "Sehr geehrter Herr …"; for a woman "Sehr geehrte Frau …". The ending -er shows the masculine, just like "Lieber Tom".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Es tut mir leid, dass ich habe nicht geantwortet.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich nicht habe geantwortet.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich geantwortet nicht habe.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich nicht geantwortet habe.
questions.explanation: After "dass" the conjugated verb goes to the end, after the participle: "dass ich nicht geantwortet habe". The first choice keeps main-clause order, the most common error.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Auto ist kaputt. ___ komme ich heute mit dem Bus."
questions.explanation: The second sentence is the consequence of the first, so "deshalb" (that's why), followed directly by the verb. "Weil" would send the verb to the end, "Denn" needs normal order, and "Trotzdem" means "nevertheless", which doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Complete: "Entschuldigung, ich ___ mich ein bisschen. Ich bin in zehn Minuten da."
questions.explanation: "sich verspäten" means to be late, and it is reflexive: "ich verspäte mich". "verschieben" means to postpone something, not to be late, and "spät" is an adjective.

questions.stem: What does "Können wir den Termin auf Donnerstag verschieben?" ask?
choices: Can we confirm the appointment for Thursday?
Can we move the appointment to Thursday?
questions.explanation: "verschieben" means to postpone or move, and "auf Donnerstag" gives the new day. To cancel is "absagen", to confirm "bestätigen".

questions.stem: Your friend writes: "Sag mir Bescheid, wenn du angekommen bist." What should you do?
choices: Pick him up when he arrives.
Let him know when you have arrived.
questions.explanation: "Bescheid sagen" means to let someone know. "wenn du angekommen bist" means when you have arrived. So he wants a message from you when you get there.

questions.stem: In an e-mail, what is "der Anhang"?
questions.explanation: "der Anhang" is the attachment: "Im Anhang finden Sie …" means "Please find … attached". The subject line is "der Betreff", and a reply or feedback is "die Rückmeldung".

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Liebe Frau Brandt, kannst du mir bitte die Aufgaben schicken? Viele Grüße"
choices: "Viele Grüße" is too informal for a teacher.
"kannst" should start with a capital letter.
questions.explanation: With "Frau Brandt" you use Sie, so the request must be "können Sie". Mixing a Sie-opening with du is a typical register mistake. "Liebe" is right for a woman, "Viele Grüße" is fine in a semi-formal e-mail, and after the opening comma the next word starts small.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Mia, es tut mir leid, ich verspäte mich um 20 Minuten, weil mein Bus nicht kommt. Kaufst du die Karten? Ich gebe dir das Geld nachher. Bis gleich! Tom" Why is Tom late?
questions.explanation: "weil mein Bus nicht kommt" gives the reason: his bus isn't coming. He asks Mia to buy the tickets and will give her the money afterwards ("nachher").

questions.stem: Which sentence accepts an invitation?
choices: Ich sage gern zu und bringe einen Salat mit.
questions.explanation: "zusagen" is to accept, the opposite of "absagen" (to decline or cancel). The other sentences cancel, ask to postpone, or say you forwarded the invitation.

questions.stem: Complete: "Bitte antworten Sie ___ bald, die Sache ist dringend."
questions.explanation: "möglichst bald" means "as soon as possible". "möglich" alone is the adjective "possible" and doesn't work before "bald"; "inzwischen" means meanwhile.

questions.stem: How many points do you need to pass the Goethe-Zertifikat A2?
choices: 60 overall, with at least 45 written and 15 speaking
questions.explanation: You need 60 of 100 points, and also at least 45 of the 75 written points and 15 of the 25 speaking points. A good written score can't make up for a very weak speaking result.

questions.stem: What do you write in the Schreiben part of the Goethe A2?
choices: A form and a short letter
An informal SMS (20–30 words) and a semi-formal e-mail (30–40 words)
questions.explanation: Schreiben has two tasks: an informal SMS of 20–30 words and a semi-formal e-mail of 30–40 words, each covering three content points. The form belongs to the A1 exam.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the speaking tasks in the Goethe A2?
choices: Asking and answering questions with word cards
Planning an appointment with your partner
questions.explanation: There is no preparation time and no presentation at A2. The three tasks are questions with word cards, talking about your life, and planning something together.

questions.stem: In the planning task your partner suggests: "Wie wäre es mit Samstag um zehn?" You have a dentist's appointment then. What is a good reply?
choices: Da kann ich leider nicht, da bin ich beim Zahnarzt. Geht es auch am Nachmittag?
Ja, gern, um zehn passt es mir gut.
questions.explanation: A good reply refuses politely, gives a reason and makes a new suggestion, so the conversation keeps going. A bare "Nein" ends it, and accepting would contradict your calendar.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann heute nicht kommen, weil ich ___."
questions.explanation: After "weil" the conjugated verb goes to the very end, after the infinitive: "weil ich arbeiten muss" (lesson 3). "muss arbeiten" is main-clause order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe einen ___ Laptop gekauft."
questions.explanation: Laptop is masculine and the accusative object; after "einen" the adjective takes -en: "einen neuen Laptop" (lesson 9). "neuer" is the nominative after "ein", as in "Das ist ein neuer Laptop".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wohin legst du das Buch?" – "Ich lege es auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: "Wohin?" asks about a movement to a place, so the two-way preposition "auf" takes the accusative: "auf den Tisch" (lesson 13). "auf dem Tisch" answers "Wo?" (where something is).

questions.stem: Which sentence is a polite request?
choices: Könnten Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?
questions.explanation: "Könnten Sie …?" is the Konjunktiv II (lesson 15), the most polite way to ask. "Ich will" sounds demanding, and a statement or bare imperative is not polite.

questions.stem: Complete: "Berlin ist ___ als München."
questions.explanation: The comparative of "groß" adds an umlaut and -er: "größer als" (lesson 12). "am größten" is the superlative, and "mehr groß" is an English-style mistake.

questions.stem: An exam instruction says: "Beachten Sie die Uhrzeit." What should you do?
choices: Look at the clock in the room.
questions.explanation: "beachten" means to pay attention to or note, and "die Uhrzeit" is the time on the clock. The instruction tells you that the time in the text matters for the answer.

questions.stem: In a listening text you hear: "Der Kurs beginnt am Montag um neun, äh, nein, um halb zehn." When does the course start?
questions.explanation: The speaker corrects himself: "nein, um halb zehn". The last information counts, and "halb zehn" is 9:30, not 10:30 or 8:30: German "halb" counts towards the next hour.

questions.stem: What does "Ich verwechsle immer die beiden Wörter" mean?
choices: I always mix up the two words.
questions.explanation: "verwechseln" means to mix up or confuse. To forget is "vergessen", to repeat "wiederholen".

questions.stem: You want to know what time the pharmacy opens on Saturday. You have its whole information leaflet. Which way of reading fits best?
choices: Skimming the whole leaflet for its topic
Scanning for Samstag and a time
Reading every sentence slowly from the start
Translating the leaflet word by word
questions.explanation: You need one fact with a typical shape (a day and a time), so you scan: let your eyes jump until you see Samstag and Uhr, then read that line. Skimming only tells you what the leaflet is about; reading everything slowly wastes time.

questions.stem: Match each way of reading to the task it fits best.
choices: Find out what a newspaper article is about
Find the price of a bike in an ad
Follow the rules for a library card exactly
questions.explanation: Skimming gives the topic, scanning finds one fact, detailed reading is for exact rules. Translating every word is not a reading strategy the lesson recommends.

questions.stem: Name the type of each numbered text on the notice board.

image.alt: A notice board with four texts: a notice from Hausverwaltung Berger saying there is no water on Tuesday 14 May from 8 to 12 because of a repair in the cellar; a poster for a summer party in the courtyard on Saturday 18 May from 4 pm, asking people to bring salad or cake; a small ad selling a blue child's bike in good condition for 40 euros, Familie Yilmaz, second floor; and a note about Mia, a grey cat with white paws, missing since Monday, with a reward of 50 euros.

questions.explanation: 1 has a sender (Hausverwaltung Berger) and An alle Mieterinnen und Mieter: a notice. 2 has huge letters, an event, a date and a time: a poster. 3 says Zu verkaufen with a price and tear-off strips: a small ad. 4 describes a missing cat and offers a Belohnung: a note.

questions.stem: Look at the notice board. According to the notice from the management, when is there no water?

image.alt: A notice board with four texts: a notice from Hausverwaltung Berger saying there is no water on Tuesday 14 May from 8 to 12 because of a repair in the cellar; a poster for a summer party in the courtyard on Saturday 18 May from 4 pm, asking people to bring salad or cake; a small ad selling a blue child's bike in good condition for 40 euros, Familie Yilmaz, second floor; and a note about Mia, a grey cat with white paws, missing since Monday, with a reward of 50 euros.

questions.explanation: The notice says: Am Dienstag, 14. Mai, gibt es von 8 bis 12 Uhr kein Wasser. Saturday from 4 pm is the summer party; Monday is when the cat went missing.

questions.stem: Look at the notice board. How many euros does the child's bike cost? Give only the number.

image.alt: A notice board with four texts: a notice from Hausverwaltung Berger saying there is no water on Tuesday 14 May from 8 to 12 because of a repair in the cellar; a poster for a summer party in the courtyard on Saturday 18 May from 4 pm, asking people to bring salad or cake; a small ad selling a blue child's bike in good condition for 40 euros, Familie Yilmaz, second floor; and a note about Mia, a grey cat with white paws, missing since Monday, with a reward of 50 euros.

questions.explanation: Scan the small ad for Euro: Kinderfahrrad, blau, gut erhalten, 40 Euro. (The 50 euros on the board are the reward for the cat.)

questions.stem: A sign says: "Der Laden öffnet erst um 10 Uhr." Ana arrives at 9:30. What does she find?
choices: The shop is only open for ten minutes.
questions.explanation: erst um 10 means "not until 10": at 9:30 it is still closed. Reading erst as nur ("only") leads to the third choice.

questions.stem: A museum sign says: "Geöffnet: täglich außer montags, 10 bis 17 Uhr." Which statement is true?
choices: The museum is open only on Mondays.
The museum is open every day, Mondays included.
The museum opens at 17 on Mondays.
The museum is closed on Mondays.
questions.explanation: außer means "except": open every day except Mondays. Missing the small word außer gives the second choice; reading it as "only" gives the first.

questions.stem: Which of these are typical clues of a small ad (Anzeige)? Select all that apply.
choices: A long quotation from a politician
questions.explanation: Small ads offer (Zu verkaufen, Biete) or want something (Suche) and usually give a price and a contact. Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren opens a formal letter, and quotations belong to news reports.

questions.stem: Fill in the small word that means "not until": "Der Arzt ist ___ ab 11 Uhr in der Praxis."
questions.explanation: erst marks a time that is later than you might expect: the doctor is not in the practice before 11. (nur would limit an amount, not a starting time.)

questions.stem: Read the report: "Neustadt: Bibliothek verleiht jetzt auch Werkzeug. … Das Leihen ist kostenlos. Man braucht nur einen Bibliotheksausweis. Er kostet für Erwachsene 12 Euro im Jahr, für Kinder und Jugendliche unter 18 nichts. Die Dinge darf man zwei Wochen behalten. Elektrische Geräte bekommt man aber erst ab 18 Jahren. … Kleidung und Möbel nimmt sie nicht an." Who can borrow an electric drill?
choices: An adult with a library card
questions.explanation: You need a library card (Man braucht nur einen Bibliotheksausweis), and electric appliances are only for people aged 18 and over (erst ab 18 Jahren). The 16-year-old has a free card but is too young for an electric drill.

questions.stem: Which questions does the lead of a news report usually answer?
choices: How the journalist feels about it
questions.explanation: The lead, the first sentence or paragraph, gives the key facts: Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? Details, quotes and the Warum? usually come later.

questions.stem: You have a reading question and a text. As in the exam tip from lesson 24, you start with the question. Put the steps of an efficient reader in order.
choices: Skim the text for its type and topic
Scan for the place where the answer must be
questions.explanation: Know what you are looking for, get an overview, find the right place, and only then read slowly. Reading in detail first wastes time on parts you don't need.

questions.stem: Read the report: "Neustadt: Bibliothek verleiht jetzt auch Werkzeug. … Das Leihen ist kostenlos. Man braucht nur einen Bibliotheksausweis. Er kostet für Erwachsene 12 Euro im Jahr, für Kinder und Jugendliche unter 18 nichts. Die Dinge darf man zwei Wochen behalten. Elektrische Geräte bekommt man aber erst ab 18 Jahren. … Kleidung und Möbel nimmt sie nicht an." Richtig oder falsch: "Die Bibliothek nimmt alte Möbel an."
choices: Falsch: Möbel nimmt sie nicht an.
questions.explanation: The library does want donations, but the last sentence says: Kleidung und Möbel nimmt sie nicht an. A reader who stops at Spenden says richtig.

questions.stem: The report says about the library's items: "Die neue Bibliothek der Dinge hat schon 120 Gegenstände. Bald sollen es 200 sein." What does the second sentence tell you?
choices: The library plans to have 200 items soon.
questions.explanation: bald (soon) and sollen describe a plan, not a fact: it has 120 now and wants 200. Taking a plan for a fact is a common reading mistake.

questions.stem: What is "der Hausschuh"?
choices: A slipper, a shoe you wear at home
questions.explanation: Read compounds from the back: the head word is Schuh, so it is a kind of shoe, one for the house. A shoe shop is das Schuhhaus, with the blocks the other way round.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Kinderzimmer" (children's room)?
questions.explanation: The head word gives the gender: das Zimmer, so das Kinderzimmer. die is the article of the plural Kinder, the modifier, which does not count.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the compound "der Wohnungsschlüssel".

image.alt: The compound der Wohnungsschlüssel in four boxes: der, Wohnung, s, schlüssel

questions.explanation: Schlüssel is the head word: it says what the thing is (a key) and gives the article der. Wohnung is the modifier: which key. The s only links the two parts and has no meaning.

questions.stem: Make one compound and write it with its article: die Sonne + die Brille = ___
questions.explanation: Head word Brille (die), modifier Sonne with the linking -n-: die Sonnenbrille, sunglasses.

questions.stem: Match each building block to its usual meaning.
choices: a person or machine that does it
a place where something is sold
questions.explanation: essbar = can be eaten, arbeitslos = without work, unbekannt = not known, der Drucker = the machine that prints, die Sauberkeit = the quality of being clean.

questions.stem: A hotel review says: "Das Frühstück war fast unbezahlbar." What does it mean?
choices: Breakfast could not be paid by card.
questions.explanation: un- (not) + bezahlen (to pay) + -bar (can be done): "not payable", so very expensive. kostenlos would mean free.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe ein Geschenk bekommen." mean?
choices: I have to give a present.
questions.explanation: bekommen is a false friend: it means "to get, receive", not "to become" (werden). das Geschenk is a present; das Gift would be poison.

questions.stem: Which German words are false friends, meaning something different from the English word they look like? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: das Gift = poison, eventuell = possibly, also = so, therefore. das Hotel and die Information mean what they look like.

questions.stem: "Im Flur steht eine alte Kommode. Sie hat vier Schubladen. In der obersten liegen unsere Mützen und Schals." What is a Schublade?
questions.explanation: The context: a Kommode has four of them, and things lie in them, in the top one and the bottom one. That is a drawer (a Kommode is a chest of drawers).

questions.stem: You read "Sie lädt uns zum Essen ein." Which form do you look up in a dictionary?
questions.explanation: Dictionaries list the infinitive. lädt … ein is a separable verb with a stem change, so put the prefix back on the front: einladen (to invite).

questions.stem: Under which form do you find "Bäume" in a dictionary? Type the noun with its article.
questions.explanation: Find the singular: Bäume is the plural of der Baum (tree). The umlaut appears only in the plural.

questions.stem: Put the blocks in order to make the German word for "front door key".
questions.explanation: A front door key is a Schlüssel, so Schlüssel goes last as the head word. Which key? The one for the Haustür: der Haustürschlüssel.

questions.stem: "die Sauberkeit" is built from which word?
questions.explanation: sauber (clean) + -keit (a quality) = cleanliness. sauer (sour) and saugen (to suck) only look similar.

questions.stem: Someone says about a film: "Der Film war unheimlich." What did they most likely mean?
questions.explanation: unheimlich means creepy or eerie (and in speech also "incredibly", as in unheimlich nett). It is a reminder that un- + a root is a guess you must check, not a rule.

questions.stem: You hear: "Ham wir noch Milch?" How is this written in standard German?
questions.explanation: ham is the spoken reduction of haben. Reductions hit small words like haben and nicht; the noun Milch stays clear.

questions.stem: Match each spoken form to the written form.
questions.explanation: Ich hab = ich habe, nich = nicht, 'nen = einen, grad = gerade, vorm = vor dem. nein is shortened to nee, which is not in the list.

questions.stem: What does "halt" add in "Der Bus fährt halt nur stündlich."?
choices: It means the bus stops here.
It means the bus is late.
It says that is just how it is.
questions.explanation: halt is a modal particle: it adds an attitude ("that's just how it is, nothing to be done") but no new fact. As an exclamation, Halt! means "Stop!", but not here.

questions.stem: Timo says: "Wir treffen uns um sieben, nee, warte, um halb acht." When are they meeting?
questions.explanation: After a correction (nee, warte) the last version counts: um halb acht, 7:30. halb acht is half to eight, so 8:30 is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: Name the numbered columns of this departures board.

image.alt: A departures board with four trains and no column headings

questions.explanation: Read down each column, for example the second train: 14:12 (Zeit, departure), ICE 578 (Zug), Hamburg-Altona (Nach, destination), 7 (Gleis, platform), ca. 15 Min. später (Hinweis, a delay).

questions.stem: You hear: "Information zur S 2 in Richtung Flughafen, Abfahrt 14 Uhr 20: Die S-Bahn fährt heute von Gleis 2." Which platform do you go to?

image.alt: A departures board: 14:05 RE 7 to Köln Hbf, platform 3; 14:12 ICE 578 to Hamburg-Altona, platform 7, about 15 minutes later; 14:20 S 2 to Flughafen, platform 1, today platform 2; 14:31 RB 48 to Bonn, platform 5, cancelled.

questions.explanation: The announcement changes the platform for today: heute von Gleis 2. The board also says heute Gleis 2; platform 1 is the usual one.

questions.stem: You hear: "Die RB 48 nach Bonn, Abfahrt 14 Uhr 31, fällt heute aus. Die nächste Verbindung nach Bonn ist um 15 Uhr 31." Clara wanted the 14:31 train. How many minutes must she wait for the next one? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: fällt aus means cancelled. From 14:31 to 15:31 is 60 minutes.

questions.stem: Write the number you hear as digits: "achtundvierzig"
questions.explanation: German says the units first: acht-und-vierzig = eight and forty = 48. Writing 84 is the typical mistake.

questions.stem: Put the parts of this station announcement in the usual order.
questions.explanation: Announcements go: attention (where) → which train → what is different → apology or what to do. Listen hardest right after the train is named.

questions.stem: Which of these words are often used as modal particles in spoken German? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: ja, doch and mal (and halt, eben, denn) add attitude: Das ist ja teuer! Komm doch mit! Kannst du mal helfen? Bahnhof is a noun and morgen an adverb of time; both carry information.

questions.stem: Which tag question is typical of southern Germany and Austria?
questions.explanation: gell? (or gelt?) is southern and Austrian. ne? is typical of the north, nicht wahr? is careful speech anywhere, and na ja is a filler word, not a tag question.

questions.stem: A friend says: "Wir sehen uns um halb drei." What time is that?
questions.explanation: halb drei is half way to three: 2:30. English "half three" (3:30 in British English) makes 3:30 the tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which note is written well in Stichworte for this message: "Wir treffen uns am Samstag um halb acht vorm Kino"?
choices: Timo hat gesagt, dass wir uns am Samstag treffen.
Treffen um halb, nicht Bahnhof, ne?
questions.explanation: Stichworte keep the facts (day, time, place) and drop everything else. The second is a whole sentence and too slow; the third and fourth lose the time.

questions.stem: On the Berlin U-Bahn you hear: "Zurückbleiben, bitte!" What should you do?
questions.explanation: zurückbleiben means to stay back: the doors are about to close, so don't try to get on.

questions.stem: Which tense does the narrator of a German fairy tale normally use?
questions.explanation: Stories are narrated in the simple past (Präteritum): Sie nahm den Vogel. The characters' speech uses the present and perfect: Du hast mir geholfen.

questions.stem: Match each simple past form to its infinitive.
questions.explanation: Strong verbs change their vowel; the consonants stay: tr-g, fl-g, gr-b, h-ß, r-f. fliehen (to flee) has the past floh, and halten has hielt.

questions.stem: What is the traditional last line of a German fairy tale?
choices: Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute.
questions.explanation: "And if they haven't died, they are still alive today." Es war einmal is the first line, and Eines Tages moves the story forward.

questions.stem: Put the events of the fairy tale "Lina und der Vogel" in order.
choices: Lina pflegte den Vogel sieben Tage lang.
Der Vogel sang: „Grab unter dem alten Baum!“
Lina fand eine Kiste voll Gold.
questions.explanation: Problem (illness), the hero goes out and meets a helper, a kind act, the helper's advice, the reward. This is the usual path of a fairy tale.

questions.stem: In the fairy tale, why couldn't the bird fly?
questions.explanation: Er konnte nicht fliegen, denn sein Flügel war verletzt: its wing was injured. denn gives the reason.

questions.stem: Type the modern German form of "balde" (from Goethe's poem).
questions.explanation: balde is an older form of bald (soon). Goethe uses it so that it rhymes with Walde.

questions.stem: Label the numbered parts of the landscape with the words from the poem and the lesson.

image.alt: An evening mountain landscape with peaks, treetops, two birds in a tree, a forest and a walker with a stick

questions.explanation: der Gipfel is the summit of the mountain, der Wipfel the top of a tree, die Vögel the birds, der Wald the forest and der Wanderer the walker. There is no river (Fluss) or bridge (Brücke) in the picture.

questions.stem: What is "Vögelein" in "Die Vögelein schweigen im Walde"?
questions.explanation: -lein makes a diminutive, usually with an umlaut: der Vogel → das Vögelein, little birds. Modern German more often says Vögelchen.

questions.stem: Which words in Goethe's poem are older or poetic forms that you shouldn't use in an everyday e-mail? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Ruh = Ruhe, im Walde = im Wald, spürest = spürst. Hauch (breath) and Gipfeln (dative plural of Gipfel) are normal modern German.

questions.stem: The first four lines of the poem end with Gipfeln, Ruh, Wipfeln, du. What is their rhyme scheme?
questions.explanation: Gipfeln rhymes with Wipfeln (lines 1 and 3: a), Ruh with du (lines 2 and 4: b): abab. The last four lines are cddc.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Büchlein" (little book)?
questions.explanation: Diminutives with -chen or -lein are always neuter: das Büchlein, das Vögelein, even though der Vogel is masculine.

questions.stem: Fill in the infinitive: "schwieg" comes from ___.
questions.explanation: schweigen (to be silent): schwieg, hat geschwiegen. Think of the consonants schw-g.

questions.stem: When and where did Goethe write the poem "Über allen Gipfeln ist Ruh", by most accounts?
choices: In 1780, on the wall of a hut on a hill near Ilmenau
In 1815, in a letter from Weimar
In 1823, as a song text for Schubert
In 1812, for the Grimms' collection of fairy tales
questions.explanation: By most accounts he wrote it in pencil on the wall of a wooden hut on the Kickelhahn near Ilmenau in September 1780. 1815 is when Goethe published it in his collected works (an unauthorised printing had appeared in 1800), and Schubert set it to music later.

questions.stem: What does "Spürest du kaum einen Hauch" mean?
choices: You feel hardly a breath of air.
You can hardly see the trees.
questions.explanation: kaum = hardly, der Hauch = a breath, a light breath of wind. Everything in the poem is still.

questions.stem: Complete with the past participle of "umziehen" (to move house): "Wir sind 2015 nach Wien ___."
questions.explanation: umziehen is separable, so -ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: um + ge + zogen = umgezogen. It's movement from one home to another, which is why the sentence uses sind.

questions.stem: Name the stages of a life shown in the numbered pictures.

image.alt: Five numbered pictures on a timeline: a pram, a graduation cap, two wedding rings, a moving van with boxes and a rocking chair.

questions.explanation: The pram stands for die Geburt (birth), the graduation cap for der Abschluss (a qualification), the rings for die Hochzeit (wedding), the moving van for der Umzug (a move to a new home) and the rocking chair for die Rente (retirement, pension). die Kindheit is a whole period of life, and der Lebenslauf is the CV that lists these events.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its past participle.
questions.explanation: -ieren verbs take no ge-: studiert. Verbs with an inseparable prefix take no ge- either, so verlassen and bekommen look like their infinitives. nennen is a mixed verb: new vowel and -t, genannt. aufwachsen is separable: auf + ge + wachsen. "gestudiert" and "genennt" are the typical mistakes.

questions.stem: Which verbs form the perfect with sein? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: aufwachsen (ist aufgewachsen), sterben (ist gestorben) and werden (ist geworden) are changes of state, so they take sein. heiraten (hat geheiratet) and verlassen (hat verlassen, it has an accusative object: Ich habe meine Heimat verlassen) take haben.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "In 2010 I moved to Hamburg." Start with the year.
questions.explanation: 2010 bin ich nach Hamburg umgezogen. The year stands alone in position 1 (no "in"), so the auxiliary bin follows in position 2, then the subject ich; the participle umgezogen goes to the end of the sentence bracket.

questions.stem: Complete with the simple past of "können": "Mit sechs ___ ich schon lesen."
questions.explanation: Modal past: drop the umlaut and add -te: können → konnte. The ich form has no ending after -te. Not "könnte", which means "could" in the sense of "would be able to" (lesson 15).

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this old school report (Zeugnis).

image.alt: A school report from Grundschule Lindenweg for Peter Wolf with four numbered parts: 3b next to his name, the word Mathematik in the list of subjects, the grade 4 next to it, and a signature at the bottom.

questions.explanation: 3b is the class (die Klasse): the third year, group b. Mathematik is a subject (das Fach) and 4 is its grade (die Note); in Germany 1 is the best grade. The signature at the bottom is die Unterschrift.

questions.stem: Match each simple past form to its infinitive.
questions.explanation: Strong verbs change their vowel: gehen → ging, kommen → kam, geben → gab (es gab = there was), finden → fand. wissen is a mixed verb: new vowel and -te, wusste. The past of sehen is sah.

questions.stem: Which are correct simple past forms of modal verbs? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: konnte (können), mochte (mögen, with g → ch) and durften (dürfen) are right: no umlaut, -te. möchten has no simple past of its own (use wollte), and müsste, with an umlaut, is a different form meaning "would have to" (lesson 15); the past of müssen is musste.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "As a child I wasn't allowed to watch TV."
questions.explanation: Als Kind durfte ich nicht fernsehen. "Als Kind" is position 1, the modal durfte is in position 2, the subject follows, and the infinitive fernsehen goes to the end with nicht just before it.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence "Ich kann nicht kommen, …" by putting the words in order.
questions.explanation: …, weil ich heute arbeiten muss. weil starts the clause, the subject comes right after it, and the conjugated verb (the modal muss) goes last of all, after the infinitive arbeiten.

questions.stem: How does each person feel? Name the numbered faces.

image.alt: Five numbered faces: a big smile, a frown with a tear, angry eyebrows with clenched teeth, wide eyes with an open mouth, and a wavy mouth with a drop of sweat.

questions.explanation: 1 smiles: glücklich (happy). 2 frowns and cries: traurig (sad). 3 has angry eyebrows and clenched teeth: wütend (furious). 4 has wide eyes and an open mouth: überrascht (surprised). 5 has a wavy mouth and is sweating: nervös (nervous).

questions.stem: Complete with the perfect of "anrufen" (to call): "Ich bin enttäuscht, weil du nicht ___ ___."
questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause the auxiliary goes last of all: weil du nicht angerufen hast. anrufen is separable, so the participle is an + ge + rufen = angerufen.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich glaube, dass er recht hat.
Ich glaube, dass er hat recht.
Weil es regnet, nehme ich den Bus.
Weil es regnet, ich nehme den Bus.
questions.explanation: With dass the verb goes to the end (dass er recht hat); without dass the second part is a main clause (er hat recht). Mixing the two (dass er hat recht) is wrong. A weil clause in position 1 is followed directly by the main verb: verb, comma, verb (regnet, nehme ich).

questions.stem: Match each German adjective to its meaning.
questions.explanation: froh = glad, wütend = furious, enttäuscht = disappointed, überrascht = surprised, stolz = proud (stolz auf + accusative = proud of). "nervous" is nervös and "satisfied" is zufrieden.

questions.stem: Fill in als, wenn or ob: "___ ich klein war, hatten wir einen Hund. ___ ich heute einen Hund sehe, denke ich an ihn. Ich weiß nicht, ___ ich wieder einen Hund möchte."
questions.explanation: Als ich klein war: one period in the past. Wenn ich heute einen Hund sehe: every time, in the present. Ich weiß nicht, ob …: an indirect yes/no question (you can say "whether" in English).

questions.stem: Which word fills each gap?
left: ___ ich ein Kind war, wohnten wir in Bonn.
Weißt du, ___ der Zug fährt? – Um 8.15 Uhr.
Ich weiß nicht, ___ sie mitkommt oder nicht.
___ es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
questions.explanation: als: one period in the past (als ich ein Kind war). wann: the question asks for a time, and the answer is a time (um 8.15 Uhr). ob: a yes/no question made indirect ("whether she's coming or not"). wenn: a condition with a result.

questions.stem: In which sentences is "wenn" correct in the gap? Select all that apply.
choices: ___ ich nach Hause komme, koche ich immer zuerst Tee.
___ ich 2019 in Rom war, hat es jeden Tag geregnet.
___ du Hilfe brauchst, ruf mich an.
Ich weiß nicht, ___ er heute kommt.
questions.explanation: wenn is right for something that happens every time (… nach Hause komme, koche ich immer …) and for a condition (wenn du Hilfe brauchst). One stay in the past takes als: Als ich 2019 in Rom war. An indirect question takes ob or wann, never wenn: Ich weiß nicht, ob er heute kommt.

questions.stem: Ask politely whether the shop is open on Monday. Put the words in order after "Können Sie mir sagen, …"
questions.explanation: Können Sie mir sagen, ob Sie am Montag geöffnet haben? A yes/no question becomes indirect with ob; the subject pronoun Sie comes right after ob, and the conjugated verb haben goes to the end. The sentence as a whole is a question, so it ends with a question mark.

questions.stem: How do you say "I don't know if she's at home"?
choices: Ich weiß nicht, wenn sie zu Hause ist.
Ich weiß nicht, ob ist sie zu Hause.
Ich weiß nicht, ob sie zu Hause ist.
Ich weiß nicht, wann sie zu Hause ist.
questions.explanation: "If" here means "whether", so German uses ob, with the verb at the end: ob sie zu Hause ist. wenn never starts an indirect question; "ob ist sie" keeps question word order; wann means "when", which changes the meaning.

questions.stem: A short biography in an encyclopedia is usually written in which tense?
questions.explanation: Written stories, including biographies, use the simple past: Sie heiratete 1872. The perfect is the tense of conversation; the present is only for what is still true today.

questions.stem: Complete with the simple past of "heiraten": "1872 ___ sie den Ingenieur Carl Benz."
questions.explanation: heiraten is weak. Its stem heirat- ends in -t, so it adds -ete: sie heiratete. "heiratet" without the final -e is the present tense.

questions.stem: Complete with the simple past of "aufwachsen": "Sie ___ in Pforzheim ___."
questions.explanation: wachsen is strong (wachsen – wuchs – gewachsen), so the er/sie form is wuchs with no ending. aufwachsen is separable: in a main clause the prefix goes to the end: Sie wuchs in Pforzheim auf.

questions.stem: Match each infinitive to its simple past (er/sie form).
questions.explanation: Each follows an ablaut pattern: ei → ie (bleiben, blieb), ie → o (fliegen, flog), i → a (finden, fand), e → a (sprechen, sprach), a → u (fahren, fuhr). Strong verbs never add -te, so "fuhrte" and "bleibte" are wrong.

questions.stem: Put the events of Bertha Benz's life in order, from the earliest.
choices: Carl bekommt ein Patent für den Motorwagen.
Bertha fährt mit ihren Söhnen nach Pforzheim.
questions.explanation: Born 1849, married 1872, patent 1886, the trip to Pforzheim on 5 August 1888, died 1944 in Ladenburg at 95.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this German CV (Lebenslauf).

image.alt: A German CV with six numbered parts: a photo at the top right, four section headings whose text is hidden, and a place, date and signature at the bottom. Under heading 2: name, date of birth and address. Under heading 3: two jobs with dates. Under heading 4: a degree and the Abitur. Under heading 5: three languages with levels.

questions.explanation: Name, date of birth and address are the Persönliche Daten. Jobs go under Berufserfahrung (work experience), the degree and the Abitur under Ausbildung (education), the languages under Sprachkenntnisse. A printed CV often ends with place, date and signature. The photo is optional today.

questions.stem: Which are strong verbs, with a new vowel and no -te in the simple past? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: fahren – fuhr, sterben – starb and bleiben – blieb change their vowel and take no -te. heiraten (heiratete) and gründen (gründete) are weak.

questions.stem: In the text, why did Bertha Benz buy fuel in a pharmacy in Wiesloch?
choices: Carl had told her to stop there.
Her mother worked in the pharmacy.
It was cheaper than at the petrol station.
There were no petrol stations yet, and the fuel was sold in pharmacies.
questions.explanation: "Tankstellen gab es noch nicht, und der Wagen brauchte Ligroin, eine Art Benzin aus der Apotheke." Carl knew nothing about the trip, and there were no petrol stations to compare with.

questions.stem: Read: "Bergauf war der Motor zu schwach, und die Söhne mussten oft schieben." What happened?
choices: Uphill the engine was too weak, so the sons often had to push.
The sons often wanted to drive uphill.
The engine broke down, and the sons went home.
The sons were too weak to push the car uphill.
questions.explanation: bergauf = uphill, schwach = weak, mussten = had to (simple past of müssen), schieben = to push. It was the engine that was too weak, not the sons.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Nach dem Abitur studierte sie Medizin, und dann sie arbeitete in Wien."
choices: Nach dem Abitur should be Nach Abitur
dann sie arbeitete should be dann arbeitete sie
questions.explanation: dann is in position 1 of its clause (after und, which doesn't count), so the verb follows straight away: und dann arbeitete sie in Wien. studierte and arbeitete are the right simple past forms.

questions.stem: Tomasz has had his own workshop since June 2025 and still has it. Complete his biography: "Seit Juni 2025 ___ er eine eigene Werkstatt."
questions.explanation: With seit and something that is still true today, German uses the present: Seit Juni 2025 hat er … The simple past hatte and the perfect hat gehabt would mean it's over.

questions.stem: Complete: "2005 ___ sie in Graz eine kleine Firma." (gründen, simple past)
questions.explanation: gründen is weak, and its stem ends in -d, so it adds -ete: gründete. "gegründet" is the participle and would need hat.

questions.stem: In a German tabular CV, in what order are the entries in each section usually listed today?
questions.explanation: Today a Lebenslauf usually starts each section with the current or most recent entry (seit 06/2025 …) and goes back in time. A biography, by contrast, tells the story oldest first.

questions.stem: Anna says: "Ich habe keinen Hunger." Which sentence reports this correctly in everyday German?
choices: Anna hat gesagt, dass ich keinen Hunger habe.
Anna hat gesagt, dass sie hat keinen Hunger.
Anna hat gesagt, dass sie keinen Hunger hat.
Anna hat gesagt, dass sie keinen Hunger hatte.
questions.explanation: ich becomes sie (Anna), the verb goes to the end, and the tense stays as Anna said it: dass sie keinen Hunger hat. "dass ich …" forgets to change the pronoun; "hatte" would mean she wasn't hungry at some earlier time.

questions.stem: Ben asked you: "Kommst du mit?" Report it: "Ben hat gefragt, ___ ich mitkomme."
questions.explanation: "Kommst du mit?" is a yes/no question, so the reported question starts with ob (whether), and mitkomme joins up at the end.

questions.stem: Lisa asked you: "Wo wohnst du?" Report it: "Lisa hat gefragt, wo ich ___."
questions.explanation: The question was put to you, so du becomes ich, and the verb takes the ich form: wohne. It goes to the end of the clause, after the question word wo.

questions.stem: Lena told you: "Ruf mich morgen an!" Report it with a form of "sollen": "Lena hat gesagt, ich ___ sie morgen anrufen."
questions.explanation: A command is reported with sollen: ich soll sie anrufen (in speech also ich sollte sie anrufen). mich becomes sie, because Lena is now "she".

questions.stem: Your friend asked you: "Wann holst du mich ab?" Report it: "Sie hat gefragt, …"
questions.explanation: Sie hat gefragt, wann ich sie abhole. du becomes ich and mich becomes sie; the question word wann stays at the front, the subject pronoun comes next, then the object pronoun, and the separable verb joins up at the end.

questions.stem: Max said these things to you. Match each one to how you report it: "Max hat gesagt / gefragt, …"
questions.explanation: A statement takes dass (and Max's ich becomes er); a yes/no question takes ob; a W-question keeps its question word; a command becomes sollen. Max's du means you, so it becomes ich.

questions.stem: Tim asked you: "Hast du heute Zeit?" Which are correct ways to report this? Select all that apply.
choices: Tim hat gefragt, ob ich heute Zeit habe.
Tim wollte wissen, ob ich heute Zeit habe.
Tim hat gefragt, wenn ich heute Zeit habe.
Tim hat gefragt, ob ich habe heute Zeit.
Tim hat gefragt, ob du heute Zeit hast.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with ob and the verb at the end; fragen and wissen wollen both work. wenn can't start a reported question, "ob ich habe" leaves the verb in the wrong place, and "ob du … hast" forgets that Tim's du is you, so it becomes ich.

questions.stem: In the text "Das Gerücht im dritten Stock", what did Herr Weber really tell Frau Kühn?
choices: He is moving to Vienna in May.
He will be at his daughter's in Vienna for three weeks in May, and he asked her to water his plants.
His daughter is moving into his flat.
He wants to give his plants to Jonas.
questions.explanation: "Ich bin im Mai drei Wochen bei meiner Tochter in Wien. Können Sie meine Blumen gießen?" He was going on holiday. The idea that he was moving out grew as the message was passed on.

questions.stem: Frau Kühn told Jonas: "Er hat gefragt, ob wir seine Blumen gießen können." What did Jonas tell Mia?
choices: that Herr Weber said they should take his plants
that Herr Weber asked them to water his plants
that Herr Weber was moving to Bonn
questions.explanation: Jonas whispered: "Er hat gesagt, wir sollen seine Blumen nehmen." He turned "water" into "take", which is how a message changes in Stille Post.

questions.stem: A news report says: "Die Ministerin sagte, sie sei sehr zufrieden." What does the form "sei" show?
choices: that the sentence is a question
that it will happen in the future
that the minister is giving an order
that the reporter is passing on what the minister said
questions.explanation: sei is the Konjunktiv I of sein. News reports use it to mark reported speech: the reporter passes on the minister's words without claiming they're true. In conversation you'd say: Sie hat gesagt, sie ist sehr zufrieden.

questions.stem: You call a colleague, but someone else answers: "Frau Ott ist leider nicht im Büro." What is that person most likely to say next?
choices: Kann ich Sie mit Frau Ott verbinden?
questions.explanation: "Kann ich etwas ausrichten?" = Can I take a message? ausrichten means to pass on a message. weitersagen is to tell others (often what shouldn't be passed on); "Haben Sie etwas ausgerichtet?" asks whether you passed something on, and "Kann ich Sie mit Frau Ott verbinden?" (put you through to her) makes no sense if she isn't there.

questions.stem: Your mother says to you: "Dein Bruder hat meinen Schlüssel." You tell your brother. Which is right?
choices: Mama hat gesagt, dass du ihren Schlüssel hast.
Mama hat gesagt, dass dein Bruder meinen Schlüssel hat.
Mama hat gesagt, dass du meinen Schlüssel hast.
Mama hat gesagt, dass er ihren Schlüssel hat.
questions.explanation: You're talking to your brother, so "dein Bruder" becomes du; your mother is now "she", so "meinen Schlüssel" becomes ihren Schlüssel. "meinen" would mean your own key.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: Sie hat gefragt ob ich mitkomme.
Sie hat gefragt, ob ich mitkomme.
Sie hat gefragt, ob ich mitkomme?
Sie hat gefragt, ob ich komme mit.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the main clause from the ob clause, the separable verb joins up at the end (mitkomme), and because the whole sentence is a statement it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in the bathroom.

image.alt: A bathroom with a mirror, a toothbrush in a cup, a bar of soap, a towel on a rail, and a jar of cream and a comb on a shelf, with six numbered markers

questions.explanation: 1 der Spiegel (mirror), 2 die Zahnbürste (toothbrush), 3 die Seife (soap), 4 das Handtuch (towel), 5 die Creme (cream), 6 der Kamm (comb). Toothpaste (die Zahnpasta) and shampoo (das Shampoo) are not in the picture.

questions.stem: Type the reflexive pronoun for each blank: "Ich ziehe ___ an." (I get dressed.) and "Ich ziehe ___ eine Jacke an." (I put on a jacket.)
questions.explanation: In the first sentence there is no other object, so the reflexive pronoun is accusative: mich. In the second, eine Jacke is the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun moves to the dative: mir.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Wir haben uns im Urlaub gut erholt.
Er hat sich beim Fußball verletzt.
questions.explanation: Correct: "Wir haben uns … erholt" (uns for wir, perfect with haben), "Ich putze mir die Zähne" (dative mir because die Zähne is the object) and "Er hat sich … verletzt". Wrong: "Ich bin mich erkältet" (reflexive verbs take haben: Ich habe mich erkältet) and "Du wäschst sich" (sich is only for er/sie/es, sie and Sie; with du it is dir: Du wäschst dir die Hände).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Today I got changed quickly."
questions.explanation: Heute takes position 1, so the conjugated verb habe comes second and the pronoun subject ich follows it. The reflexive pronoun mich comes straight after the subject pronoun, and the participle umgezogen goes to the end: Heute habe ich mich schnell umgezogen.

questions.stem: Match each reflexive verb to its meaning.
choices: to recover or get some rest
questions.explanation: sich beeilen = to hurry, sich erholen = to recover, get some rest, sich langweilen = to be bored, sich ärgern = to be annoyed, sich erkälten = to catch a cold. "To be boring" is not a reflexive verb: Der Film ist langweilig.

questions.stem: Type the question words: "___ wartest du?" – "Auf den Bus." and "___ wartest du?" – "Auf meine Schwester."
questions.explanation: warten auf + accusative. To ask about a thing (the bus), use the wo-word: Worauf wartest du? To ask about a person (my sister), keep the preposition and add the accusative wen: Auf wen wartest du?

questions.stem: Match each verb to its fixed preposition and case.
questions.explanation: warten auf + Akk, teilnehmen an + Dat, sich interessieren für + Akk, Angst haben vor + Dat, sich kümmern um + Akk, träumen von + Dat. für and um are always accusative and von always dative; an and vor are the ones to learn with each verb.

questions.stem: Which answers are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Freust du dich auf die Party? – Ja, ich freue mich darauf.
Wartest du auf Tom? – Ja, ich warte darauf.
Denkst du an den Termin? – Ja, ich denke daran.
Sprichst du oft mit Lena? – Ja, ich spreche oft mit ihr.
Hast du Angst vor der Prüfung? – Ja, ich habe Angst davon.
questions.explanation: For things, answer with da(r)- + the verb's own preposition: darauf (auf die Party), daran (an den Termin). For people, use the preposition + a pronoun: mit ihr. "Ich warte darauf" can't refer to Tom, a person: say "Ich warte auf ihn". Angst haben vor needs davor, not davon.

questions.stem: Lena got flowers from a friend yesterday. Complete her message: "Ich habe mich sehr ___ die Blumen gefreut!"

image.alt: A timeline: sich freuen über points to something you already have or that happened; sich freuen auf points to something still coming

questions.explanation: Lena already has the flowers, so she is pleased about them: sich freuen über + accusative. sich freuen auf is for something that is still coming (Ich freue mich auf die Ferien). an and für don't go with sich freuen.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "What did you (all) talk about yesterday?"
questions.explanation: The wo-word worüber (sprechen über) is the question word in position 1, the conjugated habt comes second, then the subject ihr, the time word gestern, and the participle gesprochen at the end.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things.

image.alt: Six things with numbered markers: a necklace, a ring, an umbrella, sunglasses, a wallet and a parcel

questions.explanation: 1 die Kette (necklace), 2 der Ring (ring), 3 der Regenschirm (umbrella), 4 die Sonnenbrille (sunglasses, singular like die Brille), 5 das Portemonnaie (wallet), 6 das Paket (parcel). There is no perfume (das Parfüm) or bracelet (das Armband) in the picture.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Have you shown it to her yet?"
questions.explanation: With two pronouns the accusative comes first: es (it) before ihr (to her). Both pronouns come straight after the subject du, then schon, and the participle gezeigt goes to the end.

questions.stem: Replace both objects with pronouns: "Ich schenke meinem Bruder das Buch." → "Ich schenke ___." Type the two pronouns in the right order.
questions.explanation: das Buch (accusative) → es; meinem Bruder (dative) → ihm. With two pronouns the accusative comes first: Ich schenke es ihm.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Der Schal passt gut zur Jacke.
questions.explanation: Correct: "Die Schuhe gefallen mir" (the plural thing is the subject, so gefallen), "Du fehlst mir" (I miss you) and "Der Schal passt gut zur Jacke" (goes well with). Wrong: helfen takes the dative (Ich helfe dir), and with two pronouns the accusative comes first (Ich gebe es ihm).

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its meaning.
questions.explanation: With fehlen the person who misses is in the dative and the one who is missed is the subject: Du fehlst mir = I miss you; Ich fehle dir = you miss me. stehen + dative = to suit, gehören + dative = to belong to, passen + dative = to suit or be convenient. "I like the jacket" would be "Die Jacke gefällt mir".

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Head and shoulders of a man with glasses and a beard, with six numbered markers

questions.explanation: 1 die Haare (hair, usually plural), 2 die Brille (glasses), 3 die Nase (nose), 4 der Mund (mouth), 5 der Bart (beard), 6 das Ohr (ear). He isn't wearing a necklace (die Kette), and his neck (der Hals) isn't numbered.

questions.stem: Type the correct form of werden: "Du ___ bestimmt eine gute Lehrerin." and "Mein Sohn ___ morgen zehn."
questions.explanation: werden is irregular: du wirst (no d), er/sie/es wird (no extra t). Mein Sohn is er, so wird; "Er wird zehn" means he turns ten.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its meaning.
questions.explanation: sympathisch is a false friend: it means likeable, not sympathetic (understanding). fleißig = hard-working, faul = lazy, ehrlich = honest, neugierig = curious (or nosy).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Correct: werden forms the perfect with sein and takes no article with a job (Sie ist Ärztin geworden); jedes is singular (jedes Kind); after etwas the adjective becomes a noun with -es (etwas Neues). Wrong: "Er hat dick geworden" (ist geworden) and "Jede Leute" (jeder is singular only: alle Leute).

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "My brother has become very quiet."
questions.explanation: The subject mein Bruder takes position 1 and the auxiliary ist position 2 (werden uses sein in the perfect). sehr goes directly before the adjective it describes, and the participle geworden goes to the end.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann ___ das gut vorstellen."
questions.explanation: sich etwas vorstellen (to imagine) has an accusative object, das, so the reflexive pronoun is dative: mir. "mich" would be "introduce myself", and sich and dir don't match the subject ich.

questions.stem: Complete: "Guten Tag! Darf ich ___ vorstellen? Ich bin Ihre neue Kollegin."
questions.explanation: She is introducing herself, and there is no other accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun is accusative: mich. "Darf ich mir … vorstellen" would need an object and mean "imagine". Ihnen would need an object too (Darf ich Ihnen meinen Mann vorstellen?).

questions.stem: Replace "den Film" with a pronoun: "Ich sehe mir den Film an."
questions.explanation: den Film becomes ihn (accusative masculine). With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: ihn mir. The dative reflexive stays mir; mich would be accusative, and ihm is dative, not accusative.

questions.stem: What does "Das kann ich mir nicht leisten." mean?
questions.explanation: sich etwas leisten (können) means to (be able to) afford something. Imagine is sich etwas vorstellen, remember is sich etwas merken.

questions.stem: Which sentence clearly means "They help each other", with no other possible meaning?
questions.explanation: einander always means "each other". "Sie helfen sich" can mean "each other" or "themselves", and "sich selbst" means "themselves". "sich einander" mixes two ways of saying it and is wrong: use einander or sich gegenseitig.

questions.stem: Put into the perfect: "Er denkt sich eine Ausrede aus." (He makes up an excuse.)
choices: Er hat sich eine Ausrede ausgedacht.
Er ist sich eine Ausrede ausgedacht.
Er hat sich eine Ausrede ausgedenkt.
Er hat eine Ausrede sich ausgedacht.
questions.explanation: Reflexive verbs use haben, the pronoun stays straight after haben, and the participle goes to the end. ausdenken is separable and mixed like denken – gedacht, so the participle is ausgedacht, not ausgedenkt.

questions.stem: Read: "Stell dir vor: Ich habe mir gestern beim Fußball den Fuß verstaucht. Jetzt muss ich mir die Spiele im Fernsehen ansehen." What happened?
choices: He imagined a football match and watched it on TV.
He broke his leg and can't watch the matches.
He hurt his friend's foot playing football.
He sprained his ankle and now has to watch the matches on TV.
questions.explanation: sich den Fuß verstauchen = to sprain your ankle; mir shows it is his own foot. sich etwas ansehen = to watch. "Stell dir vor" just means "guess what" here, not that he imagined something.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich habe mich den Arm gebrochen.
Ich habe mir den Arm gebrochen.
Ich bin mir den Arm gebrochen.
Ich habe meinen Arm mir gebrochen.
questions.explanation: den Arm is the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun is dative (mir), and the perfect uses haben. The pronoun comes before the noun object, and German uses the article, not a possessive, with your own body part.

questions.stem: Type the reflexive pronouns: "Merk ___ bitte die Adresse!" (to a friend) and "Wir haben ___ gestern die Wohnung angesehen."
questions.explanation: sich etwas merken and sich etwas ansehen both take a dative reflexive. The imperative to a friend is the du form, so dir; with wir the pronoun is uns.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Have you had a look at it (the flat) yet?"
questions.explanation: sie stands for die Wohnung (accusative) and dir is the dative reflexive. With two pronouns the accusative comes first: sie dir. Then schon, and the participle angesehen at the end.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its meaning.
choices: to remember or make a note of
questions.explanation: All five take a dative reflexive and an accusative thing. "To introduce yourself" is sich vorstellen with the accusative (Ich stelle mich vor) and has no "etwas".

questions.stem: In which sentences must the blank be a dative pronoun (mir)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is dative when the sentence has another accusative object: das, die Hand, ein neues Fahrrad. "Ich habe mich gestern verletzt" and "Darf ich mich kurz vorstellen?" have no other object, so they take the accusative mich.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Correct: "Wir schreiben uns" (we write to each other), miteinander (with each other) and "sich gegenseitig" (each other). Wrong: sich merken needs its pronoun (Ich merke mir die Nummer), and with two pronouns the accusative comes first (Ich sehe ihn mir an).

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm cold" in German?
questions.explanation: Body sensations use sein + the dative person, with no subject: Mir ist kalt. "Ich bin kalt" describes your character (a cold person). "Ich habe kalt" is French-style, not German.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann mich nicht erinnern. Sein Name fällt ___ nicht ein."
questions.explanation: einfallen takes the person in the dative and the idea (sein Name) as the subject: Sein Name fällt mir nicht ein.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mir ___ die richtigen Wörter nicht ein."
questions.explanation: The subject is die richtigen Wörter (plural), so the verb is plural: fallen. The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person in the dative.

questions.stem: Your friend tells you her cat is ill. You say: "Oh, das tut mir leid." What does that mean?
questions.explanation: Das tut mir leid expresses sympathy here: I'm sorry (to hear that). It can also be an apology, but nothing here is your fault. "I don't care" would be "Das ist mir egal"; "seems strange" is "Das kommt mir komisch vor".

questions.stem: Which sentence is the perfect of "Mir fällt nichts ein."?
questions.explanation: einfallen is built on fallen, so it takes sein; the person stays dative (mir) and the participle is eingefallen.

questions.stem: What does "Mathe fällt mir schwer." mean?
choices: Maths is heavy for me to carry.
questions.explanation: schwerfallen + dative = to be hard for someone: I find maths hard. The opposite is leichtfallen: Mathe fällt mir leicht.

questions.stem: Which sentence fits best when you say goodbye to your grandmother on the phone?
choices: Ich bin in dich verliebt, Oma.
questions.explanation: Ich hab dich lieb is warm and not romantic: right for family and close friends. "verliebt" and "Du gefällst mir" are about romance or attraction, and "Ich finde dich nett" is far too distant for your grandmother.

questions.stem: Read: "Mir ist sofort aufgefallen, dass hier alle Schüler zum Mittagessen bleiben." What does Jana say?
choices: She noticed straight away that all the students stay for lunch.
She forgot that the students stay for lunch.
She doesn't like staying for lunch.
questions.explanation: auffallen + dative = to be noticed by someone: "it struck me" = I noticed. Perfect with sein: ist aufgefallen.

questions.stem: Type one word for each blank: "Ist ___ kalt?" (asking a friend: Are you cold?) and "Nein, aber ___ ist schlecht." (No, but I feel sick.)
questions.explanation: Body sensations put the person in the dative: dir (you, informal) and mir (me). The verb stays ist because there is no real subject.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its meaning.
questions.explanation: egal sein = not to matter, leidtun with a person as subject = pity, vorkommen = to seem, schwindlig = dizzy, wichtig sein = to matter. An apology is "Es tut mir leid", not "Du tust mir leid".

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich bin schlecht, ich muss nach Hause.
Es ist mir wichtig, dass du kommst.
questions.explanation: Correct: Mir ist langweilig (I'm bored), Es ist mir wichtig, dass … (es holds position 1 for the clause), Deutsch fällt mir leicht. Wrong: "I feel sick" is Mir ist schlecht (Ich bin schlecht = I'm bad at something or a bad person), and einfallen takes sein: Mir ist nichts eingefallen.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Is it all right with you if I come later?"
questions.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb ist. Then the two pronouns: the subject es (standing for the wenn-clause) comes before the dative dir, since a short subject pronoun always comes first. The adjective recht closes the main clause, and the wenn-clause has its verb komme at the end.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I couldn't think of the names."
questions.explanation: The dative mir takes position 1, the auxiliary sind (plural, because the subject is die Namen, and sein because of fallen) comes second, then the subject, nicht, and the participle eingefallen at the end.

questions.stem: Name the numbered clothes.

image.alt: A person dressed for winter with six numbered items of clothing, from head to feet.

questions.explanation: 1 die Mütze (the woolly hat with a bobble; a hat with a brim would be der Hut), 2 der Schal (scarf), 3 die Jacke (jacket), 4 die Handschuhe (gloves, literally "hand shoes"), 5 die Hose (trousers, singular in German), 6 die Stiefel (boots).
